# THE ODYSSEY
### Retold in English, with Explanations

---

## BOOK ONE
### In Which the Gods Hold a Meeting, and a Young Man Discovers He Has a Voice

---

Before we begin, a word about beginnings.

The old poets never simply *started*. That would have seemed to them rather like sitting down to dinner without saying anything at all, or building a house without laying a foundation, or (to use a comparison they would have understood better than either) setting out on a long sea voyage without first pouring a little wine into the water for the gods and hoping they were in a good humour. A poet always began by asking for help. Not from his listeners — from a Muse.<sup><a href="#book-01-note-1">1</a></sup>

So the old poem begins with a request, and since we are going to be together for some while, you and I, I shall begin with one too, and then get on with it.

*Tell me about the man of many turnings — the one who was clever in a hundred ways and got very little good out of any of them; who wandered a long, long way after he had knocked down the holy towers of Troy; who saw the cities of many peoples and learned what was in their minds; who suffered a great deal at sea, in his own heart, struggling to keep his life and to bring his companions home. He never did bring them home, though. They died of their own foolishness, the idiots — they ate the cattle of the Sun, and the Sun took away their day of homecoming. Begin wherever you like, goddess. Begin anywhere, and tell us too.*

There. That is more or less how it went, and I have kept it, because it tells you three things straight off, and it is polite to tell people what a story is about before they are three hundred pages into it.

The first thing is that this is a story about a man who was extremely clever and it did not save him. The second is that he lost every single one of his men, and that it was not his fault, which is a thing the poem is at some pains to say early and say plainly. And the third — well, the third is the one that matters most. All of that business with the sea and the monsters and the cattle of the Sun: it is not the point of the story. It is the part everybody remembers, the way everybody remembers the dragon and not the will. The point of the story is a house. A particular house, on a small stony island, with a woman in it and a boy who has grown up in it without a father, and a great many uninvited guests eating everything in it. The sea monsters are on the way to the house. Do not lose sight of the house.

Now then.

---

By the time our story opens, the war at Troy had been over for ten years, and every Greek<sup><a href="#book-01-note-2">2</a></sup> who was going to get home had got home. They had straggled back one by one, out of the storms and the shipwrecks and the long detours, and their wives had wept over them, and they had hung up their shields and settled down to complain about the weather and the young. The rest were dead — buried under the walls of Troy, or drowned on the way back, or (in one particularly nasty case, which we will come to) murdered on their own doorsteps by people who ought to have been glad to see them.

Only one man was still out.

His name was Odysseus, he was the king of a small rough island called Ithaca off the west coast of Greece, and he was, at this moment, sitting on a beach a very long way from it, crying.

He was being kept there by a goddess called Calypso, who lived alone on an island in the middle of nowhere, who was beautiful, who was in love with him, and who had told him — quite sincerely, and more than once — that if he would only agree to stay with her she would make him immortal, and he would never grow old, and they would live together forever in a cave with vines growing over the mouth of it and four springs running clear water in four directions. She was not being cruel. She thought she was offering him the best thing anyone had ever been offered, and by most reckonings she was.

He said no. He said no for seven years. He spent his days sitting on the rocks looking east over the water, hoping to see so much as the smoke going up from the chimneys of his own house, and wishing he were dead; and at night he went back to the cave and lay down beside her because there was nowhere else on the island to lie down. That is the situation, and I want you to sit with how uncomfortable it is for a moment, because a great many people have retold this part as though it were a holiday. It was not a holiday. It was seven years of being loved by somebody you have not chosen, on an island you cannot leave.

And the gods, on the whole, were sorry for him. All of them except one.

The exception was Poseidon, who was god of the sea and of earthquakes and of horses (an odd combination until you have seen surf coming in), and who had a grudge against Odysseus of the deepest and most personal kind, which we shall come to in its proper place. It is enough for now to say that Odysseus had blinded Poseidon's son, and that Poseidon was not the sort to let that go. He could not quite kill the man outright — that was not permitted him — but he could keep him from home, and he had been keeping him from home for a decade, with the patience of water working on stone.

It happened, however, that just now Poseidon was away. He had gone off to the far south to a feast among the Ethiopians, who lived at the ends of the earth where the sun rises and sets, and who were famous for two things: being the most distant people in the world, and being unusually good hosts.<sup><a href="#book-01-note-3">3</a></sup> He would be gone some while, and he had left no one minding the door.

Which was exactly what Athena had been waiting for.

---

The gods lived on Mount Olympus, in the north, on a peak so high that it goes up out of the weather altogether; and while people down below imagined all sorts of things about their arrangements up there, the honest truth is that the arrangements were embarrassingly like a family. They ate together. They argued at the table. They took sides, and remembered slights, and worked round one another, and the whole enormous machinery of the world went grinding along beneath them as a sort of by-product of who happened to be annoyed with whom that week.

At the head of the table was Zeus, who was king, and who had been thinking about a murder.

"It really is extraordinary," he said, to no one in particular, in the tone of a man returning to a grievance he has aired before, "the way they blame us. Listen to them. Every disaster that comes to a mortal, and it's the gods, the gods, the gods — as if we sat up here inventing miseries for them. When the plain fact is that they manufacture the greater part of it themselves, out of their own recklessness, and then send up the bill to Heaven.

"Take Aegisthus. We *told* him. We sent Hermes down specially — went to some trouble about it — and said: do not murder that man, and do not marry that man's wife, because there is a son, and the son will grow up, and when he is grown he will come for you. We could not have been plainer. And he did it anyway, and the boy grew up, and came for him, exactly as advertised. And now I suppose we shall be told that was our doing as well."<sup><a href="#book-01-note-4">4</a></sup>

There was a small pause of the kind that falls when everyone at a table knows that somebody is about to use an opening.

"Father," said Athena.

Now I must tell you about Athena, since she is going to be in this story more than anyone else except the two people it belongs to. She was Zeus's daughter, and his favourite, and the goddess of exactly three things, which were: war (but only the kind that is planned and won, not the kind that is enjoyed), crafts and weaving and everything made carefully with the hands, and cleverness. That last is the important one. She was the patron goddess of good ideas, quick answers, and lies told well in a tight corner — and you can see at once why Odysseus was her particular favourite among all the men alive, because he was the finest liar in the world and she admired him for it the way a master carpenter admires a joint.

"Father," she said, "Aegisthus got what was coming to him, and so may everyone else who does what he did. But my heart is broken over Odysseus. Poor wretched man — he has been away from his own people all this time, on an island in the navel of the sea, in the house of Calypso, who keeps him there with soft words and coaxing so that he will forget Ithaca. And he cannot forget it. He would be glad to see the smoke going up from his own roof and then die. And it does not move you at all. Did he never sacrifice to you, out there beside the ships at Troy? Why are you so hard on him?"

"Child, what a thing to say." Zeus looked genuinely startled. "How could I ever forget Odysseus? There is no man alive with better sense, or who gave the gods their due more generously. It is my brother Poseidon, who is in a rage about the Cyclops — his son, whose eye Odysseus put out. He will not kill him. He simply moves him about the sea and will not let him come home. Well. Let us all put our heads together and settle it. Poseidon will have to give way. He can hardly hold out against every one of us at once."

"Then send Hermes," said Athena, who had had the plan ready for some time and was not going to waste the moment, "to Calypso's island, to tell her plainly that it is decided, and that Odysseus goes home. And I will go to Ithaca — to his son. I will put some spirit into the boy. I'll have him call the Greeks to assembly and speak out to the whole island against these men who are eating him out of house and home. And then I'll send him off to Pylos and to Sparta to ask after his father. He may hear something. And if he hears nothing, he will at least come back a man with a good name, which is worth having."

Zeus agreed, because he always did in the end, and because it was a good plan.

And Athena went down.

---

She went down from the peaks of Olympus and came to Ithaca, and stood at the outer gate of the courtyard of Odysseus's house, holding a bronze spear; and she had taken on the appearance of a man — a stranger, a sea-captain named Mentes, chief of a people called the Taphians, who were traders and part-time pirates, there being less difference between the two professions than either would have admitted.<sup><a href="#book-01-note-5">5</a></sup>

And what she saw, standing at that gate, was this.

The courtyard was full of young men. They were sprawled on the hides of oxen — oxen they had killed themselves, out of the herds of the house — and they were playing at dice, and shouting, and enjoying themselves enormously. Servants were running about among them at a half-trot, the particular half-trot of people who have been working too hard for too long with no end in sight: some mixing wine and water in the great bowls, some wiping down the tables with sponges and setting them out again, some carving up more meat than any household could afford. There were a hundred and eight of these young men. They were the sons of the best families of Ithaca and the islands round about. They had been living in that house, at that house's expense, for something over three years.

They were there to marry the queen.

Here I had better stop and explain, because this is the part that a modern reader stumbles over, and if you stumble over it now the whole book will limp.

Odysseus had been gone twenty years. There was no news of him, no body, no grave — nothing. Under the customs of the time a woman in that position was in an impossible middle place: not a wife, because her husband was almost certainly dead; not a widow, because nobody could prove it. And the kingdom was in the same middle place. Ithaca had no king, and its heir, Telemachus, had been an infant in arms when his father sailed and was now barely twenty — old enough to be angry, not yet old enough to be obeyed.

So the young men of the district had worked it out among themselves, as young men will. Whoever married Penelope would in all likelihood become king. Therefore they would all court her at once. Therefore they would all move into her house, and stay there, and eat and drink at her expense until she gave in and chose one — and the longer she held out, the more of the estate they would get through, which they did not mind in the least, because the whole point of the exercise was that the estate would eventually belong to one of them.

You will want to know why she did not simply throw them out. She could not. A woman could not order armed men off the property, and the law of that country provided her no help she could call on. You will want to know why she did not simply *say no*. Then her father would have taken her home and married her to somebody of his choosing, and the house would have passed out of Telemachus's hands entirely; and there would still have been a wedding, only now she would have no say in it at all. You will want to know why Telemachus did not throw them out, and the answer is arithmetic: one young man and a handful of loyal servants against a hundred and eight armed sons of powerful families, every one of whom had a father and brothers who would want blood if he were harmed.

They were, in short, not besieging the house. They were doing something cleverer and much crueller. They were being *guests*. And that is the joke at the black heart of this entire book, because in that world there was no law more sacred than the law of guests — and these men had turned it inside out and were wearing it as armour.<sup><a href="#book-01-note-6">6</a></sup>

---

Telemachus saw the stranger at the gate before anyone else did, because he was not enjoying the party.

He was sitting a little apart from the rest, sick at heart, doing the thing he did most days, which was to imagine his father walking in through that gate: coming in out of nowhere, scattering the suitors like poultry, taking back his own house and his own honour and his own place at the head of his own table. It is a daydream that will be familiar to anyone who has ever been young and powerless in a house full of people behaving badly. It had the particular quality of all such daydreams, that it did not make him feel better afterwards.

And then he looked up, and there was a stranger standing at the gate — waiting, being kept waiting — and Telemachus was up and across that courtyard like a shot, appalled.

He took the stranger's right hand in his own and took the bronze spear with the other, and he said: "Welcome, sir. Sit down and eat something, and afterwards you shall tell us what you need."

Notice the order of that sentence. He did not ask the man's name. He did not ask his business, or where he was from, or how long he intended to stay. That was not merely good manners; it was the law, and Telemachus was following it to the letter in a house where nobody else had followed it for three years. First you take the stranger in, and feed him, and give him a bath and clean clothes and a good chair. *Then* you ask who he is. And when he leaves you give him a present, and if he ever comes back, or his children come, or his children's children, your house and his are friends forever and neither may lift a hand against the other. It was called *xenia* — guest-friendship — and it was under the personal protection of Zeus himself, who kept a special title for the purpose: Zeus of the Strangers, god of anybody who turns up at your door with nothing.<sup><a href="#book-01-note-7">7</a></sup>

Which is why it is quite an important detail that the young man who kept the law that day, alone in that house, was giving a chair and a footstool and the best cuts of the meat to a god in disguise.

He led her in and set her spear in the rack against the great column, where his father's spears were standing — still standing, still there, and I do not think you need me to tell you what that rack of spears was doing to him every day of his life. He gave her a fine carved chair set a little apart from the crowd, with a linen cloth over it and a footstool, and drew up a seat for himself beside it, so that his guest would not have to eat within earshot of the noise and would not have to listen to men bellowing over dice while she ate.

A servant girl brought water in a golden jug over a silver basin and poured it over their hands, and set out a polished table, and the housekeeper brought bread and a great many small dishes, and the carver brought platters of meats and set gold cups beside them, and the steward went up and down keeping them filled.

And then the suitors came in.

They came in and took their places and set to, with a great deal of noise, and when they had eaten and drunk as much as they wanted they began to want other things — dancing and singing, which is the crown of a feast — and a herald put a beautiful lyre into the hands of a man named Phemius, who sang for those men because they made him, and who began to sing.<sup><a href="#book-01-note-8">8</a></sup>

And under the cover of the music, Telemachus put his head close to his guest's, so that no one else would hear, and said:

"Friend — I hope you won't take this badly. It's easy for *them*: they eat another man's living and pay nothing for it, a man whose white bones are lying out in the rain somewhere on land, or rolling in the sea's surf. If they saw him walk in through that door there is not one of them who would pray to be faster on his feet — they'd pray to be richer in clothes and gold, and much good it would do them. As it is, he has died badly, and there's no comfort anywhere, not even if somebody told me he was coming. His homecoming is finished.

"But tell me — who are you? Where do you come from? What ship? And this is what I really want to know: is this the first time you have been here, or were you a friend of my father's? A great many men used to come to this house. He got about, in his day."

And Athena — Mentes — said: "I'll tell you everything. My name is Mentes; my father was Anchialus, and I'm chief of the Taphians. I'm here with my own ship and crew, sailing the wine-dark sea to trade iron for copper. My ship's lying out of town under Mount Neion. My family and yours have been guest-friends since your grandfather's time; ask old Laertes if you doubt me. And I came because they told me your father was home. Apparently the gods have him tangled up somewhere still.

"He isn't dead, though. Odysseus is alive, and on some island, held by hard men who won't let him go. I'm no prophet and I don't read birds, but I'll tell you what I think: he will not be away much longer. He'd get out of an iron cage. He'll find a way.

"But tell me this. You're — what, Odysseus's son? You must be. That head, and those eyes; it's uncanny."

"My mother says so," said Telemachus, "and I suppose she would know. Though for my own part I sometimes wish I were the son of a man who had grown old on his own farm among his own things. As it is, I'm the son of the unluckiest man ever born. That's your answer."

Then Mentes said, "Well, the gods have not left your house without a name, whatever else they've done, if Penelope has a son like you. But now tell me about *this*." And the stranger looked out across the hall — at the shouting, and the meat going round, and the dogs, and the wreckage of it. "What is all this? A wedding? A public dinner? Because it certainly isn't people paying for their own food. They look to me like men eating another man's house down around his ears, and behaving very insolently about it. Any decent man walking in here would be disgusted."

And that opened the door, and out it all came.

"Stranger — since you ask — there was a time when this house was rich and respectable, back when *he* was still on the island. But the gods have decided otherwise, and they have made him vanish more completely than any man who ever lived. I could bear it better if he were dead. If he had gone down at Troy with his friends around him, or died in his own bed with the work of the war behind him, the Greeks would have built him a barrow, and I'd have had that at least to hand on. As it is the storm winds have carried him off with no name and no notice, and left me nothing but grief.

"And he isn't the only thing I have to cry about. Look at them. Every man of rank in Dulichium and Same and wooded Zacynthus, and every man of rank on this rock of an island, is courting my mother and wrecking my house. And she cannot refuse them — it would be the ruin of her — and she cannot bring herself to choose. And meanwhile they eat, and drink, and in a little while they will have eaten me down to nothing, and I expect me with it."

Athena was very angry when she heard that, and she said:

"By heaven, you need your father. If Odysseus were to come and stand in that doorway now, with a shield and two spears and a helmet on his head, the way I first saw him — if he came in on those men the way he was that day, they would find their marriages short and bitter. But that lies with the gods, whether he comes home and pays them out in that hall or not. So think about this instead: how are you going to get them out of the house *yourself*?

"Listen to me and do as I say. Tomorrow morning call the Greeks to assembly — all of them — and speak, and let the gods be your witnesses. Tell the suitors to go home. As for your mother, if she has a mind to marry, let her go back to her father's house, and let *them* deal with the dowry and the bride-gifts, as is proper for a daughter they think well of.

"And here is my advice for you. Take a ship — the best you can get — and twenty rowers, and go and ask after your father. Go to Pylos first, to old Nestor; and then to Sparta, to Menelaus, because he came home last of all the Greeks and he will have picked up more news than anybody.<sup><a href="#book-01-note-9">9</a></sup> If you hear your father is alive and on his way, then grit your teeth and put up with this for one more year. And if you hear he is dead, then come home, and heap up a barrow for him, and give him the funeral rites in full, and give your mother to a husband. And when that is done and finished — *then* think very carefully about how you are going to kill these men in your house, by a trick or in the open.

"You are too old to be a child any longer. Have you not heard what a name young Orestes got for himself among men, when he came home and killed the man who murdered his father? You are tall, my friend, and you are handsome, and men will be talking about you for a long time yet. Be brave.

"And now I must go down to my ship. My crew will be getting restless. See to this yourself, and remember what I've said."

"Friend," said Telemachus, "you have spoken to me like a father to his son, and I will not forget it. But stay a little longer — bathe, and rest, and let me give you a present to take home with you, something fine, something worth keeping, the way friends give to friends."

"No — don't hold me now. I am in a hurry. Whatever gift you feel moved to give me, give it to me when I come back, and let it be a good one, and you shall have as good in return."

And with that Athena went out of the hall, and up — like a bird going up, straight up out of sight.

And she left something in the young man's chest that had not been there that morning. He stood a moment where she had left him, and then he understood, in the way one does understand such things, without being told: and he went across the hall towards the suitors, and he was not the same person who had been sitting in the corner an hour before.

---

The bard was still singing. He was singing about the Greeks coming home from Troy, and about all the ways it had gone wrong for them, and the suitors were sitting quiet for once and listening.

And upstairs, Penelope was listening too. She heard it from her room above the hall, and she could not bear it, and she came down the long stairs with two maids behind her and stood by the pillar at the edge of the room with her veil across her face; and she was crying, and she said:

"Phemius — you know a hundred songs. Sing them one of those. Let them sit here and drink their wine in peace and listen to anything else at all. Only stop singing *that* one, because it breaks my heart in my breast every time, and I have a grief in this house that will not be lifted, and a man I remember every hour of every day, whose name is spoken across the whole of Greece."

And Telemachus said: "Mother — why shouldn't he sing what he likes?"

I want you to notice that this is the first thing Telemachus says in the whole poem to his own mother, and that he has just come from a conversation with a goddess.

"It isn't the poets who cause these things," he said. "Zeus causes them; he gives out what he likes to each of us, and there's no arguing with it. There's nothing wrong in singing about the Greeks' bad end. People always praise the newest song loudest, whatever it's about. Set your heart to listen. My father was not the only man who never came home from Troy; a great many others were lost as well.

"Go back upstairs, and see to your own work — your loom, and your spinning, and keep the maids at theirs. Talking is men's business, and mine most of all, since I am the master of this house."

And Penelope went back upstairs, astonished, and turned that over in her mind for a long while, and cried herself to sleep. And I confess I have never been quite sure how to take that speech — whether it is a boy trying on his father's voice and finding it a size too large, or a young man discovering that being brave and being kind are two different accomplishments and that you can manage the first before you have learned the second. Probably it is both. Most people are unbearable for a little while just after they find their courage.

The suitors, meanwhile, broke into an uproar in the shadowy hall, every one of them praying to be the man who got into her bed. But Telemachus stood up in front of the lot of them and said:

"Suitors of my mother — you insolent, overbearing men — let us enjoy our dinner, and let there be no shouting, because it is a fine thing to listen to a singer like this one. But in the morning let us all take our places in assembly, all of us, and I will make my speech to you plainly. Get out of my house. Feast somewhere else; eat your own food; go round from house to house and use up your own inheritances. Or if you think it better and more profitable to eat one man's living and pay him nothing for it — then go on doing it, and I will call on the gods, and Zeus may yet see that you are paid what you are owed; and you will die in this house, and there will be no vengeance taken for any one of you."

That silenced them. They bit their lips and stared at him, because they had never in three years heard him speak like that.

Then Antinous said — and Antinous is a man you may as well start disliking now, because you will be doing a great deal of it later — "Telemachus. The gods themselves must be teaching you to make speeches, and to make them so *boldly*. I hope Zeus never makes you king of Ithaca, even though it is yours by birth."

"Antinous," said Telemachus, "I'll say this even if it annoys you. I should be quite happy to take the kingship, if Zeus offered it. Do you think it's the worst thing that can happen to a man? There's nothing wrong with being a king: your house grows rich and you are held in honour. But there are plenty of other Greek princes on this island, young and old, and one of them can have the title, now that Odysseus is dead. What I *will* be master of is my own house, and my own servants, whom my father won for me."

And Eurymachus said, smoothly — for Eurymachus was the one who always spoke smoothly, and you should distrust him rather more than Antinous, not less — "Telemachus, which of us is to be king of Ithaca lies with the gods; but nobody is going to take your property from you while there are men living on this island. Now. Tell me about your visitor. Where was he from? What was his family? Did he bring news of your father, or was he here about some debt of his own? He got up and went off very quickly; he didn't wait to be introduced. He didn't look like a man of no account, either."

"Eurymachus," said Telemachus, "my father's homecoming is over and done with. I don't believe any news now, whoever brings it, and I have no time for prophecies. That man was an old guest-friend of my father's from Taphos: Mentes, son of Anchialus, chief of the seafaring Taphians."

So he said. And in his heart he knew perfectly well that he had been talking to a god.

Then they turned to dancing and singing again and enjoyed themselves until evening came on; and when it did, they went off to their own homes to sleep, which is the one thing that could be said in their favour.

And Telemachus went up to his own high room in the fine walled courtyard, in a place with a view all round it, and went to bed with his mind turning over and over.

Going with him, carrying blazing torches, went Eurycleia — daughter of Ops, son of Peisenor — who had been bought by his grandfather Laertes long ago, when she was a girl, for the price of twenty oxen; and who had nursed Telemachus as a baby, and loved him more than any of the servants in that house did.<sup><a href="#book-01-note-10">10</a></sup>

She opened the door for him, and he sat down on the bed and pulled off his soft tunic and put it into the old woman's hands, and she folded it and smoothed it and hung it on a peg beside the bedstead and went out of the room, drawing the door to by its silver handle and pulling the bolt home with the strap.

And there he lay all night, wrapped in a fleece, thinking about the journey Athena had told him to make.

---

## NOTES TO BOOK ONE

<a id="book-01-note-1"></a>
1. **The Muses.** Nine goddesses, daughters of Zeus and of Memory — which is exactly the right parentage, as you will see. This poem was composed before writing was in general use in Greece, and it was not read; it was *performed*, from memory, by professionals, over several evenings, probably with a stringed instrument going underneath it. A poet who could hold twelve thousand lines in his head and produce them on demand did not feel that this was a thing he was doing entirely by himself, and he did not think he was being modest when he said so. When he asked a Muse to sing *through* him, he meant it fairly literally. The daughters of Memory were the ones who kept the words safe. Whether one man called Homer made this poem, or several, or a tradition of hundreds over centuries, is a question people have been arguing about for two thousand years, and it has a name — the Homeric Question — and no answer.

<a id="book-01-note-2"></a>
2. **"Greeks."** The poem never uses the word. It calls them Achaeans, or Argives, or Danaans, more or less interchangeably, according to what fits the rhythm of the line. None of these means quite what "Greek" means today, and there was no country called Greece: there were many small kingdoms speaking related dialects who thought of themselves as one people only in certain moods — such as when sailing to Troy together. Throughout this book I say "Greeks", because saying "Achaeans" makes it sound like a story about strangers, and it is not.

<a id="book-01-note-3"></a>
3. **The Ethiopians.** Not the people of the modern country, though the name survives there. To this poet the word meant, roughly, "the people at the far edge of the world where the sun is close," and they were understood to be exceptionally pious and to give exceptionally good dinners, for which reason the gods went to visit them and were reliably unavailable. It is the ancient equivalent of a character being out of mobile reception, and the plot needs it.

<a id="book-01-note-4"></a>
4. **The murder Zeus is talking about.** Agamemnon was the commander-in-chief of the whole Greek army at Troy, the greatest king of his day. While he was away, his cousin Aegisthus seduced his wife Clytemnestra; and when Agamemnon came home in triumph after ten years of war, the two of them killed him at his own homecoming feast. Seven years later Agamemnon's son Orestes came back from exile and killed Aegisthus. — Now: keep that story in your hand for the whole of this book, because the poem is going to hold it up beside our story again and again, like a tailor holding cloth against cloth. A king comes home from Troy. There is a wife who has waited, and a son who has grown up, and men in the house who should not be there. It happened one way for Agamemnon. Everyone in this poem, gods included, is watching to see which way it will happen for Odysseus. Penelope is being measured against Clytemnestra every time she comes down the stairs. Telemachus is being measured against Orestes, and knows it, and it terrifies him.

<a id="book-01-note-5"></a>
5. **Mentes, and a word you already know.** Athena spends most of this poem in disguise, and this is the first of many. Later she will borrow the shape of another of Odysseus's old friends, an Ithacan called Mentor, to guide and advise Telemachus on his travels — which is where our word *mentor* comes from. The word entered English by a roundabout route (a French novel of 1699 that retold these events for the education of a prince), and it means what it means because of a goddess pretending to be somebody's uncle.

<a id="book-01-note-6"></a>
6. **The suitors, and why this is a horror story.** It is worth saying plainly what these men are doing, because our word "suitors" makes it sound like a Jane Austen problem. They have occupied a house whose master is missing and whose heir is a boy. They are consuming the estate deliberately — the estate they intend to inherit — as a way of applying pressure to a woman who has no legal means of removing them. They are doing this under the protection of a sacred custom, in numbers that make resistance suicide, and they are enjoying it. That is the situation, and everything else in this poem — the monsters, the shipwrecks, the twenty years — is the long way round to the door of that hall.

<a id="book-01-note-7"></a>
7. **Guest-friendship (*xenia*).** The most important social institution in this world and the hardest for us to feel from the inside, because we have police, and hotels, and passports. In a world with none of those, a traveller far from home was a man with no protection of any kind, and the only thing standing between him and being robbed and killed on any road in Greece was a religious obligation — that the stranger at your door is sacred, and that Zeus himself watches how you treat him. Feed him first; ask his name afterwards; send him away with a gift. In return, the guest owes the host courtesy, honesty, and restraint. It goes both ways, and it binds the two families permanently. Once you have this in your head, you have the moral spine of the entire poem: nearly every episode in it is a test of hospitality, passed or failed. Odysseus's whole voyage is a series of doors he knocks on. The Cyclops fails the test at one end of the scale. The suitors fail it at the other.

<a id="book-01-note-8"></a>
8. **Phemius.** Remember him. He is a professional bard in a hall he cannot leave, singing to men he did not choose to entertain — a fact that will matter very much indeed, several hundred pages from now, on a day when it is dangerous to be found in that hall. There is also a fine joke buried here, and I do not want you to miss it: this poem is being performed by a bard, in a hall, for a company of noblemen at dinner. Its audience were looking at a real Phemius while they listened. And the song he sings is *the Greeks coming home from Troy*, which is the song we are currently inside.

<a id="book-01-note-9"></a>
9. **Nestor and Menelaus.** Nestor was king of Pylos, the oldest of the Greek commanders at Troy, famous for talking a very great deal and being, on balance, worth listening to. Menelaus was king of Sparta and the husband of Helen — whose departure to Troy, willing or otherwise, started the war in the first place. He got her back, and got home last of anybody, after being blown all the way to Egypt. They are the two surviving men most likely to know something, and Telemachus's journey to them takes up the next three books.

<a id="book-01-note-10"></a>
10. **Eurycleia, bought for twenty oxen.** She is a slave. So are most of the servants in this house, and in every great house in the poem, and the text says so without embarrassment, because it did not occur to anyone that it required one. I am not going to smooth this over, and I am not going to let it pass without comment either. Hold two things at once, as the poem does: Eurycleia was purchased, like livestock, at a price the poem is happy to quote you; and Eurycleia loves this boy, and he loves her, and she is going to be one of the two or three people in the entire story who can be relied upon absolutely when everything comes apart. Both of those are true, and the second does not excuse the first. It is a very old book. Twenty oxen, and a lifetime, and a lamp in a doorway at the end of a bad day.

---

*Book Two: In Which There Is a Meeting, and a Sign in the Sky, and a Ship Sails at Night.*


<div class="page-break"></div>

<!-- Source: book/odyssey-book-02.md -->

# THE ODYSSEY
### Retold in English, with Explanations

---

## BOOK TWO
### In Which There Is a Meeting, and a Sign in the Sky, and a Ship Sails at Night

---

When Dawn came up, with her rosy fingers, Odysseus's dear son got out of bed.

I should say something about that dawn before we go any further, because you are going to meet her a great many times and I do not want you to think I have run out of ideas.

In the original, Dawn is a goddess with rose-red fingers, and she has them every single morning without exception, in this poem and in the other one, for the excellent reason that "rosy-fingered Dawn" is a block of six syllables that fits the metre exactly and can be dropped into the front of a line whenever the sun comes up. The sea is wine-dark. Ships are hollow. Athena is grey-eyed. Achilles is swift-footed even when he is sitting down sulking in a tent, which is most of the time. These are not lazy writing. They are the load-bearing timbers of a poem that had to be composed *while it was being performed*, out loud, in front of an audience, without a script; and a bard who had four hundred such phrases in his head, sorted by length, could build a line the way a mason builds a wall, reaching for the stone that fits the gap.<sup><a href="#book-02-note-1">1</a></sup>

So: rosy-fingered. Every time. I shall use it when it seems to want using, and you may take it as a small ceremonial noise the poem makes at sunrise, like a clock chiming.

---

Telemachus got up and dressed, and slung a sharp sword over his shoulder and tied good sandals on his shining feet, and came out of his room looking, the poem says, very like a god; and he told the heralds to sound the call and summon the Greeks of Ithaca to assembly.

They sounded it, and the men came in from all over the town — slowly at first, then faster, because word got round, and word had something remarkable in it. There had not been an assembly on Ithaca since Odysseus sailed for Troy.

Twenty years. Think about what that means. It is not that the island had been badly governed; it is that it had not been governed at all. No court had sat, no dispute had been judged in public, no decision had been made in the hearing of the men it fell on. Whatever machinery Ithaca once had for the ordinary business of a community had simply been let go, and grass had grown up through it, and everyone had got used to that — and the hundred and eight young men in the great house had grown from boys into men in a country where no one had asked anybody anything in front of witnesses for two decades. That is not a coincidence. That is the soil the whole disaster grew in.<sup><a href="#book-02-note-2">2</a></sup>

Telemachus went down to the meeting-place with a bronze spear in his hand and two quick dogs trotting at his heel. And Athena poured a supernatural grace over him as he came, so that the whole assembly stared as he walked in; and the elders made way for him, and he sat down in his father's seat.

The first to speak was an old, old man named Aegyptius, bent double with age and knowing a very great deal. He had had four sons. One farmed his fields at home. Two were sitting in that assembly among the suitors of Penelope, eating the estate of Odysseus with the rest. And the fourth had sailed with Odysseus to Troy in the hollow ships, and his name was Antiphus, and his father did not know what had become of him.

I am obliged to tell you what had become of him, because the poem's first audience knew it before Aegyptius opened his mouth, and the scene is built out of that knowledge. Antiphus was eaten. He was eaten alive in a cave by the Cyclops Polyphemus, in the dark, along with five of his shipmates — the very act that set Poseidon against Odysseus and is the reason none of these people have had a king for ten years past the end of the war. His father does not know. His father will never know. He is about to stand up and speak kindly to the son of the man who lost his boy, and there is nothing anyone can do about it, and the poem does not even pause. It simply lets you sit there holding it.

The old man leaned on his staff and said: "Listen to me, men of Ithaca. We have not held a session, we have not sat in assembly, since the day Odysseus went away in the hollow ships. Who has called us now? Which of the young men, or which of the older ones? Has he heard news of the army coming home, and does he mean to tell us plainly what he heard first? Or is it some other public matter he wants to raise? He seems to me a good man, and a lucky one. May Zeus bring to pass whatever good thing he has in mind."

Telemachus was very glad to hear that, and did not sit still long. He stood up in the middle of them all, and a herald put the speaker's staff into his hand, and he turned first to the old man.

"Sir, he is not far off — you are about to see him, and yes, I am the one who called you, and yes, I am in more pain than any man here. No, I have not heard news of the army coming home, and I have no other public business to raise. This is my own trouble. Two calamities have fallen on my house.

"The first is that I have lost my father — who was once *your* king, and a gentle one, like a father to every one of you. The second is worse, and it is the ruin of my whole house and everything I have. Men are courting my mother against her will — and they are the sons of the very men sitting in this assembly. They will not go to her father Icarius's house and ask him for her properly, and let him settle the bride-gifts and give his daughter to whichever man he likes best. Instead they come to my house, day after day, every day, killing my cattle and my sheep and my fat goats, feasting and drinking my bright wine, and there is no end to it. There is no man in the house like Odysseus to drive this ruin off. I cannot do it. I am not that man, not yet — and I know exactly how little I can do, and so do they.

"I tell you I would defend myself if I had the strength. This has gone beyond bearing. My house is being destroyed in a way that is not decent. Be angry, you men. Be ashamed in front of the neighbours who live round about. Be afraid of the gods, in case they turn on you in disgust at what is being done. I beg you, by Zeus and by Themis, who breaks up assemblies and calls them into session — *stop*, my friends, and leave me alone with my bitter grief. Unless — unless my father, good Odysseus, ever did some deliberate harm to the Greeks, and you are all paying me back for it out of spite. I would rather it were you eating my stores and my cattle. If you ate them I might at least be paid for them one day: I could go up and down the town pressing my claim until I got my property back. As it is you fill me with a hurt I have no way to answer."

And in a rage he threw the staff on the ground, with tears breaking out of him — and pity went through the whole assembly.

Everyone sat quite silent. No man had the heart to answer Telemachus harshly.

Except Antinous.

---

"Telemachus. That is a big speech, and an unbridled one, and you should be ashamed of yourself, trying to fix the blame on us. Your trouble is not the Greek suitors. It is your own mother, who is a past master at this sort of thing.

"Three years it has gone on — no, this is the fourth — and the whole time she has been leading us on. She holds out hope to every man of us, she sends each one private messages and encouragement, and what she is thinking is nothing like what she says.

"And here is the trick she pulled. She set up a great loom in the hall, and started weaving a wide fine web, and she said to us: *Young men, my suitors — Odysseus is dead. Be patient; do not press me to marry, however eager you are, until I finish this cloth, or all my thread will be wasted. It is a shroud for the lord Laertes (Odysseus's father), for the day when the pitiless end of death takes him. I will not have the women of this country talking against me — that a man who won so much lay dead with no proper cloth to cover him.*

"That is what she said, and we agreed, because how could we not? So she wove at the great web in the daytime — and at night, by torchlight, she unravelled it. Three years she got away with it. She fooled the Greeks. And in the fourth year, when the seasons had come round again, one of her women told us — one who knew all about it — and we caught her in the act of pulling out the beautiful cloth. So she had to finish it, whether she liked it or not.

"Now here is our answer to you, and you may hear it, and so may all the Greeks. Send your mother away. Tell her to marry whichever man her father chooses and whichever man pleases her. But if she goes on tormenting the sons of the Greeks much longer, on the strength of the gifts Athena has given her — the beautiful handwork, and the excellent mind, and the tricks, which nobody in the old stories ever had the like of — then know this: we will go on eating your living and your goods for exactly as long as she keeps to this plan of hers. She is winning a great name for herself. You are losing a great deal of property. We are not going back to our own lands, or anywhere else, until she marries one of us."

Now.

I ask you to look at what has just been handed to us, because it is the finest single piece of characterisation in the first quarter of this poem, and it comes out sideways, in a hostile speech, from a man who thinks he is complaining.

For three years — three years — a woman with no legal power, no army, no husband and no adult son held off a hundred and eight armed men *with a piece of sewing*. And notice the shape of the trick, because the shape is everything. She did not refuse them; a refusal could be overruled. She agreed. She simply attached a condition to the agreement so pious that no man in Greece could object to it without looking like a monster in front of his neighbours: I am weaving a burial cloth for my husband's elderly father, so that when he dies he will not lie uncovered and shame us all. Every man there had to nod. Every man there had to wait. And she used the one activity that was so entirely and unremarkably *women's work* that not one of them thought to check on it — for three years — and every night she picked out by torchlight what she had put in by daylight, so that the work went on forever and never grew.

Do you remember what I told you Athena was the goddess of? War, and weaving, and cleverness. Penelope, at her loom, in the dark, is all three at once.

And I want you to hold on to something else. This poem is about a man famous above all other men for being cunning, who lies his way across the entire known world; and we have not properly met him yet; and the first great feat of deception in the whole book belongs to his wife. They have been apart for twenty years, and they are still doing the same thing. That is not a detail. That is the marriage. Keep it in mind for the very end of the story, when the two of them are finally in a room together, and one of them sets a trap and the other one walks straight into it.

One thing more, and it is not a pleasant one. Antinous says a woman betrayed her — one of her own household, one who knew all about it. That is a small line, and it goes past very fast, and it will be paid for horribly. Remember that a maid told.<sup><a href="#book-02-note-3">3</a></sup>

---

Telemachus answered him.

"Antinous, I cannot possibly throw the mother who bore me and brought me up out of my house against her will — not while my father is somewhere else in the world, alive or dead. And if I sent her back to Icarius of my own accord, I would have to pay her father back a great deal, and it would go hard with me.<sup><a href="#book-02-note-4">4</a></sup> I would suffer at his hands, and the gods would give me worse, because my mother would call down the terrible Furies on me as she left the house — and I would be despised by every man alive. That word will never be spoken by me.

"If your own hearts are troubled by this, then get out of my house. Feast somewhere else. Eat your own goods, and take it in turns, going from one man's house to another. But if you think it better and more profitable to ruin one man's living and never pay for it — go on. And I will call on the gods who live forever, and see whether Zeus will let there be a settling. And you will die in this house, and there will be no payment taken for any of you."

That is the second time he has said that last sentence, and it is not a young man's bluster. It is very nearly a legal formula: it means *you will be killed lawfully, as men killed in the wrong, and no blood-price and no vengeance will be owed for you.* He is not threatening them. He is describing, quite accurately, what is going to happen in this hall in about twenty books' time, and he does not know it yet.

And Zeus, who arranges these things, sent two eagles.

They came down off a mountain peak and flew a long while on the wind, wing to wing, sailing side by side; and when they were exactly over the middle of the assembly, over all those upturned faces, they wheeled and beat their wings hard and glared down at every head, and there was death in their eyes. And then they clawed at each other's faces and necks, tearing, and swung away to the right, out over the houses of the town, and were gone.

The men stared after them, appalled, and turned it over in their minds, wondering what was coming.

And an old man named Halitherses stood up — much the best of his generation at reading birds and saying what they meant — and he said:

"Listen to me, men of Ithaca, and let me speak chiefly to the suitors, because this is rolling towards them. Odysseus is not going to be away from his people much longer. I think he is somewhere very close by at this moment, and that he is sowing the seed of death and doom for every man here — and it will not stop with them, either. A great many of the rest of us who live in bright Ithaca will suffer for it too.

"So let us think, well ahead of time, how we may put a stop to this — or rather, let *them* stop it themselves, which would be much the better way, and they had better be quick about it. I am not a beginner at prophecy; I know what I am talking about. Everything I said about that man is coming true, exactly as I said it would on the day the Greeks sailed for Troy and clever Odysseus went with them. I said he would suffer terribly, and lose all his companions, and come home in the twentieth year, unknown to everybody. And here we are."

And Eurymachus said, smoothly:

"Go home, old man. Go home and prophesy to your own children, before something unpleasant happens to them.

"I am a great deal better at reading this than you are. There are any number of birds flying about under the sun, and by no means all of them mean anything. Odysseus is dead, far away, and I only wish you had died with him — then we would not have to sit through all this prophesying of yours, and you would not be stirring up a boy who is already angry, in the hope that he will make you a present out of gratitude.

"Now, here is what I say, and it will happen. If you — an old man who knows better — talk this youngster round into losing his temper, it will be the worse for *him*, first of all, and he will still not be able to do a thing about any of it. And you, sir, we shall fine, and you will pay it, and it will hurt.

"And here is my advice to Telemachus, in front of everyone. Tell your mother to go back to her father's house. They will arrange the wedding and settle the very large bride-gifts that ought to go with a daughter people are fond of. I do not believe the Greeks will leave off this hard courtship until then. We are not afraid of anybody, and certainly not of Telemachus, however many speeches he makes. And we take no notice of prophecy — the sort of thing you dribble out, old man, that comes to nothing and only makes people hate you more."

I want to be careful here, because it would be easy to say that the difference between Halitherses and Eurymachus is that one believes in omens and the other does not, and that the poem is on the side of the believer. That is nearly right but not quite. Everyone in that assembly believed in omens; the question was always *what a given omen meant*, and men argued about that the way men argue about evidence. What condemns Eurymachus is not scepticism. It is that he does not actually offer a reading. He announces that most birds mean nothing, threatens the old man's children, promises to fine him, and repeats what he wanted anyway. He is not weighing the sign. He is refusing to be interrupted. There is a particular kind of man who calls that clear thinking, and the poem has his number.

---

Telemachus had stopped arguing.

"Eurymachus — and the rest of you proud gentlemen — I am done pleading, and I will say no more about it. The gods know, and all the Greeks know. Just give me a fast ship and twenty men to work her, and I will go up and down the sea-lanes. I am going to Sparta and to sandy Pylos to ask about my father's homecoming, and how long he has been gone. Some man may tell me. I may hear a rumour out of Zeus, which is how news mostly gets about.

"If I hear my father is alive and on his way home, then for all my weariness I will hold out one more year. And if I hear that he is dead and gone, then I will come back to my own country and heap up a mound for him, and burn the offerings on it, all that is proper and in full measure — and I will give my mother to a husband."

And he sat down. And Mentor stood up.

Mentor was an old friend of Odysseus's — the friend, in fact, to whom Odysseus had handed over the whole household on the day he sailed, with instructions to keep everything in order and obey the old man Laertes. (You will recall from Book One's notes that this is the name Athena is going to borrow, and the name our word *mentor* comes from. That is still true. This is the actual man.)

And he did not attack the suitors. Please notice this, because it is the moral centre of the entire book and it is very easy to skim past.

"Listen to me, men of Ithaca.

"Let no sceptred king from this day on be kind, or gentle, or fair-minded, or have any justice in his heart at all. Let him be harsh, and let him do wicked things — since not one man remembers Odysseus among the people he ruled, and he was as gentle to them as a father.

"I do not particularly grudge the proud suitors doing violent things out of the wickedness of their own minds. They are staking their own heads on it when they eat that man's house down and tell each other he will never come back.

"It is the *rest of you* I am angry with — the way you all sit there, saying nothing. You are many. They are few. You have never once opened your mouths to hold them back."

And a man called Leocritus answered him:

"Mentor, you troublemaker, you lunatic — what are you talking about? Setting them on to stop us? It is a hard thing to fight men over a dinner, even when you outnumber them. Why, if Odysseus of Ithaca himself came home this minute and found us feasting in his hall, and set his heart on driving us out of it — his wife would get no joy of his coming, however much she has wanted it. He would meet a very ugly end, taking on so many single-handed. You are talking nonsense.

"Come on — break it up, all of you, and go back to work. Mentor and Halitherses can see the boy off on his journey; they were friends of his father's, after all. Though I think he will sit at home a good long while yet, getting his news in Ithaca, and never make that trip at all."

And with that he dissolved the assembly, and they went off to their houses, and the suitors went to the house of Odysseus.

---

Telemachus went away by himself, down to the edge of the sea, and washed his hands in the grey salt water, and prayed.

"Hear me — you who came to my house yesterday, whoever you are, and told me to take a ship and go over the misty sea to ask about my father's homecoming. The Greeks are blocking every part of it, and the suitors most of all, in their arrogance."

And Athena came and stood beside him in the shape and the voice of Mentor, and said:

"Telemachus. You will not be a coward after this, or a fool, if you have any drop of your father's spirit in you — and he was a man who finished what he said he would do. This journey of yours will not come to nothing.

"But if you were *not* his son, and Penelope's, then I would have no hope of you finishing anything. Few sons turn out to be their fathers' equals. Most are worse. A very few are better. But you are not going to be a coward or a fool, and Odysseus's wits have not entirely failed to reach you, so there is every reason to think you will bring this off.

"Never mind what the suitors are plotting. There is no sense in them, and no justice either, and they have no idea that death is standing next to them and that they are all going to die on one day. As for your journey, it will not be delayed long. I was your father's friend, and I will find you a fast ship and come with you myself. Go home now, and mix with the suitors, and get provisions ready — wine in jars, and barley meal, the strength of men, in stout skins. I will go through the town and raise a crew of volunteers. There are plenty of ships in sea-girt Ithaca, new and old, and I will find the best of them for you, and we will get her fitted out and launched on the open sea."

And Telemachus went home.

---

He found the suitors in the courtyard, skinning goats and singeing pigs. And Antinous came straight over to him, laughing, and took him by the hand, and said his name, and said:

"Telemachus, you great orator, you unstoppable force — no more hard words and no more hard feelings. Eat and drink with us the way you used to. The Greeks will see to all of this for you: a ship and a picked crew, so that you can get to sacred Pylos quickly and hear about your noble father."

And Telemachus took his hand out of Antinous's hand.

"Antinous, there is no way in the world I can have a quiet dinner with you people, or take my ease, or enjoy myself. Was it not enough that you wore away all my best possessions while I was still a child? Now I am grown, and I have listened to what other men say, and there is a spirit rising in me — and I am going to try to send the black spirits of death down on you. I will go to Pylos, or I will go about it here in this country. I am going, and the journey I am talking about will not be for nothing — as a passenger, since I have no ship and no rowers of my own. I suppose you found that arrangement more convenient."

And he pulled his hand lightly out of Antinous's hand, easily, in front of everybody.

The suitors, meanwhile, were setting out the meal, and jeering at him, and needling him, and one of the insolent young men would say something like this:

"I do believe Telemachus is planning to murder us. He'll bring back allies from sandy Pylos, or from Sparta — he's frightfully keen on it. Or perhaps he'll get as far as Ephyra, that rich country, and bring back poison to drop in the wine-bowl and finish the lot of us."

And another would say:

"Who knows? He may go off in his hollow ship and die a long way from his friends, wandering about like his father did. That would make more work for us — we'd have to divide up all his property, and give the house to his mother, and to whichever of us marries her."

That is what they said, to a young man's face, in his own house, about his father, and about his own death. And then they went in to dinner.

---

But Telemachus went down to his father's storeroom.

It was high-roofed and wide, and it held gold and bronze in heaps, and clothing folded in chests, and quantities of fragrant olive oil. And there were great jars standing along the wall in rows against the wall, full of old sweet wine, unmixed, waiting — the god's own drink — kept there in case Odysseus ever came home after all his suffering. The doors were double, close-fitted, double-locked. And the housekeeper was in there day and night, watching over everything with a very shrewd mind indeed: Eurycleia.<sup><a href="#book-02-note-5">5</a></sup>

He called her into the storeroom and said:

"Nurse, draw off some wine for me into jars — sweet wine, the best there is after the vintage you keep for my poor lord, in case he comes home from somewhere, having got out from under death. Fill twelve, and fit them all with lids. And pour me out barley meal into well-sewn bags — twenty measures of milled barley. And keep this to yourself. Have it all put together, because I shall come for it in the evening, once my mother has gone upstairs and is thinking about her bed. I am going to Sparta and to sandy Pylos, to see if I can hear anything about my dear father coming home."

And the old nurse cried out and burst into tears.

"Dear child — how did *this* get into your head? Where are you going, an only son and a beloved one, over all that country? He is dead, that man, far from home, in some place we do not know. And the moment you turn your back these people will start plotting, and you will die by a trick, and they will divide up everything you own. Stay here and sit on your own property. There is no need for you to suffer and wander about on the barren sea."

"Courage, nurse. There is a god behind this plan. But swear to me that you will say nothing to my dear mother — not until eleven days have gone by, or twelve, or until she misses me herself and hears that I have gone. I do not want her spoiling her lovely skin with crying."

So the old woman swore the great oath of the gods, and swore it properly; and then she drew off the wine into the jars, and poured the barley meal into the well-sewn bags; and Telemachus went back into the hall and mixed with the suitors.

And Athena thought of something else.

She went through the town in the likeness of Telemachus, and stood beside each man she wanted, and told him what to do, and said: be at the fast ship this evening. And she asked Noemon, son of Phronius, for a swift ship, and he was glad to give it.

The sun went down and the streets grew dark. Then she ran the fast ship down into the sea and put in her all the gear that well-benched ships carry, and moored her at the far end of the harbour; and the good crew gathered round her, and the goddess put heart into every one of them.

And Athena thought of one thing more. She went to the house of Odysseus, and there she poured sweet sleep over the suitors — sent them wandering as they drank, and knocked the cups out of their hands. They did not sit long. They got up and went off through the town to find their beds, because sleep was falling on their eyelids and they could not keep them open.

Then grey-eyed Athena called Telemachus out of the great hall — in Mentor's shape, with Mentor's voice.

"Telemachus. Your crew are sitting at the oars already, waiting for you to start. Come on. Let us not hold up the journey any longer."

And she led the way, quickly, and he came on behind her, in her footsteps.

They came down to the sea and to the ship, and found the long-haired crew on the shore, and Telemachus said: "Come on, friends — let us fetch the provisions. Everything is stacked and ready in the hall. My mother knows nothing about it, and neither do the servants. Only one woman was told."

And he led the way, and they came behind, and they carried it all down and stowed it in the ship, the way Odysseus's dear son directed.

Then Telemachus went aboard, and Athena went first and sat down in the stern, and Telemachus sat beside her. The crew cast off the stern cables and climbed in and sat down at the oars.

And grey-eyed Athena sent them a following wind — the fresh West Wind, singing over the wine-dark sea.

Telemachus called out to his men and told them to lay hold of the tackle, and they heard him and did it. They raised the pine mast and stepped it in the hollow box and made it fast with forestays, and hauled up the white sail with twisted oxhide ropes; and the wind bellied out the middle of the sail, and the dark wave sang loud along the stem as the ship went, and she ran along on the swell, making her way.

Then they made the running-gear fast in the black swift ship, and set up mixing bowls brimming with wine, and poured out an offering to the gods who live forever and always — most of all, and above all, to the grey-eyed daughter of Zeus.

And all night long, and into the dawn, the ship ran on and cut her way.

---

## NOTES TO BOOK TWO

<a id="book-02-note-1"></a>
1. **Formulas.** In the 1930s a young American scholar named Milman Parry went to what was then Yugoslavia and recorded illiterate village singers performing enormously long heroic poems from memory, and discovered that they did it exactly this way — by assembling stock phrases of fixed metrical shape, improvising the joins. It settled an argument that had run for centuries. The repeated epithets in Homer are not decorative and they are not clumsy: they are the technology of oral composition, and to a listening audience they were not tiresome at all but reassuring, the way a returning chorus is reassuring. They are also, in translation, largely untranslatable in their original function, since English prose has no metre to fill. I keep the best of them for their flavour and let the rest go.

<a id="book-02-note-2"></a>
2. **The assembly.** Not a parliament; nobody voted, and nothing was carried by a majority. It was a gathering of the free adult men of a community, called by whoever had the standing to call it, in which a man who held the speaker's staff had the right to be heard without interruption, and in which grievances were aired in public and pressure was applied by shame. Its power was entirely a matter of opinion — which sounds weak until you remember that these were small societies where a man's standing among his neighbours was the only capital he had. That is precisely why Mentor's speech later in the book lands where it does. The assembly's one real weapon was collective disapproval, and Ithaca had spent three years declining to use it.

<a id="book-02-note-3"></a>
3. **The shroud.** A body was washed, dressed, and wrapped in cloth before burning or burial; to leave a great man uncovered was a public disgrace that fell on his family. Weaving that cloth for one's father-in-law was an act of conspicuous piety, and it also fell squarely within the work a noblewoman was expected to do — indeed the work she was *praised* for doing. This is why the trick is a masterpiece rather than merely a delay: Penelope hid three years of resistance inside the most approved behaviour available to her, and the suitors policed everything about her except the one activity they thought was harmless. — As for the woman who told: the poem will come back to this. When the reckoning arrives, it does not fall only on the suitors. Twelve of the household women are killed for having gone over to them, and the manner of it is the coldest passage in the book. I mention it now, a long way off, because I do not want it to arrive as a surprise, and because I would rather you carried the question with you through everything in between: whether these women were traitors, or captives with no good options, or both. The poem is quite sure. I am not.

<a id="book-02-note-4"></a>
4. **Why sending Penelope home would ruin him.** Marriage in this world involved property moving in both directions — gifts from the suitor's family to the bride's, and a settlement from the bride's father with her. If Telemachus sent his mother back to Icarius on his own initiative, rather than her leaving of her own accord, he would owe her father substantial restitution — and he has no cattle left to pay it with, because the suitors have eaten them. They have engineered a situation where the one thing they demand is the one thing he cannot afford. He is being asked to solve his problem by bankrupting himself.

<a id="book-02-note-5"></a>
5. **The storeroom.** Notice what wealth *is* here: no coins, because coinage had not been invented yet. Wealth was bronze and gold by weight, fine cloth, oil, wine, and above all livestock — which is why "eating the estate" is not a figure of speech but a precise description of what is happening to this family. It also explains why great households ran on gift-exchange rather than purchase, and why hospitality-gifts (see Book One, note 7) were serious economics and not just good manners. And it is why the locked room matters: a house's whole worth stood in jars against a wall, behind a double door, with one trusted old woman holding the key.

---

*Book Three: In Which an Old Man Talks a Great Deal, and Some of It Is Useful.*


<div class="page-break"></div>

<!-- Source: book/odyssey-book-03.md -->

# THE ODYSSEY
### Retold in English, with Explanations

---

## BOOK THREE
### In Which an Old Man Talks a Great Deal, and Some of It Is Useful

---

The sun came up out of the beautiful water and into the brazen sky, to shine on the gods who never die and on men who do, on the grain-giving fields of earth; and the ship came in to Pylos, the well-built citadel of Neleus.

And there were four and a half thousand men on the beach, killing bulls.

That is not a figure of speech and I have not exaggerated it. They were sitting on the shore in nine great companies, five hundred men to a company, and each company had brought nine bulls, and they were sacrificing them to Poseidon of the dark hair — eighty-one black bulls, and the fires going, and the smell of it out over the water; and Telemachus of Ithaca came sailing in out of the dawn straight into the middle of the largest religious ceremony he had ever seen in his life.

You should understand what was actually happening on that beach, because *sacrifice* is one of those words that has gone strange on us. It sounds like waste — like good meat burned up and thrown away to buy favour from heaven. It was very nearly the opposite.

Here is the arrangement. When an animal was killed, the thigh bones were cut out and wrapped in a double fold of fat, with a few raw scraps laid on top, and burned on the altar with wine poured over them; and the smoke went up, and that was the gods' portion. Everything else — all the meat, every edible ounce of it — was roasted on the spot and eaten by the people standing there. That is what those five hundred men to a company were doing. They were having dinner.

In this world you did not, as a rule, simply slaughter an animal and eat it. Killing was a religious act, and a communal one, and the meal *was* the ceremony. The god got the smoke and the bones. The men got the beef.

And the Greeks knew perfectly well that this was a strange sort of bargain, and they had a story to account for it, in which the trickster Prometheus divided up the first ox and hid the good meat inside the ugly stomach-bag, and dressed the bare bones up in glistening fat, and invited Zeus to choose; and Zeus chose the fat, and got the bones, and has been getting them ever since. Whether he was fooled or was pretending to be fooled is a question the story leaves carefully open — and the answer, I think, is that when you are telling a story about why you get to eat all the steak, it is best to be a little vague about whose idea it was.<sup><a href="#book-03-note-1">1</a></sup>

---

Athena, in the shape and the voice of Mentor, told him to get on with it.

"There is no need to be shy now, not for a moment. You crossed all that water for exactly one reason — to find out about your father — so go straight up to Nestor the horseman and ask him. He will not lie to you. He is far too sensible for that."

And Telemachus said, and I love him for it:

"Mentor — how am I to go up to him? How do I even *greet* him? I have no practice at making elegant speeches, and it is embarrassing for a young man to question an older one."

That is one of the truest lines in the poem. He has spent two books discovering his courage. He has faced down a hall of armed men and thrown the speaker's staff on the ground in front of the whole island. And now he has to walk up to a distinguished stranger and introduce himself, and he would rather do almost anything else. Courage and social nerve are different muscles, and nobody has both at twenty.

"Telemachus," said the goddess, "some of it you will think of yourself, and a god will put the rest into your head. I do not believe you were born and brought up without the gods' goodwill."

And she went off ahead of him, quickly, and he came on behind in the god's own footsteps.

---

They came up to the crowd of Pylian men sitting in their companies, and there was Nestor with his sons around him, and his people busy roasting meat and running spits through it. And when they saw strangers coming, the whole party got up together and waved them in and sat them down.

The first to reach them was Nestor's son Peisistratus, who took them both by the hand and settled them on soft fleeces on the sand between his father and his brother Thrasymedes; and he gave them helpings of the inner meat and poured wine into a golden cup and put it into Athena's hands first — because she looked the elder of the two, and that is how it was done — and said:

"Say your prayer to lord Poseidon, stranger, since you have come in on his feast. And when you have poured your offering and prayed, hand the cup to your friend so that he can pour as well. He is a young man, about my own age, and I imagine he prays like the rest of us."

I hope somebody is enjoying this as much as I am. A well-brought-up young man has just handed a golden cup to the goddess Athena and invited her to pray to Poseidon — who is the one god in the world who wants Odysseus dead, whose feast this is, and who is at this precise moment at the far ends of the earth so that Athena can get on with the rescue behind his back.

And she takes the cup. And she prays. She prays graciously and at length for glory to Nestor and his sons, and for a good return for the men of Pylos; and last of all, quietly, at the end, that Telemachus might get what he came for and go home.

She was, as I have said, the goddess of doing the sensible thing well.

---

They ate; and when they had eaten as much as they wanted, old Nestor started the talking, and asked at last who his guests were. Not before. Never before. You feed a man and then you ask his name.<sup><a href="#book-03-note-2">2</a></sup>

"Now is the proper moment to enquire, now that our guests have had their dinner. Strangers — who are you? Where do you sail from over the sea-roads? Are you here on business? Or are you cruising at random, like pirates, who wander about risking their own lives and making trouble for everybody else's?"

Telemachus took his courage in both hands — Athena had put it there — and answered.

"Nestor, son of Neleus, great glory of the Greeks. You ask where we come from, and I will tell you. We are out of Ithaca, and my errand is my own, not the state's. I am looking for word of my father, if there is any to be had anywhere: Odysseus, that great heart, who they say fought beside you once and sacked the city of Troy.

"Every other man who went to that war, we know about. We know where each of them died; we have their names. But this one Zeus has made unaccountable, and nobody can tell me where he went down — whether on land, beaten under by enemies, or somewhere out at sea in the waves.

"So I have come to your knees, in the hope that you will tell me how he died: whether you saw it yourself, or heard it from some other man wandering. His mother bore him for suffering, if anyone ever was. And do not soften it out of kindness or pity. Tell me plainly what you saw. I beg you — if my father ever promised you anything and made it good, in that country of the Trojans where we Greeks suffered so much, remember it now, and tell me the exact truth."

And Nestor took a breath.

---

Now: I must prepare you.

Nestor talks. He is the oldest of all the men who went to Troy; he has ruled through three generations of men; he has outlived nearly everyone he ever fought beside; and he cannot answer a direct question without going round by way of the entire war. In the other poem, the *Iliad*, he is famous for it, and the younger heroes can be seen visibly bracing themselves when he stands up. He is the sort of old man who says *that reminds me* and means it, and who will get to your point eventually, having said four useful things and eleven charming ones on the way.

And I want to defend him, because it is easy to find him funny and much better to find him necessary.

There was no writing worth speaking of in this world. No records, no dispatches, no lists of the dead. Everything anybody knew about a ten-year war fought overseas by men out of a hundred scattered kingdoms was stored in the memories of the men who came back, and nowhere else at all. When a man like Nestor died, the things that only he knew went out like a lamp.

That is why this journey is worth four books of a poem. Telemachus is not going to Pylos to interview a witness. He is going to the library. The library is ninety years old, has a shaky sense of what is relevant, and will not stop talking; and it is the only one there is.

So. Nestor told him about the war. About how they suffered there, the unmanageable ones, ranging the misty sea after plunder wherever Achilles led them, and fighting round the great city of Priam (last king of troy). And how the best men died there. *Ajax lies there, and Achilles, and Patroclus, who gave counsel like the gods themselves — and my own son, Antilochus, faultless and strong, a great runner and a fighter. And we suffered a great deal besides. No mortal man could tell the whole of it. If you stayed five years, six years, asking me what the Greeks went through there, you would give up and go home before I had finished.*

"For nine years we worked at them with every trick we could invent, and the god barely let us finish it. And in all that time no man tried to match himself against Odysseus in cunning, because your father won every time — if you really are his son. I am astonished, looking at you. Even the way you talk is his; you would not think a young man could sound so like him. In all those years he and I never once spoke on opposite sides, in assembly or in council.
