Now, on the last night, with the oath sworn and the leaving agreed and everything he was frightened of taken off the table, the poem says they took their pleasure of it. Both sentences are in the book. I do not think the poem is confused. I think it is describing seven years of something that had a great deal of coercion in it and was not made of nothing else, which is an uncomfortable and adult thing for a poem to notice, and it notices it without comment and moves on to the carpentry.

---

Because in the morning there is carpentry, and this is the first thing in the whole book that we see Odysseus actually *do*.

Four books we have been hearing about him. He is the cleverest man alive; he thought of the horse; he crawled into Troy in rags; he held a man's mouth shut in the dark. All hearsay, all in the past tense, all told by other people at dinner. And here he is at last, in the present tense, doing something — and what he does is *build a boat*, correctly, from felling to launching, in four days, and the poem tells you exactly how.

He put on the clothes she gave him. She gave him a great axe, bronze, sharpened on both edges, sitting well in the hands, with a good olive-wood handle fitted to it; and then a smoothing adze. And she led him to the far end of the island where the tall timber was — alder and poplar and fir going up to the sky, long seasoned and dry, that would float light for him. And when she had shown him where it grew she went back to her house.

And he started cutting. It went quickly. He brought down twenty trees and trimmed them with the bronze, and planed them expertly, and trued them to a chalked line. Then she brought him augers, and he bored every timber and fitted them to each other and hammered them home with pegs and joints.

He made the floor of it as broad as a man who knows the trade lays out the bottom of a wide merchant ship. He set up the decking, fitting it to close-set ribs, and finished it off with long gunwales down the sides. He made a mast, and a yard to fit it. And he made a steering oar to hold her on course. And he fenced the whole thing about with willow withies to keep the water off, and put in a good deal of loose ballast. And Calypso brought him cloth to make the sail with, and he made that expertly too. And he lashed on the braces and the halyards and the sheets. And then he levered her down on rollers into the bright sea.

Four days, and it was finished; and on the fifth she let him go.

Now — you may skip a passage like that. Most readers do; it reads like an instruction manual with the poetry switched off. I would like you not to skip it, for two reasons.

The first is that the audience did not skip it. These were island people. A very large number of the men listening had built or repaired a boat, and every one of them could hear the difference between a poet who knew what an adze was and a poet who did not. That passage is the poem showing its papers.

The second is more important. This man is about to spend nineteen books being famous for lying. He will invent five false lives, at least, and tell them beautifully to people who deserve better. It matters enormously that the first thing we ever watch him do with his own hands is make something true — measure it, line it, peg it, and make it hold.

Keep that in mind. He is a carpenter. It comes up again, a very long way from here, in a room he built himself, and it settles everything.

---

She bathed him and dressed him in sweet-smelling clothes, and put aboard a skin of dark wine, and a bigger one of water, and a leather bag of provisions with plenty of good things in it; and she sent him a following wind, warm and gentle. And he spread his sail to it, delighted, and sat down and steered with the oar, expertly, and sleep never fell on his eyelids.

He watched the Pleiades (star constellation), and Boötes going down late, and the Bear — which men also call the Wain — that turns round in one place and keeps a lookout on Orion, and is the only one that never bathes in the Ocean.

Calypso had told him to keep that one on his left hand as he crossed. And he did.<sup><a href="#book-05-note-4">4</a></sup>

Seventeen days he sailed, and on the eighteenth the shadowy mountains of the Phaeacians' country came up, the nearest part of it to him, and it lay there on the misty sea like a shield.

And Poseidon came back from the Ethiopians.

He was a long way off, in the mountains of the Solymi, and he saw him — saw him out there on the sea, sailing — and the anger went all through him, and he shook his head and said to his own heart:

"Well. So the gods have changed their minds about Odysseus while I was away with the Ethiopians. He is nearly at the country of the Phaeacians, where it is laid down he escapes the great net of misery that has hold of him.

"But I think I can still drive him a good long way into trouble."

I want to be sure the timing has registered, because the poem has arranged it with real cruelty. Poseidon went off to the ends of the earth in the first hundred lines of Book One, and the entire rescue was scheduled into his absence. Twenty days were needed. He has come home on the eighteenth.

He gathered the clouds together and took his trident in his hands and stirred up the sea, and he called up every storm of every wind at once, and covered the land and the water together with cloud, and night came down out of the sky. The East Wind and the South Wind fell on each other, and the hard-blowing West, and the North that is born in the bright air and rolls a great wave in front of it.

And Odysseus's knees went, and his heart, and he said to himself:

"This is bad. What finally becomes of me?

"I am afraid the goddess told me nothing but the truth when she said I would have my fill of suffering at sea before I got home. All of it is coming true. Look at the sky. Zeus is roping the clouds round the whole of it; the sea is churning; every wind there is has jumped on me at once. Now I am certain to be destroyed.

"Three times, four times over, luckier were the Greeks who died back there on the wide plain of Troy, doing a favour to the sons of Atreus (Agememnon and Menaleus). I wish I had died there. I wish it had been me, on the day the Trojans in their crowds were throwing their bronze-headed spears at me over the body of Achilles. Then I would have had my rites, and the Greeks would have carried my name. As it is, it is laid down that I am taken by a miserable death."

And as he said it a great wave came down on him from above, terribly, driving, and spun the raft round; and he was thrown clear of the timbers, and the steering oar went out of his hands. The mast broke in the middle under the awful blast of the mixed winds, and the sail and the yard went far out into the water. And the wave held him under a long time. He could not get up quickly out from under the rush of it, because the clothes Calypso had given him weighed him down.

At last he came up, and spat the bitter brine out of his mouth, and it was running down off his head in streams. And even then, wrecked as he was, he did not forget his raft. He went after it through the waves and got hold of it and pulled himself into the middle of it and sat there, dodging the end of his life; and the big waves took it and carried it up and down the current — the way the North Wind in autumn drives thistles across a plain, and they stick together as they go.

---

But Ino saw him.

She was Cadmus's daughter, with the pretty ankles; and once she had been a mortal woman who spoke like one, and now she has a share of honour in the salt water and they call her Leucothea, the White Goddess. And she pitied him, wandering out there, in that much trouble.

She came up out of the water like a gull on the wing and settled on the raft, and said:

"Poor man. Why does Poseidon hate you so unspeakably, that he plants all this trouble for you?

"He will not finish you, though, however much he wants to.

"Now do this. You do not look like a fool. Take those clothes off, and let the raft go where the winds take it, and swim for it with your arms — strike out for the land of the Phaeacians, where it is laid down that you get out of this alive.

"Here. Take this veil, this immortal thing, and spread it under your chest, and then you need not be afraid of suffering or of dying. But when you get your hands on dry land, untie it and throw it back into the wine-dark sea, well away from the shore, and turn your own head away as you do it."

And she gave him the veil, and went back down into the surging water like a gull, and the black wave closed over her.<sup><a href="#book-05-note-5">5</a></sup>

And the man who had endured everything thought it over, and did not like it.

"No. No — I am afraid some god is weaving me another trap, telling me to leave the raft. I am not doing it yet. That land she says I can escape to is a long way off; I saw it with my own eyes.

"Here is what I will do, and it seems the best plan. As long as the timbers hold in their joints, I will stay here and put up with it, whatever it costs. And when a wave finally smashes the raft to pieces, then I will swim; there will be nothing better to think of by then."

And while he was still turning that over, Poseidon raised a great wave, terrible and hard and arching over, and drove it down on him.

The way a strong wind hits a heap of dry chaff and scatters it every way at once — that is how it scattered the long timbers. And Odysseus got astride a single plank, riding it like a man riding a horse, and stripped off the clothes Calypso had given him and got Ino's veil round his chest and tied it, and put his arms out and threw himself head first into the sea to swim.

And the lord of the earthquake (Poseidon) saw him, and shook his head, and said: "Right. Now go and drift about like that, in real misery, until you fall in with people the gods have favoured. I do not think you will find your suffering small." And he lashed his horses and drove away to Aegae, where his famous house is.

And Athena, daughter of Zeus, thought of something else.

She stopped the tracks of all the other winds and told them to fall off and go to sleep, and she raised the fast North Wind and broke the seas down in front of him, so that he could reach the Phaeacians, who love the oar, and get away from death.

---

Two nights and two days he drifted on the heavy swell, and his own heart told him a great many times that he was going to die.

But when the third morning came, the wind fell and there was a windless calm; and he lifted up on a big wave and looked out, straining, and saw land close by.

And it came to him the way it comes to children when their father's life begins again — a man who has lain a long time in a sickness, wasting, with some hard spirit wearing away at him, and then, thank god, the gods let him go; and that is how welcome the land looked to Odysseus, and the trees on it. And he swam hard, driving to get his feet on solid ground.

But when he was as close in as a man's voice will carry, he heard the sea booming on the reefs. Great waves were roaring against the dry land and breaking, and everything was covered in spray; there were no harbours and no roadsteads for a ship, nothing but jutting headlands and rocks and cliffs.

And his knees went, and his heart, and he said to himself:

"So Zeus lets me see land I never hoped to see, and I have cut my way through all that water — and now there is no way out of the grey sea at all.

"Sharp rocks outside, and the surf howling round them, and the cliff going up sheer, and deep water close in with no place to stand on my two feet and get clear of it. If I try to climb out, a big wave will pick me up and throw me on the stone, and it will have been a wasted effort.

"And if I swim on further, looking for a beach that slopes, or a river mouth, I am afraid the storm will pick me up again, groaning as I go, and carry me back out into the fish-filled sea. Or some god will send a monster up at me out of the water. Amphitrite keeps a great many of those, and I know how much the famous Earthshaker hates me."

And while he was turning it over, a big wave carried him in at the rough shore. He would have been stripped of his skin and had his bones smashed, if Athena had not put it into his mind to grab at a rock with both hands as he came in; and he held on, groaning, until the great wave went by.

He got past that one. And then the backwash hit him as it came out, and struck him hard, and threw him far out to sea again.

And the way the pebbles come away stuck all over the suckers of a squid when it is dragged out of its hole — that is how the skin came off his strong hands on the rock. And the great wave closed over him.

Then and there the wretched man would have died before his time, if Athena had not given him a clear head. He came up out of the surge that was vomiting in against the land, and swam along outside it, watching the shore, hoping for a beach that sloped, or a river mouth.

And swimming, he came to the mouth of a river with a good current; and that seemed the best place to him, clear of rocks, and sheltered from the wind.

And he felt the water running out, and he prayed in his heart:

"Hear me, lord, whoever you are. I have come to you, as a man comes to what he has been praying for, running from the sea and from Poseidon's threats. Even the immortal gods respect a man who arrives as a wanderer — and that is what I am now, coming to your current and to your knees after a great deal of suffering. Pity me, lord. I claim to be your suppliant."

And the river checked his current, and held the wave back, and made calm water in front of him, and brought him safe into his own mouth.

And he came out with both his knees bent under him and his strong hands hanging, because the salt water had beaten the heart out of him. His whole body was swollen and the sea was running out of his mouth and his nostrils in streams. He lay there without breath and without a word, hardly able to move, and a terrible tiredness had come over him.

And when he got his breath back and the spirit came together in him again, he untied the goddess's veil and dropped it into the river running out to sea. A big wave carried it back down the current, and Ino caught it in her hands.

And he crawled up out of the water and lay down in the reeds and kissed the earth that gives men grain.

---

And then, because he was still in the world and the world does not stop, he had a new problem, and he put it to himself:

"What now? What finally becomes of me?

"If I keep watch by the river through this miserable night, I am afraid the hard frost and the wet dew together will finish me off — weak as I am, with the breath barely in me — and the wind off a river blows cold before dawn.

"And if I climb the slope into the dark wood and lie down in the thick brush, and the cold and the tiredness let go of me, and sweet sleep comes — I am afraid I become prey and a meal for wild animals."

And thinking it over, that seemed the better of the two; and he went up into the wood, and found a place near the water, in a clearing.

He crawled in under a pair of bushes growing out of the same spot: one of them a wild olive, one a grafted olive. No wet wind ever blew through them; the sun never struck through them with its rays; the rain never got through, they were grown together so close. And Odysseus crawled in under them and at once heaped himself a wide bed with his own hands, because there was a great drift of fallen leaves lying there — enough to cover two men or three, in the winter season, however hard the weather.

And when he saw it he was glad, and he lay down in the middle and poured the leaves over himself.

The way a man on a lonely farm, out at the edge of everything, with no neighbours, buries a burning log in the black embers and keeps the seed of the fire alive so that he does not have to go somewhere else to fetch it — that is how Odysseus lay covered over in the leaves.

And Athena poured sleep over his eyes and closed the lids of them, so that the exhaustion he had suffered would let go of him soonest.

---

## NOTES TO BOOK FIVE

<a id="book-05-note-1"></a>
1. **Tithonus.** Dawn's husband, and a joke the poem does not stop to make, though it puts him in the first line of a book about a man refusing to be made immortal. Dawn fell in love with a mortal prince and asked Zeus to make him deathless, and Zeus granted exactly what she asked for — and she had forgotten to ask for youth. So Tithonus did not die. He got older, and older, and older, past strength, past sight, past speech, until in the end there was nothing left of him but a voice, and she shut him in a room, and he is in there still. The Greeks had a number of stories about people acquiring immortality and every single one of them is a horror story. It is worth carrying that into the cave with you when Calypso makes her offer.

<a id="book-05-note-2"></a>
2. **Calypso, and what a nymph is.** Her name is built on the Greek verb *kalyptō*, to cover, to conceal, to hide away — the same root as the veil Ino gives him later in this book. She is, by name, the Concealer, and what she conceals is a man: for seven years nobody in the world, god or mortal, knew where Odysseus was. — As for what she is: a nymph is a minor female divinity attached to a place, a spring, a tree, a stretch of coast. Deathless, but not an Olympian; powerful in her own patch and nowhere else. Note what she cannot do. She cannot defy Zeus. She cannot build a ship. She cannot leave. She has spent seven years on an island in the middle of the sea with one man and no way of going anywhere either, and there is a reading of this book — not the only one, but a real one — in which two prisoners are talking to each other on that beach and only one of them knows it.

<a id="book-05-note-3"></a>
3. **The oath by the Styx.** The Styx is a river of the underworld, and swearing by its water is the one oath even the gods cannot wriggle out of. Hesiod (playwright like Homer), who is precise about the penalties, says a god who swears falsely by it lies breathless and speechless for a year, cut off from nectar and ambrosia, and is then barred from the councils and the feasts of the other gods for nine more. — What matters here is that Odysseus demands it. A goddess who has just been ordered by the king of the gods to release him tells him he is free to go, and his response is to require a legally binding oath, and hers is to laugh and call him a rogue and give him one. That is the relationship in miniature. It is also, exactly, why he is going to survive the next nineteen books: he does not believe good news.

<a id="book-05-note-4"></a>
4. **Steering by the Bear.** Greek sailing was mostly coastal and mostly in daylight and mostly in summer, hopping from headland to headland; there was no compass, no chart, and no instrument of any kind. What there was, was the sky. The constellation the poem calls the Bear or the Wain — our Plough, or Big Dipper — is circumpolar in these latitudes, which is what the poem means by saying it is the only one that never bathes in the Ocean: it wheels round the pole all night and never sets. So it is always in the north. And if you keep the north on your left hand, you are sailing east. That is the whole of Calypso's sailing direction, and it is a real one; a man could cross with it. Notice also that Odysseus does not sleep for seventeen days and nights. He is single-handing a small boat across open water with no crew to take a watch, and the poem knows precisely what that costs.

<a id="book-05-note-5"></a>
5. **Ino, who is called Leucothea.** She had been a mortal woman: a princess of Thebes, sister to the mother of Dionysus, and she took the infant god in and nursed him — for which Hera drove her mad, and she went off a cliff into the sea with her own son in her arms, and the sea took her in and made her a goddess. She now spends her immortality pulling drowning men out of the water. Bear that in mind when a veil comes up out of the sea and a voice says *you need not be afraid of dying*; the poem has chosen, out of everyone available, the one divinity in the Mediterranean who knows from the inside what it is to go under. — And notice what Odysseus does with the help: he takes it, thanks nobody, and then refuses to follow the instructions until the raft is smashed out from under him. He is right, too. She told him to abandon a floating vessel two days from land. Being rescued by a goddess is not the same as being told the truth by one, and he has learned to tell the difference.

---

*Book Six: In Which a Girl Does the Washing, Plays a Ball Game, and Finds Something Dreadful in the Bushes.*


<div class="page-break"></div>

<!-- Source: book/odyssey-book-06.md -->

# THE ODYSSEY
### Retold in English, with Explanations

---

## BOOK SIX
### In Which a Girl Does the Washing, Plays a Ball Game, and Finds Something Dreadful in the Bushes

---

So the man who had endured everything slept there, buried in his leaves, worn out with exhaustion.

And Athena went to the town of the Phaeacians.

They had lived once in a wide open country called Hyperia, next door to the Cyclopes — who were stronger than they were, and violent, and kept raiding them. So their king Nausithous had got them up and moved the whole nation to Scheria, far away from everybody who works for a living, and run a wall round the town and built houses and put up temples for the gods and marked out the fields. But he had gone down into the dark by now, and Alcinous ruled there, and the gods had taught him what he knew.

Hold on to that piece of family history for three books. These people are refugees. They live at the far edge of the world in a walled town full of gardens and dancing and ships, and the reason they live there is that they could not go on living next to the Cyclopes.<sup><a href="#book-06-note-1">1</a></sup>

---

Athena went to the house, and into a richly-made room where a girl was sleeping who looked like one of the immortals in shape and in her face: Nausicaa, the daughter of great-hearted Alcinous. Two maids slept on either side of the doorposts, and they had beauty from the Graces, and the shining doors were shut.

And the goddess went through like a breath of air and stood over the girl's head, and took on the look of the daughter of Dymas, a man famous for his ships — a girl of her own age, and dear to her.

"Nausicaa. How did your mother come to have such a careless daughter?

"Your good clothes are lying about the place unwashed, and your marriage is very close, when you will have to be beautifully dressed yourself and find clothes for the people who walk with you. That is how a good name gets built up among people, and how a father and a mother are made glad.

"So let us go washing as soon as it is light. I will come with you and work beside you, so that you get it all done quickly, because you are not going to be unmarried much longer. The best men in the whole country here are already asking for you, and you are Phaeacian yourself.

"Go on — ask your father, first thing in the morning, for the mules and the wagon to carry the sashes and the robes and the bright coverlets. It is much better than walking. The washing pools are a long way from the town."

And she went away to Olympus, where they say the gods have their seat forever. The wind does not shake it, and the rain never wets it, and the snow never comes near it; there is a great clear air spread cloudless over it, and a white light running along it; and there the blessed gods take their pleasure, all their days.

---

Dawn came up on her fine throne and woke Nausicaa, and she wondered at the dream, and went through the house to tell her parents about it.

She found her mother indoors, sitting at the hearth with her women round her, spinning yarn dyed with the purple of the sea. And she caught her father in the doorway on his way out to a meeting of the chiefs, where the Phaeacian nobles were calling him.

And she stood in front of him and said:

"Daddy — could you get the wagon out for me? The high one, with the good wheels. I want to take the good clothes down to the river to wash; they are all lying dirty.

"And it is only right that you should have clean clothes on you when you sit in council with the leading men.

"And there are five sons of yours in this house — two of them married, and three of them fine young bachelors who are always wanting freshly washed things to wear when they go out dancing. And I am the one who has to think about all of it."

That is what she said, because she was too shy to mention her own marriage to her father.

But he understood every word of it, and he answered:

"I do not grudge you the mules, child, and I do not grudge you anything else. Go on. The servants will get the wagon out for you, the high one with the good wheels and the box on top."

I would like to stop here for a moment, having just come out of the North Wind and the squid and the drowning, and point out that we are now in a domestic comedy and it is one of the best-observed things in ancient literature.

A girl has had a dream that has made her think about getting married, and she wakes up embarrassed about it, and she goes to her father and constructs an entire practical case for a trip to the river which is about everybody's laundry except her own. Your council robes, father. The boys' dancing clothes. And the poem tells you plainly what she is doing — *she was too shy to mention her own marriage* — and then tells you, in the next line, that he knew perfectly well.

And he does not tease her. He does not say *ah, so that's it*. He gives her the wagon and the mules and asks no questions, and goes off to his meeting.

There is a great deal of grand machinery in this poem — gods in council, storms raised by tridents, oaths sworn on the rivers of the dead. This is the other thing it can do, and it does it in nine lines: a father and a daughter, both of them knowing exactly what the conversation is about, and neither of them saying so, out of kindness.

---

The servants brought out the mule wagon and yoked the mules, and the girl carried the good clothes out of the room and packed them in. And her mother put a chest of food in for her, all sorts of good things, and something to go with it, and poured wine into a goatskin bag; and she gave her a golden flask of soft olive oil, for the girl and her women to rub on themselves after bathing.

And Nausicaa took the whip and the shining reins and cracked the whip to start them, and there was a clatter of mules, and they pulled steadily, carrying the clothes and the girl — not alone; her women went along with her.

They came to the beautiful stream of the river, where the washing pools were, always full, with plenty of clear water welling up through them, enough to clean the dirtiest things. And they turned the mules loose out of the wagon and drove them along the eddying river to graze on the honey-sweet clover, and took the clothes down off the wagon in armfuls and carried them into the dark water and trod them in the pits, racing each other at it.

And when they had washed everything and got all the dirt out, they spread it in rows along the shore, where the sea washed the shingle cleanest.

Then they bathed and rubbed themselves with the oil, and had their meal on the river bank, and waited for the sun to dry the clothes.<sup><a href="#book-06-note-2">2</a></sup>

And when they had all had enough to eat, they threw off their headscarves and played at ball, and Nausicaa of the white arms led the singing for them.

The way Artemis (god of the hunt) who showers arrows goes down a mountain — down the long ridge of Taygetus, or Erymanthus — happy among the boars and the running deer, and the wild nymphs, the daughters of Zeus, play along with her, and Leto is glad in her heart, because her girl holds her head and her forehead higher than all of them and is easy to pick out, though every one of them is lovely: that is how the unmarried girl stood out among her women.

---

And when she was about to yoke the mules and fold the good clothes and go home, Athena thought of something else — so that Odysseus would wake up, and see her, and be brought into the city.

The princess threw the ball at one of her women and missed her, and it went into a deep eddy of the river.

And they all screamed.

And Odysseus woke up.

He sat up and turned it over in his mind. *What now? Whose country am I in this time? Are they violent and wild, with no sense of right, or do they take strangers in, and do they have god-fearing minds? Something went past me just then that sounded like girls — nymphs, who live on the steep tops of the mountains and the springs of the rivers and the grassy meadows? Or am I somewhere near people who use speech? Well. I shall go and look for myself.*

And he crawled out from under the bushes, and with his great hand he broke off a leafy branch to hold in front of himself and cover what a man does not want seen.

And he came out.

The way a lion goes, bred in the mountains, sure of his own strength, driving on through rain and wind with his eyes on fire, in among the cattle or the sheep or the wild deer of the hills — his belly tells him to go, and he will try even a well-fenced fold: that is how Odysseus was about to come among those girls with their beautiful hair, naked as he was. He had no choice left.

And he was horrible to look at, all crusted over with dried sea-salt.

And they ran. They ran in every direction, along the spits of the beach.

Only the daughter of Alcinous stood still, because Athena put courage in her heart and took the fear out of her legs; and she stood and faced him.

---

And Odysseus had a decision to make, and it took him about a second and a half.

The correct and binding way to beg a stranger for your life in this world was to get down and take hold of their knees with one hand and their chin with the other. It was a physical act and it worked like a legal one: once you were holding on, the person you were holding was under an obligation the gods were watching, and to shake you off was a serious impiety. It is the strongest claim a helpless person can make. Every instinct this man has, after twenty years of getting out of things, is to make the strongest claim available.

And he looked at her — a girl on a beach, on her own, ten feet from a naked stranger the size of a lion with salt in his beard — and worked out that if he touched her she would never forgive him, and that he would win the argument and lose the case.

So he stayed where he was, and used words instead. He made a soft and cunning speech.<sup><a href="#book-06-note-3">3</a></sup>

"I am at your knees, my lady. Whatever you are — a goddess, or a mortal woman.

"If you are a goddess, one of those who hold the wide sky, then I take you for Artemis, the daughter of great Zeus: you have her looks, and her height, and the way she is put together.

"And if you are one of the mortals who live on the earth, then three times blessed is your father, and your honoured mother, and three times blessed your brothers. Their hearts must warm right through with pleasure every time they watch you go into the dancing — a young shoot like you.

"And blessed beyond all of them, in his heart, is the man who wins the argument with his gifts and takes you home.

"I have never seen anything like you with my own eyes — no man, no woman. I am afraid, looking at you.

"Once, on Delos, beside the altar of Apollo, I saw a young palm shoot coming up out of the ground. I had gone there too, with a great many men behind me, on a journey that was going to end badly for me. And I stood and stared at that tree for a long time, and could not stop, because no shaft like it had ever come up out of the earth.

"And that is how I feel now, my lady. I am amazed by you, and I am afraid, and I do not dare to take hold of your knees.

"Hard grief has come on me. Yesterday, on the twentieth day, I got out of the wine-dark sea. All that time the swell and the racing storms carried me away from the island of Ogygia (where Calypso lived). And now some god has thrown me down here to suffer some more — because I do not think it is over. I think the gods have a good deal more in store for me before it is finished.

"Pity me, my lady. You are the first person I have come to, after everything I have been through, and I do not know one other human being in this country. Show me the town, and give me a rag to throw round myself — anything, whatever you had the clothes wrapped in when you came.

"And may the gods give you everything your heart wants: a husband, and a house, and *one mind between you*. There is nothing better in this world, nothing stronger, than a man and a woman keeping house together with one mind. It is a great pain to the people who hate them, and a joy to the people who love them — and they know it themselves, better than anyone."

---

I said in Book One that we would be a while getting to the point of this poem, and that the point was a house.

That is the point of the poem. He has just said it, in the last sentence of that speech, on a beach, to a stranger, holding a branch.

The word is *homophrosynē*, and there is no clean English for it. Like-mindedness. Same-thinkingness. Two people whose minds run the same way. He does not say love, and he does not say fidelity, and he does not say passion — all of which he could have said and none of which are the thing he means. He means the arrangement in which two people want the same things and think about them in the same way and can therefore trust each other, and he says that when it exists it is a weapon against your enemies and a comfort to your friends, and that the two people inside it know something the people outside it do not.

He has one. It is nineteen hundred miles away and he has not seen it for twenty years and he is not sure it is still there.

And he wishes it on a girl he met four minutes ago, as a blessing, in the middle of begging her for a scrap of cloth to cover himself with.

That is the sentence to carry with you into the rest of this book. Everything Odysseus turns down — a goddess, deathlessness, the girl who is about to appear in his path, the kingdom that will be offered to him with her — he turns down because of a thing he can describe in one clause and cannot get home to.<sup><a href="#book-06-note-4">4</a></sup>

---

And Nausicaa answered him.

"Stranger — you do not strike me as a bad man, or a stupid one.

"Zeus himself hands out good luck to people, to bad men and good men, whichever way he likes; and he has given you this, I suppose, and you have to put up with it.

"But now, since you have arrived at our city and our country, you shall not go short of clothing, or of anything else that a suppliant who has been through it deserves when he comes to us.

"I will show you the town, and tell you the name of the people. The Phaeacians hold this city and this land. And I am the daughter of great-hearted Alcinous, and the strength and the power of the Phaeacians rest on him."

And she called to her women, who had run off.

"Stand still! Where are you running to, at the sight of a man?

"You surely do not think he is an enemy? There is no man alive, and never will be, who comes to the country of the Phaeacians carrying war. We are very dear to the immortals. And we live out here at the edge of things, in the middle of the surging sea, the last people anywhere, and no other human beings have anything to do with us.

"This is some unlucky man who has come here off his course, and we have to look after him now. All strangers and beggars come from Zeus, and a small gift is a welcome one.

"So give the stranger food and drink, women, and wash him in the river, somewhere out of the wind."

They stopped, and called to each other, and settled him in a sheltered place as Nausicaa told them; and they laid out clothes for him, a cloak and a tunic, and gave him the golden flask of soft oil, and told him to wash in the streams of the river.

And Odysseus said: "Girls — stand back over there while I get the salt off my shoulders myself, and rub the oil on. It has been a long time since my skin had any oil on it. I am not going to wash in front of you. I am ashamed to stand naked among girls with lovely hair."

So they went away and told the princess.

And he washed the brine off his back and his broad shoulders, and scrubbed the crust of the sea out of his hair. And when he had washed and oiled himself all over and put on the clothes the unmarried girl had given him, Athena made him look taller and stronger, and made the hair come down curling off his head like hyacinth flowers.

The way a skilled craftsman washes gold over silver — a man Hephaestus and Athena have taught the whole art, so that everything he finishes has grace in it — that is how she poured grace over his head and shoulders.

And he went off and sat down apart on the beach, shining with good looks and grace.

And the girl looked at him.

And she said to her women: "Listen to me. This man has not come among the Phaeacians against the will of the gods. A moment ago I thought he was appalling. Now he looks like the gods who hold the wide sky.

"I wish a man like that might be called my husband, living here, and that it might please him to stay.

"Well. Give the stranger food and drink, women."

They heard her and did as she said; and they put food and drink in front of him, and the man who had endured everything ate and drank like an animal, because it had been a very long time since he had tasted anything.

---

Then Nausicaa thought of the rest of it.

She folded the clothes and put them in the good wagon, and yoked the strong-hoofed mules, and got up herself; and she called Odysseus over and told him what to do, and there is more calculation in it than most people notice.

"Get up now, stranger, and come into the town, and I will send you on to the house of my father, who is a wise man, where I promise you will meet the best of the Phaeacians.

"But do it like this — you do not seem to me to lack sense.

"While we are going through the fields and the farmland, come along quickly behind the wagon with the women; I will lead the way.

"But when we are about to enter the city — there is a high wall round it, and a fine harbour on either side of the town, and the entrance is narrow; the curved ships are drawn up along the road, and every man has his own slip for his; and there is the meeting-ground round the beautiful temple of Poseidon, built of quarried stone set deep in the earth; and there the men see to the tackle of the black ships, the cables and the sails, and there they plane down the blades of the oars — because the Phaeacians do not care about bows and arrows; it is masts and oars and balanced ships they care about, and they love crossing the grey sea in them —

"when we are about to enter the city, I want to keep away from their nasty talk, in case somebody blames me afterwards. There are some very insolent men about, and one of the worse sort might say this if he met us:

"*Who is this tall handsome stranger with Nausicaa? Where did she pick him up? Some husband for herself, no doubt. Perhaps she has taken in some wandering man off a ship — some foreigner, since we have no neighbours. Or some god she has been praying hard for has come down out of the sky in answer, and she will have him for the rest of her days. Better if she has gone out and found herself a husband somewhere else, since she is clearly too good for the Phaeacians here at home — and there are plenty of them courting her, and good men too.*

"That is what they would say, and it would be thrown at me afterwards. And I would blame another girl who behaved like that — who went about with men before her wedding day, with her father and mother still living, and without their knowing.

"So do this instead. There is a grove of Athena beside the road, a poplar wood, with a spring running in it and a meadow round about — my father's estate, and his orchard in full bloom, as far out of town as a man's shout will carry.

"Sit down there and wait, for as long as it takes us to get into the city and reach my father's house. And when you think we have got there, then go into the town yourself and ask for the house of my father, great-hearted Alcinous. It is easy to recognise; a small child could take you to it. None of the other Phaeacian houses are built anything like it.

"And when the house and the courtyard have closed round you, go quickly through the hall until you reach my mother. She sits at the hearth in the firelight, leaning against a pillar, spinning sea-purple yarn — a wonder to look at — with her women sitting behind her.

"My father's chair is against the same pillar, and he sits in it drinking his wine like an immortal.

"Go straight past him. Put your arms round my mother's knees, if you want to see the day of your homecoming quickly and with gladness, however far away your home may be.

"If she takes to you in her own mind, then there is hope for you — that you will see the people you love, and get back to your own well-built house and your own country."

---

There is a great deal in that speech and I want to take two things out of it.

The first is the practical brilliance of it, which is of a piece with everything else in this book. She has looked at a man who cannot walk into a foreign city alone and unknown, and she has designed him a way in: an approach route, a waiting point, a landmark, and — crucially — the name of the one person in the building whose good opinion decides everything. She is seventeen years old, if that. She would have made an excellent minister.

The second is what it costs her.

She has just told a strange man, out loud, in front of her women, that she wishes he could be her husband. And now she is arranging to be seen arriving home alone.

Not because she has changed her mind. Because there are men in her town who talk, and she knows exactly what they will say, and she can quote it — she performs the sneer, word for word, in the voice they would use. *She's picked up some sailor. She's too good for the local boys.* She has clearly heard it said about somebody else. And then she says the hardest sentence in the book: that she would think badly of a girl who did that.

She is a princess of a people who are the finest sailors in the world, at the edge of the earth, dear to the gods, walled and rich and safe from every enemy — and she cannot walk into her own town beside a man without it costing her something she cannot get back.

So she sends him round the long way, and she drives home by herself, and that is very nearly the last we shall hear from her.

---

She cracked the whip and the mules went on, and stepped out well, and they made good time; and she drove carefully, so that the women and Odysseus, on foot, could keep up, and she used the whip with judgement.

And the sun went down, and they came to the famous grove, the sacred ground of Athena, and Odysseus sat down there.

And he prayed to the daughter of great Zeus:

"Hear me, child of Zeus who holds the storm cloud — Unwearied One. Hear me now, since you did not hear me before, when the famous Earthshaker was smashing me.

"Let me come to the Phaeacians as a man they will care for and pity."

So he prayed, and Athena heard him.

But she did not show herself to him face to face, not yet. She was keeping out of the way of her father's brother (Poseidon) — who was still burning with anger against the godlike man, and would go on being angry until he reached his own country.

---

## NOTES TO BOOK SIX

<a id="book-06-note-1"></a>
1. **The Phaeacians.** They are the hinge of the whole poem and it is worth knowing what they are before you meet them. For five books we have been in the ordinary world — Ithaca, Pylos, Sparta, places with politics and taxes and inheritance law. For the next four books we will be somewhere else entirely, and after that we go into a world of one-eyed giants, witches, singing monsters and the country of the dead. The Phaeacians stand exactly on the border. They are recognisably a real society, with a king and a council and a harbour and gossip; and they are also a fairy-tale people, dear to the gods, living past the edge of the map, whose ships need no steersman and know by themselves where every man wants to go. Everything before them is history. Everything after them is a story told at their dinner table — because it is here, and only here, that Odysseus tells his own adventures, in his own voice, to an audience. Keep that in view. From Book Nine to Book Twelve, the most famous events in this poem come to you as a shipwrecked man's after-dinner account of himself, given to strangers he needs something from. — And note the one hard fact in their history: they emigrated because they could not live near the Cyclopes. The monsters are not in another kind of world from this one. They are just up the coast.

<a id="book-06-note-2"></a>
2. **The laundry.** Trampled in stone pits with the feet, rinsed, and spread out on the shingle at the tide line, where the sea has scoured the pebbles clean and the salt and sun bleach the linen. It is heavy physical work and it takes all day, and it is being done by the king's daughter with her own feet, on an outing she had to ask permission for. This is worth registering because it is easy to picture these households wrongly. Nobody is idle. Penelope weaves; Helen spins with a golden spindle and keeps a work-basket at her chair; Arete will be found spinning in the firelight; the queen of the Phaeacians and the princess of the Phaeacians both work with their hands, and it is a mark of standing rather than the opposite. The distinction that mattered was not between working and not working. It was between working in your own house and working in somebody else's.

<a id="book-06-note-3"></a>
3. **Suppliancy, and the touch he does not make.** To supplicate formally was to take hold of a person's knees with one hand and their chin or beard with the other, and then to speak. The physical hold was the point: it made the claim binding, put the suppliant under the protection of Zeus, and made refusal a religious offence rather than merely a rudeness. It is what Odysseus is about to do to the queen, on this girl's own instructions, with his arms round her knees at the hearth. — Here he declines it, and says so out loud, and dresses the refusal up as awe: *I am amazed by you, and I do not dare*. Read it as flattery and it is charming. Read it as tactics and it is one of the shrewdest things he does in the poem. He gives up the strongest available claim on her, in exchange for her not being frightened of him — and he is right, because the claim would have been worth nothing from a naked stranger who had just grabbed a girl on an empty beach, and her goodwill is worth everything. He also, and this matters, does not lie to her. He tells her the truth about Ogygia and the twenty days. He lies to nearly everyone else on this island. He does not lie to her.

<a id="book-06-note-4"></a>
4. **Like-mindedness (*homophrosynē*).** The poem's own definition of a good marriage, given in this speech and nowhere else so plainly: not desire, not loyalty, not even love, but two people whose minds work the same way. It is a startling thing to find as the stated ideal in a heroic poem from the eighth century before Christ, and it is worth saying that the poem means it structurally and not just sentimentally. It is the reason Penelope's shroud trick was set beside Odysseus's cunning in Book Two. It is the reason the last recognition in this book, twenty thousand lines from here, is not a matter of scars or proofs of identity but of one person laying a trap and the other spotting it. And it is the standard by which the poem quietly judges the other marriages it shows you: Menelaus and Helen, who love each other and tell incompatible stories over a drugged bowl; Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, who came to a very great oneness of purpose indeed, and it was murder.

<a id="book-06-note-5"></a>
5. **"Go straight past my father."** The oddest instruction in the book, and the poem does not explain it here. A shipwrecked stranger arriving at a foreign court is told to walk past the king on his throne without stopping and throw his arms round the queen's knees — and told it by the king's own daughter, as though it were obvious, and told that everything depends on the queen's opinion. Alcinous rules the Phaeacians and the strength and power of the people rest on him; his daughter says so herself, thirty lines earlier. And it is his wife you supplicate. The explanation, such as it is, arrives at the start of the next book, and I will let it arrive there rather than spoil it; but note in the meantime that this is the third great house we have visited, and that in Sparta it was Helen who identified the guest, named him, and controlled the room, and in Ithaca it is Penelope's decision that everything is waiting on. This poem is extremely interested in what wives actually decide, as against what kings appear to.

---

*Book Seven: In Which There Is a Garden That Is Always in Fruit, and a Queen Who Recognises the Laundry.*


<div class="page-break"></div>

<!-- Source: book/odyssey-book-07.md -->

# THE ODYSSEY
### Retold in English, with Explanations

---

## BOOK SEVEN
### In Which There Is a Garden That Is Always in Fruit, and a Queen Who Recognises the Laundry

---

So he prayed there in the grove, while the strong mules carried the girl on into the town.

And when she came to her father's famous house she pulled up at the gateway, and her brothers came out and stood round her looking like immortals, and unyoked the mules and carried the clothes indoors; and she went off to her own room. And her old nurse lit the fire for her — Eurymedousa, who had been brought over from Apeira long ago in the curved ships, and had been picked out of the plunder and given to Alcinous, because he was king over everybody and the people listened to him as though he were a god. She had brought Nausicaa up in that house, and now she lit the fire and set about getting her supper.<sup><a href="#book-07-note-1">1</a></sup>

And Odysseus got up to go into the town.

Athena, who was looking after him, poured a thick mist round him as he went, in case one of the great-hearted Phaeacians should meet him on the road and pass some remark and ask him who he was. And just as he was about to step into the town she came to meet him herself, in the shape of a young girl carrying a water pitcher; and she stood there in front of him, and Odysseus said:

"Child, could you take me to the house of a man called Alcinous, who is king over the people here? I am a stranger. I have been through a great deal. I have come a long way, out of a distant country, and I do not know a single soul who lives in this town."

"Certainly, sir," said Athena. "I will show you the house; my own father lives close by it. But go quietly, and let me lead the way, and do not look at anybody and do not ask anybody anything. These people are not very tolerant of strangers, and they do not exactly make a foreigner welcome. What they trust is their fast ships, and crossing the great gulf of the sea, because Poseidon (god of the sea, and the one who has been keeping Odysseus from home these ten years) gave them that."

I hope you have noticed that this is not at all what the girl on the beach told him a few hours ago, and I think the difference is worth a moment of our time before we go in through the gate. Nausicaa said that all strangers and beggars come from Zeus, that a small gift is a welcome one, and that her people are dear to the gods; and she was speaking honestly and out of a generous nature, and every word of it was true. Athena, who has been watching this nation for rather longer than seventeen years, says: keep your head down, they do not much care for outsiders. And that is true as well. The Phaeacians are about to treat this man magnificently — feed him, bathe him, entertain him, load him with gold and carry him home for nothing — and they are also, every one of them, going to make him prove himself first, and one of them is going to insult him to his face in public before the day is out. Hospitality in this world is a law; but laws are kept by people, and people are a mixed business, and a poem that told you otherwise would not be worth reading.

---

She led the way, quickly, and he came along behind her in the goddess's own footsteps; and the Phaeacians, the famous sailors, never noticed him going through the middle of their town, because Athena would not allow it. And as they walked she told him about the woman whose knees he was going to take hold of.

"That house you asked about, sir — the king sits in it, and his wife is called Arete, and she comes of the very same stock the king himself comes from.

"Poseidon began that line, with Periboea, who was the loveliest woman of her time and the youngest daughter of Eurymedon, who was king over the Giants once, and destroyed them, and himself along with them. Poseidon lay with her and she bore a son, Nausithous, who ruled the Phaeacians; and Nausithous had two sons, Rhexenor and Alcinous.

"Apollo (god of prophecy, and of the bow, whose arrows bring sudden death) shot Rhexenor down when he was newly married and had no son in the house, and he left one daughter behind him: Arete. And Alcinous made her his wife, and honours her as no other woman on this earth is honoured — no other woman anywhere who keeps a house under a husband.

"That is the honour she has, and has always had, from her own children, and from Alcinous himself, and from the people, who look at her as though she were a god and speak to her that way when she goes through the town. There is nothing lacking in her own good sense either, and she settles quarrels, even quarrels between men, for the people she thinks well of.

"If she takes to you in her own mind, then there is hope for you: that you will see the people you love, and get back to your own high-roofed house and your own country."

And with that Athena went away over the barren sea, and left lovely Scheria behind her, and came to Marathon and to Athens of the wide streets, and went into the strong house of Erechtheus.

---

Now, at the end of the last book I pointed at Nausicaa's instruction — walk straight past my father and put your arms round my mother's knees — and told you that the explanation was coming and that I would let it arrive in its own good time rather than spoil it. Here it is; and I have to tell you, in all honesty, that it does not explain anything at all.

What we are given is a family tree. A god fathered the line; the elder brother died young leaving one daughter; her uncle married her; and she is honoured as no woman on earth is honoured. And then the same fact three more times over, which is generally a sign that somebody is filling a silence: her children honour her, her husband honours her, the people honour her like a god when she walks down the street.

Notice what is missing from all of that. There is no office. She is not a priestess, and not a judge, and not a co-ruler under any constitutional arrangement that anybody troubles to name; and the one line in the whole speech that describes her actually doing something — that she settles disputes, *even between men* — is thrown out in half a breath as though it followed naturally from what has gone before, which it does not. It follows from nothing. It simply sits there, remarkable and unexplained, in the middle of a genealogy.

So we have been handed an answer with a hole in the middle of it, and the hole is the shape of a woman with real power that nobody in the building can quite account for. And I have come to think that this is the truth of the matter rather than a failure of the poem, because there have been such women in every society that has ever existed, including a great many societies with no legal room for them whatsoever, and the way you can always tell is exactly this: everybody knows to go to her, nobody can point to the rule that says so, and if you ask a local why, you are given a genealogy and a list of the people who respect her.

There is one other thing in that speech which slides past very fast, and I shall mention it once and then leave it alone. She is his brother's daughter, and he married her, and the poem reports this in the same breath as everything else without the smallest flicker of embarrassment — because to its first audience this was not scandal but administration. A royal house that has suddenly lost its heir has a succession problem and a property problem at the same moment, and marrying the orphaned niece to her nearest kinsman solves both of them at a stroke.<sup><a href="#book-07-note-2">2</a></sup>

---

Then Odysseus came to the famous house, and stopped where he was, with his heart turning over a great many things, before he stepped onto the bronze threshold.

Because there was a brightness like the sun and the moon over that high-roofed house. The walls ran bronze on both sides, all the way in from the threshold, with a cornice of dark blue enamel round the top of them. Golden doors shut the strong house in; silver doorposts stood on the bronze threshold, with a silver lintel above and a golden handle. And on either side of the doors there were dogs made of gold and silver, that Hephaestus (the lame smith of the gods, who makes everything the immortals cannot make for themselves) had built with his own skill and knowledge, to keep watch over the house of great-hearted Alcinous — deathless dogs, that do not grow old, ever.

Inside, chairs stood along the wall on both sides, the whole way in from the threshold, and light finely-woven covers were thrown over them, the work of the women of the house; and the Phaeacian leaders sat there to eat and drink, because there was always something going on. And there were young men made of gold standing on their well-built pedestals, holding burning torches in their hands, to light the hall at night for the people at dinner.<sup><a href="#book-07-note-3">3</a></sup>

And there were fifty serving women in that house. Some of them grind the yellow grain at the millstone; others weave at the loom, or sit twirling the spindles, and their hands move like the leaves of a tall poplar; and the close-woven linen is so smooth that the oil runs off it. For the Phaeacian men are the best sailors in the world at driving a fast ship over the sea, and their women are the best in the world at the loom, because Athena gave them the skill for it, and good sense besides.

And outside the courtyard gate there was an orchard of four acres, with a hedge running round both sides of it and tall trees flourishing inside: pears and pomegranates and apples with their bright fruit, and sweet figs, and olives in their prime. And the fruit of those trees never dies and never fails, winter or summer, the whole year round; there is always a west wind blowing there, and it is always bringing some fruit on and ripening others, so that pear grows old upon pear, and apple upon apple, grape upon grape and fig upon fig. And there was a vineyard rooted in the same ground, heavy with grapes, and part of it a level drying-floor where the bunches lie in the sun; and other clusters they are gathering, and others they are treading; while in the front rows the unripe grapes are still dropping their blossom, and others just beginning to darken. And at the far end of the vineyard there were neat beds of vegetables of every kind, green all the year. And two springs ran there: one of them led all through the garden, and the other going the other way, out under the courtyard threshold and up towards the high house, and the townspeople came and drew their water from that one.

That was the gods' shining gift in the house of Alcinous.

---

And Odysseus stood outside in the road and looked at it, and I should like to stand there with him a moment, because he has been in a rich house before and this is not the same thing at all.

You will remember Menelaus's palace in Book Four, where this same young man's own son stood in the doorway and said out loud that it must be what the house of Zeus looks like inside, and was gently corrected by his host. But that house was full of *treasure*: gold and amber and ivory and silver, every piece of it carried home in a ship, and every piece of it a receipt for eight years of wandering about the eastern sea while his brother was being murdered at his own front door. Menelaus recited the inventory and then told the boy, in the same breath, that he would hand over two thirds of it tomorrow to have the dead men back.

This is not treasure. What Odysseus is looking at over that hedge is a working farm with the seasons taken out of it.

And I would ask you to notice what the poem chooses to dwell on, at length and with evident pleasure, in the wealthiest house it will ever show us. Not the gold. The gold gets a line and a half. It is the fruit that gets the paragraph: four acres of pears and figs and olives, and a vineyard standing at every stage of the year all at once, some of it being picked and some of it being trodden and some of it still in flower; and the vegetable beds; and the two springs, one of which is led out under the wall so that the neighbours can fill their jars at the king's water. The marvel of the place is not that its owner is rich. It is that nothing there ever fails, and nobody there ever has to wait.

That is a fairy-tale, of course, and the poem knows quite well that it is a fairy-tale; no one has ever farmed a country where the wind is always westerly and the apples are always coming. But it is a very particular fairy-tale, and it is precisely the one that a farming people would dream, because it is made entirely out of the absence of the things that frighten them. No hungry gap in February. No hail the week before harvest. No year when the olives simply do not come.

And there is a man standing at the gate looking at it who has been at sea for ten years; whose own orchard is on a stony island where the goats do better than the grain; and whose father, at this moment, is sleeping in the ashes by the fire with the servants, out in the real dirt and the actual weather, grieving.

He looks at it for a long time. Then he goes in.

---

Inside, the Phaeacian leaders were pouring the last of their wine to Hermes (the messenger of the gods, and the one who walks with travellers), which is what they always did at the end of an evening before they began thinking about bed. And Odysseus went through the house wrapped in the thick mist Athena had poured round him, until he came to Arete and to the king, and threw his arms round Arete's knees.

And at that moment the miraculous mist fell away from him, and every person in that hall found themselves looking at a man who had not been there a second before. They went silent. They stared. They wondered.

And he made his appeal.

"Arete, daughter of godlike Rhexenor. I come to your husband, and to your knees, and to these guests, after a very great deal of suffering. May the gods grant them all good lives, and may every man here hand on to his children the wealth in his house and whatever honour the people have given him. But arrange an escort for me, so that I can get to my own country quickly. I have been away from the people I love a long time, and I have suffered."

And he sat down in the ashes of the hearth, beside the fire.

And nobody said a single word.

---

That is the most awkward pause in the poem so far, and it deserves to be looked at rather than hurried past, because a great deal is going on inside it.

A man has appeared out of nothing in the middle of a closed room and taken hold of the strongest position their law allows to a helpless person: his arms are round the queen's knees, which puts him under the protection of Zeus himself and makes shaking him off an act of impiety rather than mere rudeness. Then he lets go and sits down in the fireplace — in the ash, at the hearth, which is at once the sacred centre of the house and the coldest and lowest place in it to put a guest. It is a gesture of complete self-abasement, and, this being Odysseus, it is also completely unanswerable. Every person in that room now has a religious problem sitting in their fire, and not one of them can think what to say about it.

What breaks the silence is an old man. Echeneus was the oldest Phaeacian present and the best speaker among them, and he knew a great many old things; and he said, in effect, what everybody in the room should have said several seconds earlier — that this would not do, that it did the king no credit to have a stranger sitting on the ground in the ashes, that everybody was holding back and waiting for him, and that the man should be got up out of the fireplace at once and put in a silver-studded chair, and the wine mixed, and a proper supper brought out of the stores.

And two things happen next which I would not like you to miss, because they are small and they tell you a great deal about how this poem thinks good rule works. The first is that the correction comes from the oldest man in the room, in front of the whole council, and the king takes it instantly and without the smallest flicker of resentment — which is the point. Good kingship in this poem is not a matter of never getting it wrong; it is a matter of what happens when a man of ninety tells you that you have. And the second is that when Alcinous needs a seat of honour for the stranger, he turns his own favourite son out of one: he tells Laodamas, who was sitting next to him and whom he loved best, to get up and go and sit somewhere else. That is how honour worked in a world with no money in it. There were only so many good chairs, and giving one to somebody always meant taking it away from somebody else, and everybody in the hall saw who moved.

---

Then a maid brought water in a beautiful golden jug and poured it out over a silver basin for him to wash his hands, and drew up a polished table beside him; and the housekeeper brought bread and a great many good things out of her stores; and the man who had endured everything ate and drank.

And Alcinous told the herald to mix the bowl and serve everyone in the hall, so that they could pour out to Zeus, who walks in beside anybody who deserves respect. And when they had poured, and drunk as much as they wanted, the king dismissed the council for the night. In the morning, he said, they would call in more of the elders and entertain the stranger properly and make good sacrifices, and then see about his escort, so that this man could get to his own country without trouble and without pain, however far away it was; and after that he would suffer whatever his fate was, and whatever the heavy Spinners spun into his thread on the day his mother bore him.<sup><a href="#book-07-note-4">4</a></sup>

"But if he is one of the immortals come down out of the sky," he added, "then the gods are up to something new. Because up to now they have always shown themselves to us plainly whenever we make them a proper sacrifice, and they sit down and eat beside us; and if one of us meets them out on the road on his own, they do not hide themselves, because we are close to them — the way the Cyclopes are, and the wild tribes of the Giants."

And Odysseus said:

"Alcinous, get that out of your head. I am nothing like the immortals who hold the wide sky, not in my body and not in what I am. I am like men who die.

"Whoever you know who carries the heaviest load of sorrow among human beings — I will set my griefs against theirs and match them. And I could tell you a great deal more, and everything I have suffered through the will of the gods.

"But let me eat, in spite of my grief. Because there is nothing more shameless than a man's cursed belly, which insists on being remembered, however badly he is hurt and however much sorrow he has in his mind. I have sorrow in my mind. And it keeps telling me to eat and drink, and it makes me forget everything I have been through, and it will not stop until it is filled.

"But hurry, all of you, at first light. Put me down on my own country, wretched as I am. I have suffered enough. Let the life leave me the moment I have seen my own property, and my servants, and my great high-roofed house."

---

That is one of the strangest and best speeches in the poem, and it is not heroic in the least, and that is exactly the point of it.

A man is being asked, in the politest possible terms, whether he might not be a god in disguise. And his answer is that he is not, and his proof is that he is hungry.

Set it for a moment beside the other poem, because the two of them are arguing here and it is worth hearing the argument. In the *Iliad*, when Achilles's dearest friend is killed and he is torn to pieces by grief, they bring him food and he will not touch it; and his refusal to eat is presented as the true and towering response of a great soul, so that in the end a goddess has to come down and feed him in secret because he will not do it for himself. Grief in that poem is a thing you starve on. It lifts you clear of the ordinary business of the body and sets you above other men.

This poem does not believe a word of it.

What this poem says, through the mouth of a man sitting in borrowed clothes at a stranger's table, is that the belly is shameless; that it nags; that it will not permit you to concentrate properly on your own tragedy. However much you have lost, however far from home you are, however many of your friends have been eaten or drowned in front of you, there comes a point in the afternoon when the appalling fact is that you would like your dinner — and you will eat it, and while you are eating it you will actually stop thinking about the thing for a few minutes, which is somehow the most humiliating part of the whole business.

And he is not saying this lightly or as a joke. He says it with real bitterness — *the cursed belly*, the thing that makes you forget. He would very much rather be the sort of man who cannot eat. He is not that sort of man. Almost nobody is.

And the poem's judgement on him, offered quietly and without any fuss at all, is that this is not a failure. It is how a person gets through twenty years. The man who can eat when he is heartbroken is the man who is still alive when the ship goes down; and the reason he gets home in the end is not that his grief was smaller than anybody else's. It is that he kept eating.

---

Then they poured the last of the wine and went off home to bed, and Odysseus was left in the hall with Arete and Alcinous sitting beside him, while the maids cleared the dishes away.

And Arete spoke first, because she had recognised the clothes. She had looked at the cloak and the tunic on his back and known them at once, having made them herself with her own women.

"Stranger. There is something I should like to ask you first, myself. Who are you? Where are you from? Who gave you those clothes? Did you not say you came here wandering, over the sea?"

And Odysseus told her — and told her the truth, which is worth pausing on, because he is going to spend a great deal of the rest of this poem doing nothing of the kind. He told her about the island of Ogygia and the goddess Calypso; about the ship split open by lightning and the crew drowned, and nine days clinging to the keel; about the seven years, and the offer of deathlessness that never once persuaded him; about the raft, and the seventeen days of open water, and Poseidon smashing him within sight of land; about the river, and the leaves.

And then he came to the part with the girl in it, and there he was careful.

"And I saw your daughter's maids playing on the shore, and her among them, looking like a goddess; and I asked her for help. And she showed better sense than you would ever expect from somebody of that age — you do not generally find young people being sensible; they are usually thoughtless. She gave me bread, and red wine, and had me washed in the river, and gave me these clothes. That is the truth, painful as it is to tell."

And Alcinous said: "Stranger, there is one thing my child did not handle properly. She should have brought you here herself, with her women, since it was to her that you first appealed."

And Odysseus lied to him.

"Sir, do not blame your blameless daughter for that. She did tell me to follow her with the women. I was the one who refused. I was afraid, and I did not want you to be angry at the sight of it. We are a suspicious lot, we people on this earth."

---

I have been waiting several books to say this, so you will forgive me for stopping in the middle of a dinner party to say it properly.

That is the first lie we ever watch Odysseus tell. Not the first he has ever told, of course — this is the man who walked into Troy dressed as a beggar and walked out again over a pile of bodies, and we have heard two separate people describe it — but it is the first one told in the present tense of this poem, in front of us, in a room, in real time. And from here to the very last pages he will be lying almost continuously: false names, false countries, four or five entirely invented lives, told to swineherds and beggars and princes and, in the end, to his own wife.

And this first one is a lie told by a shipwrecked stranger with nothing in the world, to the king whose goodwill is the only thing standing between him and dying on that island, for the sole purpose of lifting a mild fatherly criticism off the shoulders of a seventeen-year-old girl who helped him.

He gains nothing whatever by it. It costs him a small risk, at the worst possible moment to be taking small risks. And notice precisely where the falsehood lies, because it is beautifully placed: he does not lie about whether she behaved well. He lies about *whose decision it was*. He takes her careful calculation about the gossips in the town — which she made deliberately, and explained to him at length on the road — and quietly moves it onto his own account, where a father's disapproval cannot reach it.

Keep that firmly in mind two hundred pages from now, when he is telling an enormous falsehood to somebody who loves him and you find yourself wondering what to think. It is the same faculty at work. Lying is not a moral quality in this man at all; it is a tool, and it does whatever the hand holding it wants done. Which is why the interesting question about him is never *is he lying* — he is, almost always — but *what is he protecting*.

---

And Alcinous answered him, and it must be said that Alcinous is a thoroughly decent man.

"Stranger, my heart is not the kind that gets angry for no reason. Everything is better done properly. By Father Zeus, and Athena, and Apollo — a man like you, thinking the way I think, I could wish you would have my daughter, and be called my son-in-law, and stay here. I would give you a house and everything in it, if you stayed of your own free will. But nobody in this country will hold you against it; Zeus forbid.

"Your escort I shall fix for tomorrow, so that you may know it is settled. You will lie down and sleep, overcome, while they row you over the calm water until you reach your own country and your own house, or wherever else you like — even if it is further off than Euboea, which the people here say is the furthest place there is. Some of our men saw it once, when they carried Rhadamanthus over to visit Tityos; and they went all that way and came home again the same day without turning a hair.

"You will find out for yourself how good my ships are, and how good my young men are at throwing up the sea with the flat of an oar."<sup><a href="#book-07-note-5">5</a></sup>

And Odysseus was delighted, and prayed aloud: "Father Zeus, let Alcinous do everything he has said. Let his fame never go out over the grain-giving earth. And let me get to my own country."

Now I want you to notice what he did not say, because the silence is the whole of it.

A king has just offered him a daughter, a house, an estate and a place among a people the gods sit down to dinner with; and has said, in the same breath and with real grace, that he will not be held to any of it and may leave whenever he likes. It is the third such offer he has been made in this poem — a goddess offered him deathlessness, a girl on a beach said out loud in front of her maids that she wished he could be her husband, and now this — and it is by some way the best-made of the three, coming from a good man who means it kindly and who has taken care to leave the door open behind it.

And Odysseus neither accepts nor refuses. He prays for a safe journey, out loud, in front of the man who has just made the offer, and lets that stand as his answer.

There is nothing else to be said, and he knows it. He said the true thing yesterday morning, on a beach, to this man's daughter, when he had nothing on but a branch: that there is nothing in this world better or stronger than a man and a woman keeping house together with one mind between them. He has one. It is a very long way from here, and he has not seen it for twenty years, and he is not certain it is still there. Everything he turns down, he turns down for that.

---

Then Arete told her women to put a bed under the covered walk, and to lay beautiful purple blankets on it and spread rugs over them and put fleecy cloaks on top for a covering. And they went out of the hall with torches in their hands, and when they had made the bed up they came and stood beside Odysseus and said: "Come and lie down, stranger; your bed is made."

And he was very glad to sleep.

So the man who had endured everything slept there, in the corded bed, under the echoing colonnade. And Alcinous lay down in an inner room of the high house, and his wife lay beside him, and she had made up the bed.

---

## NOTES TO BOOK SEVEN

<a id="book-07-note-1"></a>
1. **Eurymedousa.** She was taken from a place called Apeira in the curved ships and given to Alcinous as his share of the plunder, because he was king; and then she raised his daughter. She gets two lines and no further mention, and she is the fourth household we have been shown — after Ithaca, Sparta and Pylos — in which the woman who brought up the children arrived as somebody's property. The pattern is worth naming plainly this once and then leaving alone: whenever this poem wants to show you a house running warmly and well, there is a woman at the centre of the domestic arrangements who was carried there in a ship against her will. See Book One, note 10, and Book Four, note 1.

<a id="book-07-note-2"></a>
2. **Arete.** On the marriage: an uncle marrying his brother's orphaned daughter would have raised no eyebrows in a royal house that had just lost its heir, since it kept the succession, the property and the claim inside one family at a single stroke. Greek practice in later centuries permitted marriage between an uncle and a niece for exactly this reason — an heiress with no brothers was very often married to her nearest kinsman on the father's side, precisely so that the estate should not walk out of the family.
