The poem states it flatly because to its audience it was administration and not scandal. — On the name: it stands close to a Greek verb meaning to pray for or to entreat, and so carries a faint shadow of *the one who is prayed to*, which suits a woman whose knees a suppliant is instructed to grasp; and it is also close to *aretē*, excellence. The Greeks enjoyed this sort of resonance and were not at all systematic about it. I would not build very much on it, but it is there.

<a id="book-07-note-3"></a>
3. **The gold dogs and the gold torch-bearers.** These are not ornaments. The dogs are deathless and ageless and they are on guard, and the young men holding the torches are standing on pedestals doing a job of work; they are made things that function — machines in the shape of servants and animals, built by the smith of the gods — and they are among the earliest of their kind in European literature. Hephaestus does this elsewhere too: in the *Iliad* he owns twenty tripods on golden wheels that roll into the gods' assembly by themselves and roll home again afterwards, and he is attended by handmaids made out of gold who can think and speak and have strength in them. What strikes me most is how completely untroubled everybody is. Nobody in this poem finds the golden dogs uncanny, or asks whether they are alive, or wonders what they do when the smith is not watching. They are simply the finest work of the finest craftsman there is, and the mark of the finest house there is, and the guests walk past them in to dinner.

<a id="book-07-note-4"></a>
4. **The Spinners.** The Fates: three of them in the developed mythology, one who spins the thread of a life, one who measures it and one who cuts it. But notice how lightly the poem holds all this. Alcinous says the stranger will suffer whatever was spun for him at his birth, and then in the very same speech makes elaborate practical arrangements to see that he suffers as little as possible — and nobody present feels the least tension between the two. That is characteristic. Fate in this poem is not a machine that removes choice; it is closer to the shape of a life as seen from the outside, or from the end. People still deliberate, take advice, change their minds and are held responsible for what they do; and Zeus himself, in the first hundred lines of Book One, complains bitterly that men blame the gods for troubles they have manufactured entirely on their own.

<a id="book-07-note-5"></a>
5. **Euboea, and the size of the world.** Alcinous names Euboea as the furthest place his people have ever heard of, out at the very rim of things, so distant that his sailors still talk about the voyage. Euboea is a long island lying off the east coast of mainland Greece, close enough to the shore in places to shout across. It is, in other words, extremely near — near to Athens, near to Boeotia, near to the poet and near to his audience. The joke is aimed gently at the Phaeacians: for all their magical ships, their sense of the world is a fairy-tale sense, and the ends of the earth to them are somebody else's back garden. It is also, in a poem so preoccupied with distance, a quiet piece of consolation. The furthest place in the world is a day's sail, if you have the right ship.

---

*Book Eight: In Which a Blind Man Sings, a Young Man Is Rude About Sport, and a Stranger Cries Into His Cloak.*


<div class="page-break"></div>

<!-- Source: book/odyssey-book-08.md -->

# THE ODYSSEY
### Retold in English, with Explanations

---

## BOOK EIGHT
### In Which a Blind Man Sings, a Young Man Is Rude About Sport, and a Stranger Cries Into His Cloak

---

When Dawn came up, rosy-fingered, Alcinous got out of bed, and so did Odysseus, the sacker of cities; and the king led the way down to the Phaeacian meeting-ground, which is laid out beside the ships.

Athena went through the town in the likeness of the king's own herald, stopping beside one man after another. "Come along, leaders and counsellors of the Phaeacians — come to the assembly and hear about the stranger who has arrived at the house of Alcinous. He has been driven over the sea, and he looks like one of the immortals."

And she poured a supernatural grace over Odysseus's head and shoulders and made him taller to look at, and broader, because she wanted the Phaeacians to find him formidable and worth respecting — and because he was going to have to get through a great many tests before the day was out. It looks like a party, this day. It is an examination.

The seats filled up, and the crowd stared at him, and Alcinous stood and spoke.

"A stranger — I do not know who — has come to my house, wandering, out of the east or out of the west, and he is asking for an escort. Let us get one ready, the way we always do; nobody who comes to my house sits about here for long, grieving over his send-off.

"So drag a black ship down to the bright sea, a new one on her first voyage, and pick out fifty-two young men from the whole country, the best there are. Lash the oars in place and then come up to my house and get a meal inside you. That is my instruction to the young men. As for the rest of you — the sceptred kings — come to my house, so that we can entertain our guest properly indoors. Nobody refuse.

"And send for Demodocus, the singer whom heaven has favoured. The god gave him song beyond anybody else, to delight us however his heart moves him to sing."

So the ship was hauled down and the mast stepped and the oars fitted into their leather loops, and they moored her out in deep water and went up to the great house. The colonnades and the courtyards and the halls filled with men, young and old, and there were a great many of them; and Alcinous killed twelve sheep for them, and eight white-tusked boars, and two shambling oxen, and they dressed them and got a very fine dinner ready.

And the herald came bringing the singer, whom the Muse loved above other men, and to whom she had given good and evil together: she took his eyes away, and she gave him sweet song.<sup><a href="#book-08-note-1">1</a></sup>

He was given a silver-studded chair in the middle of the diners, backed against a tall pillar; and the herald hung the clear-toned lyre on a peg above his head and showed him how to reach up and take it down, and put a basket beside him and a good table and a cup of wine to drink when he wanted it.

And when they had all eaten and drunk as much as they wanted, the Muse stirred the singer to sing about the famous deeds of men — out of a song whose fame had gone right up into the wide sky in those days.

He sang about the quarrel of Odysseus and Achilles: how the two of them had once fallen out at a rich feast of the gods, with terrible words, and how Agamemnon had been secretly delighted to see the best of the Greeks quarrelling, because Apollo (god of prophecy, and of the bow) had told him at Delphi that this would be the sign. And it was the beginning of the disaster that rolled over the Trojans and the Greeks alike, by the will of Zeus.

And Odysseus took the great purple cloak in his strong hands and drew it down over his head and hid his handsome face, because he was ashamed to be seen crying by the Phaeacians. Every time the singer stopped he would push the cloak back and wipe the tears away and take his two-handled cup and pour an offering to the gods; and every time the singer started again — because the Phaeacian nobles kept urging him on, they were enjoying the story so much — he would cover his head and cry.

He got away with it. Nobody noticed except Alcinous, who was sitting next to him and could hear him breathing.

Consider what has just happened, because as far as anybody can tell it had never happened in a story before. A man is sitting in disguise at a foreign dinner table listening to a professional performer sing a well-known number about the Trojan war, and he is in it — not as a veteran in the audience but as one of the two men the song is about; and the crowd, who have heard it before and like it, are calling for more. That is what undying fame turns into. It becomes something a stranger performs at parties, in a town you have never visited, to people who will applaud and then ask for the one about the horse; and the man it belongs to sits under his cloak and waits for it to stop so that he can wipe his face and pour his wine like everybody else.

---

Alcinous, who was quick, said that they had all had enough of dinner and the lyre and had better go out to the games — so that the stranger could tell his friends at home how far the Phaeacians outdid everybody at boxing and wrestling and jumping and running.

Out they went, with a great crowd behind them, and a number of fine young men stood up to compete. Their names, and I give them because they are worth having, were Acroneus and Ocyalus and Elatreus, Nauteus and Prymneus and Anchialus, Eretmeus and Ponteus and Proreus, Thoon and Anabesineus and Amphialus; and Euryalus, who was as good as murderous Ares to look at, the best-built of all the Phaeacians after the faultless Laodamas; and the three sons of Alcinous, Laodamas and Halius and Clytoneus.<sup><a href="#book-08-note-2">2</a></sup>

Clytoneus won the footrace by a distance. Euryalus won the wrestling, Amphialus the jump, Elatreus the discus, and Laodamas the boxing.

And when they had enjoyed the games, Laodamas said: "Friends, let us ask the stranger whether he knows any sport. He is not badly built — look at his thighs and his calves, and those arms, and the thick neck on him. There is a great deal of strength there, and he is not past it either; he has just been broken up by hard usage. There is nothing on earth like the sea for finishing a man off, however strong he is."

So he went and stood in the middle and said, politely: "Come and try, sir, if you know any games. You look as if you would. There is no greater glory for a man, as long as he lives, than what he can do with his hands and his feet. Come and have a try, and shake the cares off your heart. You will not be kept waiting for your journey much longer; the ship is launched and the crew are ready."

"Laodamas, why are you all pressing me and making fun of me? I have more grief in my mind than games. I have been through a great deal and worked very hard, and I am sitting here in your assembly wanting to go home, and asking your king and your people for it."

And Euryalus answered him to his face, and insulted him.

"No. I did not think you looked like a man who knows about contests — not the sort men hold everywhere. You look more like a man who goes up and down in a ship with a lot of oars, in charge of a crew of traders, keeping an eye on his cargo and watching his freight charges and his greedy profits. You do not look like an athlete."

That is not an insult about sport, and I hope you heard what it actually was. He is saying: you are in business; you are the sort of man who counts things. To a young nobleman of this world there was no deeper cut available, since the whole value system he was raised in held that a gentleman shows his quality with his body, in public, for honour — and that a man who works for gain is a lesser article. It also happens to be aimed at somebody who has spent ten years calculating, weighing, counting his men and getting what he could out of every place he landed in, and who is at this moment working a room in order to extract a passage home. Which is very likely why it lands.

And Odysseus looked at him from under his brows.

"That was ugly, sir, and you talk like a reckless man. The gods do not give every good thing to every man — not beauty and brains and eloquence together. There is a man whose looks are nothing much, and the god crowns his words with a shape, and people watch him with pleasure; he speaks steadily on, with a winning modesty, and he stands out in any gathering, and when he walks through the town men look at him as if he were a god. And there is another man who is as handsome as the immortals, and there is no grace in anything he says.

"You, for instance. You are outstanding to look at; a god could not improve you. And your mind is empty.

"You have stirred me up. I am not a beginner at games, whatever you say; I was among the best of them while I could still trust my youth and my hands. Now I am held down by hardship and pain, because I have got through a good deal of war and a good deal of heavy water. Even so — I will try. Your words bit me, and you have provoked me."

And he got up, still in his cloak, and picked up a discus: a big one, bigger and thicker and a great deal heavier than the ones the Phaeacians had been throwing at each other. He swung it and let it go, and the stone hummed as it went; and the Phaeacians, the long-oared men, the famous sailors, ducked at the noise of it going over.

It went past every one of their marks. It flew light out of his hand.

And Athena, in the shape of a man, set the marker down where it fell and called out: "Even a blind man could find your mark, stranger, feeling for it — because it is not mixed in with the crowd of them at all. It is out in front, well out. Take heart about this event. There is not a Phaeacian here who will reach it, let alone pass it."

And Odysseus was delighted, because there was somebody in that crowd who was on his side; and being thoroughly wound up by now, he challenged the lot of them.

"Reach that, young men. And when you have, I shall throw another one as far or further. Anybody else who feels moved to it — since you have made me angry — come out. Boxing, wrestling, running, I do not care. Any Phaeacian you like, except Laodamas, because he is my host, and only a lunatic quarrels with the man who is feeding him.

"I am not bad with any of the usual weapons. I know how to handle a polished bow. I would be first to hit my man in a crowd of enemies, even with a lot of my own friends standing beside me shooting at the same target. There was only one man at Troy who beat me with a bow, and that was Philoctetes. Beyond him I say I am far the best of everyone alive now who eats bread on this earth — though I would not set myself against the men of former times, not against Heracles, and not against Eurytus of Oechalia, who used to shoot against the immortals themselves, which is why Eurytus did not live to be old; Apollo was angry with him and killed him, because he had challenged him to a shooting match.

"And I can throw a spear further than another man can shoot an arrow. It is only in the footrace that I am afraid one of you might beat me. I have been badly knocked about in a great deal of water, with no steady food on board, and my legs have gone."

Everybody went very quiet. And of all the things this man might have boasted about — he is an eloquent liar with twenty years of material — he chose the bow, which nobody had asked about and on which he was not going to be tested. It is the first time in eight books that a bow has been mentioned. I should keep it, if I were you.

Alcinous stepped in and smoothed the whole thing over, and did it beautifully.

"Stranger, nothing you have said is ungracious. You wanted to show what is in you, because you were angry, and because this man stood up in front of everybody and insulted you. No one who knew how to talk sense would find fault with your quality.

"But listen now, so that you can tell your own heroes about it later, when you are at dinner in your own house with your wife and children and you happen to think of us. We are not perfect boxers, and we are not wrestlers. But we run fast, and we are the best seamen there are. And we love our dinner, and the lyre, and dancing, and clean clothes, and hot baths, and bed.

"Come on then — the best dancers among the Phaeacians. Dance. So that the stranger can tell everyone at home how far we are ahead of the rest of the world at sailing and running and dancing and song. And somebody fetch Demodocus his clear-toned lyre."

He does not scold Euryalus in public, you notice; he accepts the visitor's anger as reasonable, changes the subject, and changes it to the thing his people are honestly best at — telling the truth about what they are not good at while he is about it. There is no shame in him at all.

---

So they cleared a dancing floor and widened the ring, and the boys who were best at it, in the first bloom of youth, struck up and beat out the holy dance with their feet; and Odysseus stood watching the twinkle of the feet, and was amazed.

And the singer struck the lyre and began a song, and it was a rude one.

He sang about Ares (god of war) and Aphrodite (goddess of love): how they first went to bed together in the house of Hephaestus (the lame smith of the gods, and her husband), secretly, and how Ares gave her a great many presents and disgraced the marriage bed.

And the Sun, who sees everything, saw them, and went and told him.

And when Hephaestus heard the story that goes to the heart, he went off to his forge with murder in his mind and put the great anvil on the block, and hammered out chains that could not be broken and could not be got out of, so that the two of them would stay exactly where they were put. And when the trap was made he went to the bedroom where his own bed stood and threw the chains all round the bedposts in a circle, and hung a great many more of them down from the roof beam, fine as spider silk, so fine that not one of the blessed gods could see them. It was very cunning work. And when he had got the whole thing round the bed he pretended to leave for Lemnos, which was his favourite place in the world.

Ares was not keeping a blind watch. He saw the great craftsman go, and came to the house wanting Aphrodite, and found her just back from her father's, and took her hand. "Come to bed, love. Hephaestus is not at home; he has gone off to Lemnos."

And she thought it was a very good idea.

So the two of them went to bed and lay down — and the chains came down round them, and they could not move a limb or lift anything, and then they understood that there was no getting out of it.

And back came the great lame god, having turned round before he ever reached Lemnos, because the Sun had been keeping watch for him. He stood in the doorway of his own house with a savage rage on him and gave a dreadful shout, and called out to all the gods:

"Father Zeus, and the rest of you blessed immortals — come here and look at this. It is a joke, and it is not to be borne. Because I am lame, Aphrodite is always insulting me, and she loves destructive Ares because he is handsome and sound in the legs, and I was born crooked. And nobody is to blame for that but my two parents, who should have thought twice.

"Come and see where those two are sleeping — in my bed — and how it hurts me to watch it. I do not think they will want to lie like that much longer, however much they are in love. But my trap and my chain will hold them until her father gives me back every one of the courtship gifts I paid over for that shameless girl. His daughter is beautiful, and she has no self-control."

And the gods came crowding to the house with the bronze floor. Poseidon (god of the sea) came, and Hermes the runner came, and lord Apollo who works from far off came. The goddesses stayed at home, every one of them, out of modesty.

And the gods stood in the doorway, and unquenchable laughter went up among the blessed gods when they saw the cleverness of it. And one would look at the man next to him and say: "Bad deeds do not prosper. The slow one catches the quick one. Look at Hephaestus — slow as he is, and lame — catching Ares, who is the fastest of all the gods on Olympus. And now he owes the fine for adultery."

And Apollo said to Hermes: "Would you be willing to sleep in bed beside golden Aphrodite, even held down by those heavy chains?"

And Hermes said: "I only wish it, lord Apollo. Let there be three times as many chains, and no way out of them, and let all of you gods look on, and all the goddesses too — I would still sleep beside golden Aphrodite."

And the immortals roared with laughter.

Only Poseidon did not laugh. He kept asking Hephaestus to let Ares go, and in the end offered to stand surety and pay the fine himself if Ares defaulted; and Hephaestus said, well, if Ares runs off owing me, I shall be chaining *you* up instead — and released them. And the moment the chains were off the two of them jumped up and went: Ares straight to Thrace, and Aphrodite to Cyprus, to Paphos, where she has her sanctuary and her fragrant altar; and there the Graces bathed her and rubbed her with the immortal oil that shines on the gods who live forever, and dressed her in beautiful clothes, a wonder to look at.<sup><a href="#book-08-note-3">3</a></sup>

That was the singer's song, and Odysseus enjoyed it as much as anybody.

I hope you enjoyed it too, and I hope you also noticed what the Phaeacians did not, which is that they have just been told the plot. A wife; a husband who finds out; a lie about where he is going; a trap built in secret out of the one thing he is better at than anybody alive; and everybody caught in it at once, in the hall, with the whole household looking on. The only reason it is a comedy is that nobody in it can die. Take the immortality away and it is Agamemnon at his own homecoming dinner with twenty men behind the door — the same story exactly, and human beings stay dead. Which is why this poem can put its funniest scene in the middle of its saddest evening and not think itself frivolous.

---

Then Halius and Laodamas danced on their own, because nobody could match those two; and they took a beautiful purple ball, and one would lean back and throw it up towards the shadowy clouds and the other would spring off the ground and catch it easily before his feet came down. And when they had finished with throwing it straight up they began passing it back and forth, dancing all the while, and the other young men stood round the ring beating time, and a great noise of it went up.

"My lord," said Odysseus, "you said your dancers were the best. There it is, exactly as you said. I am astonished, looking at it."

Alcinous was very pleased, and turned to the Phaeacians. "The stranger seems to me a man of excellent sense. Let us give him a proper guest-gift. Twelve kings rule in this country as leaders, and I am the thirteenth. Let every one of us bring him a clean cloak and a tunic and a talent of gold, and let us bring it all together now, so that the stranger can go in to dinner with the gifts in his hands and a glad heart. And Euryalus is to make it up with him, in words and with a present, because what he said was not decent."

They all agreed, and Euryalus did it, and did it well. He gave him a bronze sword with a silver hilt and a scabbard of new-sawn ivory round it, worth a great deal. "Sir, and father — if anything was said here that was out of order, let the storm winds pick it up and carry it off. And may the gods let you see your wife, and get you home to your own country; you have been away from your friends far too long, and suffering."

"And to you, my friend — good luck, and may the gods give you a good life, and may you never miss this sword you have just given me, having made it right with words." And he slung it over his shoulder.

The sun went down, and the splendid gifts were carried up to the house, and Alcinous told Arete to bring out the best chest there was and put a fresh cloak and tunic in it herself; and he added a beautiful gold cup of his own, so that the stranger would remember him every time he poured a drink for the gods at home. And Arete told her women to set the great cauldron on the fire and heat a bath; and she packed the chest with the clothes and the gold, and said:

"Look at the lid yourself now, and tie it up quickly with a knot of your own — so that nobody robs you on the voyage, while you are lying asleep in the black ship."

And Odysseus heard her, and fitted the lid down at once, and put a cunning knot on it that lady Circe had taught him, long ago.

You have not met her yet. He does not explain. He simply ties the knot, and the poem tells you where he learned it and moves on — and there is a name sitting in the middle of that sentence which means nothing to anybody in the room and everything four books from now.

Then the housekeeper told him to get into the bath, and he was glad to see the warm water, because he had not been looked after like that since he left Calypso's house.

---

And when the women had bathed him and rubbed him with oil and put a fine cloak and tunic on him, he came out and went towards the men who were drinking their wine.

And Nausicaa was standing by the doorpost of the strong-built hall.

She looked at him, and she was amazed, and she said: "Goodbye, stranger. When you are back in your own country, remember me sometimes — because it is to me, first of anybody, that you owe your life."

"Nausicaa, daughter of great-hearted Alcinous — if Zeus grants that I get home and see my day of homecoming, then there, every day of my life, I will pray to you as to a god. Because you gave me my life, girl."

And he went and sat down beside the king.

That is the last we see of her. She does not weep, and she does not ask him to stay, and she asks for the smallest thing she could possibly have asked for, on the strongest grounds there are — which is that he would be dead in the reeds without her.

---

They were carving the meat and mixing the wine, and the herald came up leading Demodocus and set him down among them, propped against a tall pillar. And Odysseus cut a piece off the chine of a white-tusked boar, a rich piece with plenty of fat along both sides, and there was more left on it than he kept for himself; and he called the herald over.

"Give this to Demodocus, so that he can eat it; I want to say something civil to him, sorry as I am. Singers get honour and respect from every man on earth, because the Muse has taught them the paths of song and she loves the whole tribe of them."

And the herald carried it over and put it in the hands of the great man, and he took it and was glad. And when they had eaten, Odysseus said to him:

"Demodocus, I praise you above every mortal man. Either the Muse taught you or Apollo did, because you sing the fate of the Greeks so very rightly — everything they did and suffered and worked through — as if you had been there yourself, or heard it from a man who was.

"So change to another part of it now, and sing about the making of the wooden horse: the one Epeius built with Athena's help, and which Odysseus got up into the citadel by a trick, filled with the men who sacked Troy. If you can tell me that part of it in the right order, I shall say to every man alive that a god was generous to you and gave you divine song."

He asked for it, you notice. Nobody made him. He has spent the whole day pulling a cloak over his head to get through this man's songs, and now he puts down his cup and asks, politely, by name, for the one that is entirely about him.

The singer began, and took it up from where the Greeks burned their huts and went aboard and sailed away, and the men with Odysseus were already sitting inside the horse in the Trojans' own meeting-place, because the Trojans had dragged it up there themselves. And it stood there while they sat round it arguing, and they could not decide, and there were three ways it might have gone: split the hollow wood open with the pitiless bronze; or drag it to the top of the rock and push it over; or leave it standing as a great offering to please the gods. And that was the way it was going to end, because it was laid down that they would be destroyed when their city closed round that great wooden horse with all the best of the Greeks inside it.

And he sang how the sons of the Greeks poured out of the horse and sacked the city; how they went through it, this way and that, wrecking the steep town; and how Odysseus went like Ares to the house of Deiphobus with Menelaus beside him, and dared the most terrible fight of all there, and won it through great-hearted Athena.

That is what the famous singer sang. And Odysseus melted, and the tears ran down his cheeks out of his eyes and wetted them.

And the way a woman cries, falling on the body of her own husband, who has gone down in front of his city and his people trying to hold the day of destruction away from his town and his children; and she sees him dying, gasping for breath, and winds herself round him and shrieks aloud; and behind her men are hitting her back and her shoulders with the butts of their spears, driving her off into slavery, to have hard work and misery, and her cheeks waste with the most pitiful grief —

that is how Odysseus cried, and the tears were pitiful under his eyelids.

---

The poem has just compared him to a woman being dragged away from her husband's body on the night her city fell, and there are women in exactly that position, at Troy, on that specific night, because of the wooden horse. Which he built; and which he has just asked, by name, to hear a song about; and which he is weeping at.

I have read a good many attempts to soften that and I do not believe any of them. It has been coming since Book Three, when Nestor mentioned in passing that Athena turned against her own side over what the Greeks did in that city; the whole homeward voyage is the invoice. And here, at the moment of maximum self-pity, the poem reaches out without a word of comment and hands him the grief of the people he did it to. It does not say he deserves it. It says: this is what that felt like, and now it is what you feel like. And then it goes straight back to the story.

---

Nobody noticed him crying except Alcinous, who was sitting next to him and could hear him. And Alcinous stopped the music.

"Let Demodocus put the lyre down. Not everybody here is enjoying this. Ever since we sat down to dinner and the singer started, our guest has not once stopped grieving; some very heavy sorrow has got into him. Let the singer stop, so that all of us can enjoy ourselves together, hosts and guest alike. Everything we are doing is being done for our honoured visitor: the escort, the gifts, the friendship. Any man with the least sense treats a stranger and a suppliant like a brother.

"So do not go on hiding what I am about to ask you behind some clever evasion. Tell me the name they call you at home — your mother and your father, and the people in your town. Nobody in the world is nameless, good or bad; parents give a name to everyone once they are born.

"And tell me your country and your people and your city, so that the ships can carry you there by thinking about it. Because our ships have no steersmen and no steering oars, the way other ships do. They understand by themselves what men are thinking and what they want; they know every city and every rich field there is, and they cross the open water at enormous speed, wrapped in mist and cloud, and there is never the least fear of damage or of going down.

"Though I did hear my father Nausithous say, once, that Poseidon was angry with us for giving everybody safe passage home. He said that one day a well-built Phaeacian ship, coming back from an escort, would be smashed on the misty sea, and a great mountain would be set down over our city. That is what the old man said. The god may bring it about, or leave it undone, whichever pleases him.<sup><a href="#book-08-note-4">4</a></sup>

"But come — where have you been driven to? What countries did you reach, what people? Were they cruel and wild, with no sense of right, or did they take strangers in, and have they god-fearing minds?

"And tell me why you cry. Why does your heart go, inside you, when you hear about the fate of the Greeks and of Troy? The gods made that. They spun destruction for those men, so that there would be a song in it for people who have not been born yet.

"Did some relation of yours die in front of Troy? A good man — a son-in-law, or a father-in-law? They are the nearest to us after our own blood. Or was it a companion? A man who understood you? Because a companion with an understanding mind is no worse a thing than a brother."

---

## NOTES TO BOOK EIGHT

<a id="book-08-note-1"></a>
1. **The songs we have lost, and what a bard actually was.** Demodocus sings three times in this book, and every one of his songs is a summary of a story that existed and is now gone. The quarrel of Odysseus and Achilles comes from no poem we possess; nor does the wooden horse, which — and this surprises people — does not appear in the *Iliad* at all. That poem ends with Hector's funeral, before the horse, before the fall, before any of it. What survives to us are two poems out of a whole library: there was once a cycle of epics covering the entire war from its causes to the last homecoming, and they were known and quoted and loved, and they have all vanished, leaving titles, summaries, and quotations in other men's books. When Demodocus takes requests he is thumbing through a shelf that no longer exists. — Which also tells you what a working singer was. Not a man who recited one long poem, but a man with an enormous repertoire who could start anywhere in it, at a customer's request, and take it up in the right order. Note too what the Muse gave and took: the blindness and the song arrive together, in the same line, as a single transaction. Later ages built a legend that Homer himself was blind, and this passage is very likely where they got it.

<a id="book-08-note-2"></a>
2. **The Phaeacian athletes' names.** Read them again. Acroneus is roughly Topship; Ocyalus is Swiftsea; Nauteus is Sailor; Prymneus is Sternman; Eretmeus is Oarman; Ponteus is Seaman; Proreus is Prowman; Thoon is Speedy; Anchialus is Seaside; Amphialus is Sea-all-round. Even the king is Alcinous, "strong of mind," his father was Nausithous, "swift with ships," and his daughter Nausicaa has ships in her name as well. An entire nation of sailors is walking about with sailing for a surname, and a Greek audience got the joke instantly and for nothing — which is exactly the sort of pleasure that evaporates in translation. It is the kind of thing an English reader would meet if a village of blacksmiths turned out to be called Forge, Hammer, Smith, Anvil and Sparks.

<a id="book-08-note-3"></a>
3. **The fine for adultery.** There is law in the joke, and the law is the point of the ending. Hephaestus does not want revenge; he wants to be paid. He demands that Aphrodite's father hand back the courtship gifts — the substantial property a suitor transferred to a bride's family to make a marriage — on the grounds that the goods were paid over for a wife who has not behaved like one. And Poseidon settles the matter by standing surety, like a man guaranteeing a neighbour's debt. That is not divine justice; it is property, and a bad debt, and every man listening had seen something of the kind settled in his own village. Which makes the joke sharper than it looks: the gods on Olympus are not living in some other moral universe. They are living in a Greek village with no funerals.

<a id="book-08-note-4"></a>
4. **The prophecy hanging over the Phaeacians.** Alcinous mentions it in passing, in the middle of a boast, and then shrugs — the god may do it or not. It is worth pinning down, because it is the one dark thing in this bright country and it is stated plainly. These people ferry everybody home; it is their national vocation, and their pride, and the reason the gods sit down to dinner with them. And Poseidon resents it, being the god who keeps men *from* getting home, and there is an old warning in the family that the price will eventually be a wrecked ship and a mountain dropped on the harbour. Hold on to it. The poem has not raised it for atmosphere.

---

*Book Nine: In Which the Stranger Gives His Name at Last, and Tells About a Cave.*


<div class="page-break"></div>

<!-- Source: book/odyssey-book-09.md -->

# THE ODYSSEY
### Retold in English, with Explanations

---

## BOOK NINE
### In Which the Stranger Gives His Name at Last, and Tells About a Cave

---

Before he answers, I am going to get out of the way, because for the next four books the story is not mine to tell.

He is about to say his own name aloud for the first time in this poem, and then he is going to keep talking until the end of Book Twelve — the giant, the witch, the singers on the rock, the country of the dead, all of it. It is the most famous stretch of storytelling in Europe, and almost none of it happens where people think it does. It happens in a dining hall on Scheria, after supper, in the mouth of a shipwrecked man describing himself to a king whose ships he needs. There are no witnesses left; every man who sailed with him is dead. His audience are a people who packed up and emigrated because they could not go on living next to the Cyclopes. And there is a ship in the harbour outside that has not sailed yet.

So when the prose says *I* from here on, it is Odysseus and not me. Where a line breaks across the page like the one below, that will be me coming back for a moment, and then going away again.

---

Lord Alcinous, most distinguished of all your people — it is a fine thing to listen to a singer like this one, with a voice like a god's. I do not think there is any better end than this: good cheer through a whole people, and men sitting in rows down a hall listening to a singer, and the tables beside them full of bread and meat, and a steward drawing wine out of the bowl and carrying it round and filling the cups. That seems to me about the most beautiful thing there is.

But your heart has turned to asking me about my miseries, so that I shall cry even harder than I have been. What shall I tell you first, then? What last? The gods have given me a great many.

My name first, so that you know it, and so that if I get out from under the day of my death I shall be your guest-friend afterwards, even though I live a long way off.

I am Odysseus, the son of Laertes. Men know me for every kind of trick, and my fame has gone up to the sky.<sup><a href="#book-09-note-1">1</a></sup>

I live in Ithaca, where you can see for miles. There is a mountain on it, Neriton, with the leaves shaking on it, and it stands out. There are islands round about, close in to each other — Dulichium, and Same, and wooded Zacynthus. Mine lies low, and furthest out in the sea towards the dark; the others lie away towards the dawn and the sun. It is rough country, but it raises good young men, and I have never seen anything sweeter than a man's own land.

Calypso kept me in her hollow cave, a goddess, and she wanted me for her husband. Circe kept me in her house on Aeaea, and she wanted the same. Neither of them ever persuaded my heart. There is nothing sweeter than your own country and your own parents — not if you live in a rich house somewhere else, in a foreign country, away from them.

Very well. I shall tell you about the miserable voyage home that Zeus gave me out of Troy.

---

The wind carried me from Troy to the Cicones, at Ismarus. I sacked the town and killed the men. We took their wives out of it, and a great deal of property, and divided it up so that nobody went short of a fair share.

Then I told my men to run for it, quickly. The fools would not listen. There was a great deal of wine drunk, and they slaughtered a great many sheep on the beach, and cattle with their shambling walk and their bent horns.

And meanwhile the Cicones went and called the other Cicones, their neighbours inland, who were more numerous and better men, and knew how to fight from a chariot and on foot as well. They came at first light, as thick as the leaves and the flowers come in spring, and a bad fate from Zeus stood beside us, and we suffered a great deal. They set the battle up beside the ships and we threw our bronze spears at each other; and all morning, while the sacred day was still growing, we held them off, though there were more of them. But when the sun moved round to the hour when a man unyokes his oxen, then the Cicones broke us, and the Greeks gave way.

Six armed men off each ship were killed. The rest of us got away, and got out from under our death.

---

That is the first adventure, and it is the one most people have never heard of, and I should not like you to go past it. Before there is a single monster in this poem the hero stops at a town on the way home from a war that is already over and takes it — and says so himself, in his opening sentence, with no provocation offered and none expected. *We took their wives out of it and divided them up so that nobody went short.* One book ago the poem compared this man, at length and with no comment whatever, to a woman being beaten away from her husband's body and driven off into slavery. Here is the same sentence from the other side, in his own mouth, at dinner, as background. He is not confessing. It has not occurred to him that there is anything to confess, and that is precisely why it is worth a moment of your time.

The other thing in it is the shape of the disaster, which you will meet again: he told them to go, and they would not, and it cost seventy-two men. Remember the form of words, because he is scrupulous about it, and there is a place further on where he cannot use it.

---

Zeus who gathers the clouds set the North Wind on us, an enormous storm, and covered the land and the sea alike with cloud, and night came rushing down out of the sky. The ships were driven sideways, and the sails torn into three and four pieces by the force of it. We got them down and rowed hard for the shore, and lay there two nights and two days, eating our hearts out with exhaustion and pain.

On the third morning we stepped the masts and hoisted the white sails and sat still, and the wind and the steersmen kept us straight; and I would have got home to my own country without a scratch. But as I was rounding Cape Malea the swell and the current and the North Wind pushed me off and drove me past Cythera.

For nine days after that I was carried over the fish-filled sea by ruinous winds. On the tenth we came ashore in the country of the Lotus-eaters, who eat a flowering food. We went ashore and drew water, and my men had a meal beside the fast ships; and when we had had food and drink I sent some of them off to find out what sort of men lived there and ate the bread of that country — two, and a third as a herald with them.

They went, and fell in with the Lotus-eaters. And the Lotus-eaters did not plan any harm to my men at all. They gave them lotus to taste.

And whoever ate that honey-sweet fruit no longer wanted to bring back a report, or to come back at all. They wanted to stay there among the Lotus-eaters, chewing the lotus, and forget the way home.

I brought them back to the ships crying, and I had to use force. I dragged them under the benches and tied them up, and told the rest of my trusty companions to get aboard the fast ships in a hurry, in case one of them ate the lotus and forgot about going home. They went aboard at once and sat down at the oars and struck the grey water with the blades.

---

From there we sailed on with our hearts full of trouble, and came to the country of the Cyclopes — a violent and lawless people.

They put nothing in with their own hands and they plough nothing. They trust the gods for it, and everything comes up for them unsown and unploughed: wheat, and barley, and vines with great heavy clusters that make wine, and the rain of Zeus swells it all. They have no assemblies for making decisions, and no laws. They live on the tops of the high mountains in hollow caves, and each one lays down the rules for his own wives and children, and none of them takes any notice of the others.<sup><a href="#book-09-note-2">2</a></sup>

There is a wooded island lying across the mouth of their harbour — neither close in nor far out — and it is full of wild goats without number, because no human foot disturbs them there. No hunters go through it, the sort who wear themselves out in the woods going over the tops of the mountains. It is not grazed by flocks and it is not ploughed; it goes unsown and unbroken all its days, empty of men, and it feeds bleating goats.

Because the Cyclopes have no ships with painted cheeks, and there are no shipwrights among them who might build them well-benched vessels to get things done — going across to other men's towns, the way people constantly do go over the sea to one another. Men like that would have made this island a good place to live in.

It is not a bad island at all. It would bear anything in season. There are soft watered meadows along the shore of the grey sea; vines would never fail there; the ploughing is level; they could cut a deep crop off it every summer, because the soil underneath is rich. And there is a harbour where you need no moorings — no anchor stones, no stern cables. You run in and lie there as long as your sailors feel like it and until the wind gets up. And at the head of the harbour bright water runs out from under a cave, and poplars grow round it.

That is where we sailed in. Some god guided us through a black night; there was nothing to see. The fog lay thick round the ships and the moon did not show in the sky, but was shut up in cloud. Not one of us saw that island with his eyes, and we never saw the long waves rolling in to the beach either, until we had run the ships aground. We took down the sails and went out onto the shore of the sea, and slept there, and waited for the bright morning.

---

That, if you will forgive me for pointing at it, is a colonist talking. Water supply, anchorage, soil, level ploughing, two crops off it and vines that would never fail; and nobody living there, and the people across the water with no ships to do anything about it. Read his description of the Cyclopes again and it turns out to be the same passage: no hulls, no shipwrights, no assemblies, no laws, no farming, and every household answering to nobody. That is a checklist, and every item on it is something he has. This poem was made in a century when Greeks were pouring out across the Mediterranean in exactly such ships, looking at exactly such coasts, and finding people on them who did not farm as Greeks farmed — and were therefore not, in the settlers' judgement, really using the place. I shall not tell you what to make of it. I only say that when a man in a story remarks that the natives are savages who have never made anything of a fine piece of land, you are hearing a very old sentence, and it is worth hearing it as one.

---

When the dawn came up we walked round the island and admired it, and the nymphs put the mountain goats up for us so that my men could eat. We got our curved bows out of the ships, and our long boar-spears, and split into three parties and started shooting, and the god gave us a satisfying bag: twelve ships were with me, and nine goats fell to each of them, and for me alone they cut out ten.

So all day until sunset we sat and feasted on meat past counting and sweet wine. The red wine had not run out yet; there was still plenty, because we had all drawn off a great deal in jars when we took the sacred citadel of the Cicones. And we looked across at the country of the Cyclopes, which was very close, and saw smoke, and heard voices, and the noise of sheep and goats. And when the sun went down and the darkness came, we lay down to sleep on the beach.

In the morning I called my men together. "The rest of you stay here, my trusty companions. I am going over with my own ship and my own crew to find out about these people — whether they are violent and wild and unjust, or whether they take strangers in, and have god-fearing minds."

We rowed across, and it was not far, and right at the edge of the land we saw a cave, high up, with laurels round the mouth of it. A great many flocks were penned there for the night, sheep and goats, and round it there was a yard built high with quarried stone and tall pines and oaks with their high crowns. A giant of a man slept in there. He pastured his flocks alone, and a long way off, and he did not go near anybody else; he kept apart, and his mind was lawless. He was a monstrous piece of work — not like a man who eats bread, but like a wooded peak standing up by itself in a range of high mountains, away from the others.

I told the rest of my companions to stay and guard the ship, and I picked out the twelve best of them and went. And I took a goatskin of dark sweet wine with me, which Maron had given me — the son of Euanthes, the priest of Apollo (god of prophecy, and of the bow) who protects Ismarus — because we had protected him and his wife and his child, out of respect, since he lived in the wooded grove of Apollo. He gave me splendid presents: seven talents of well-worked gold, and a mixing bowl of solid silver, and then wine, twelve jars of it, all of it neat, a drink for gods. Not one of the servants in his house knew about that wine, and not one of the maids — only himself and his wife and one housekeeper. And whenever they drank it he would pour one cup of it into twenty measures of water, and a smell would come up off the bowl that was sweet past describing; and it was not a time when anybody wanted to hold back.<sup><a href="#book-09-note-3">3</a></sup>

I filled a big skin with that and took it, and food in a bag as well. Because straight away, in my proud heart, I had a feeling that a man was going to come at us — a great brute, clothed in enormous strength, who knew nothing about justice or law.

---

We got to the cave quickly, and he was not in it; he was out pasturing his fat flocks. So we went in and looked round at everything. There were crates loaded with cheeses, and the pens were crowded with lambs and kids, each lot penned separately: the spring ones in one place, the summer ones in another, and the newborn in a third. And there were vessels swimming with whey, pails and bowls, all well made, and he did his milking into them.

And straight away my men started begging me to take some of the cheeses and go — to come back and drive the kids and the lambs out of the pens to the fast ship and sail off over the salt water.

And I would not listen to them. It would have been very much better if I had. But I wanted to see him, and I wanted to see whether he would give me guest-gifts.

He was not going to turn out delightful to my companions when he appeared.

So we lit a fire and made an offering, and helped ourselves to the cheeses and ate, and sat in the cave waiting until he came back with his flock. He came carrying an enormous weight of dry wood to burn at his supper, and threw it down inside the cave with a crash; and we bolted in terror to the deepest corner of it. He drove his fat flocks into the wide cave — all the ones he milked; the males, the rams and the he-goats, he left outside in the deep yard. Then he lifted a great doorstone and set it in place. It was huge. Two and twenty good four-wheeled wagons could not have shifted it off the ground. That was the size of the rock he put in his doorway.

Then he sat down and milked the ewes and the bleating goats, all of it in order, and put the young under each one. And half the white milk he curdled and gathered up and stored in wicker baskets; and the other half he stood in vessels, so that he could take it and drink it at his supper.

And when he had got through all his work, he lit his fire — and saw us.

"Strangers, who are you? Where do you sail from over the watery ways? Are you here on business, or do you wander about at random, like pirates, who wander about risking their own lives and bringing trouble to other people?"

Our hearts broke in us at that: we were terrified by the deep voice of him and by the size of him. But even so I answered him.

"We are Greeks. We are coming from Troy, and all sorts of winds over the great gulf of the sea have driven us off course — making for home, we came another way, by another road. That is how Zeus wanted it, I suppose. We say we are men of Agamemnon's army, whose fame is the greatest under heaven just now, so great a city did he sack and so many people did he destroy.

"And we have come to your knees, hoping you will give us a guest's welcome, or make us some other present, which is the right of strangers. Respect the gods, sir. We are your suppliants. Zeus is the avenger of suppliants and strangers — Zeus of the Strangers, who walks in beside honourable travellers."

And he answered me straight out of a pitiless heart.

"You are a fool, stranger, or you have come a very long way, telling me to be afraid of the gods and keep clear of them. The Cyclopes do not care about Zeus who holds the storm cloud, or about any of the blessed gods, because we are a great deal stronger than they are. I would not spare you or your companions to avoid making an enemy of Zeus. Not unless my own heart told me to.

"But tell me — where did you leave your ship when you came? Somewhere far along the coast, or close by? I should like to know."

He was testing me. He did not get anywhere; I know too much. And I answered him with a crooked answer. "Poseidon (god of the sea) smashed my ship. He drove it against the rocks at the edge of your country and brought it up against a headland, and the wind carried it in off the sea. I got out from under a sheer destruction, with these men here."

He did not answer me a word. He sprang up and put his hands on my companions, and grabbed two of them together and knocked them against the ground like puppies, and their brains ran out and wetted the earth. He cut them up limb from limb and made his supper of them. He ate like a lion bred in the mountains, and left nothing: the guts, the flesh, the bones with the marrow in them.

We cried, and lifted our hands up to Zeus, watching this appalling thing done, and there was nothing we could do; helplessness held our hearts.

And when the Cyclops had filled his enormous belly with human meat and milk drunk neat on top of it, he lay down inside the cave, stretched out among his sheep. And I made a plan in my great heart to go up close to him and draw my sharp sword off my thigh and stab him in the chest, where the midriff holds the liver, feeling for the place with my hand. And another thought held me back. We would have died there too, and died on the spot, because there was no way our hands could have pushed that enormous stone off the high doorway.

So we waited, groaning, for the bright morning.

---

When Dawn came up he lit his fire and milked his fine flocks, all of it in order, and put the young under each one; and when he had got through all his work he grabbed two more of my men and made his meal. And when he had eaten he drove his fat flocks out of the cave, lifting the great doorstone easily — and then he put it back, the way a man puts the lid back on a quiver. And with a great deal of whistling he turned his flocks up towards the mountain, and left me there, working out how to do him harm.

And this is the plan that seemed best to my heart.

There was a great club of the Cyclops's lying beside a pen: green olive wood, which he had cut so that he could carry it when it had dried out. Looking at it, we thought it about the size of the mast of a black ship, a twenty-oared merchantman, broad in the beam, that crosses the great gulf of the sea. That was its length, and that was its thickness. I stood over it and cut a fathom's length off it and handed it to my companions and told them to smooth it down. They made it even, and I stood over it and sharpened the end, and then took it and hardened it in the blazing fire. And I hid it carefully under the dung, of which there was a great deal spread about the cave.

And I told the others to draw lots, to see which of them would have to take the risk with me — to lift that stake and grind it into his eye when sweet sleep came over him. And the lot fell on the four I would have picked myself, and I counted as the fifth with them.

He came back in the evening with his fine-fleeced flock, and this time he drove all of them into the wide cave and left nothing in the deep yard outside. Either he had begun to suspect something, or a god told him to. Then he lifted the great doorstone and set it in place, and sat down and milked, all of it in order, and put the young under each one. And when he had got through all his work he grabbed two more men and made his supper.

And then I stood close to him with an ivy-wood bowl of the dark wine in my hands.

"Cyclops — here. Have some wine, now you have eaten human meat, so that you know what sort of drink our ship was carrying. I was bringing it to you as an offering, in case you might pity me and send me home. But you are past all bearing. You cruel thing — how is any man in the world ever going to come to you after this? You have not behaved rightly."

He took it and drank it, and he was terribly pleased with the sweet drink, and asked for another. "Give me more, generously, and tell me your name — now, at once — so that I can give you a guest-gift, one you will be glad to have. The grain-giving earth grows wine of great clusters for the Cyclopes too, and the rain of Zeus swells it. But this is a runnel of ambrosia and nectar."

So I handed him the flaming wine again. Three times I brought it and gave it to him, and three times he drank it down, the fool. And when the wine had got round the Cyclops's wits, I spoke to him with honeyed words.

"Cyclops, you asked me my famous name. I shall tell you. And you give me the guest-gift you promised me.

"Nobody is my name. Nobody is what they call me — my mother, and my father, and all my companions."

And he answered me out of a pitiless heart. "Nobody I shall eat last, after all his companions. The others first. That is your guest-gift."<sup><a href="#book-09-note-4">4</a></sup>

---

He went over backwards and lay with his thick neck bent to one side, and sleep that beats everything took hold of him; and the wine came up out of his throat with gobbets of human flesh in it, and he vomited in his drunken sleep.

And I drove the stake in under the deep ashes until it should get hot, and talked to all my men and put heart into them, so that nobody would lose his nerve and back out. And when the olive stake was on the point of catching fire, green as it was, and was glowing terribly, I brought it up out of the fire; and my companions stood round me, and some god breathed a great courage into us.

They took the olive stake, sharp at the end, and drove it into his eye. And I leaned on it from above and spun it.

The way a man bores a ship's timber with an auger, and the men below him keep it turning with a strap, holding the two ends, and it runs round and round and does not stop: that is how we held the fire-pointed stake in his eye and spun it, and the blood ran out round the hot thing. The flame singed his eyelids and his brow all round as the eyeball burned, and the roots of it crackled in the fire.

The way a smith plunges a great axe or an adze into cold water to temper it, and it screams aloud — because that is what gives iron its strength — so his eye hissed round the olive stake.

He screamed horribly and the rock rang with it, and we bolted away in terror. And he pulled the stake out of his eye, thick with blood, and threw it away from him, raving; and he shouted aloud to the Cyclopes who lived round about in caves on the windy heights.

They heard him and came from all directions and stood round the cave and asked him what was the matter. "What is wrong with you, Polyphemus? Why are you shouting like this through the immortal night and keeping us all awake? No mortal man is driving your flocks off against your will, surely? Nobody is killing you, surely, by force or by trickery?"

And out of the cave the mighty Polyphemus answered them: "My friends — Nobody is killing me. By trickery. Not by force."

And they answered him with words that went straight out of them and away. "Well, if nobody is doing you violence, and you are on your own, there is no escaping a sickness that comes from great Zeus. Say a prayer to your father, the lord Poseidon."

And off they went. And my own heart laughed inside me, that my name and my faultless scheme had taken them all in.

---

The Cyclops, groaning and in agony, felt about with his hands and took the stone away from the doorway, and sat down in the entrance himself with his arms spread wide, to catch anybody who tried to go out among the sheep. That is evidently how much of a fool he thought I was.

And I was planning how it might turn out best — how I might find some way out of death for my companions and for myself. I wove every kind of trick and scheme, as a man does when his life is at stake, because a great evil was very near.

And this is the plan that seemed best. There were rams there, well fed, thick in the fleece, big handsome animals with wool as dark as violets. I bound these together, silently, with the twisted withies the monster used to sleep on: three at a time, and the middle one of each three carried a man, and the two on the outside walked alongside and covered him. Three sheep to each man. And for myself there was a ram, far the best of the whole flock. I got hold of him by the back and curled myself up under his shaggy belly and lay there, and gripped that marvellous fleece with my hands, twisted into it, and held on with a steady heart.

And so, groaning, we waited for the bright morning.

When Dawn came up the males rushed out to pasture, and the females bleated round the pens unmilked, because their udders were bursting. And their master, worn out with the pain of it, felt along the backs of all the sheep as they stood up in front of him — and never noticed, the fool, that my men were tied underneath the chests of the woolly animals.

The last of the whole flock to go out was the ram, weighed down with his own fleece and with me, and I was thinking hard. And the mighty Polyphemus felt him and said:

"Ram, my old friend. Why are you going out of the cave last of the flock, like this? You have never before been left behind by the sheep. You were always far the first to graze the tender bloom of the grass, striding out; the first to reach the running rivers; and the first to want to come home to the fold in the evening. And now you are the last of them all.

"You must be grieving for your master's eye. A bad man blinded it, with his wretched companions, after breaking my wits down with wine. Nobody. And I do not say he has got out from under his death yet.

"If only you could feel with me, and had speech, and could tell me where he is dodging about away from my anger. Then his brains would be knocked out all over the floor of this cave, and my heart would get some relief from the trouble that worthless Nobody has brought on me."

And he let the ram go out through the door.

And when we had got a little way from the cave and the yard, I got out from under the ram first, and then untied my companions. And quickly, keeping turning to look behind us, we drove those long-striding animals, rich with fat, down to the ship. And our companions were very glad to see us, the men who had got away from death — and they started to cry for the others. But I would not let them cry. I stopped each man with my eyebrows, and told them to throw all that fine-fleeced stock aboard at speed and sail out on the salt water. They went aboard at once and sat down at the oars and struck the grey water with the blades.

---

And when I was as far off as a man's shout will carry, I called back to the Cyclops, jeering at him.

"Cyclops. So it was not some weakling's companions you were going to eat by main force in your hollow cave. Your own foul deeds were bound to come down on your own head, you brute — you did not shrink from eating guests in your own house. So Zeus has paid you, and the other gods with him."

That made him angrier still. He broke the top off a great hill and threw it, and it landed in front of the dark-prowed ship, and the sea heaved up under the stone, and the backwash off the deep water carried the ship in and drove it towards the land. I got hold of a long pole and shoved us off, and gave my men the nod to throw themselves on the oars; and they bent to it and rowed.

And when we were twice as far out as before, I started calling to the Cyclops again — and my men were all round me trying to stop me, one after another, with soft words. "You reckless man. Why do you want to provoke a wild creature like that? He threw something into the sea just now that drove the ship back to land, and we thought we were finished. If he hears one of us make a sound, he will smash our heads and the ship's timbers together with a jagged lump of rock, that is how far he throws."

They said that, and they did not persuade my great heart. I called out to him again with my anger up.

"Cyclops. If any mortal man ever asks you about the shameful blinding of your eye, tell him this: that Odysseus blinded it, the sacker of cities, the son of Laertes, whose home is in Ithaca."

---

That is the most expensive sentence anybody speaks in this poem.

Everything up to it has been faultless. The false name worked so well that the neighbours went home; the men came out under the bellies of the sheep; he is at sea, out of reach, with the wine and the cheeses and the flocks aboard, having beaten something forty times his size by pure invention and lost nobody in the escape. And then he turns round and hands the creature his name, his father's name and his address, with his own crew hanging off his arms begging him not to.

He is never stupid, and he is not being stupid here. He is doing something the Greeks understood far better than we do and had no word of reproach for: he is claiming the deed, because a story with nobody's name on it is not a story, and because a man who has spent his life being famous cannot bear to have been Nobody at the one moment it counted. In the older poem men die on purpose to have their names said afterwards; that is the whole economy of the thing, and every person in that Phaeacian hall grew up inside it. This poem, being the sequel, shows you the bill. He is ten years from home, and every man on those twelve ships is going to die, and it begins here, with a shout across the water that nobody asked him to make — and he tells the story himself, at dinner, to a king, and does not leave the bit out.

---

He groaned, and answered.

"So the old prophecies have come home. There was a prophet here, a good man and a tall one, Telemus the son of Eurymus, who was outstanding at prophecy and grew old among the Cyclopes as their prophet. He told me all of this would happen in time — that I would lose my sight at the hands of Odysseus.

"But I was always expecting a big handsome man to turn up here, with enormous strength in him. And now a little one, a nothing, a weakling, has put my eye out, after knocking me down with wine.

"Come here, Odysseus, and let me give you guest-gifts, and let me urge the famous Earthshaker (Poseidon) to send you on your way. I am his son, and he says he is my father. And he will cure me, if he chooses to, and nobody else will — none of the blessed gods and no mortal man."

"I only wish I could take the life and the soul out of you as surely as I know the Earthshaker will never cure that eye."

And then he prayed to the lord Poseidon, stretching his hands up towards the starry sky.

"Hear me, Poseidon, holder of the earth, with the dark hair. If I am really yours, and you say you are my father, then grant that Odysseus, the sacker of cities, the son of Laertes, whose home is in Ithaca, may never reach his home.

"And if it is laid down that he is to see his own people and come to his well-built house and his own country — then let him come late, and in a bad way, having lost all his companions, in someone else's ship. And let him find trouble in his house."

That was his prayer, and the god with the dark hair heard him.<sup><a href="#book-09-note-5">5</a></sup>

And then the Cyclops picked up a much bigger stone and swung it and threw it with immeasurable force, and it fell just behind the dark-prowed ship, and only just missed the end of the steering oar. The sea heaved up under the stone, and the wave carried the ship forward and drove it on to the far shore.

---

We came back to the island where the rest of the ships were lying together, and our companions were sitting round them crying, waiting for us and expecting the worst. We ran her ashore and stepped out onto the beach, and got the Cyclops's flocks out of the hollow ship, and divided them up so that nobody went short of a fair share. But the ram — my well-greaved companions gave that to me alone, over and above the division, when the flocks were shared out.

And I sacrificed it on the beach to Zeus of the dark clouds, the son of Cronos, who rules over everybody, and burned the thigh pieces.

And he took no notice at all of my sacrifice. He was thinking about how every one of my well-benched ships and every one of my trusty companions might be destroyed.

So all that day until sunset we sat and feasted on meat past counting and sweet wine. And when the sun went down and the darkness came, we lay down and slept on the shore of the sea. And when the rosy-fingered Dawn came up I roused my companions and told them to get aboard and cast off the cables. They went aboard at once and sat down at the oars and struck the grey water with the blades.

And from there we sailed on, glad to be out from under our death, and grieving in our hearts for the dear companions we had lost.

---

## NOTES TO BOOK NINE

<a id="book-09-note-1"></a>
1. **The name he finally gives.** Greek names carried their meanings on the surface, the way English surnames do — Baker, Smith, Fletcher — and everybody heard them. This one is built on a verb meaning to hate, to be furious with, to cause pain, and it runs in both directions at once: the man who is hated, and the man who deals out trouble. The Man of Wrath, roughly, or the Man Others Have It In For. It is not a compliment and was never meant as one, and there is a story about how he came by it which the poem is keeping until much later. — Which makes his self-introduction worth reading twice. He gives his name, and his father's, and then in the same breath tells a room full of strangers how famous it is. Eight books of anonymity, and the first thing he does with the name is polish it.

<a id="book-09-note-2"></a>
2. **What "lawless" means here.** The Greek word is *themis* and its plural: not statutes, but the settled customs by which decisions get made and quarrels judged — what is done, what is not done, and who says so. The Cyclopes have none, and it is worth setting out the poem's indictment in full, because it amounts to a definition of civilisation by its absence: no assemblies where matters are decided in common; no customary law; no agriculture; no ships; no shipwrights; no traffic with other communities; and each male laying down the law inside his own cave and taking no interest whatever in anyone else's. — Notice what is *not* on that list. Nobody says they are stupid, and nobody says they eat people; Polyphemus turns out to eat people, but that is his own contribution, and the charge against his whole nation is that they do not farm, do not sail, and do not hold meetings. To this poem a household that answers to nobody is not free. It is the definition of a monster.

<a id="book-09-note-3"></a>
3. **Maron's wine, and how the Greeks drank.** One cup to twenty of water, and still so strong that nobody could stop — an extreme ratio, quoted precisely to tell you this is no ordinary wine; the ordinary run was something nearer one to three or four. But the important thing for a modern reader is the practice itself. Greeks watered their wine as a matter of course, always, and the mixing bowl standing in the middle of every hall in this poem is there for exactly that purpose. Drinking it neat was what foreigners did, and barbarians, and men who came to a bad end. So when the Cyclops takes the bowl three times and swallows it undiluted, a Greek audience did not need to be told he was making a mistake; they had just watched him do something no civilised person at that dinner would have done.

<a id="book-09-note-4"></a>
4. **"Nobody."** The most famous pun in European literature, and it does not survive the crossing into English, so here is what is actually happening. The name he gives is *Outis*, which is simply the Greek for "no one" — which is why the neighbours outside the cave go away again: they ask whether somebody is killing him, he shouts back the word for nobody, and they take it as an answer rather than as a name. That much comes across in translation. — What does not come across is the second turn of the screw. When those neighbours frame their question, the Greek idiom requires a different form of the negative, and the phrase that comes out — *mē tis*, "if nobody" — is indistinguishable in sound from *mētis*, the ordinary word for cunning, the practical intelligence that finds a way out. It is Odysseus's own defining quality, and the poem uses it of him constantly. So the Cyclopes stand outside the cave and unknowingly announce the exact truth: *cunning is killing you*. And a few lines later Odysseus tells us his heart laughed at how his name and his faultless scheme had taken them in — using, of course, the same word. It is a triple joke, set up and paid off across forty lines, and airtight in Greek. I can explain it to you. Nobody can translate it.

<a id="book-09-note-5"></a>
5. **The curse, which is also the synopsis.** Count the terms of that prayer. Let him not get home at all — and if he must, then let him come *late*; let him come *in a bad way*; let him have *lost every one of his companions*; let him arrive *in a ship belonging to somebody else*; and let him *find trouble in his house*. Every one of those comes true exactly, including the ship, which is at this moment tied up in the harbour outside the hall where he is telling the story. The whole remaining shape of the poem sits in a blind man's prayer on a beach, and the man it was aimed at is reciting it aloud, from memory, to the people whose ship will fulfil the fourth clause. This is characteristic: the poem tells you what is going to happen with striking regularity, and it costs nothing, because knowing the destination has never yet spoiled the road.

---

*Book Ten: In Which There Is a Bag of Wind, a Good Deal of Bad Luck with Doors, and a Woman with a Wand.*


<div class="page-break"></div>

<!-- Source: book/odyssey-book-10.md -->

# THE ODYSSEY
### Retold in English, with Explanations

---

## BOOK TEN
### In Which There Is a Bag of Wind, a Good Deal of Bad Luck with Doors, and a Woman with a Wand

---

We are still in the hall on Scheria, after supper, and the cups are still going round. Twelve ships came out of Troy under his command, and one of them has been emptied in a cave. In this book he loses the other eleven, and I mention it now because the poem is not going to give you time to notice.

---

We came to the island of Aeolia, where Aeolus lives, the son of Hippotas, whom the immortal gods love. It is a floating island, and there is a wall of unbreakable bronze running all the way round it, and the rock goes up sheer.

He has twelve children in his palace: six daughters and six sons in the prime of their youth. And he gave the daughters to the sons as their wives. They eat, always, beside their own father and their good mother, with an endless supply of good things in front of them; and by day the house is full of the smell of cooking and echoes with the sound of the flutes in the courtyard; and at night they sleep beside their honourable wives on blankets and corded bedsteads.<sup><a href="#book-10-note-1">1</a></sup>

We came to their city and their fine house, and he gave me a month of hospitality and asked me about everything — about Troy, and the ships of the Greeks, and the way the Greeks came home. And I told him the whole of it, in the right order.

And when I asked him for my road, he did not refuse me anything, and he got the escort ready. He gave me a bag made out of the hide of a nine-year-old ox, flayed whole, and in it he had tied up the courses of all the boisterous winds — because Zeus had made him the steward of the winds, to stop any of them or start any of them, whichever he liked. And he lashed the bag down in the hollow ship with a shining silver cord, so that not the smallest breath could get out of it. And then he sent me the West Wind to blow, to carry the ships and the men along.

He was not going to bring it off. We were destroyed by our own stupidity.

Nine days we sailed, night and day alike. And on the tenth our own fields came up over the water — and we were near enough to see men tending their fires.

And then sweet sleep came over me, because I was exhausted. I had been handling the sheet myself the whole way and never given it to anybody else, so that we would get home faster.

And my companions started talking to each other. They had decided I was carrying gold and silver home from Aeolus, and this is the sort of thing they said, looking at one another:

*It is extraordinary how this man is loved and honoured by everybody, whatever city and country he comes to. He is bringing home a great deal of fine plunder out of Troy, and we — who have made exactly the same journey — are going home with empty hands. And now Aeolus has given him all this out of friendship. Come on, let us have a quick look and see what it is, and how much gold and silver is in that bag.*

And that was the plan that won, and they untied the bag, and all the winds burst out. The storm snatched them up straight away and carried them out to sea, crying, away from their own country.

And I woke up, and turned it over in my faultless heart — whether to go over the side and die in the water, or to endure it in silence and stay among the living. I endured it, and stayed, and covered my head and lay down in the ship. And they were carried back to the island of Aeolia by that evil blast, and my companions were groaning.

---

Everybody remembers that as the crew being greedy and stupid, so it is worth looking at what they actually say to each other. Not *let us steal it*: rather, *we did the same ten years he did, and he is going home rich and we are going home with nothing* — and then, how much is in there? They think it is treasure because a king who entertained them for a month has given their captain a large heavy sealed sack, lashed down with silver cord, and in nine days and nine nights nobody has told them what is in it; and because he has not let another man touch the steering sheet in all that time, which is either magnificent seamanship or a commander who does not trust his crew, and looks identical from the rowing bench.

He never told them. That is the whole of it, and you can hear it in what is missing: nowhere does he say *I explained what Aeolus had given me and warned them*. At the Cicones his defence was precise and he repeated it — I told them to run; they would not listen. He is scrupulous about that formula, and here he cannot use it. What went wrong on that ship went wrong before anybody touched the cord.

---

We went ashore and drew water, and my companions had a meal beside the fast ships.
