And when we had had food and drink I took a herald and one companion and went up to the famous house of Aeolus, and found him at dinner with his wife and his children. We came in and sat down on the threshold beside the doorposts, and they were astonished.

*How did you get here, Odysseus? What evil spirit has been at you? We sent you off with great care, so that you would reach your own country and your house and anything else you love.*

And I answered them with a sick heart. *My wretched companions ruined me — and a cruel sleep along with them. Put it right, my friends. You have the power.*

That is what I said, speaking gently. And they went dead silent. And their father answered:

*Get off this island. Now. You are the most contemptible thing alive. It is against all right for me to help a man on his way when the blessed gods hate him. Get out. You have come here hated by the immortals.*

And he drove me out of the house, and I was groaning heavily.

We sailed on from there with our hearts full of trouble, and the men's spirits were worn down by the hard rowing, because of our own foolishness; and there was no sign of a passage anywhere. Six days we sailed, night and day alike. And on the seventh we came to the steep citadel of Lamus — to Telepylus of the Laestrygonians, where one herdsman calls to another as he drives his flock in, and the other answers him as he drives his out. There a man who never slept could earn double wages: one lot for herding cattle, and another for pasturing white sheep. The paths of the night and of the day are close together there.<sup><a href="#book-10-note-2">2</a></sup>

We came into a splendid harbour, with a sheer cliff running unbroken along both sides of it, and two headlands jutting out opposite each other at the mouth, and the entrance is narrow. And every one of the other captains steered his curved ship inside, and they moored them close together in the hollow of the harbour — because there is never a swell in there, great or small, but a bright calm all round.

I alone kept my black ship outside. I moored her at the very edge, with the cables made fast to a rock.

Then I climbed a rugged lookout and stood there. There was no sign of work — no oxen, no men — nothing but smoke going up off the land. So I sent men to go and find out what sort of people ate the bread of that country: two of them, and a herald as a third.

They went ashore and followed a smooth road, the one the wagons use to bring wood down from the mountains to the town. And in front of the town they met a girl drawing water, the strong daughter of Antiphates the Laestrygonian, who had come down to the clear-running spring. They went up and asked her who was king of these people, and she pointed out her father's high-roofed house at once.

They went in and found his wife inside — as big as a mountain top — and they loathed the sight of her. And she called Antiphates in from the meeting-place, who set about arranging a miserable death for them. He grabbed one of my men on the spot and made his meal of him. The other two bolted and got back to the ships.

And he raised the cry through the town, and the powerful Laestrygonians heard it and came from every direction, thousands of them, and they were not like men at all but like giants. And they threw rocks down at us off the cliffs, boulders a man could barely lift. And an appalling noise went up out of the ships: men dying and timbers being smashed at the same time. And they speared them like fish and carried them home for a disgusting supper.

And while they were killing the men inside the deep harbour, I drew the sharp sword off my thigh and cut through the cables of my dark-prowed ship, and shouted to my own crew to fall on the oars if they wanted to get out of it. And every man of them threw the water up in terror of dying. And my ship got out past the beetling cliffs into the open sea, and was glad of it.

The rest went down there together.

---

Five hundred and forty men, give or take, and eleven ships, gone in about a page. Nobody is named; there is no last stand and no dying speech; and every one of those men had come through ten years at Troy and had somebody at home counting. They die at a pretty anchorage without a fight, and the one man who lives does so because his ship was tied to a rock outside a harbour that every other captain in the fleet had sensibly gone into. Whether that was caution or luck he does not say, and I notice he does not explain it either.

---

We sailed on, glad to be out from under our death, and grieving for the dear companions we had lost. And we came to the island of Aeaea, where Circe lives — the goddess with the braided hair, terrible, who speaks like a human being, the full sister of the deadly-minded Aeetes. Both of them were born of Helios who gives light to men, and of Perse their mother, the daughter of Ocean.

We brought the ship into a harbour that will hold a ship, and some god guided us; and there we lay for two days and two nights, eating our hearts out with weariness and pain. On the third morning I took my spear and my sharp sword and went up quickly from the ship to a place with a view, hoping to see some work of men's hands and hear a voice. And I saw smoke coming up off the wide-wayed earth, through the thick brush and the woods, from the house of Circe.

And I thought about going down to look into it; and what seemed best, thinking it over, was to go back to the fast ship and give my men a meal, and then send some of them to find out. And on the way, when I was close to the ship, one of the gods took pity on me, alone as I was, and sent a great stag with tall antlers right across my path, going down to the river out of his woodland pasture to drink, because the heat of the sun was on him.

I hit him in the middle of the back as he came out, and the bronze spear went straight through, and he dropped in the dust screaming, and the life went out of him. I put my foot on him and pulled the spear out; and then I picked willow shoots and twisted a rope of them, a fathom long, and bound the feet of that great animal together, and slung him round my neck and carried him down to the black ship, leaning on my spear — because there was no possibility of carrying him on one shoulder with one hand; he was a very big beast.

And I threw him down in front of the ship and roused my men, going up to each one and speaking to him gently. *Friends. We are not going down into the house of Hades before our day comes, whatever grief we are in. Come on: while there is still food and drink in the fast ship, let us remember to eat, and not waste away with hunger.*

They did as I said at once. They uncovered their heads on the shore of the barren sea and stared at the stag, because he was a very big beast; and when they had had their fill of looking at him they washed their hands and got a magnificent dinner ready. So all that day until sunset we sat and feasted on meat past counting and sweet wine; and when the sun went down and the darkness came, we lay down to sleep on the shore of the sea.

---

When Dawn came up I called them all together.

*Listen to me, my companions, for all the bad things you have suffered. My friends, we do not know where the darkness is and we do not know where the dawn is; we do not know where the sun that shines on men goes down under the earth, or where he comes up. So let us think quickly whether there is any plan left. I do not believe there is. I climbed a rugged lookout and I saw that this is an island, and the endless sea has it in a crown, and it lies low. And in the middle of it, with my own eyes, I saw smoke, through the thick brush and the woods.*

And their spirits broke in them, because they remembered what Antiphates the Laestrygonian had done, and the violence of the great-hearted man-eating Cyclops. They cried aloud and let the big tears fall. And no good came of their crying.

So I counted off my well-greaved companions into two parties and appointed a leader for each. I led one; godlike Eurylochus led the other. And we shook the lots quickly in a bronze helmet, and the lot of great-hearted Eurylochus jumped out. So he went, and twenty-two companions with him, crying. And they left us behind, crying too.

In the glades they found the house of Circe, built of polished stone in a place with a view all round it. And there were mountain wolves round it, and lions, which she had bewitched herself by giving them evil drugs. They did not attack my men. They stood up on their hind legs and fawned on them, wagging their long tails — the way dogs fawn round their master when he comes back from dinner, because he always brings them something. That is how the wolves with their strong claws and the lions fawned round my men. And my men were terrified, looking at those dreadful animals.

They stood in the gateway of the goddess with the beautiful hair, and they could hear Circe inside, singing in a lovely voice, going up and down in front of a great web, imperishable, the kind of work goddesses do: fine and lovely and full of light.

And Polites spoke first, a leader of men, the dearest and steadiest of all my companions. *Friends. There is somebody inside, going up and down in front of a great web and singing beautifully; the whole floor rings with it. Some goddess, or some woman. Let us call out to her at once.*

So they called, and she came out and opened the shining doors and asked them in. And they all followed her inside, in their innocence. Eurylochus alone stayed behind; he suspected it was a trap.

She brought them in and sat them down on chairs and benches, and mixed them cheese and barley meal and yellow honey into Pramnian wine — and into the food she stirred ruinous drugs, so that they would completely forget their own country. And when she had given it to them and they had drunk it off, she struck them with her wand at once and penned them in the pigsties.

And they had the heads and the voices and the bristles and the bodies of pigs. But their minds were the same as before, exactly.

So there they were, shut in, and crying; and Circe threw down acorns and beech mast and cornel berries for them to eat, the things that pigs lying in the mud always eat.

---

Eurylochus came straight back to the fast black ship to tell us about our companions and the miserable fate they had met. He could not get a single word out, however much he wanted to; his heart was struck through with a terrible grief and his eyes were full of tears. And when we had all questioned him in amazement, at last he told us what had happened.

And I slung my silver-studded sword over my shoulder, the great bronze one, and my bow, and told him to lead me back by the same road. And he took hold of my knees with both hands and begged me. *Do not take me back there against my will. Leave me here. I know you will never come back yourself, and you will not bring any of the others either. Let us get out of here quickly with the men we have got. We may still escape the evil day.*

*Eurylochus, you stay here then. Stay in this place and eat and drink beside the hollow black ship. I am going. A hard necessity is on me.*

So I went up from the ship and the sea. And when I was going through the sacred glades and was about to reach the great house of Circe, Hermes of the golden wand met me on my way, looking like a young man with the first down on his lip, at the age when youth is at its most charming. And he took my hand and said my name.

*Where are you off to now, you unlucky man, going alone over the hills, and you do not know the country? Your companions are penned in Circe's house, in close-fitting sties, like pigs. Have you come to set them free? I do not think you will get away yourself either. You will stay where the others are.*

*But listen. I will get you out of it. Take this good herb and go to Circe's house, and it will keep the evil day off your head. And I will tell you all of Circe's deadly tricks. She will mix you a drink and put drugs into the food. And even so she will not be able to bewitch you, because the good herb I am giving you will not let her.*

*And when Circe strikes you with her long wand, then draw the sharp sword off your thigh and go at her as though you meant to kill her. And she will be terrified, and she will tell you to go to bed with her. And do not refuse the bed of a goddess then — not if you want her to release your companions and look after you. But make her swear the great oath of the blessed gods first: that she will not plot any new harm against you, so that she does not make you a weakling and unman you when she has you stripped.*

And the slayer of Argus (Hermes) gave me the herb, pulling it out of the ground, and showed me what it was like. Its root was black and its flower was as white as milk. *Moly*, the gods call it. It is hard for mortal men to dig, but the gods can do anything.<sup><a href="#book-10-note-3">3</a></sup>

Then Hermes went away to high Olympus, and I went on to Circe's house, and my heart was very dark as I went.

---

I stood in her gateway and called; and she came out at once and opened the shining doors and asked me in. And I followed her, sick at heart. She sat me down on a silver-studded chair, beautifully made, with a footstool under my feet, and mixed me a drink in a golden cup, and put a drug into it, with murder in her mind.

And when she had given it to me and I had drunk it off — and it did not bewitch me — she struck me with her wand. *Now go to the sty and lie down with the rest of your friends.*

And I drew the sharp sword off my thigh and went at her as though I meant to kill her. And she gave a great cry and ran in under the blade and got hold of my knees, and her words came out fast.

*Who are you? Where do you come from? Where is your city, and where are your parents? I am amazed that you drank these drugs and were not bewitched. No other man alive has ever withstood this drug once it has gone past the barrier of his teeth. But there is a mind in you that cannot be got round.*

*You must be Odysseus. You must be. The man of many turns, whom the god of the golden wand always told me would come here, on his way back from Troy in a fast black ship. Come — put the sword back in its sheath. Let the two of us go to bed together, so that we may lie down and make love and trust each other.*

*Circe. How can you tell me to be gentle with you? You have turned my companions into pigs in your own house, and now you have got me here and you are plotting something, and you tell me to go into your room and up into your bed — so that when you have me stripped you can make me a weakling and unman me. I am not going up into your bed unless you can bring yourself, goddess, to swear me a great oath that you are not planning any new harm against me.*

And she swore it at once, the way I told her to. And when she had sworn it and got through the whole of the oath, I went up into Circe's beautiful bed.<sup><a href="#book-10-note-4">4</a></sup>

---

I said in Book Five that this man does not believe good news and that it would keep him alive; and there it is again, word for word, from a different mouth in a different house. But something else happens here that happens nowhere else in the poem, and I should like it on the record before we go on: he does not solve this one. Every other trap in these four books he gets out of with his own head — the false name, the sheep, the stake in the fire, the rock at the harbour mouth. Here a god walks up to him on a garden path and hands him the antidote, the tactics and the script, and he does exactly as he is told, and it works exactly as he was told it would.

---

While I was in her bed, four handmaids were working in the house — the ones who keep house for her, born of the springs and the groves and the sacred rivers that run down to the sea. One threw beautiful purple covers over the chairs with linen underneath; one drew silver tables up in front of the chairs and set golden baskets on them; the third mixed honey-sweet wine in a silver bowl and set out gold cups; and the fourth brought water and lit a great fire under a big cauldron.

And when the water boiled in the bright bronze she sat me in a bath and washed me, mixing it warm to my liking, and poured it over my head and my shoulders until she had taken the weariness that eats a man's spirit out of my limbs. And when she had washed me and rubbed me with rich oil and put a fine cloak and tunic on me, she led me in and sat me down on a silver-studded chair with a footstool.

And a maid brought water in a gold jug and poured it over a silver basin for me to wash my hands, and drew a polished table up beside me; and the housekeeper brought bread and a great many good things, giving freely of what she had. And she told me to eat.

And I did not want it. I sat there with my mind on other things, and my heart saw trouble coming.

And when Circe saw me sitting like that, not putting my hands out to the food, she came and stood beside me. *Why are you sitting there like a man who has lost his tongue, eating your own heart, and not touching food or drink? Do you suspect some other trick? There is no need. I have already sworn you a powerful oath.*

*Circe — what man with any decency in him could bring himself to taste food or drink before he had got his companions free and seen them with his own eyes? If you really mean it kindly, then let them go.*

So Circe went out through the hall with her wand in her hand, and opened the doors of the sty, and drove them out. They looked like nine-year-old boars. They stood there facing her, and she went through them and rubbed each one with a different drug. And the bristles fell off them — the bristles the ruinous drug had grown on them — and they turned back into men. Younger than they had been before, and much better looking, and taller.

And they knew me, and every man of them took my hand. And a longing to weep came over all of them, and the house rang with it, terribly. And the goddess herself was moved to pity.

---

She told me to go down to the ship and haul her out and stow the gear in the caves, and then come back with the rest of my men. I went, and found them beside the fast ship crying, letting the big tears fall.

And the way farmyard calves come round the herd of cows coming back to the yard when they have had their fill of grass — all of them skipping together in front of them, and the pens no longer hold them, and they run round their mothers lowing without stopping — that is how those men crowded round me, in tears, when their eyes saw me. And it felt to them exactly as though they had got home; as though this were their own country, and the city of rugged Ithaca itself, where they were born and brought up.

And I told them to haul the ship out and stow the gear, and then follow me to Circe's sacred house. And every one of them obeyed at once, except Eurylochus, who tried to hold them all back.

*Where are we going, you poor fools? Why are you so hungry for trouble that you would go down to Circe's house — where she will turn the whole lot of us into pigs or wolves or lions, and we will be made to guard her great house for her? It is exactly what the Cyclops did, when our companions went into his yard, and this reckless Odysseus went with them. They died there too, through his stupidity.*

And when he said that I thought hard about drawing the long sword off my sturdy thigh and taking his head off and rolling it on the ground, close relation by marriage though he was. But my companions held me back with soft words, and said to leave him by the ship to look after it. So they went up from the ship and the sea; and Eurylochus did not stay behind either. He came with us. He was afraid of my terrible anger.

Meanwhile Circe had bathed the rest of my companions in her house and rubbed them with rich oil and put fleecy cloaks and tunics on them; and we found them all having a good dinner in the hall. And when they saw each other face to face and knew each other, they wept and wailed, and the house rang round them.

And the goddess came and stood beside me. *Son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many devices. Do not go on raising this great lamentation any longer. I know myself what you have all suffered on the fish-filled sea, and how unfriendly men have done you harm on land. Come. Eat food and drink wine, until you get the spirit back in your breasts that you had at the beginning, when you first left your own country, rugged Ithaca. As you are now, you are withered and dispirited, always thinking about your hard wandering, and there is never any gladness in your hearts, because you have been through a great deal.*

And we did as she said. And we stayed there day after day, for a full year, feasting on meat past counting and sweet wine.

---

A year.

Set it beside Ogygia. He was with Calypso seven years, which is a great deal longer, and the poem takes enormous trouble to tell us what those years were like: he sat on the rocks every day and cried and looked at the water, the sweetness went out of his life, and he lay beside her unwilling beside the willing one. Here he stays a year in a beautiful house with a goddess who looks after him extremely well, and the poem records not one day of grief. No rocks, no weeping, no looking at the sea. The wine goes round and the meat comes in and the year goes by. And it is not Odysseus who ends it. It is the men — the same men he went unarmed into a witch's house to rescue — who have to take him aside and say, in effect, *sir. Ithaca.* And he goes to her that night and asks to be released, and she releases him at once, and never argues, and never held him at all.

I shall ask the question once and then leave it alone: what exactly was he doing for a year? Not because I think he had stopped wanting to go home — I do not believe he stopped for an hour in twenty years, and the poem has proved it to me more than once — but because wanting to go home and going home are different things, and this is the most honest thing in the book about how people fail to do what they want most. Not by choosing against it. By being comfortable, among friends, for a while, and then for a while longer.

---

When the year was up and the seasons had come round again, my trusty companions called me out. *Strange man. It is time you thought about your own country — if it is really laid down that you are to be saved and get back to your high-roofed house and your own land.*

And my proud heart was persuaded. So all that day until sunset we sat feasting; and when the sun went down and the darkness came, they lay down to sleep through the shadowy hall. But I went up to Circe's beautiful bed and took hold of her knees, and the goddess listened to me.

*Circe. Keep the promise you made me — to send me home. My spirit is set on it now, and so are my men's; they wear my heart away, sitting round me grieving, whenever you happen to be somewhere else.*

*Son of Laertes, Odysseus of the many devices. Do not stay in my house any longer against your will. But there is another journey you have to make first. You must go to the house of Hades and dread Persephone, to consult the spirit of Teiresias of Thebes — the blind prophet, whose mind is still whole. Persephone has granted understanding to him alone, dead as he is. The others go flitting about as shadows.*

And my heart broke when I heard it. I sat there on the bed and cried, and I did not want to go on living and see the light of the sun any more. And when I had had enough of crying and rolling about, I answered her. *Circe — who is going to guide us on that journey? Nobody has ever got to Hades in a black ship.*

And she told me, and I shall set down what she said exactly as she said it, because I did every part of it afterwards, in order, and my life turned on it.

*Do not give a thought to wanting a guide beside the ship. Set up the mast and spread the white sail and sit down; the breath of the North Wind will carry her. And when you have crossed the stream of Ocean, where there is a level shore and the groves of Persephone — tall poplars, and willows that drop their fruit — then beach your ship there and go yourself to the mouldering house of Hades. There the river of fire and the river of wailing run into Acheron, and there is a rock where the two roaring rivers come together.*

*Then go close in, hero, and do exactly as I tell you. Dig a pit, about a forearm's length each way. And pour a drink offering round it to all the dead: first with milk and honey, then with sweet wine, and the third time with water. And sprinkle white barley meal over all of it.*

*And make a long prayer to the strengthless heads of the dead. Promise them that when you get to Ithaca you will sacrifice a barren heifer in your halls, the best you have, and pile the altar with good things; and that to Teiresias by himself you will sacrifice a ram, a black one, all black, the finest in your flocks.*

*And when you have finished praying to the great crowds of the dead, then sacrifice a ram and a black ewe, turning their heads towards the darkness — but turn yourself away, facing towards the streams of the river. And then a great many souls of the dead and gone will come.*

*Then call your companions and tell them to flay the sheep that are lying there killed by the pitiless bronze, and to burn them, and to pray to the gods. And you: draw the sharp sword off your thigh, and sit there, and do not let the strengthless heads of the dead come near the blood until you have asked Teiresias. And the prophet will come to you very soon, and he will tell you your way, and the stages of it, and how you are to get home over the fish-filled sea.*

---

And the Dawn came up on her golden throne while she was still speaking. And she put a cloak and a tunic on me, and dressed herself in a long shining robe, finely woven and lovely, and put a beautiful golden belt round her waist and a veil over her head.

And I went through the house rousing my men, standing over each one and speaking gently. *Do not go on lying there sleeping. Let us go. Lady Circe has told me everything.*

And their proud hearts were persuaded. But not even from there did I get all my men away unhurt.

There was one called Elpenor, the youngest of them, not very brave in a fight and not very sound in the head, who had lain down apart from the others on the roof of Circe's house, wanting the cool air, because he was heavy with wine. And he heard the noise and the stir of his companions moving about, and jumped up suddenly, and forgot to go back down by the long ladder, and fell headlong off the roof; and his neck was broken out of its spine, and his soul went down to the house of Hades.<sup><a href="#book-10-note-5">5</a></sup>

And I said to the others as they came: *You think you are going home now. Circe has marked out another road for us — to the house of Hades and dread Persephone, to consult the soul of Teiresias of Thebes.*

And their spirits broke in them when they heard it. They sat down where they were and cried and tore their hair. And no good came of their crying.

And while we were on our way down to the fast ship and the shore of the sea, grieving and letting the big tears fall, Circe went on ahead of us and tied a ram and a black ewe beside the black ship.

She passed us easily. Who could see a god going to and fro, if the god did not wish it?

---

## NOTES TO BOOK TEN

<a id="book-10-note-1"></a>
1. **The house of Aeolus.** Six sons, six daughters, and the daughters married to the brothers — stated in one line, with no comment, as part of a description of a happy and well-run household. It is worth stopping on, because the poem plainly does not intend it as horror. Aeolus is a favourite of the gods, generous, hospitable and helpful, and his home is the most perfectly self-contained thing in the book: an island that floats free of any coast, with a wall of unbreakable bronze round it, where the family eat together every day and there is music in the courtyard and nobody ever has to go outside for anything, including a spouse. Greek myth has other such families and generally attaches no scandal to them at the level of gods and half-divine beings; the rules that governed actual Greek households were not thought to apply upward. What the detail is *for*, I think, is the enclosure. This is a household that needs nothing from the world — which makes what happens next exact. The one thing Aeolus gives away is a sealed bag, and when it is opened and the man comes back, the door shuts and does not open again. Perfectly self-sufficient people can afford to be perfectly unforgiving.

<a id="book-10-note-2"></a>
2. **"Where the paths of night and day are close together."** A herdsman driving his flock in at dusk calls out and is answered by one driving out at dawn, and a man who could do without sleep might draw two wages a day. That is a description of a place where the nights are so short they barely happen — high-latitude summer, where the light never entirely goes. Nobody knows what to do with it. It sits in the middle of a Mediterranean poem, unexplained, and it has been argued over for two thousand years: a garbled traveller's report carried south along the amber routes; a memory of a Norwegian summer that reached Greece through four sets of hands; a coincidence; an invention that happens to describe something real. I have no answer and neither has anybody else. But it is worth knowing that the strangest line in the strangest book of this poem is not about a monster. It is about the light.

<a id="book-10-note-3"></a>
3. **Moly.** Black root, milk-white flower, hard for mortals to dig — and the poem tells you that *moly* is what the gods call it, which is one of a small handful of places in Homer where we are told that the immortals have their own names for things and that this is not the human one. People have been trying to identify the plant for a very long time, and the most persistent modern candidate is the snowdrop, which grows wild in Greece, has a dark bulb and a white flower, and contains a compound that is a genuine antidote to the class of poisons that produce delirium and hallucination — the sort of thing you might get from thorn-apple or henbane, both of which grow in the region and both of which have been used to make people compliant. On that reading Circe's drink is a real drug and Hermes' herb a real counter to it, and somebody in the Bronze Age Aegean knew it. It is a lovely theory and I would not bet the house on it. What is certain is the shape of the thing: the goddess who knows every drug is defeated by a better one, handed over by a god who does not stay to watch.

<a id="book-10-note-4"></a>
4. **What Circe threatens.** Hermes' warning is specific, and the Greek is blunter than English likes to be: when she has him naked and unarmed she will make him worthless and not a man. It carries both senses at once, cowardice and unmanning, and the poem does not separate them, because in this world they were not separate. What is being described is the standard fear about a woman with power over a man in a bedroom, and the standard defence is a binding oath sworn before the act. — Note what the scene does structurally. He arrives with a sword out, and the encounter is settled on his terms: she swears, he goes to bed with her, and afterwards she is his ally for a year and gives him the sailing directions that save his life. It is a seduction converted into a treaty. Whether one should read her as beaten, or as having got precisely what she wanted from the start, the poem leaves entirely open — and I notice that she was expecting him. Hermes had told her, years before, that he would come.

<a id="book-10-note-5"></a>
5. **Elpenor.** The youngest man aboard, no good in a fight, not clever, drunk, asleep on a flat roof for the cool air; he hears everyone moving, jumps up, forgets there is a ladder, and breaks his neck. It is the least heroic death in the poem and quite possibly in all Greek literature, and it takes four lines. Every other man who dies in these four books is eaten by something, or drowned, or crushed by a rock thrown by a giant; this one falls off a roof at a party. I mention it because it would be easy to read as a throwaway, and it is not: he is going to matter, very shortly, and the poem's willingness to spend real feeling on a man it has just told you was neither brave nor bright is one of the more decent things about it.

---

*Book Eleven: In Which He Digs a Hole, and the Dead Come Up to Talk.*


<div class="page-break"></div>

<!-- Source: book/odyssey-book-11.md -->

# THE ODYSSEY
### Retold in English, with Explanations

---

## BOOK ELEVEN
### In Which He Digs a Hole, and the Dead Come Up to Talk

---

This is the middle — not roughly the middle, but the middle. Everything before this book goes away from home and everything after it comes back towards home, and the hinge is a hole in the ground at the edge of the world with a man sitting beside it holding a sword. It is also the first descent to the country of the dead in European literature, and every one that came afterwards walks in its footprints. One warning and then he can have it back: about halfway through, the poem will stop him and take us out to the dining hall for a few minutes. That is not a join in the manuscript. Wait for it.

---

We went down to the ship and dragged her into the bright water and put the mast and the sail in her, and took the sheep aboard, and went aboard ourselves, in a bad way, letting the big tears fall. And Circe sent us a following wind behind the dark-prowed ship, a good companion, to fill the sail. All day her sail was stretched as she crossed the sea, and the sun went down and all the ways grew dark.

And she came to the edge of deep-flowing Ocean, where the country and the city of the Cimmerian people are, wrapped in fog and cloud. The shining sun never looks down on them with his rays — not when he climbs up towards the starry sky, and not when he turns back down again — and a deadly night is stretched over those wretched people.

We ran the ship ashore and got the sheep out, and went along beside the stream of Ocean until we came to the place Circe had described. There Perimedes and Eurylochus held the animals, and I drew the sharp sword off my thigh and dug the pit, a forearm's length this way and that. And I poured the offering round it to all the dead: first with milk and honey, then with sweet wine, and the third time with water; and I sprinkled white barley meal over all of it. And I prayed hard to the strengthless heads of the dead, and promised them that when I got to Ithaca I would sacrifice a barren heifer in my halls, the best I had, and pile the altar high with good things; and that to Teiresias by himself I would offer a ram, black all over, the finest in my flocks.

And when I had finished praying I took the sheep and cut their throats over the pit, and the dark blood ran into it.

And they came up out of the darkness underneath. Brides came, and unmarried boys, and old men who had suffered a great deal, and soft young girls with hearts new to grief; and a great many men wounded with bronze spears, killed in war, still in their bloodied armour. They came crowding round the pit from every direction with an unearthly crying, and a pale fear took hold of me.

And I told my companions to flay the sheep and burn them and pray to the gods — to mighty Hades and to dread Persephone (his queen, who rules the dead beside him). And I drew the sharp sword off my thigh and sat there, and would not let the strengthless heads of the dead come near the blood until I had asked Teiresias.<sup><a href="#book-11-note-1">1</a></sup>

---

The first soul that came was my own companion Elpenor. He had not been buried under the wide-wayed earth; we had left his body in Circe's house, unwept and unburied, because another task was pressing us.

I cried when I saw him. *Elpenor — how did you get down here under the fog and the dark? You have come quicker on foot than I did in my black ship.*

And he groaned and answered me. *Son of Laertes. An evil fate from some god did for me, and an immeasurable quantity of wine. I lay down on Circe's roof and never thought to go back down by the long ladder, and I came down head first, and my neck was broken out of its spine.*

*And now I beg you by the ones left behind, who are not here — by your wife, and by your father who brought you up, and by Telemachus, the only son you left in your halls — because I know that when you go from here you will bring your ship in at Aeaea again — there, my lord, remember me. Do not go away and leave me unwept and unburied and turn your back on me, or I may become a reason for the gods to be angry with you. Burn me with my armour, all that I have, and heap up a mound for me on the shore of the grey sea, for an unlucky man, so that people yet to come will know. Do that for me. And plant on the mound the oar I used to row with, when I was alive and with my companions.*

*I will do all of it, my poor friend. I will see to it.*

So the two of us sat there exchanging these unhappy words, I on one side holding my sword over the blood, and the ghost of my companion on the other side, saying a great deal.

---

And then came the soul of my dead mother, Anticleia, the daughter of great-hearted Autolycus, whom I had left alive when I sailed for holy Troy. I cried when I saw her, and I pitied her in my heart. And even so I would not let her come near the blood, however badly it hurt, until I had asked Teiresias.

And the soul of Teiresias of Thebes came, holding a golden staff, and he knew me.

*Son of Laertes. Why have you left the light of the sun, you unlucky man, and come to see the dead and this place where there is no joy? Stand back from the pit and hold that sharp sword away, so that I can drink the blood and tell you the truth.*

I stepped back and pushed the silver-studded sword into its sheath. And when he had drunk the dark blood, the faultless prophet spoke.

*You are asking about a sweet homecoming, glorious Odysseus. And a god is going to make it hard for you. Because I do not think you will get past the Earthshaker (Poseidon). He has stored up anger against you in his heart, and he is furious about his own dear son, whose eye you put out.*

*Even so, you may still get home, though you will suffer for it — if you can hold your own spirit in, and your companions'. When you first bring your ship in at the island of Thrinacia, escaping the violet sea, you will find the cattle grazing there, and the fat flocks of Helios, who sees everything and hears everything. If you leave those alone and keep your mind on getting home, then all of you may still reach Ithaca, badly off as you will be. But if you harm them, then I am telling you now: destruction for your ship and for your men. And if you get out of it yourself, you will come home late, and in a bad way, having lost every one of your companions, in somebody else's ship. And you will find trouble in your house — arrogant men eating up your living, courting your godlike wife and offering her bride-gifts.*

*But you will pay them out for their violence when you come. And when you have killed the suitors in your own halls, whether by a trick or openly with the sharp bronze — then go. Take a well-made oar and go on until you come to men who know nothing about the sea, and eat their food without salt in it, and have never heard of ships with painted cheeks, or of the shaped oars that are the wings of ships. And I will tell you a very clear sign, and you will not miss it. When another traveller meets you on the road and says you have a winnowing fan on your broad shoulder — then plant your shaped oar in the ground, and make a fine sacrifice to the lord Poseidon: a ram, a bull, and a boar that mates with sows. And go home, and offer sacred hecatombs (great sacrifices, like 100 cattle) to the immortal gods, to all of them in their order.*

*And death will come to you far from the sea. A very gentle death. It will take you when you are worn down with a sleek old age, and your people will be prosperous around you. That is the truth I am telling you.*

*Teiresias — I suppose the gods themselves have spun all this out. But tell me this. I see the soul of my dead mother there. She sits by the blood without a word, and she cannot bring herself to look straight at her own son, or speak to him. Tell me, lord — how can she know who I am?*

*That is easily said. Any one of the dead you let come near the blood will speak the truth to you. Any one you refuse will go back again.*

And the soul of lord Teiresias went away into the house of Hades, having said his prophecy.

---

And I stayed where I was until my mother came up and drank the dark blood. And she knew me at once, and cried.

*My child. How did you come down here under the murky dark, and you alive? It is hard for the living to see these things. There are great rivers between, and terrible waters, and Ocean first of all, which nobody can cross on foot; you must have a well-built ship. Have you only now come here from Troy, wandering all this time with your ship and your men? Have you not been to Ithaca yet? Have you not seen your wife in your own house?*

*Mother — necessity brought me down to Hades, to consult the soul of Teiresias. I have not been near Greece yet. I have not set foot on my own country. I have been wandering, and there has been nothing but trouble, since the first day I followed Agamemnon to Ilium (Troy). But tell me this truly. What death took you? Was it a long illness? Or did Artemis (goddess of the hunt, whose arrows bring a quiet death to women) come and kill you with her gentle shafts? And tell me about my father, and about the son I left behind. Is my position still theirs? Or does some other man hold it now? And tell me about my wife — what she intends, and what is in her mind. Is she still with the boy, keeping everything safe? Or has one of the Greeks married her by now?*

*She is still in your halls, and her heart is steady, and she is enduring it. The nights waste away for her, wretchedly, and the days, and she is crying. Nobody holds your position. Telemachus keeps your lands undisturbed, and dines at the feasts a man who deals out judgements ought to dine at; everybody invites him.*

*But your father stays out on the farm and does not come into the town at all. He has no bedstead now, and no cloaks, and no bright coverlets. In the winter he sleeps in the house where the servants sleep, in the ashes by the fire, and wears bad clothes. And when the summer comes, and the rich autumn, there are beds of fallen leaves heaped low all over the slope of his vineyard, and he lies down on those, grieving, feeding a great sorrow in his heart and longing for you to come back. And a hard old age has come on him.*

*And that is how I died too. It was not the sharp-eyed archer goddess who came and killed me in my house with her gentle arrows, and it was not a disease, the sort that most often takes the spirit out of the limbs by a horrible wasting. It was missing you. It was longing for you, and for your good sense, glorious Odysseus, and for your kindness. That took my honey-sweet life away.*

And I wanted to take hold of the soul of my dead mother. Three times I went for her, and my heart urged me to hold her. Three times she went out of my hands like a shadow, or like a dream. And the grief in my heart got sharper every time.

*Mother — why do you not stay for me, when I want to hold you? Why can we not put our arms round each other, even here in Hades, and take our fill of cold grieving? Is this some phantom that dread Persephone has sent me, to make me cry even harder?*

*My child. Most unlucky of all men. Persephone is not deceiving you. This is simply the way it is with mortals when a person dies. The sinews no longer hold the flesh and the bones together. The great force of the blazing fire destroys all that, as soon as the life leaves the white bones. And the soul flutters off like a dream and goes to and fro.*

*Get back to the light, quickly. And take all of this in, so that you can tell your wife afterwards.*

---

That last instruction is the thing to keep. She does not say *remember me*, or *avenge me*, or *bury me properly*. She has one child in front of her whom she died of missing, and what she does with her few words is send him home to somebody else and give him something to say when he gets there. It is the only thing left that she can do about twenty years of waiting for a man to walk in at the door.

---

Then Persephone sent up the souls of the women, all of them the wives and daughters of great men, and they gathered in a crowd round the dark blood; and I drew the long sword off my thigh and would not let them all drink together, but let them come one at a time, and each of them told me her lineage.

Tyro came, who fell in love with a river and was loved by Poseidon in the river's shape, and bore Pelias and Neleus. Antiope came, who bore Amphion and Zethus, the two who first built the foundations of seven-gated Thebes and walled it, because for all their strength they could not live in Thebes without walls. And Alcmene came, who bore Heracles to Zeus; and Megara, the daughter of Creon, whom Heracles married.

And I saw the mother of Oedipus, the beautiful Epicaste, who did a monstrous thing without knowing what she was doing, and married her own son; and he had killed his own father and married her. And the gods made it known among men straight away. And he stayed on in lovely Thebes, ruling the Cadmeans, suffering, through the destructive plans of the gods. And she went down into the house of Hades, having tied a noose to a high roofbeam, in the grip of her own grief. And she left him pains past counting — everything a mother's avenging Furies bring about.<sup><a href="#book-11-note-2">2</a></sup>

And Chloris came, and Leda who bore Castor and Polydeuces, whom the earth holds, and they are alive, and even under the earth they have honour from Zeus, and live on alternate days and are dead on alternate days. And Iphimedeia came, who bore Otus and Ephialtes, the two tallest and handsomest men the grain-giving earth ever fed after Orion: at nine years old they were nine cubits across and nine fathoms tall, and they threatened to raise war against the immortals themselves, and set about piling Ossa on Olympus and Pelion on Ossa so as to climb into the sky — and they would have brought it off, if they had reached the full measure of manhood, but Apollo killed them both before the down flowered on their cheeks.

And I saw Phaedra, and Procris, and beautiful Ariadne, the daughter of Minos, whom Theseus tried to bring from Crete to holy Athens and got no joy of, because Artemis killed her first on the island of Dia. And Maera, and Clymene, and hateful Eriphyle, who took gold as the price of her own husband.

I could not tell you or name all of them, all the wives and daughters of heroes that I saw; the immortal night would be used up first. And it is time to sleep, either on board the fast ship with my crew, or here in your house. My escort is a matter for the gods and for you.

---

That is the sound of a man putting his cup down. He has been talking since dinner; he has just walked a hall full of listeners along a wall of famous names; and he has stopped in the middle of it and said, in effect, *goodness, look at the time.*

---

And the whole room stayed silent, held in the spell of it, through the shadowy hall. And the first person to speak was the queen.

"Phaeacians. What do you make of this man — his looks, his size, and the balance of the mind inside him? He is my guest, but every one of you has a share in the honour of him. So do not be in a hurry to send him off, and do not be mean with your gifts to a man in such need. You have a great deal of treasure lying in your houses by the will of the gods."

And the old lord Echeneus said: "Friends, our wise queen has not spoken wide of the mark, and not wide of what we were all thinking. Do as she says — though the word and the deed rest with Alcinous here."

And Alcinous said: "What she says will stand, as surely as I am alive and rule over the Phaeacians who love the oar. Let our guest hold on, however much he wants to be off, until tomorrow — until I have made the gifts complete. The escort will be the men's business, and mine most of all, since the power in this country is mine."

And Odysseus said: "Lord Alcinous. If you told me to stay here for a year, and were getting my escort ready and giving me splendid gifts, I would take that too. It would be much better to reach my own country with a fuller hand; I would be more respected, and better loved, by every man who saw me come home to Ithaca."

And Alcinous said: "Odysseus — looking at you, we do not take you for a cheat or a liar, the sort the black earth breeds in great numbers, men who fashion falsehoods out of things nobody could ever check. There is a shapeliness on your words, and there is a good mind inside you. You have told your story with skill, the way a singer does.

"But tell me this. Did you see any of your godlike companions down there — men who went with you to Ilium (Troy) and met their fate? The night is long. Immeasurably long. It is not time to sleep in the hall yet. Tell me the marvellous things. I could hold out until the bright dawn, if you could bear to stay in this hall and tell me your troubles."

---

A king has just praised his guest for not being the sort of man who invents stories out of things nobody can verify, and has given as his reason that the man tells a story as well as a professional storyteller. The evening's material so far has included a one-eyed giant, a floating island, a woman who turns men into pigs and a conversation with the dead. I do not think Alcinous is a fool — he has been the most sensible man in four books — and I think the poem is grinning at us over its own frame. Note what else the interval does. The cups come back, and the queen says *do not be mean with your gifts*, and the guest replies that he would happily stay a year if the presents were good enough, because he would rather arrive home rich. He is not confessing at a dinner party. He is earning his fare.

---

Lord Alcinous — there is a time for many words and there is a time for sleep. But if you are still eager to listen, I would not grudge you things more pitiful still: the sufferings of my companions, who got out from under the war-cry of the Trojans and then died on the way home, through the will of an evil woman.

When Persephone had scattered the souls of the women, there came the soul of Agamemnon, grieving; and round him were gathered the others who had died with him in the house of Aegisthus. He knew me at once when he had drunk the dark blood. He wept shrilly and stretched his hands out towards me, wanting to hold me; but there was no strength left in him, and none of the force his supple limbs used to have.

I cried when I saw him. *Most glorious son of Atreus, lord of men. What death took you? Did Poseidon take you on your ships, raising a foul blast of cruel winds? Or did enemies do it on dry land, while you were cutting out their cattle and their fine flocks, or fighting for a city and its women?*

*It was not Poseidon on the ships, and it was not enemies on dry land. Aegisthus arranged my death and my fate, and killed me with the help of my accursed wife. He asked me to his house. He gave me dinner. And he killed me the way a man kills an ox at the manger.*

*So I died the most pitiful death. And round me my companions were slaughtered without a pause, like white-tusked pigs killed in the house of a rich and powerful man for a wedding or a feast day. You have been present at the killing of a great many men, cut down one at a time or in the press of a battle. But you would have been sorriest of all in your heart if you had seen that: how we lay in the hall among the mixing bowls and the loaded tables, and the whole floor swam with blood.*

*And the most pitiful thing I heard was the voice of Cassandra, whom treacherous Clytemnestra (Agememnon's wife, remarried to Aegisthus, and Helen's twin sister) killed beside me. And I lifted my hands and beat the ground with them as I died, with the sword in me. And that shameless woman turned her back and walked away. She would not even use her hands to close my eyes and shut my mouth, though I was going down to Hades.*

*So there is nothing more terrible, nothing more shameless, than a woman who can put a thing like that in her mind. I thought I was coming home welcome to my children and my household. And she has poured shame on herself, and on the women who come after her, and even on the decent ones.*

*Zeus has been terribly hard on the house of Atreus (Agememnon's father) from the beginning, through the plans of women. A great many of us died for Helen's sake, and Clytemnestra was laying her trap for you while you were far away.*

*So never be gentle to your own wife either. Do not tell her every plan you know. Tell her part, and keep part hidden. Though death will not come to you from your wife, Odysseus. She is far too sensible, and knows too well what good counsel is — Penelope, the daughter of Icarius. We left her behind a young bride when we went off to the war. There was a boy at her breast, an infant. He must be sitting among grown men by now, and lucky, because his father will see him when he comes, and he will put his arms round his father, which is how it should be. My wife did not let me have my fill of looking at my own son. She killed me first.*

*And here is one more thing; put it away in your mind. Bring your ship in to your own dear country secretly, not in the open. There is no trusting women.*

*But tell me — have you heard anything about my son? Is he alive? Because noble Orestes is not dead anywhere on this earth.*

*Son of Atreus, why ask me this? I have no idea whether he is alive or dead, and it is a bad thing to talk empty as the wind.*

So the two of us stood there exchanging these unhappy words, grieving, letting the tears fall.

---

And then came the soul of Achilles, and of Patroclus, and of faultless Antilochus, and of Ajax, who was the best of the Greeks in looks and in build after the son of Peleus. And the soul of Achilles knew me.

*Son of Laertes. You reckless man. What enormous thing will you think of next? How did you dare to come down to Hades, where the senseless dead live, the worn-out images of men?*

*Achilles, son of Peleus — far the strongest of the Greeks. I came for Teiresias, to see if he could tell me any plan for getting back to rugged Ithaca. Because I have not been near Greece yet, or set foot on my own country, and I have had nothing but trouble. But you, Achilles — no man was ever more blessed than you, and no man ever will be. When you were alive we Greeks honoured you like a god, and now you are down here you rule mightily among the dead. So do not grieve at being dead, Achilles.*

*Do not talk to me smoothly about death, glorious Odysseus. I would rather be alive and working the soil for another man — a landless man, with nothing much to live on — than be king over all the dead who are used up.*

That is Achilles, who was offered the choice in the older poem between a long quiet life at home and a short one ending under the walls of Troy with a name that would never die, and who took the short one on purpose, knowing the terms; and who is the reason that poem exists. He has had a while to think about it. The *Iliad* is a poem about a young man choosing glory over length of life, and the *Odyssey* puts that young man in a hole in the ground and asks him how it went.

*But tell me about my son. Did he follow you to the war, to be a leader? And tell me about noble Peleus, if you have heard anything. Do the Myrmidons still honour him, or do they treat him badly through Greece, because old age has him by the hands and feet? I am not up there under the sun's rays to help him — not the man I used to be, when I killed the best of their army on the wide plain of Troy. If I could come to my father's house like that for even a little while, I would make my strength and my untouchable hands something to be afraid of, for anyone doing him violence.*

And I told him about Neoptolemus: that I had brought him myself from Scyros; that in council he was always first to speak and never got it wrong, and only Nestor and I could beat him at it; that in the fighting he never stayed in the crowd but ran far out in front, and gave way to nobody, and killed a great many men. And I told him about the horse — how all the best of us sat inside it, and the leaders were weeping and their legs were shaking, and I never once saw that young man's fine skin go pale or saw him wipe a tear off his face; he kept begging me to let him out, handling his sword-hilt and his heavy bronze spear. And I told him that when we had sacked the steep city of Priam he went aboard his ship with his share and a fine prize, without a scratch on him.

And the soul of Achilles went away over the field of asphodel with long strides — glad, because I had told him his son was outstanding.

---

The other souls of the dead and gone stood about grieving, and each one asked me about the people they cared for. Only the soul of Ajax kept away, still furious about the victory I had won over him beside the ships, in the contest for the armour of Achilles.

I wish I had never won a contest like that. For the sake of that armour the earth closed over a head like his — Ajax, who was above all the other Greeks in his looks and in what he did, after the son of Peleus.

And I spoke to him gently. *Ajax, son of faultless Telamon. Were you not going to forget your anger with me, even in death, over that ruinous armour? The gods made it a disaster for the Greeks. Such a tower of a man we lost in you. We grieve for you constantly, the way we grieve for the life of Achilles; and nobody is to blame but Zeus, who hated the Greek army terribly and laid your fate on you. Come here, my lord. Hear what I am saying. Put down your anger and your lordly spirit.*

He did not answer me. He went off into the darkness after the other souls of the dead.

Even then he might have spoken to me, angry as he was, or I to him — but the heart in my breast wanted to see the souls of the others.

In a book whose entire machinery exists to make the dead speak, one man is addressed by name, apologised to, praised and begged, and turns round and walks away without a syllable. And notice what it costs the speaker: *I wish I had never won a contest like that* is the only place in twenty-four books where Odysseus wishes he had lost. He does not say it about the Cyclops's eye, or the horse, or the town at Ismarus. He says it about a prize he won fairly.

---

And I saw Minos, the son of Zeus, holding a golden staff, sitting and giving judgements to the dead; and they sat and stood about him through the wide-gated house of Hades, asking him to settle their cases. And after him I saw huge Orion, driving the wild beasts together over the field of asphodel, the same ones he killed himself on the lonely hills, with an unbreakable bronze club in his hands.

And I saw Tityos, the son of Earth, lying on the ground; he covered nine acres of it. Two vultures sat on either side of him tearing at his liver, going right into the flesh, and his hands could not push them off. He had laid hands on Leto as she was going to Delphi.

And I saw Tantalus, in hard pain, standing in a pool with the water up against his chin. He looked like a man dying of thirst and he could not get anything to drink: every time the old man stooped down, mad for a drink, the water was swallowed away and vanished, and the black earth showed round his feet. And there were tall trees over his head dropping their fruit down at him — pears and pomegranates and shining apples and sweet figs and ripe olives — and every time he reached up for them, the wind tossed them away to the shadowy clouds.

And I saw Sisyphus, in violent pain, wrestling a monstrous stone with both arms. He would brace his hands and feet and shove it up towards the top of a hill; and just as he was about to get it over the crest, the weight of it would turn him back, and the shameless stone would come rolling down to the flat ground again. And he would strain and shove it back up, and the sweat poured off his limbs, and the dust rose off his head.<sup><a href="#book-11-note-3">3</a></sup>

And after him I saw the mighty Heracles — his phantom. He himself is among the immortal gods, enjoying their feasts, and he has Hebe for a wife. Round him there was a clamour from the dead like the noise of birds, and they scattered everywhere in terror; and he came on like the black night, with his bow bare and an arrow on the string, glaring terribly, like a man about to shoot. There was a fearful belt about his chest, a golden baldric, and marvellous things were worked on it: bears and wild boars and lions with their eyes flashing, and battles and fighting and killings and men being slaughtered. I hope whoever put his craft into that belt never made another one.

He knew me the moment he saw me. *Son of Laertes. Are you dragging out a bad destiny too, the same as the one I carried under the rays of the sun? I was the son of Zeus, and I had trouble past all measuring. I was made subject to a man far worse than I was, and he laid hard labours on me. He even sent me down here once, to bring up the hound — because he thought there could be no harder task; and I brought the hound up and led him out of Hades, and Hermes guided me, and Athena.*<sup><a href="#book-11-note-4">4</a></sup>

And he went back into the house of Hades.

But I stayed there, in case some other one of the heroes who died long ago might come, and I might have seen the men I wanted to see, Theseus and Peirithous. But before that, the tribes of the dead came thronging up with an unearthly cry, and a pale fear took hold of me, in case dread Persephone should send me up the head of the Gorgon out of the house of Hades.

So I went back to the ship at once and told my men to get aboard and cast off the cables. They went aboard and sat down at the oars. And the current carried us down the stream of Ocean; oars first, and after that a fair wind.

---

## NOTES TO BOOK ELEVEN

<a id="book-11-note-1"></a>
1. **The pit, the blood, and where this is.** Three things a modern reader needs, and none of them are what most people expect. — *First:* he does not go down. Circe's directions send him to the far edge of Ocean, to a beach, where he digs a small pit and the dead come *up*. There is no descent, no gate, no guide, no tour; he never sets foot in the house of Hades and never sees it. The full underworld journey — the crossing, the ferryman, the levels — is later machinery, mostly Virgil's and Dante's, and it is not here. — *Second:* the blood. The dead in this poem are not spirits in the modern sense but worn-out images, without strength, without voice, and without recognition; they cannot even *know* him until they have drunk. What the blood gives back, briefly, is not life but the power to remember and to speak, which is why he has to sit there rationing it with a sword, and why his own mother sits by the pit in silence and cannot look at her son. — *Third:* this is not hell. As promised in Book Four, note 5: there is no judgement at the door, no sorting, no reward for the good and no fire for the wicked. Everybody goes to the same grey place, Achilles and Agamemnon and Elpenor who fell off a roof, all together. Minos is down there judging, but look at what he is doing — settling disputes *among* the dead, the way a king settles disputes among the living. He is a magistrate, not St Peter.

<a id="book-11-note-2"></a>
2. **Oedipus, three hundred years before Sophocles.** Here is the whole story as this poem has it: he killed his father and married his mother in ignorance; the gods made it known at once; his mother hanged herself; and *he went on ruling in Thebes*. He is not blinded. He does not put out his own eyes; there is no exile, no wandering, no daughter leading him by the hand to Colonus. He suffers, and he keeps the throne. Set that beside what happens to the material later, when the Athenian tragedians take hold of it and make the discovery and the self-blinding the whole point, and you have the same lesson as Book Three, note 4, on Orestes. These stories were not fixed. The versions we treat as *the* myth are almost always somebody's later, harder-edged rewrite. Homer knew a different one and told it in nine lines, on the way past.

<a id="book-11-note-3"></a>
3. **What the three punishments have in common.** Tityos assaulted Leto. Tantalus and Sisyphus are here for offences the poem does not spell out, but the tradition is consistent that both personally cheated or insulted the gods — Tantalus by abusing their hospitality, Sisyphus by trying to outwit death itself. Every one of the three is being punished for an offence *against a god*, personally, and not for wickedness in general. This is the Elysium note from Book Four arriving from the other side, and worth stating plainly because it cuts against everything later readers brought with them: there is no ordinary moral accounting in this afterlife. Bad men who did not offend the gods are not punished, and good men who did not please them are not rewarded. There are three individuals in agony, and everybody else is simply dead, in the grey, forever. When Achilles says what he says thirty lines later, this is the place he is talking about.

<a id="book-11-note-4"></a>
4. **Heracles in two places at once.** He is standing in front of Odysseus with an arrow on the string — and the poem stops to tell you that this is only his phantom, and that Heracles himself is up on Olympus at the feast, married to the goddess of youth. Both statements are in the text, one line apart. This is the plainest theological contradiction in Homer and there is no reconciling it: either a man's shade goes to the grey place or he becomes a god, and Heracles is doing both. Most scholars think the Olympus line is a later addition, patched in by somebody who could not bear to have the greatest hero of them all shuffling about in the dark with everybody else. I mention it because it is a useful reminder of what this text is. It is not one man's manuscript. It is a tradition that was sung and re-sung and repaired for centuries before anyone wrote it down, and occasionally you can see the join.

---

*Book Twelve: In Which There Is Singing, a Choice Between Two Deaths, and the Last of the Ships.*


<div class="page-break"></div>

<!-- Source: book/odyssey-book-12.md -->

# THE ODYSSEY
### Retold in English, with Explanations

---

## BOOK TWELVE
### In Which There Is Singing, a Choice Between Two Deaths, and the Last of the Ships

---

This is the last of the four books he tells himself, and it is the one where everything runs out: the ship, the men, the food, all of it, until there is one man in the water holding two pieces of wood. I mention it in advance because the poem will not stop to mark it. He simply gets to the end, and stops, and turns back into a guest who has talked rather too long.

---

When our ship had left the stream of Ocean and come to the wave of the wide sea, and to the island of Aeaea, where the house of early Dawn is and her dancing floors and the risings of the sun — we ran her ashore on the sand and went out onto the beach, and there we slept and waited for the bright morning.

And when Dawn came up I sent my companions to Circe's house to fetch the body of dead Elpenor. We cut logs quickly and buried him on the furthest point of the headland, grieving, letting the big tears fall. And when the corpse and the dead man's armour had burned, we heaped up a mound and dragged a standing stone onto it, and on the very top of the mound we planted his oar.

And Circe knew perfectly well that we had come back from the house of Hades, and she dressed and came down quickly, and her women came with her carrying bread and a great deal of meat and sparkling red wine. And the shining goddess stood among us.

*You reckless men. You have gone down alive into the house of Hades. You will be twice dead, when other men die only once. Come — eat here, and drink wine, all day long. And at first light you shall sail; and I will show you the way and make every part of it plain, so that you do not come to grief through some miserable piece of bad planning, on the sea or on the land.*

And our proud hearts agreed to that. So all day until sunset we sat and feasted on meat past counting and sweet wine; and when the sun went down and the darkness came, they lay down to sleep beside the ship's cables. But she took me by the hand and sat me down away from the others, and lay down beside me and asked about every single thing; and I told her all of it, in the right order. And then she said this.

---

*All of that is finished, then. Now listen to what I tell you — and a god himself will remind you of it.*

*You will come first to the Sirens, who bewitch every man who comes near them. Whoever comes on them without knowing, and hears the Sirens' voice, his wife and his little children never stand round him and welcome him home again. The Sirens bewitch him with their clear singing, sitting in a meadow; and there is a great heap of men's bones round about them, rotting, with the skin shrivelling on them.*

*Drive past. And knead sweet wax and stop up your companions' ears, so that none of them can hear. But if you want to hear it yourself, then have them tie you hand and foot in the fast ship, standing upright against the mast-step, with the ropes made fast to the mast itself — so that you can listen to the voices of the two Sirens and enjoy it. And if you beg them and order them to let you go, then let them tie you down with more ropes still.*

*And when your companions have driven the ship past them, then I am not going to tell you which of two roads you should take. You must work that out in your own mind. I shall describe them both.*

*On one side there are overhanging rocks, and the great wave of dark-eyed Amphitrite (Poseidon's wife, who breeds the monsters of the sea) roars against them. The blessed gods call them the Wandering Rocks. Nothing that flies gets past — not even the timid doves that carry ambrosia to father Zeus; the smooth rock always takes one of them, and the father sends another up to make the number right. And no ship of men that ever came there has got away; the waves of the sea and the blasts of destroying fire carry off ships' timbers and men's bodies together. One seagoing ship alone ever sailed past — the Argo, that everybody sings about — on her way home from Aeetes; and even her the wave would have thrown against the great rocks, but Hera (queen of the gods) sent her through, because Jason was dear to her.*<sup><a href="#book-12-note-1">1</a></sup>

*On the other side there are two cliffs. One of them reaches the wide sky with its sharp peak, and a dark cloud stands round it and never streams away, and there is never clear air about the top of it, in summer or in autumn. No mortal man could climb it, not if he had twenty hands and twenty feet, because the rock is smooth, like something polished. And halfway up that cliff there is a misty cave, facing west, towards the darkness. That is where you will steer your hollow ship past, glorious Odysseus. A strong man shooting from a ship could not reach that cave with an arrow.*

*And Scylla lives in it, yelping horribly. Her voice is no bigger than the voice of a new-born puppy, but she herself is a dreadful monster; nobody would be glad to look at her, not even a god. She has twelve feet, all of them dangling, and six necks, immensely long, and on each of them an appalling head with three rows of teeth in it, thick and close together, full of black death. She is sunk to her middle inside the hollow cave, but she holds her heads out beyond the terrible gulf and fishes there, sweeping round the rock for dolphins and sea-dogs and whatever bigger thing she can catch. No sailors have ever yet got past her and been able to boast that their ship came through untouched. She takes a man in each head, and carries him off out of the dark-prowed ship.*

*The other cliff is lower — you will see; they are close together, and you could shoot an arrow across. On that one there is a great fig tree covered in leaves, and underneath it divine Charybdis sucks the black water down. Three times a day she throws it up, and three times she sucks it down, terribly. Do not be there when she sucks it down. Nobody could save you from destruction then, not even the Earthshaker.*

*Go close along Scylla's cliff instead, and drive the ship past fast. It is far better to grieve for six of your companions than for all of them together.*

*Goddess, tell me this truly. Could I somehow get clear of deadly Charybdis and still fight the other one off, when she goes for my men?*

*You obstinate man. So your mind is on fighting again, and on hard work. Will you not give way even to the immortal gods? She is not mortal. She is an immortal evil — terrible, savage, impossible to fight. There is no defending yourself. Running is best. If you stop to put your armour on beside that rock, I am afraid she will come out at you again with as many heads as before, and take as many men. Drive past hard, and shout for Crataiis, who is Scylla's mother, and who bore her as a curse to men. She will stop her coming a second time.*

*Then you will reach the island of Thrinacia. And there a great many cattle of Helios (the Sun, who sees everything and hears everything) graze, and his fat flocks: seven herds of cattle, and as many fine flocks of sheep, and fifty in each. They bear no young and they never die, and goddesses are their shepherds. If you leave those alone, and keep your mind on getting home, then you may still all reach Ithaca, badly off as you will be. But if you do them any harm, then I am telling you now: destruction for your ship and your men. And if you get out of it yourself, you will come home late and in a bad way, having lost every one of them.*

And the Dawn came up while she was still speaking; and the shining goddess went away up the island.

---

Almost everybody arrives at the Sirens carrying the wrong picture, and it is not the reader's fault but two and a half thousand years of paintings. Homer never describes them. Not their faces, not their bodies, not their number beyond Circe's passing *the two Sirens*; and there is no suggestion anywhere of the bedroom about them. The bird-bodies came later out of vase-painting, the fish-tails out of a medieval muddle with mermaids, and the seductress with the comb and the mirror is largely the nineteenth century. What the poem gives is a meadow, a heap of men with the skin drying on their bones, and a song — and when we hear the song, in a page or two, it will turn out to be an offer of *knowledge*. We know what happened at Troy, they sing, and everything that happens anywhere on the earth. Come and be told; you will go away knowing more.

Which means the hook is baited with precision for exactly one man's weakness, and it is not lust. It is the thing that took him into a stranger's cave to see what gift he might be given, and up every lookout on every island, and down to a pit at the edge of the world to ask the dead questions after he already had his answer.

---

So I went to the ship and roused my men, and Circe sent us a following wind behind the dark-prowed ship, a good companion, filling the sail. And then I spoke to my companions, sick at heart.

*Friends. It is not right that only one or two of us should know the prophecies Circe told me. I shall tell you, so that we may all know them, and then either die, or get away from death and out from under our fate. First of all she told us to keep away from the voices of the marvellous Singers, and from their flowering meadow. She said I alone might listen. But you must tie me with hard bonds, standing upright against the mast-step, with the ropes made fast to the mast itself. And if I beg you and order you to let me go, then you must tie me with more ropes still.*

And meanwhile the ship came quickly to the island of the Sirens, because a fair wind drove her. And then the wind dropped, all at once, and there was a windless calm, and some god put the swell to sleep. My companions stood up and furled the sail and stowed it, and sat down to the oars and made the water white with the polished pine.

And I took a great round cake of wax and cut it up small with the sharp bronze and worked it in my strong hands; and the wax grew warm quickly, because of the great pressure and the rays of the lord Sun; and I went along the line and stopped the ears of every man of them. And they tied me hand and foot in the ship, upright against the mast-step, with the ropes made fast to the mast; and then they sat down and struck the grey sea with their oars.

And when we were within calling distance, driving hard, the Sirens saw the fast ship coming close, and they raised their clear song.

*Come here, famous Odysseus, great glory of the Greeks. Stop your ship, so that you can listen to the two of us. No man has ever yet driven his black ship past this place without listening to the honey-sweet voice out of our mouths. Every man has gone away delighted with it, and knowing more than he did. Because we know everything — everything the Greeks and the Trojans suffered on the wide plain of Troy, by the will of the gods. And we know everything that happens on the fruitful earth.*

That is what they sang, in beautiful voices, and my heart wanted to listen. And I made signs with my eyebrows to my companions to untie me. They fell forward on the oars and rowed; and Perimedes and Eurylochus got up at once and tied me with more ropes, and pulled them tighter.

And when they had rowed past, and we could no longer hear the Sirens' voices or their song, my trusty companions took the wax out of their ears and untied me.<sup><a href="#book-12-note-2">2</a></sup>

---

Odysseus could have stopped his own ears, of course. There was wax enough, and nothing in Circe's instructions obliged him to listen; she offered it as an option, and it is the option nobody sensible would take. So he deafened every man aboard and had himself made helpless instead, and arranged to be the only person in the world who has heard that song and lived — and, as it happens, the only man on that ship who would ever be in a position to tell anybody about it. Which he is doing, at this moment, at dinner.

---

And the moment we had left that island behind, I saw smoke, and a great wave, and I heard a booming. And the oars flew out of their hands in terror, and all the oars splashed down along the current, and the ship stopped dead where she was.

And I went along the ship and stood over every man and heartened him with soft words. *Friends. We are not exactly ignorant of trouble. This is no worse than when the Cyclops shut us in his hollow cave by main force. Even out of that we got away, by my courage and my planning and my wits; and I think we shall remember this one too, one day.
