So come — hit the deep surf of the sea with your oars, and see whether Zeus will let us get out from under our destruction. And you, steersman — here are your orders, and keep them in your mind. Hold the ship out beyond that smoke and that surf, and hug the cliff on the other side, and do not let her drift off the other way without your noticing, or you will throw us all into disaster.*

And they did as I said, quickly.

I did not say a word to them about Scylla — a trouble there was no dealing with — in case my companions were frightened and stopped rowing and huddled together down inside the ship. And at that point I let Circe's grim instructions go clean out of my head, when she told me not to arm at all. I put my famous armour on, and took two long spears in my hands, and went up onto the fore-deck, because that was where I expected rocky Scylla to appear from first. And I could not make her out anywhere. My eyes got tired with staring, everywhere, up at that misty rock.

So we sailed up the narrow strait, and we were crying: Scylla on one side, and on the other divine Charybdis sucking the salt sea water down horribly. When she threw it up, she seethed and bubbled all over in a churning mess, like a cauldron on a great fire, and the spray flew high overhead and fell on the tops of both cliffs. And when she sucked the salt water down, the whole inside of her showed, churning, and the rock roared terribly all round, and the sea floor showed underneath, black with sand. And a green fear took hold of my men.

We were looking at *her*, frightened of dying — and Scylla took six of my companions out of the hollow ship, the six best of them in strength and in their hands.

I turned my eyes back to the fast ship, looking for my men, and I saw their feet and their hands already above me as they were lifted up. And they screamed and called out to me by name, that one last time, with their hearts in agony.

The way a fisherman on a jutting rock, with a long pole, throws his bait down as a trap for the little fishes, and when he catches one he pulls it up and out and throws it on the shore, writhing: that is how they were pulled up towards the rocks, writhing. And there in her doorway she ate them, while they screamed and stretched their hands out towards me, in the most terrible struggle of all.

That was the most pitiful thing my eyes ever saw, out of everything I suffered searching out the ways of the sea.

---

That is the only place in the poem where somebody is told the exact price of a course of action in advance and pays it deliberately. Circe does not hint and she does not speak in riddles: one way loses the whole ship, the other loses six men, and six is better than all. He does the arithmetic and takes the six. It is the correct decision, and a commander who refused it would kill everybody — but it is worth saying plainly that this is what command is, in a way the older poem never quite has to face, since in the *Iliad* men die in battle facing an enemy, and here six men who have done nothing are given away in advance on a goddess's recommendation.

And they are not told. He says so, and gives his reason, and the reason is professional and almost certainly right: had they known there was something overhead that could not be fought, they would have dropped the oars, and then the ship would have drifted, and Charybdis would have had all of them. Nevertheless he stood in the bows in full armour with two spears, watching for her, having been told plainly that arming was useless and would only cost him a second six. He did it anyway; he could not help it. So the picture to carry out of this book is of a man in armour at the front of a ship, staring up at a cliff for something he has been assured he cannot fight, while behind him the men he did not warn pull at their oars in ignorance and six of them go up off the deck like fish on a line.

---

So we got clear of the rocks and of Charybdis and of Scylla; and then we came to the island of the god, where the fine broad-browed cattle of the Sun were, and his many fat flocks. And while I was still out at sea in the black ship I could hear the lowing of cattle being penned, and sheep bleating. And into my mind came the words of the blind prophet Teiresias, and of Circe, who had both told me very strictly to keep away from that island.

So I spoke to my companions, sick at heart, and told them both prophecies and named both sources, and said: drive the black ship past the island.

And their spirits broke in them. And Eurylochus answered me straight away, and there was hate in it.

*You are a hard man, Odysseus. There is more strength in you than in other men and your limbs never get tired. You must be made entirely of iron, if you will not let your companions — worn out with hard work and lack of sleep — set foot on dry land, where we might get a decent supper ready on an island in the sea. Instead you tell us to go blundering off through the fast-coming night, driven away from the island over the misty water.*

*It is out of the night that the hard winds come, the ones that break ships up. How is any man to get out from under a sheer destruction, if a squall comes suddenly out of the South Wind or the blustering West — the ones that most often smash a ship apart, whatever the gods who rule us may want? No. Let us give way to the black night now and get our supper, and stay beside the fast ship. In the morning we will go aboard and put out into the wide sea.*

That is the best speech Eurylochus ever makes and nearly all of it is true. The men are exhausted; they have just watched six friends lifted off the deck and eaten; night is coming; and everything he says about the weather is not merely reasonable but professionally right. He is a seaman making a seaman's case. He is also entirely wrong, for the oldest of reasons: he does not know what his captain knows. He has not stood beside a pit in the dark and heard a dead prophet name that island. He is arguing about the weather with a man who is not arguing about the weather.

And all the rest of them agreed with him. And then I knew that some god was arranging trouble for us.

*Eurylochus, you force my hand; I am one man against all of you. Very well. But all of you swear me a great oath: that if we find a herd of cattle or a big flock of sheep, no man will kill a single cow or a single sheep out of the wicked folly of his heart. Sit quietly and eat the food that immortal Circe gave us.*

And they swore it, exactly as I told them to. And we moored the well-built ship in a hollow harbour beside a spring of sweet water, and my companions went ashore and made supper skilfully. And when they had put away all desire for food and drink, they began to weep, remembering the companions Scylla had taken and eaten. And a sweet sleep came over them while they were crying.

---

Then in the third watch of the night Zeus got up a screaming wind and an extraordinary storm, and hid the land and the sea alike in cloud, and night came rushing down out of the sky. And when Dawn came up we hauled the ship in and made her fast in a hollow cave, where the nymphs had their dancing floors and their seats. And I called them all together and said: friends, there is food and drink in the fast ship; let us keep our hands off these cattle, in case we come to harm; these belong to a dreadful god, the Sun, who sees everything and hears everything.

And their proud hearts agreed.

And then the South Wind blew for a whole month, and no other wind came at all, except the East and the South. Now as long as my men had food and red wine, they kept their hands off the cattle, because they wanted to live. But when all the provisions in the ship were used up, they had to go roving after game, whatever they could get: fish, and birds, anything that came to their hands, with bent hooks — because hunger was wearing away their stomachs.

And I went up the island to pray to the gods, hoping one of them would show me a way home. And when I had got away from my companions I washed my hands somewhere out of the wind and prayed to all the gods who hold Olympus.

And they poured a sweet sleep over my eyelids.

And Eurylochus began to put an evil plan to my companions.

*Listen to me, my companions, for all the bad things you have suffered. Every kind of death is hateful to us miserable men. But dying of hunger, and meeting your fate that way, is the most pitiful of all. Come on. Let us drive off the best of the Sun's cattle and sacrifice to the immortals who hold the wide sky. And if we ever get back to Ithaca, our own country, we will build a rich temple to the Sun straight away and put a great many fine offerings in it. And if he is angry about his straight-horned cattle, and wants to wreck our ship, and the other gods agree with him — then I would rather lose my life all at once, with one gulp at the wave, than be squeezed slowly to death on a desert island.*

And all the rest of them agreed with him. And at once they drove off the best of the Sun's cattle from close by. And they stood round them and prayed to the gods, pulling the soft leaves off a tall oak, because they had no white barley on the ship. And when they had prayed and cut the throats and flayed them, they cut out the thigh pieces and covered them with a double fold of fat and laid raw meat on top; and they had no wine to pour over the burning offerings, so they poured water instead, and roasted all the entrails.

And at that moment the sweet sleep went off my eyelids, and I went down to the fast ship and the shore of the sea. And when I was close to the ship the warm smell of the fat came round me, and I cried out to the immortal gods: *Father Zeus, and the rest of you blessed gods who live forever — you lulled me into a pitiless sleep, to destroy me. And my companions, left to themselves, have planned a monstrous thing.*

---

There is the pattern this poem has been assembling since the beach at Ismarus, complete at last. He warned them, in full, with both sources named. He lost the argument. He took the only step left and made them swear an oath, and they swore it and meant it. And then the wind blew for a month, and the food ran out, and he was up a hill asleep.

---

And Lampetie went as a messenger to the Sun to tell him we had killed his cattle. And he spoke among the immortals, furious.

*Father Zeus, and the rest of you blessed gods — take vengeance on the companions of Odysseus, who have insolently killed my cattle, the cattle I always took pleasure in, going up into the starry sky and turning back down again to earth. If they do not pay me a proper compensation, I shall go down into the house of Hades and shine among the dead.*

*Sun — go on shining among the immortals and among mortal men on the grain-giving earth. I shall very soon strike their fast ship with a bright thunderbolt and smash it to pieces in the middle of the wine-dark sea.*

(I had that from Calypso of the beautiful hair. She told me she had heard it herself from Hermes the messenger.)<sup><a href="#book-12-note-3">3</a></sup>

And when I got down to the ship I rebuked them, going from one to another. And we could find no remedy: the cattle were already dead. And then the gods began showing us portents. The hides crawled. The meat on the spits bellowed, both the roasted and the raw. And there was a noise like the voice of cattle.

For six days my trusty companions feasted on the best of the Sun's cattle. And when Zeus brought on the seventh day, then the wind stopped raging in a storm, and we went aboard at once and put out into the wide sea, and set up the mast and hoisted the white sail.

---

But when we had left that island behind, and no other land showed, nothing but sky and sea, then Zeus set a black cloud over the hollow ship, and the sea went dark underneath it.

She did not run for very long after that. The West Wind came at once, shrieking, blowing in a great tempest, and the blast of it snapped both the forestays of the mast; and the mast fell backwards, and all the gear spilled down into the bilge; and the mast caught the steersman on the head in the stern of the ship and smashed every bone in his skull together, and he went down off the deck like a diver, and his proud spirit left his bones.

And Zeus thundered at the same moment and threw his bolt into the ship. And she shuddered from end to end, struck by the bolt of Zeus, and filled with the smell of sulphur; and my men fell out of her. They were carried on the waves round the black ship like sea-crows, and the god took away their homecoming.

And I kept going up and down the ship until the sea tore the sides away from the keel, and the wave carried the bare hull along. And it broke the mast off level with the keel — and the backstay had been thrown over it, a rope made of oxhide — and with that I lashed the keel and the mast together, and sat on the two of them, and was carried along by the ruinous winds.

Then the West Wind stopped raging. And the South Wind came on quickly, bringing pain to my heart, because it meant I would have to measure out the road back to deadly Charybdis all over again. All night I was carried, and at sunrise I came to Scylla's cliff and to terrible Charybdis. And she was sucking the salt sea water down.

And I sprang up towards the tall fig tree and got hold of it and hung on like a bat. There was nowhere I could get a footing or climb up: the roots were far below and the branches were out of reach above, long and heavy, and they overshadowed Charybdis. And I held on grimly and waited for her to spit the mast and the keel up again. And they came at last, to my great relief. At the hour when a man gets up from the assembly and goes to his supper — a man who has been settling a great many quarrels among young men who want a judgement — at that hour the timbers came out of Charybdis.

And I let go with my hands and feet and dropped, and came down with a crash in the water beside those long timbers; and I got up on them and rowed along with my hands. And the father of gods and men did not let Scylla catch sight of me. Otherwise I would not have got out from under a sheer destruction.

Nine days I was carried, and on the tenth night the gods brought me to Ogygia, where Calypso lives, who took me in and looked after me.

But why should I tell you all this? I told it to you and your good wife yesterday, in this house, and I hate telling a story twice when it has already been told properly.

---

And he stops there, which is a very fine last line: not a flourish, not a summary and certainly not a moral, but a small piece of good manners. *You have heard the rest. It would be rude to repeat myself.* It closes the frame, too. From here to the end there is no more first person and no more monsters. The next time we see him he will be asleep in the bottom of somebody else's boat, and when he wakes he will be on a beach he does not recognise, in his own country, and he will start lying again for quite different reasons.

I shall take it back from here.

---

## NOTES TO BOOK TWELVE

<a id="book-12-note-1"></a>
1. **The Argo, and a poem that is not this one.** Circe drops the name of another ship and another voyage as though everybody knew all about it, which they did — the story of Jason and the golden fleece was old and famous when this poem was young. Notice how the reference is made: not *there was a ship called Argo*, but *the Argo that everybody sings about*, which is one poet acknowledging a rival hit. It is the clearest single sign that the two poems we have are survivors from a whole crowded literature. There were epics about Thebes, about the war before the war at Troy, about the homecomings of all the other Greek captains, about Heracles, about the Argo; there were men who could sing every one of them; and all of it is gone, except the odd line quoted by a later writer, and except for moments like this, where one poem waves at another across the water as it goes past.

<a id="book-12-note-2"></a>
2. **The Sirens, and what they are not.** Homer never describes them: not their faces, not their bodies, not their number beyond Circe's passing *the two Sirens* — nothing but a meadow, a heap of rotting men, and a voice. The bird-bodies come from Greek vase-painting and funerary sculpture; the fish-tails come from a medieval muddle with mermaids in the north; and the seductress with the comb and the mirror is largely the nineteenth century, which had its own reasons for wanting the danger at sea to be a woman. What the poem does give, and gives precisely, is the content of the song, and it is a promise of knowledge: we know what happened at Troy, and we know everything that happens on the earth. That is what is written on the hook. The bones in that meadow belong to men who stopped rowing because they wanted to be told something.

<a id="book-12-note-3"></a>
3. **How he knows what Zeus said.** This is one of my favourite lines in the poem and it is nearly always skipped. Odysseus has just reported a private conversation on Olympus between the Sun and the king of the gods — and he stops dead, mid-story, to tell his audience where he got it. Calypso told him; and she said Hermes had told her. Think what that means: somewhere on that island, in the middle of those seven years, a goddess and a man sat down and she passed on a piece of divine gossip about the day his crew died, which she had from the messenger of the gods, and he has carried it ever since and is retailing it now at a dinner party. The poem makes nothing of it. It simply notes the chain of custody, the way a careful witness does — and it is the only place in four books where the teller stops to explain how he came by something he could not have seen. It is exactly the sort of thing an honest man does, and exactly the sort of thing a very good liar does, and there is no way on earth to tell which from the outside.

<a id="book-12-note-4"></a>
4. **The cattle of the Sun, and a promise kept.** Turn back to the first page of Book One and look at what the poem chose to say about the crew in its opening breath: that they died through their own recklessness, the fools, because they ate the cattle of the Sun, and the Sun took away their day of homecoming. That is the only specific event in the entire twelve-year voyage that the poem announces in advance. Not the Cyclops, not the witch, not the descent to the dead. This. Which tells you what the poem thinks the story of the crew actually is; and it has now delivered exactly what it promised, eleven books later, with the reasons attached — they were starving, they had sworn an oath, their captain was asleep on a hillside, and the man who talked them into it made a speech about how a quick death is better than a slow one.

<a id="book-12-note-5"></a>
5. **Between Scylla and Charybdis.** The phrase has been in English for centuries and most people who use it do not know it means something quite specific: not merely two dangers, but two dangers of *unequal and known* cost, where the whole art lies in choosing the smaller deliberately and paying it. The rock will certainly take six men; the whirlpool may take everybody. Circe's advice is not to be brave and not to be clever — it is to steer close to the thing that will definitely maim you in order to stay clear of the thing that might destroy you altogether. People have been trying to put the pair on a map since antiquity, the usual candidate being the Strait of Messina, which has a real tidal race in it; I would not lean on it. Charting this poem is a very old amusement that has produced a large library and no agreement whatever, and the poem is doing something more interesting than describing a coastline. It is describing a decision, of a kind anybody who has had to make one will recognise, and it has been lending people the words for it ever since.

---

*Book Thirteen: In Which a Man Is Carried Home Asleep, and Does Not Know Where He Is.*


<div class="page-break"></div>

<!-- Source: book/odyssey-book-13.md -->

# THE ODYSSEY
### Retold in English, with Explanations

---

## BOOK THIRTEEN
### In Which a Man Is Carried Home Asleep, and Does Not Know Where He Is

---

I have the story back, and I should say at once that everything is about to change. For twelve books we have been travelling, and if you have been keeping a map in your head it is by now a large and crowded one. From here there is no map at all. We arrive in one small place and stay in it for twelve books and never leave, and the whole of the rest of this poem happens on a rocky island you could walk across in a day, mostly indoors, and mostly among people talking to one another. The monsters are finished; there is not another one in the book. What takes their place is a farmhouse, a pigsty, a hall full of young men eating another man's dinner, and a woman upstairs who has been thinking for twenty years — and I will say plainly that I find the second half the greater achievement, because anybody with a good imagination can put a giant in a cave, and it takes something else to make you hold your breath over a husband and wife who both know more than they are saying.

---

They all sat in silence, held in the spell of it, through the shadowy hall. And Alcinous answered him:

"Odysseus — since you have come to my house with its bronze floor and its high roof, I do not think you will be driven off your course again, badly as you have suffered. And to every one of you here, who are always drinking the sparkling wine of the elders in my halls and listening to the singer, I say this. There are clothes already stored in the polished chest for the stranger, and worked gold, and all the other gifts the Phaeacian counsellors brought here. Come — let us each of us give him a great tripod and a cauldron as well; and then we will collect it back from the people afterwards, because it is a hard thing for one man to give freely without being repaid."

That pleased them all, and they went off home to bed. And when Dawn came up they hurried down to the ship carrying the bronze; and the king himself went about the ship and stowed everything under the benches with his own hands, so that none of it would get in the crew's way when they were pulling on the oars.

Then they went back to the house and made a feast, and Alcinous sacrificed an ox to Zeus; and they burned the thigh pieces and enjoyed a splendid dinner, and Demodocus sang among them, the singer whom the people honoured.

But Odysseus kept turning his head towards the blazing sun, willing it to set, because he was longing to be gone. The way a man longs for his supper when a pair of wine-dark oxen have been dragging the jointed plough through fallow ground all day for him, and the sun going down is a very welcome thing, so that he can go to his supper at last, and his knees ache as he walks — that is how welcome the setting of the sun was to Odysseus.

"Lord Alcinous, most distinguished of all your people. Pour your libations now and send me off unharmed; and my good wishes to all of you. Everything my heart wanted is done: my passage home, and gifts given in friendship. May the gods make them prosper for me. And may I find my faultless wife at home when I come, and everyone I love unhurt. And may all of you here make your wedded wives and your children glad, and may the gods grant you every kind of excellence, and may no trouble ever come near your people."

They all approved. And Odysseus stood up and put his two-handled cup into Arete's hands. "Fare well, queen, all your years, until old age comes, and death, which come to everybody. I am going now. May you have joy in this house of your children and your people, and of Alcinous the king."

And with that he stepped over the threshold. Heralds went with him down to the fast ship, and Arete sent her women too: one carrying a clean cloak and tunic, and one bringing the strong chest, and another with bread and red wine. And when they had got it all aboard, they spread a rug and a linen sheet for Odysseus on the deck at the stern of the hollow ship, so that he could sleep soundly. And he went aboard and lay down in silence.

They sat down in order at the oars and cast the cable off the pierced stone, and leaned back and threw up the sea with their blades. And a sweet sleep fell on his eyelids: unbroken, very sweet, and extremely like death.

The way four stallions harnessed abreast on a plain spring forward together under the lash, and rise high in their stride and get through the road quickly — that is how the stern of that ship lifted, and behind her the dark wave of the loud-roaring sea went seething past. She ran on, steady and safe, and not even the wheeling hawk could have kept up with her, which is the fastest thing that flies. So she ran, cutting the waves, carrying a man whose mind was like the mind of the gods, who had suffered a great many griefs in his heart, and who was now asleep, quite still, and had forgotten everything he had suffered.

---

And when the brightest star came up, the one that most often announces the light of early Dawn, the seafaring ship drew in to the island.

There is a harbour there belonging to Phorcys, the old man of the sea, in the country of Ithaca; and two headlands run out into it, sheer on the seaward side but sloping down towards the harbour, and they keep off the great waves that hard winds raise outside, so that inside, once they have come to their anchorage, well-benched ships can lie without any mooring at all. And at the head of the harbour there is a long-leaved olive tree, and close beside it a lovely cave, full of shadow, sacred to the nymphs who are called Naiads. Inside it there are mixing bowls and jars made of stone, and the bees store their honey in them; and there are long looms of stone, where the nymphs weave their sea-purple webs, and it is a wonder to see; and there is water in there, always running. And it has two doors. One faces the North Wind, and that is the way men go down into it. The other faces the South, and belongs to the gods; and men do not go in that way at all. It is the road of the immortals.<sup><a href="#book-13-note-1">1</a></sup>

They rowed in there, knowing the place from old days; and the ship ran up onto the beach for half her length, driven on by the hands of the rowers. And they lifted Odysseus out of the hollow ship, still in the linen sheet and the bright rug, and laid him down on the sand, overpowered with sleep. And they carried out the goods the Phaeacians had given him and piled it all together beside the trunk of the olive tree, well off the road, in case some traveller came by and robbed him before he woke.

Then they went home again.

---

But Poseidon had not forgotten the threats he made against Odysseus long ago, and he went to ask Zeus what he meant to do about it.

"Father Zeus. I shall not be honoured among the immortal gods any longer, when mortal men do not honour me in the least — the Phaeacians, who are of my own blood. I always said Odysseus would get home only after a great deal of suffering; I never denied him a homecoming altogether, since you had promised him one and bowed your head on it. And now they have carried him asleep in a fast ship over the sea and set him down in Ithaca, and given him gifts past counting — bronze and gold and woven cloth, more than he could ever have brought out of Troy if he had come home unhurt with his fair share of the plunder."

"What a thing to say, wide-ruling Earthshaker. The gods do not dishonour you at all; it would be a hard business to assail the eldest and best of us with dishonour. And if any man gives way to his own strength and does not honour you, you always have your revenge afterwards. Do whatever you like, and whatever pleases your heart."

"I would have done it long ago, exactly as you say — but I always hold back from your anger and keep out of its way. What I should like now is to smash that beautiful Phaeacian ship on the misty sea as she comes back from her escort duty, so that they will stop this business and give up ferrying men about. And I should like to put a great mountain over their city."

"Here is what seems best to me. When all the people are looking out from the town, watching her come on — then turn her into a stone close inshore, a stone shaped like a fast ship, so that everyone will marvel at it. And then put your great mountain over their city."

So Poseidon went to Scheria and waited there. And when the seafaring ship came in, running fast and close, the Earthshaker came up to her and struck her flat with the palm of his hand and turned her into stone, and rooted her to the bottom by pressing down; and then he went away.

And the Phaeacians stood talking to one another, and one would look at the man beside him and say: "Who has bound our fast ship on the sea as she was running home? We could see the whole of her a moment ago."

And Alcinous spoke among them. "This is the fulfilment of the old prophecy my father used to tell me. He said Poseidon was angry with us because we give safe passage to everybody, and that one day, as a beautiful Phaeacian ship came home from an escort, the god would smash her on the misty sea and put a great mountain over our city. That is what the old man said. And now all of it is coming true.

"So let every one of us do as I say. Stop escorting mortals, from now on, whoever comes to our city. And let us sacrifice twelve chosen bulls to Poseidon, and hope he may pity us and not put a long mountain over our town."

And they were frightened, and got the bulls ready. So they were praying to the lord Poseidon — the leaders and the counsellors of the Phaeacian people — standing about the altar.

---

And there the poem leaves them, and never goes back. We are not told whether the mountain fell.

The last we see of the kindest people in this book — who took a naked stranger off a beach, fed him before asking his name, gave him a chair their own prince had to get out of, loaded him with treasure and refused to be thanked, and carried him home for nothing while he slept — is a crowd of them at an altar with twelve bulls, praying that a hill will not come down on their harbour. I have found no way of making that comfortable. Alcinous did not overreach; he kept the law of guest-friendship rather better than it required. What has happened is that a nation whose whole vocation is carrying lost men home has crossed a god whose particular business, for twenty years, has been stopping one lost man from getting home — and has done it by being good at the thing they are good at. Their virtue is the offence. And the poem stops the sentence halfway, so that we are left with the raised hands and the shadow of a hill that may or may not be coming.<sup><a href="#book-13-note-2">2</a></sup>

---

And Odysseus woke up in his own country, and did not know it. He had been away a long time; and besides, Athena had poured a mist round the place, so that she could make him unrecognisable to everyone and tell him what he needed to know, and so that his wife and his townspeople and his friends should not know him until the suitors had paid for every one of their offences. So everything looked strange to its own master: the long paths, and the harbours where ships can lie, and the steep rocks, and the trees in leaf.

He sprang up and stood and looked at his own country, and groaned, and struck both his thighs with the flat of his hands.

"What is it now? Whose country have I come to this time? Are they violent and wild and unjust, or do they welcome strangers, and have they god-fearing minds? And where am I to take all this property? And where am I to go myself?

"I wish it had stayed with the Phaeacians. I could have gone to some other great king, who would have entertained me and sent me on my way. As it is, I do not know where to put this, and I am not going to leave it here for somebody else to walk off with.

"It seems the Phaeacian leaders were not so wise and just after all. They have taken me to the wrong country. They said they would bring me to Ithaca, and they have not done it. May Zeus of the suppliants pay them out.

"But come — let me count my goods and see whether they have gone off with anything in their hollow ship."

And he counted the beautiful tripods and the cauldrons, and the gold, and the fine woven cloth. And not one thing was missing. And then he cried for his own country, dragging himself along the shore of the loud-roaring sea, grieving heavily.

---

Home at last, after twenty years, and the first thing he does on the soil of Ithaca is take an inventory. I would not make him small for it — he has woken alone on an unknown beach with no crew, no ship and a heap of portable wealth lying in the open, which in this world is less a fortune than a reason for somebody to kill you. But notice that he finds nothing missing, and it does not shift him an inch: the Phaeacians have done exactly what they promised and stacked his treasure under a tree with more care than most men would take with their own, and he counts every cup and goes on grieving. He has been right to be suspicious so often that his mind runs there before his eyes can argue. The mist that is really keeping him from recognising the place is not entirely the goddess's.

---

Then Athena came up to him in the likeness of a young man, a shepherd of sheep, delicate-looking, the way kings' sons are, with a well-made double cloak round his shoulders and a javelin in his hand. And Odysseus was glad to see him.

"Friend — since you are the first person I have met in this place — good day to you. Do not come at me with any ill will. Save these goods of mine, and save me. I pray to you as I would to a god, and I have come to your knees. Tell me this truly. What country is this? What people? Is it one of the clear-seen islands, or some coast of the mainland sloping down to the sea?"

"You must be a fool, stranger, or you have come a very long way, if you are asking about this country. It is not so nameless as all that. A great many people know it. It is rugged, and no good for driving horses; but it is not a poor place either, for all that it is narrow. There is grain here past describing, and wine as well; and there is always rain on it and fresh dew; it is good country for goats and for cattle; there is timber of every kind, and the watering places never fail. So the name of Ithaca, stranger, has reached even to Troy, which they tell me is a long way from the land of Greece."

And the heart of the much-enduring man leapt, and he was glad because of his own country. And then he did not tell her the truth. He held back the thing he had been about to say, always turning over some very shrewd counsel in his breast.

"Yes — I heard of Ithaca even in Crete, out over the sea; and now I have come here myself, with these goods. And I left as much again behind for my children when I ran, because I killed a man: the son of Idomeneus, Orsilochus, who was quicker on his feet than anybody in the whole of Crete. He wanted to rob me of my plunder from Troy, that I had gone through so much for, because I would not do his father a favour and serve under him at Troy, but had my own command. I struck him with a bronze-tipped spear as he came in from the field; I lay in wait for him beside the road with one companion, and a black night covered the sky, and nobody saw us.

"And when I had killed him I went to a ship at once and begged the lordly Phoenicians, and gave them as much plunder as satisfied them. I asked them to take me and set me down at Pylos, or at Elis. But the force of the wind drove them away from there, very much against their will; they were not trying to cheat me. And we came here off our course in the night. We rowed into the harbour with a great deal of trouble, and not one of us gave a thought to supper, badly as we wanted it; we simply got out of the ship and lay down. And a sweet sleep came over me, tired as I was; and they took my goods out of the hollow ship and set them down beside me where I was lying on the sand, and went aboard, and sailed for Sidon. And I was left behind, sick at heart."

And Athena smiled at him, and stroked him with her hand.<sup><a href="#book-13-note-3">3</a></sup>

---

She turned into a woman then, tall and beautiful and skilled at glorious handiwork.

"He would have to be a cunning man, and a thief, who could get past you in any kind of trickery — even if it were a god who met you. You terrible man. Crafty-minded. Never tired of deceiving. So even in your own country you were not going to give up your tricks and your lying stories, which you love from the bottom of your heart.

"Come — let us not talk about it any more. The two of us know all about craft. You are far the best of all men at planning and at speaking, and I am famous among all the gods for wisdom and for sharpness. And you did not know Athena, the daughter of Zeus, who always stands beside you and guards you in every trouble — and who made you loved by all the Phaeacians.

"And I have come here now to weave a plan with you, and to hide the goods the Phaeacians gave you, because I put it in their minds; and to tell you how much you still have to suffer in your own well-built house. Endure it. You must. And do not tell anybody, man or woman, that you have come back from your wandering. Take a great deal of pain in silence, and put up with men's violence."

"Goddess, it is hard for a mortal man to know you when he meets you, however clever he is, because you take whatever shape you please. But I do know this: you were kind to me in the old days, all the while we sons of the Greeks were fighting at Troy. And when we had sacked the steep city of Priam (Troy) and gone away in our ships, and a god scattered the Greeks — after that I never saw you. I never noticed you coming aboard my ship to keep grief away from me. I went on wandering with a torn heart until the gods let me out of it.

"So now I beg you by your father — because I do not believe I have come to Ithaca; I think I am roaming about in some other country and you are saying this to mock me — tell me whether I really have come home."

"That is always the way your mind runs. And that is exactly why I cannot abandon you when you are in trouble — because you are civil, and quick-witted, and steady. Any other man coming home from wandering would have rushed off gladly to see his children and his wife in his own halls. You do not even want to *ask* about them, or find anything out, until you have first put your wife to the test — who is sitting in your halls exactly as she always was, and the nights and the days waste away for her, miserably, while she cries.

"I was never in any doubt about it myself. I knew you would come home, after losing all your companions. But I did not want to fight with Poseidon, my father's brother, who nursed his anger against you and was furious because you blinded his own son.

"But come, and I will show you the country of Ithaca, so that you can be sure."<sup><a href="#book-13-note-4">4</a></sup>

And she scattered the mist, and the land appeared. And Odysseus was glad, delighted with his own country, and kissed the grain-giving earth; and he lifted his hands and prayed to the nymphs. "Naiad nymphs, daughters of Zeus — I never expected to see you again. Now I greet you with these loving prayers. And we shall give you gifts as we used to, if the daughter of Zeus is kind and lets me live, and brings my dear son up to be a man."

---

That exchange is the hinge of the whole second half, and it goes past very lightly because she is laughing at him while she says it. *Any other man would have run home to his wife and children; you will not even ask after them until you have tested her.* His mother is dead of missing him and he has spoken to her ghost; his father is sleeping in the ashes; his son has grown up without ever seeing his face; and his wife has held off a hundred and eight armed men with a loom and her wits. He has landed, and his first instinct is not to find them but to find out. Athena is not scolding him — she admires it, and it is why she has stayed — but the poem is not the goddess, and it will spend ten books making us feel what it costs.

---

Then they sat down together beside the trunk of the sacred olive and planned death for the suitors.

"Son of Laertes. Think how you are going to get your hands on those shameless men, who have been lording it in your halls for three years now, courting your godlike wife and offering her wedding gifts. And she is forever grieving for you to come home, and she holds out hope to all of them, and makes each man promises, and sends them messages — and her mind is on something else entirely."

"Well. So I was very nearly going to die in my own halls the way Agamemnon died, if you had not told me all this, goddess. Come — weave me a plan, so that I can pay them back. And stand beside me, and put the same courage and daring into me that you did when we untied the shining diadem of Troy. If you would stand by me with that much fire in you, lady goddess, I would fight three hundred men."

"I shall be with you, certainly, and I shall not lose sight of you when we are about this work. And I think a good deal of the floor is going to be spattered with the blood and brains of the men who are eating up your living.

"Come now — I shall make you unrecognisable to everybody. I shall shrivel the good skin on your supple limbs, and take the fair hair off your head, and put a rag round you that anybody would shudder to see a man wearing; and I shall film over your eyes, that were so fine before — so that you look contemptible to all the suitors, and to your wife, and to the son you left behind.

"And you go first of all to the swineherd, who looks after your pigs. He is loyal to you, and fond of your son, and fond of steady Penelope. You will find him sitting with the swine, beside the Raven's Rock and the spring of Arethusa, eating acorns and drinking the black water — the things that make swine run to good fat. Stay there, and sit with him, and ask him about everything, while I go to Sparta to call your son home."

"Then why on earth did you not tell him, when you knew the whole of it? Was it so that he could wander about the barren sea in misery as well, while other men eat his living?"

"Do not let him weigh on you. I sent him myself, and I went with him, so that he might come out of it with a good name. He is not suffering at all; he is sitting comfortably in the house of Menelaus with an endless supply of everything beside him. There are young men lying in wait for him in a black ship, meaning to kill him before he can get back. I do not think it will happen. I think the earth will cover a few of those suitors first."

And with that she touched him with her wand. She shrivelled the good skin on his supple limbs and destroyed the fair hair on his head and put an old man's skin all over him, and filmed over his eyes, which had been so fine. And she put a different cloak on him, and a tunic — filthy things, torn, blackened with foul smoke — and over it all she threw the big hide of a fast deer, worn bald. And she gave him a staff, and a shabby bag full of holes with a twisted cord to sling it by.

And when they had settled everything the two of them parted; and she went off to Sparta, to fetch his son.<sup><a href="#book-13-note-5">5</a></sup>

---

## NOTES TO BOOK THIRTEEN

<a id="book-13-note-1"></a>
1. **The cave with two doors.** A cave at the head of the harbour, sacred to the water-nymphs, with stone mixing bowls and stone looms inside it, bees making honey in the jars, water always running, and two entrances — a northern one for men and a southern one that only gods use. It is a beautiful piece of description and later readers could not leave it alone. There survives a whole treatise on it, written some nine hundred years after the poem by the philosopher Porphyry, arguing that every detail is an allegory of the soul's descent into the body and its return: the cave is the material world, the honey is the pleasure that traps us, the two doors are the gates by which souls come into life and go out of it, and so on for many pages. I mention it partly because it is charming and partly as a warning, since this poem attracts that kind of reading the way a wall attracts ivy, and the ivy is often lovely and occasionally tells you more about the reader than the wall. At the plain level the cave is doing something simple and rather good: he is being put ashore, unconscious, at the threshold of a place where the gods have their own private door.

<a id="book-13-note-2"></a>
2. **The sentence that is never finished.** The prophecy was planted in Book Eight, note 4, where Alcinous mentioned it in the middle of a boast and shrugged it off. It has now half come true: the ship is stone. Whether the mountain came down, the poem does not say. Ancient readers argued about it hard, and the argument turned on one Greek word in Zeus's instructions, which can be read either as *and cover their city* or as *but do not cover their city* — the whole fate of a nation resting on a syllable, with some manuscripts and some ancient critics going each way. So the ambiguity may not merely be the poem declining to tell us; it may be built into the text at the level of the grammar, and it has been unresolved since antiquity. I find I would rather it stayed that way. A poem that has spent three books teaching you to love a people, and then puts them at an altar under a shadow and looks away, is doing something no tidier ending would do half so well.

<a id="book-13-note-3"></a>
3. **The Cretan lies.** This is the first of several — he will tell four or five more before the poem ends, to the swineherd, to the suitors, to Penelope and to his own father — and they are worth watching as a set, because they are not improvisations. They are variations on one story, told with such consistency that scholars call them the Cretan tales: he is always a Cretan of good family, there is always a killing or a wrong done to him, there is always a flight by sea, and there are almost always Phoenician traders involved. He can produce it under any pressure, in any company, at any length. Two things make Crete a good choice. It was a real and famous place with a real and famous king, far enough from Ithaca to be unverifiable but close enough to be plausible, and exactly the sort of place a wandering man of rank might genuinely have come from. And Cretans already had a certain reputation in the Greek world for telling stories; the proverb about Cretan liars is later than this poem, but the joke it draws on is not. When Odysseus wants a false name and a false country, he reaches for the one that comes with a wink attached.

<a id="book-13-note-4"></a>
4. **Why Athena stayed away.** She gives her reason plainly, and it is worth having, because it explains how the gods work here and will save a good deal of puzzling later. She did not abandon him and was never in doubt that he would survive; she simply would not fight her uncle. Poseidon was angry, Poseidon had a right to be angry, and no other god was going to stand in his way while the anger lasted — not out of fear exactly, but because that is not how these gods deal with one another. They do not overrule; they wait. Zeus does the same thing in this very book: told that his brother wants to punish a whole nation, he says, in effect, *please yourself.* So divine favour in this poem is not protection. Athena loves this man and has loved him for twenty years, and it did not save one of his ships or one of his men. What it does is arrive at the right moment with the right information, once the other god's back is turned. Worth knowing, when people call the *Odyssey* a poem in which the gods look after their favourites.

<a id="book-13-note-5"></a>
5. **The beggar's kit, and a debt paid.** Note what she gives him: a staff, and a bag with holes in it on a twisted string. That is the whole equipment of a professional beggar in this world, and beggary was a recognised way of living rather than a simple catastrophe — a man went from house to house, was given scraps, carried them in the bag, and had a place, of a low kind, in the order of things. Hospitality worked at the bottom of society as well as the top, and there were rules about it that men were expected to keep even towards the poorest arrival; much of what happens in the next eight books turns on who keeps them. — And there is a larger thing here. In Book Nine this man stood in the stern of a ship, out of danger, with his crew hanging off his arms begging him to be quiet, and shouted his own name across the water to a blinded giant, because he could not bear that the deed should belong to nobody. It cost him ten years. He is now going to walk into his own house in a filthy hide with a holed bag over his shoulder and not say that name to a living soul for eight books, while men throw furniture at him. Of everything the wand does to him on that beach, that is the real disguise, and it is the hardest thing this poem ever asks him to do.

---

*Book Fourteen: In Which a Swineherd Gives Away What He Cannot Spare, and Is Told a Great Many Lies.*


<div class="page-break"></div>

<!-- Source: book/odyssey-book-14.md -->

# THE ODYSSEY
### Retold in English, with Explanations

---

## BOOK FOURTEEN
### In Which a Swineherd Gives Away What He Cannot Spare, and Is Told a Great Many Lies

---

He went up from the harbour by a rough track, through wooded country and over the hills, to the place Athena had told him of, where he would find the good swineherd, who looked after his property better than any of the servants Odysseus had ever acquired.

He found him sitting in the doorway of his yard — a high yard, built in the open with a view all round, big and handsome, and standing free. The swineherd had built it himself for the pigs of his absent master, without saying anything to his mistress or to old Laertes: he had quarried the stones and put a hedge of wild pear along the top. And outside he had driven in a stockade of split oak stakes, all round, close together, taking the dark part of the wood. And inside the yard he had made twelve sties, side by side, for the sows to sleep in, and fifty breeding pigs were penned in each. The boars slept outside; there were far fewer of them, because the lordly suitors kept eating them and thinning them down, since the swineherd had to send them the pick of his fattest hog every day. There were three hundred and sixty left. And four dogs lay beside them, like wild beasts, which the swineherd had reared himself.

The dogs saw Odysseus and came at him barking, and he sat down cunningly and let the staff drop out of his hand. And there in his own farmyard he would have been badly mauled, but the swineherd came out fast on quick feet, and the leather fell out of his hands as he ran through the doorway shouting, and he drove the dogs off in all directions with a shower of stones.

"Old man, the dogs very nearly tore you to pieces, all in a moment, and you would have poured shame all over me. And the gods have given me plenty else to grieve about. Here I sit mourning for a master who was like a god, and rearing fat hogs for other men to eat, while he is very likely somewhere in a foreign country going hungry — if he is even alive and still sees the light of the sun.

"Come along in, old man. Come into the hut. When you have had bread and wine and eaten your fill, you can tell me where you are from and what you have suffered."

And the good swineherd led him in and sat him down, throwing down a great heap of brushwood and spreading over it the shaggy hide of a wild goat, which he slept on himself, and it was big and thick. And Odysseus was glad to be received like that, and said so.

"Stranger, it would not be right for me to turn away a stranger, not even one worse off than you. All strangers and beggars come from Zeus. What we give is small, and welcome; that is the way with servants, who live in fear when young men are the masters. The gods have certainly blocked the homecoming of the man who would have been fond of me and given me things of my own — a house, and a piece of land, and a wife other men wanted — the sort of thing a kind master gives a servant who has worked hard for him and whose work the gods have prospered. My work has prospered here. He would have looked after me handsomely if he had grown old in this place. But he is dead.

"I wish Helen's whole tribe had been wiped out root and branch, since she loosened the knees of so many men."<sup><a href="#book-14-note-1">1</a></sup>

---

He got up at once and pulled his belt tight round his tunic and went out to the sties where the young pigs were penned, and picked out two and brought them in and sacrificed them both, and singed them and cut them up and spitted them. And when he had roasted it all he brought it and set it in front of Odysseus, hot, still on the spits, and sprinkled white barley meal over it; and he mixed honey-sweet wine in an ivy-wood bowl and sat down opposite and told him to eat.

"Eat now, stranger — such as servants have. Sucking pigs. The suitors eat the fatted hogs, and they have no thought in their minds of the anger of the gods, and no pity.

"The blessed gods do not love a cruel action. They honour justice, and the right things men do. Even men who go out raiding another man's country, and Zeus grants them plunder and they load their ships and come home — even on their hearts there falls a heavy fear of what the gods will do.

"But these men know something. They have heard the voice of some god about my master's grim death, and so they will not court honestly and they will not go back to their own houses, but eat up his goods at their ease, insolently, and spare nothing. Every day and every night that comes from Zeus they slaughter victims, and not one or two either; and they draw the wine off and waste it.

"His living was enormous. No lord had so much, not on the dark mainland and not on Ithaca itself. Twenty men together have not so much wealth. I will count it for you. Twelve herds of cattle on the mainland, and as many flocks of sheep, and as many droves of pigs, and as many wide-ranging herds of goats, all pastured by hired men and by his own herdsmen. And here in Ithaca there are eleven herds of goats grazing at the far end of the island, with good men watching them; and every day each man drives in a beast for the suitors, the best of the fattened goats he has. And I look after these pigs and guard them, and pick out the best boar and send it up to them."

Odysseus ate the meat and drank the wine, ravenously, and said nothing, sowing trouble for the suitors. And when he had eaten and his heart was satisfied, the swineherd filled the bowl he had been drinking from himself and handed it over, brimming; and Odysseus took it, and was glad.

"Friend — who is this man who bought you with his own property? You say he was rich and powerful, and that he died for Agamemnon's honour. Tell me his name. I may know him. Zeus and the other immortals know whether I have seen him and can bring you news. I have wandered a great deal."

"Old man, no wanderer who came here with news of him would ever persuade his wife and his dear son. Men who need a lodging tell lies as they please and are not interested in telling the truth. Anybody who turns up on Ithaca goes straight to my mistress and spins her a tale, and she takes them in kindly and asks about everything, and the tears run down her face, which is what a woman does when her husband has died somewhere else.

"You would soon make up a story yourself, old man, if somebody gave you a cloak and a tunic for it.

"But by now the dogs and the swift birds will have torn the skin off his bones, and the life will have left him. Or the fish will have eaten him in the sea, and his bones will be lying on some beach wrapped in sand. So he has died out there; and there is grief left for all his friends afterwards, and for me most of all. I shall never find so kind a master again, wherever I go — not if I went back to the house of my own father and mother, where I was born and where they brought me up.

"And I do not grieve so much for them, badly as I want to see them with my own eyes in my own country, as I am taken with longing for Odysseus, who is gone. I shrink from saying his name, stranger, even though he is not here. He was extremely fond of me and cared about me in his heart. I call him *honoured sir*, though he is a long way off."

---

I should like to introduce this man properly, because we have just met the most decent person in the poem and he is going to be in it for the rest of the way.

Eumaeus keeps pigs. He is a slave; he says so himself in the second sentence he speaks, and mentions, without any particular weight, that the master who bought him has been gone twenty years and that he has kept the herd up regardless. He has built the yard he is standing in with his own hands, quarried the stone himself, hedged it and stockaded it, and done the whole thing on his own initiative without troubling the mistress or the old man. And he has done it for a household that has not sent him an order in two decades.

Notice what he does when a filthy old vagrant with a holed bag comes out of the woods. He drives the dogs off, apologises for them, gives up his own bed of brushwood and goat hide, kills two of the pigs he is answerable for, and hands over his own drinking bowl full. He has nothing whatever, and he gives away rather more of it than he can afford, to a stranger with no claim on him at all, because all strangers come from Zeus.

Up at the house, a hundred and eight men of good family are eating the same estate at the rate of a hog a day, and have been for three years.

The poem does not point at that. It does not need to; it simply puts the two households side by side and lets you look. But it does do one thing here that it does almost nowhere else, and it is a very strange and touching mannerism: when Eumaeus speaks, the poem sometimes turns and addresses him directly — *and you said to him in reply, swineherd Eumaeus* — as though the poet had temporarily forgotten he was narrating and had begun talking to the man instead.<sup><a href="#book-14-note-2">2</a></sup>

---

"Friend, since you deny it altogether and say he will never come back — well, I will not merely say it, I will swear it. Odysseus is coming home. And let me have my reward for the news the moment he sets foot in his own house: dress me in a cloak and a tunic, good clothes. Before that I will not take anything, badly as I need it. I hate a man who gives way to poverty and tells lies as much as I hate the gates of death.

"Let Zeus be my witness first of all, and this table of hospitality, and the hearth of Odysseus that I have come to. All of it will happen exactly as I say. Within this very month Odysseus will come here. As the old moon goes out and the new one comes in, he will come home; and he will take his revenge on every man who is dishonouring his wife and his son."

"Old man, I shall never pay you that reward, and Odysseus is not coming home. Drink your wine in peace and let us talk about something else; do not remind me of it. The heart in my breast hurts when anybody mentions my honoured lord.

"We will let the oath alone. But I do wish Odysseus would come, as I want him to, and Penelope too, and old Laertes and godlike Telemachus. And now I am grieving without stopping for the boy — for Telemachus, whom the gods reared like a young tree, and I used to think he would be no worse than his father among men, a wonder to look at. And some god, or some man, has upset the balance of his mind, and he has gone off to sacred Pylos after news of his father; and the lordly suitors are lying in wait for him on the way home, so that the line of Arceisius may be wiped out of Ithaca and leave no name.

"But let him be, whether he is caught or gets away. Tell me about your own troubles. Who are you? Where do you come from? What ship did you come on? How did the sailors bring you to Ithaca?"

---

"I will tell you all of it truly. I only wish the two of us had food and sweet wine enough to sit here in the hut and feast quietly while other people did the work — then I could talk for a whole year and not get to the end of my heart's troubles.

"By birth I am from Crete, and my father was a rich man. He had a great many other sons born and brought up in his halls, lawful sons of a wedded wife; and my mother was a bought woman, a concubine. But Castor son of Hylax honoured me exactly as he honoured his lawful sons, and he was honoured like a god among the Cretans for his good fortune and his wealth and his fine sons. And the fates of death carried him off to the house of Hades, and his sons divided up the property and cast lots for it, and gave me a very small share and a house.

"But I married a wife from a rich family, on my own merits, because I was no fool and no coward. All that is gone now; though I think you can tell what the crop was by looking at the stubble.

"Ares and Athena gave me courage. Whenever I picked the best men for an ambush, sowing trouble for the enemy, my proud heart never once saw death in front of it: I would leap out far ahead of everybody and take my man with the spear if he gave ground at all. That is what I was like in war. Work was never dear to me, nor keeping a careful house and rearing fine children; what I loved was ships with oars, and battles, and polished spears and arrows — grim things, that other people shudder at. I suppose some god put that in my heart. Different men take joy in different work.

"Before the sons of the Greeks ever set foot in Troy, I had nine times been the leader of men and fast ships against foreign parts, and a great deal fell into my hands. I took my pick of it and drew plenty more by lot, and my house grew rich quickly, and I became a man to be feared and respected among the Cretans.

"And when Zeus arranged that hateful expedition which loosened the knees of so many men, they told me and famous Idomeneus to lead the ships to Troy, and there was no way of refusing; the people's voice was too hard against it. Nine years we sons of the Greeks fought there, and in the tenth we sacked the city of Priam (Troy) and went home in the ships, and a god scattered the Greeks.

"And Zeus arranged trouble for me. I stayed one month only, enjoying my children and my wedded wife and my property; and then my heart told me to fit out ships and sail to Egypt with a crew of good men."

And he told the swineherd the whole of it: how nine ships were fitted out and the men came quickly; how they feasted six days and sailed on the seventh with a fair North Wind, easily, as if going downstream, and came to Egypt on the fifth day. How he told his crews to stay by the ships and sent scouts up to the lookout places — and how they gave way to their own insolence instead and went straight off and plundered the Egyptians' beautiful fields, and carried off the women and the little children and killed the men. How the cry reached the city, and the people came out at dawn, and the whole plain filled with foot soldiers and chariots and the flash of bronze; and how Zeus put a coward's panic into his companions and none of them dared stand, so that a great many were cut down with the sharp bronze and the rest were led away alive to work as slaves.

"And Zeus put this into my mind — and I wish I had died in Egypt then and met my fate there, because there was still more sorrow waiting to welcome me. I took the helmet off my head at once and the shield off my shoulders and threw the spear out of my hand, and went straight to the king's chariot and took hold of his knees and kissed them. And he protected me and pitied me, and put me in the chariot and took me home with me weeping. A great many of them came at me with their ash spears, wanting to kill me, because they were extremely angry. But he kept them off, and had a proper regard for the anger of Zeus who protects strangers, and who is angrier than anyone at wicked deeds."

He stayed there seven years, he said, and gathered a great deal of property among the Egyptians, because everybody gave him something. And in the eighth year a Phoenician came along, a man well practised in deceit, a greedy rogue who had already done a great deal of harm to people; and he talked him round and took him to Phoenicia, where his house and his goods were, and kept him a full year. And when the months and days had gone by and the year had come round again, he put him on a ship for Libya, having lied that he was to carry a cargo with him — and meaning in fact to sell him there for a very large price.

"I went with him, suspecting it, because I had no choice. And the ship ran before a fresh North Wind, out in mid sea beyond Crete; and Zeus arranged destruction for them. When we had left Crete and no other land showed, nothing but sky and sea, then the son of Cronos set a black cloud over the hollow ship and the sea went dark beneath it, and he thundered and threw his bolt into her. She shuddered from end to end, struck by the bolt of Zeus, and filled with the smell of sulphur, and every man fell out of her. They were carried on the waves round the black ship like sea-crows, and the god took away their homecoming.

"And Zeus himself, though my heart was in agony, put the enormous mast of the dark-prowed ship into my hands, so that I might get out from under my destruction even yet. I got my arms round that and was carried along by the ruinous winds. Nine days I was carried, and on the tenth black night a great rolling wave put me ashore in the country of the Thesprotians. And there the king of the Thesprotians, the hero Pheidon, looked after me for nothing, because his own son came on me lying there beaten down with cold and exhaustion, and raised me up by the hand and took me to his father's house, and gave me a cloak and a tunic to wear.

"And it was there I heard about Odysseus."

---

That, if I may say so, is a masterpiece, and the reason I have let it run at this length is that it is going to happen four more times before the poem ends and this is the one where you can watch the machinery.

Look at the shape of it. A Cretan of good family; a wrong done at the division of an inheritance; a life of raiding and ships; Troy; a disastrous eastern voyage; a treacherous Phoenician; a shipwreck in which everyone drowns but the teller; a rescue by a kind king. Almost all of it is untrue and every part of it is *nearly* his own life, turned a few degrees. He really did go to Troy and really did come home by way of eleven disasters and really was the only man of his crew to live. He is not inventing a stranger. He is telling his own story with the names filed off, which is why he can do it at this length without a stumble, and why it will come out the same shape again to the next four people who ask.

And there is one true thing buried in the middle of it, which is the whole point of the exercise: *Odysseus is alive, he is close by, and he is coming.* The lie is the delivery system.<sup><a href="#book-14-note-3">3</a></sup>

---

He told him the rest: that the king had entertained Odysseus on his way home and showed him the treasure Odysseus had gathered, bronze and gold and worked iron, enough to keep a man's household to the tenth generation; that Odysseus had gone up to Dodona to ask the great oak of Zeus how he should come back to his own country after so long, openly or in secret; and that the king had sworn, pouring a libation with his own hands, that the ship was launched and the crew ready to take him home.

"But he sent me off first, because a Thesprotian ship happened to be leaving for Dulichium. He told them to take me carefully to king Acastus. And they decided among themselves to do me harm instead, so that I should come to complete misery. When the ship was well out from land they set about making me a slave. They stripped the cloak and tunic off me and put this filthy rag on me instead, and this tunic, torn, the ones you can see with your own eyes.

"And in the evening they came in to the fields of Ithaca, and tied me up in the well-benched ship with a twisted rope, and went ashore in a hurry and had their supper on the beach. And the gods themselves undid the knot for me, easily; and I wrapped the rag round my head and slid down the smooth lading-plank and put my chest to the water and swam off with both hands, and very soon I was well clear of them. Then I went up into a thicket of flowering brush and lay there crouching, and they went about groaning and looking; and when they thought there was no profit in searching any further they went back aboard.

"And the gods hid me easily, and brought me here to the farm of a man who understands things. So it seems it is still my lot to live."

"You poor man. You have stirred my heart up with all that. But you have not got it right about Odysseus, and you will not persuade me. Why does a man like you have to lie for no reason?

"I know how it stands with my master's homecoming. He was hated by all the gods, utterly, or they would have let him die at Troy, or in the arms of his friends when he had wound the war up. Then the whole Greek army would have made him a tomb, and he would have won great glory for his son as well. Now the storm winds have snatched him away without a word said.

"And I keep to myself here with the pigs, and I do not go to the city, unless sensible Penelope tells me to come, when news has arrived from somewhere. And then they all sit round the newcomer and question him closely — the ones who are grieving for their long-absent lord, and the ones who are delighted, eating up his living for nothing.

"But I have had no appetite for asking questions since an Aetolian took me in with a story. He had killed a man and wandered a long way, and came to my house, and I treated him kindly. He told me he had seen Odysseus in Crete with Idomeneus, mending his ships after a storm had broken them up, and said he would come in the summer or the autumn, bringing a great deal of treasure and his godlike crew.

"So you, old man of many sorrows — since a god has brought you here to me — do not try to please me with lies. It is not for that I shall respect you and treat you as a friend. It is out of fear of Zeus who protects strangers, and out of pity for you."

"You have a very slow heart in your breast, if not even an oath brings you round. Come then, let us make a bargain, and let the gods on Olympus be witnesses. If your master comes back to this house, you shall dress me in a cloak and a tunic and send me on my way to Dulichium, which is where I want to go. And if he does not come as I say, then set your men on me and throw me off a great cliff, so that the next beggar thinks twice about lying to you."

"Stranger — that would do wonders for my good name and my reputation among men, now and in the future: to bring you to my hut and give you hospitality and then kill you. What a light heart I should have when I said my prayers to Zeus afterwards.

"But it is time to eat. I wish the men would come, so that we could get a good supper ready in the hut."

---

They came in with the pigs and penned them, and there was an enormous squealing as the sows were shut up. And the swineherd called out to his men to bring in the best boar, so that he could kill it for a stranger from far away — "and we shall get something out of it too, who have suffered a long time over the white-tusked swine, while other men eat what we work for and pay nothing."

He split the logs with the pitiless bronze, and they brought in a very fat boar five years old and stood it by the hearth. And the swineherd did not forget the immortals, because he had good sense: as a first offering he cut hairs from the head of the white-tusked boar and threw them in the fire, and prayed to all the gods that clever Odysseus might come back to his own house. Then he struck it with a billet of oak that he had left over from splitting, and the life left it; and they cut the throat and singed it and jointed it. And the swineherd laid raw pieces from every limb on the rich fat, and threw them into the fire sprinkled with barley meal; and they cut up the rest and spitted it and roasted it and drew it off and heaped it all on platters.

And the swineherd stood up to share it out, because he had a fine sense of what was fair, and divided the whole of it into seven portions. One he set aside with a prayer for the nymphs and for Hermes; and the rest he handed round to each man. And he honoured Odysseus with the long chine of the white-tusked boar, and made his master's heart glad.<sup><a href="#book-14-note-4">4</a></sup>

"Eumaeus — may you be as dear to father Zeus as you are to me, since you honour a man in my state with the best of what you have."

"Eat, my strange guest, and enjoy what there is. The god gives one thing and holds back another, whatever he pleases, because he can do anything."

So they ate, and when they had finished, Mesaulius cleared the food away — a man the swineherd had got for himself while his master was gone, without troubling his mistress or old Laertes; he had bought him from the Taphians with his own goods. And they put out their hands to the food, and when they had had enough of eating and drinking they turned their minds to bed.

---

And a bad night came on, black, and Zeus rained the whole of it, and the West Wind blew hard and wet.

And Odysseus said something, to try the swineherd out — to see whether he would take his own cloak off and give it to him, or tell one of his men to, since he was so careful of him.

"Listen to me now, Eumaeus, and all the rest of you. I am going to make a boast and tell you something, because the wine is telling me to, crazy wine, which sets even a sensible man singing and laughing softly, and gets him up to dance, and brings out a word that would have been better left in. Since I have started, I shall not hold it back.

"I wish I were young, and my strength what it was, on the day we laid an ambush under the walls of Troy. Odysseus was leading it, and Menelaus, and I was the third in command, because they asked for me.

"When we got to the city and the steep wall, we lay down in the thick brush among the reeds and the marsh, crouching under our arms; and night came on, a bad one, with the North Wind dropping, and frost; and snow came down over us like hoar frost, cold, and ice was forming on our shields.

"Now all the others had cloaks and tunics and slept comfortably with their shoulders covered by their shields. But I had left my cloak behind with my men when I set out, like a fool, because I did not think I would be cold; so I came along with nothing but a shield and a bright kilt.

"And in the third watch of the night, when the stars had gone over, I nudged Odysseus with my elbow — he was lying next to me — and he was awake at once.

"*Son of Laertes, I shall not be among the living much longer. This cold is finishing me. I have no cloak. Some god fooled me into coming out in a tunic, and now there is no way out of it.*

"And he had a thought in his mind on the instant, being the sort of man he was for planning as well as fighting. And he said quietly: *Be quiet, in case one of the other Greeks hears you.* And then he raised his head on his elbow and said:

"*Listen, friends. A dream has come to me in my sleep, a warning. We have come a very long way from the ships. I wish somebody would go and tell Agamemnon, in case he sends more men up from the ships.*

"And Thoas the son of Andraemon jumped up straight away and flung off his purple cloak and set off running for the ships. And I lay down gladly in his cloak, and Dawn came up on her golden throne.

"I wish I were young now, and my strength what it was. Then one of the swineherds in this farm would give me a cloak — out of friendliness, and out of respect for a good man. As it is, they look down on me, because I have poor clothes on my body."

And the swineherd said:

"Old man, that is a good story you have told, and there is not a word in it out of place or wasted. So you shall not go short of clothing or anything else that a hard-pressed suppliant deserves when he meets one — for tonight. In the morning you will be flapping about in your own rags again, because we have no store of cloaks here and no spare tunics; each man has one. But when the dear son of Odysseus comes, he will give you a cloak and a tunic himself and send you wherever your heart wants to go."

And he jumped up and made him a bed near the fire and threw sheepskins and goatskins over it; and Odysseus lay down, and Eumaeus threw over him a great thick cloak, which he kept beside him for a change of clothing when a really bad storm came on.

---

That is the most charming thing in the book and I do not want it to go past unadmired.

He wants a blanket. He is a guest in a hut where there is exactly one spare cloak in the world and its owner is going out into the rain in a few minutes; and rather than ask, which would embarrass everybody, he tells a story — announcing at the top that the wine is making him boastful, so that nobody has to take it seriously — in which a cold night is solved by a clever trick, and in which he casts himself in a small part and gives the clever trick to Odysseus.

And Eumaeus, who has already said out loud that men in need make up tales for a cloak and a tunic, listens to a tale that is transparently a request for a cloak and a tunic, praises it as a good story with not a word out of place, and hands over his own cloak with the gentlest possible caveat — *for tonight; in the morning you will be in your rags again; we are not rich here.*

Neither of them mentions what is actually happening. They are both far too well-mannered.

---

So Odysseus slept, and the young men slept beside him. But the swineherd did not choose to sleep in there, away from the pigs; he got himself ready to go out, and Odysseus was glad to see how well he looked after his master's property while his master was far away.

First he slung a sharp sword over his broad shoulders, and then put on a very thick cloak against the wind, and picked up the fleece of a big well-fed goat, and took a sharp javelin to keep off dogs and men.

And he went off to lie down where the white-tusked boars were sleeping, under a hollow rock, out of the North Wind.

---

## NOTES TO BOOK FOURTEEN

<a id="book-14-note-1"></a>
1. **A swineherd who curses Helen.** It is worth registering how far the war reaches. Eumaeus has never been to Troy, has no rank, owns nothing, and lives at the far end of a small island looking after pigs; and his considered opinion, offered in his first speech, is that Helen's whole family should have been destroyed. Twenty years earlier a quarrel in a palace on the mainland took his master away, and everything that has gone wrong in his life since has come out of it — the lost prospects, the house he was never given, the estate being eaten in front of him. When the poem wants to show you the cost of the war it does not go to a battlefield. It goes to a farm.

<a id="book-14-note-2"></a>
2. **"And you said to him, Eumaeus."** Several times in the next few books the poem stops narrating this man and starts *addressing* him, switching into the second person for a line — you said, you answered — and then switching back. It is a small thing and it has fascinated readers for a very long time.
