Only a handful of characters in Homer are ever spoken to like this: Patroclus in the *Iliad*, and Menelaus, and here a slave who keeps pigs. Nobody knows for certain why. The dullest explanation is metrical convenience, and it may be right. The explanation most readers prefer, and I confess I am one of them, is that the poet grew fond of him. It is the only place in this poem where the teller's own affection leaks visibly through the surface of the telling, and it happens to the poorest man in the story.

<a id="book-14-note-3"></a>
3. **The Cretan tales.** This is the longest of them and the best place to watch how they are built, since he will do it four more times — to the suitors, to Penelope, and to his own father. They are not improvisations but variations on one standing story: a Cretan of good family, an inheritance grievance, a life of raiding, Troy, a voyage east that goes wrong, treacherous Phoenicians, a shipwreck nobody else survives, and a rescue by a decent stranger. What makes it work is that it is his own life at a few degrees' offset, so that he never has to invent anything from nothing and never contradicts himself. And every version carries the same small true cargo, planted where a listener will not notice it being planted: *Odysseus is alive and close by.* He is not lying instead of telling the truth. He is lying in order to deliver it.

<a id="book-14-note-4"></a>
4. **Seven portions, and the chine.** Watch the swineherd carve, because the whole social order is in it. He divides the meat into seven equal shares, one for each man present, which is the mark of a fair division and the reason the poem says he had a good sense of what was right; then he sets one share aside for the nymphs and for Hermes, who looks after herdsmen and travellers, before anybody eats. And then he takes the long chine — the best cut on the animal, the piece reserved for the guest of highest standing — and gives it to the filthy old beggar sitting by his fire. It is exactly what Odysseus himself did for the blind singer at the Phaeacian dinner, and the poem notes, in one line, that it made his master's heart glad. Eumaeus does not know he is honouring his master. He is simply honouring a guest, which is what he would have done for anybody.

---

*Book Fifteen: In Which a Young Man Comes Home by the Back Way, and an Old Slave Remembers Being a Prince.*


<div class="page-break"></div>

<!-- Source: book/odyssey-book-15.md -->

# THE ODYSSEY
### Retold in English, with Explanations

---

## BOOK FIFTEEN
### In Which a Young Man Comes Home by the Back Way, and an Old Slave Remembers Being a Prince

---

Athena went to Sparta, to remind the son of Odysseus about going home and to hurry him along.

She found him and Peisistratus lying in the porch of the house of Menelaus. Nestor's son was fast asleep, but no sweet sleep held Telemachus; he was awake all through the immortal night, worrying about his father. And the goddess stood over him.

"Telemachus, it is not right to go on wandering far from home, leaving your property behind with men as insolent as that in your house. Take care they do not divide it all up and eat it, and your journey turn out to have been for nothing.

"Rouse Menelaus and get him to send you off, so that you may still find your excellent mother at home. Her father and her brothers are already urging her to marry Eurymachus, who is outbidding all the other suitors in presents and keeps raising his offer. Take care she does not carry off something from your house against your will.

"You know how it is with a woman's heart: she wants to build up the house of the man who marries her, and of her earlier children and the husband who is dead she takes no more thought and asks no questions. So go home and hand everything over to whichever of the servant women seems best to you, until the gods show you a wife of your own.

"And there is another thing I want to tell you. The best of the suitors are lying in wait for you in the strait between Ithaca and rugged Samos, meaning to kill you before you can reach home. I do not think it will happen; sooner than that the earth will cover a few of the men who are eating up your living.

"Keep your ship well away from the islands and sail through the night. Whichever god is watching over you will send a wind behind you. And when you reach the nearest headland of Ithaca, send the ship and the crew on to the town, and go yourself first of all to the swineherd, who keeps your pigs and is loyal to you. Sleep there, and send him into the town to tell sensible Penelope that you are safe and have come back from Pylos."

And with that she went away to Olympus.

Telemachus woke Nestor's son with a touch of his heel. "Get up, Peisistratus. Bring out the horses and put them under the yoke, and let us be on our way."

"Telemachus, however much we want to go, there is no driving through a dark night. It will be dawn soon enough. Wait until the hero Menelaus brings the gifts out and puts them in the chariot and sends us off with a kind word. A guest remembers, all his days, the host who showed him friendship."

---

I shall not detain you over Athena's opinion of women, which is brisk, cynical and tactically shaped for a young man she wants on a ship by morning. It is worth noticing only because the poem puts it in the mouth of a goddess who knows perfectly well that it is not true of Penelope, and who has just finished telling Odysseus how faithfully his wife has held the house. She is not describing anybody. She is getting a boy to move.

---

When Dawn came up, Menelaus got out of bed and came to them; and Telemachus dressed quickly and asked to be sent home.

"Menelaus, send me back now to my own country. My heart is set on getting home."

"Telemachus, I shall not keep you here long when you want to be off. I disapprove of a host who is excessive in his kindness quite as much as one who is excessive the other way. Moderation is better in everything. It is as bad to press a guest to stay when he does not want to as it is to hold one back who is eager to go. One should look after a guest properly while he is there, and let him go when he wishes.

"But wait until I bring the gifts out and set them in the chariot, and until I tell the women to get a meal ready in the hall, out of the plenty we have. It is honour and glory and profit together to have dinner before setting out over a very wide stretch of country."

That is a small speech and I like it very much. Everything in this poem turns on the treatment of guests, and here is a man who has been thinking about the mechanics of it — who has worked out that the fault of holding somebody too long and the fault of pushing them out of the door are the same fault, and that the whole art of it is in reading what the other person actually wants. It is worth setting beside the household we visited at the end of the last book, where a slave with one spare cloak and no property at all arrived at precisely the same conclusion by himself.

Menelaus went down to the treasure chamber with Helen and his son Megapenthes, and chose a two-handled cup, and had the boy carry a silver mixing bowl. And Helen went to the chests where her embroidered robes lay, that she had made herself, and lifted out the largest and the most beautifully worked, which lay underneath all the others and shone like a star.

"Take this, dear child. Here is a gift from me, a keepsake from the hands of Menelaus, for you to use when you pour to the gods. Hephaestus made it, and Phaedimus the king of the Sidonians gave it to me when his house sheltered me on my way home."

And Helen put the robe into his hands. "I have a present for you too, dear child, a memory of Helen's hands — for your bride to wear on the day of your marriage, which you are longing for. Until then let it lie in your mother's keeping. And may you come with joy to your well-built house and your own country."

They poured the last of the wine and got into the chariot and drove out through the gateway. And as they went, Telemachus prayed to Athena; and while he was praying an eagle came over on the right with a great white goose in its talons, a tame bird out of the yard, and the men and women came running and shouting after it. And the eagle swung in close and darted away to the right, in front of the horses. And they were glad to see it, and their hearts warmed.

Peisistratus spoke first. "Consider, Menelaus, whether the god has shown this sign for the two of us, or for you."

And Menelaus began to think it over, so as to answer properly — and Helen got in before him.

"Listen to me. I shall prophesy, as the immortals put it in my heart and as I believe it will come out. That eagle came from the mountain where he was born and where his brood is, and took a goose that had been reared in the house. Just so will Odysseus come home after many hardships and much wandering, and take his revenge. Or he may be at home already, sowing trouble for every one of the suitors."

"May Zeus grant it," said Telemachus. "Then I would pray to you as I would to a god."

---

That is the last thing Helen says in the poem, and she is the only person in it who reads an omen without being asked and turns out to be exactly right.

She was extremely good at this in Book Four as well, when she looked at a boy who had just arrived and named his father before anybody else in the room had thought to. Her husband is still working out what to say — the poem is quite explicit that he is composing an answer — and she interrupts him and gets it right, and the reading she gives is one nobody else in that courtyard could have given, because it takes an eagle carrying off a domestic bird from a house full of shouting people and sees the point of view of the household. She has been the goose. She knows what it looks like from underneath.

---

They came to Pherae and slept at the house of Diocles, and drove on next morning to Pylos. And there Telemachus said: "Peisistratus, will you promise me something and do it? We are guest-friends from our fathers' time, and we are of an age, and this journey will make us closer still. Do not take me past my ship, but leave me there — or the old man will keep me in his house out of pure kindness, and I need to get home."

Nestor's son turned it over and decided how to do it properly, and swung the horses down to the shore, and unloaded the gifts into the stern of the ship, and told him to hurry aboard before the old man heard of it and came down to fetch him.

And as the crew were making ready, a stranger came up — a man from a long line of prophets, who had killed a man of his own tribe in Argos and was on the run with the dead man's brothers hunting him. His name was Theoclymenus, and he asked whose ship it was and begged to be taken aboard.

"Stranger, I shall not refuse you. Come with us, and you shall have what we have."<sup><a href="#book-15-note-1">1</a></sup>

They took his bronze spear and laid it along the deck, and he came aboard and sat down beside Telemachus; and they cast off, and Athena sent them a fair wind that came on strong out of a clear sky, so that the ship might run through the salt water as fast as possible.

---

Meanwhile Odysseus and the swineherd were having their supper in the hut, and the other men with them; and when they had eaten enough, Odysseus tried him again, to see whether he would still be kind and tell him to stay on at the farm, or send him off to the city.

"Listen, Eumaeus, and all of you. In the morning I want to go into the town and beg, so as not to wear you and your men out here. Just give me your advice and a good guide to take me there; and once I am in the city I shall have to wander about on my own and see whether anybody will give me a cup of water and a piece of bread. I could go to the house of Odysseus and take my news to sensible Penelope, and mix with the arrogant suitors — they have plenty; they might give me a dinner. I would do whatever they wanted, and do it well. Because Hermes, who gives grace and fame to every kind of work, has given me a gift for service: nobody could match me at splitting kindling, or getting a dry fire going, or carving and roasting meat, or pouring the wine — all the things that lesser men do for their betters."

And the swineherd was extremely upset.

"Good heavens, stranger — how did a notion like that get into your head? You must be very keen to die on the spot, if you really want to go into that crowd of suitors, whose insolence and violence reach the iron sky.

"Their servants are nothing like you. They are young men in fine cloaks and tunics, with their hair oiled and their faces handsome, and the polished tables in there are loaded with bread and meat and wine.

"Stay here. Nobody finds you a nuisance — not I, and not one of my men. And when the dear son of Odysseus comes, he will give you a cloak and a tunic and send you wherever you want to go."

"Eumaeus, may you be as dear to father Zeus as you are to me, for stopping my wandering and my miserable homelessness. There is nothing worse for a man than a life on the road; but it is for the sake of the cursed belly that men put up with such misery.

"But since you are keeping me here and telling me to wait for him — tell me about the mother of Odysseus, and the father he left behind on the threshold of old age. Are they still alive and looking at the light of the sun, or are they dead and gone into the house of Hades?"

"Laertes is alive. But he prays to Zeus constantly that the life may waste out of his body in his own halls, because he grieves terribly for his son who is gone, and for the wife he married, and it was her death that hurt him most and brought him to an early old age.

"She died of grief for her famous son, a pitiful death — and may nobody die that way who lives here and is a friend of mine.

"While she was alive, sorry as she was, it was always a pleasure to me to ask after her and to talk to her, because she brought me up herself along with her own daughter Ctimene, the youngest of her children. I was brought up with her, and her mother honoured me only a little less. And when the two of us reached the age everybody wants to reach, they married her to a man in Same and got a great many presents for her; and me the lady dressed in a cloak and a tunic, very fine clothes, and gave me sandals for my feet, and sent me out to the farm. And she loved me more in her heart than ever.

"Now I go without all that. But the blessed gods make the work I stay at prosper, and out of it I have eaten and drunk and given to people who deserved it. From my mistress there is nothing pleasant to be had these days, not a word and not a kindness, since that trouble fell on the house — overbearing men. And servants very much need to talk to their mistress and ask her things, and eat and drink there, and carry something back to the fields with them. Those are the things that warm a servant's heart."

---

"Then you must have been a small child, Eumaeus, when you were brought so far from your own country and your parents. Tell me — was the city sacked where your father and your lady mother lived? Or were you left alone with the sheep or the cattle, and enemies took you in their ships and sold you into this man's house, and he paid a good price for you?"

"Stranger, since you ask me that, listen quietly and enjoy yourself and sit and drink your wine. These nights are enormous. There is time to sleep and time to enjoy listening, and you need not lie down before you have to; too much sleep is wearisome. Let the rest of these go outside and sleep, and at first light have their breakfast and go out with the master's pigs. But the two of us will stay in the hut and drink and eat and take a certain pleasure in going over each other's miseries — because afterwards a man does find pleasure even in his troubles, when he has suffered a great deal and wandered a great deal.

"There is an island called Syrie, if you have ever heard of it, above Ortygia, where the sun turns. It is not so very full of people, but it is a good country, rich in cattle and rich in sheep, full of vines and full of wheat. Famine never comes to those people, and no other hateful sickness comes upon them; but when the generations grow old in the town, Apollo comes with Artemis and kills them with his gentle arrows.

"There are two cities there, and everything is divided between them; and my father was king over both — Ctesius, the son of Ormenus, a man like the immortals.

"And Phoenicians came there, men famous for their ships, greedy rogues, with a great many trinkets in their black ship. Now there was a Phoenician woman in my father's house, tall and beautiful and skilled at fine handwork, and the crafty Phoenicians talked her round. One of them got her while she was washing clothes, lying with her beside the hollow ship; and afterwards he asked her who she was and where she came from, and she pointed at once to my father's high-roofed house.

"*I come from Sidon, rich in bronze, and I am the daughter of Arybas, who was very wealthy. Taphian pirates carried me off as I was coming in from the fields, and brought me here and sold me into this man's house, and he paid a good price for me.*

"And the man said: *Would you like to come home with us, then, and see the high-roofed house of your father and mother, and the two of them? Because they are still alive, and people say they are rich.*

"And the woman said: *That might be done, if you sailors would swear me an oath to bring me home unharmed.*

"So they all swore it. And when they had sworn and finished the oath, the woman said: *Now be quiet. Let none of your crew speak to me if he meets me in the street or at the well, in case somebody goes to the house and tells the old man, and he suspects and ties me up in cruel bonds and plans destruction for the lot of you. Keep it to yourselves, and get your cargo bought as fast as you can. And when the ship is loaded, send word to me quickly up at the house, because I shall bring gold as well, whatever comes to my hand. And I will tell you something else I would gladly give as my passage money. There is a child of my master's in the house that I nurse, a knowing little thing, who runs out of doors along with me. I would bring him aboard, and he would fetch you an enormous price wherever you sold him among people of another language.*

"And with that she went back up to the house.

"And they stayed there a whole year and got a great deal of goods into their hollow ship. And when the ship was loaded and it was time to go, they sent a man up to give the woman the word. He came to my father's house, a crafty fellow, with a gold chain strung with amber beads; and the maids in the hall and my lady mother handled it and looked at it and offered him a price — and he nodded to the woman without a word, and then went back to the hollow ship.

"And she took me by the hand and led me out of the house. In the front hall she found the cups and the tables of the men who had been dining with my father and had just gone out to the assembly, and she hid three goblets in the fold of her dress and carried them off; and I went along after her, in complete innocence.

"The sun went down and all the ways grew dark, and we came quickly to the harbour, where the Phoenicians' fast ship was. They put us aboard and sailed, and Zeus sent a following wind. Six days we sailed, night and day alike; and when Zeus brought on the seventh, Artemis of the arrows struck the woman, and she dropped into the bilge like a sea-bird going down.

"And they threw her overboard, to be a meal for the seals and the fishes; and I was left there with my heart aching. And the wind and the water carried them to Ithaca, and there Laertes bought me with his own property.

"And that is how I came to see this country with my eyes."

So the two of them talked, and slept only a little, because Dawn came up quickly on her golden throne.

---

I do not think I need to say very much about that, but I will say two things.

The first is that this man is a king's son. He was born a prince on an island with two cities in it, and his father ruled both, and he was stolen at about five years old by a woman who had herself been stolen, and sold, and was trying to get home — and who used him as her fare. She died six days out and was thrown into the sea, and the child went on to Ithaca and was bought by an old man who was kind to him. He has kept pigs for that family for fifty years and calls his absent owner *honoured sir* and will not say his name.

The second is what he does with the story. Look at how he begins it: *these nights are enormous; there is time to sleep and time to enjoy listening.* He settles his guest with a drink, sends the other men off to bed so as not to bore them, and observes, quite deliberately, that going over old griefs together is a pleasure once the griefs are old enough. He is not complaining and he is not asking for sympathy. He is doing the thing a good host does on a long night, which is to offer a story in return for a story — and the man he is offering it to has just told him a magnificent pack of lies and is sitting there in disguise in his own farmhouse listening to the true one.<sup><a href="#book-15-note-2">2</a></sup>

---

And meanwhile Telemachus and his crew were coming in to the shore. They furled the sails and unstepped the mast and rowed her in to the anchorage and moored her, and got out and had their meal on the beach.

"Take the ship on to the town now," said Telemachus. "I am going out to the fields and the herdsmen. In the evening, when I have looked over my land, I shall come down to the town; and in the morning I shall give you a good dinner of meat and sweet wine as your wages for the journey."

And Theoclymenus said: "And where am I to go, dear child? Whose house shall I make for, among all the men who rule in rugged Ithaca? Or shall I go straight to your mother's house, and yours?"

"At any other time I would tell you to go to my own house; there is no lack of hospitality there. But it would be the worse for you now, because I shall be away and my mother will not see you. She does not appear often before the suitors in the hall; she keeps apart from them, upstairs, at her loom. But I can name you another man to go to: Eurymachus, the splendid son of Polybus, whom the people of Ithaca look at nowadays as though he were a god. He is much the best of them, and the keenest to marry my mother and have the honour that was Odysseus's.

"But Zeus, who lives in the sky, knows whether he will not bring the day of doom down on all of them before any wedding."

And as he said it a bird flew over on the right: a hawk, the swift messenger of Apollo, with a dove in his talons, plucking her; and the feathers came drifting down to the ground between Telemachus and the ship.

And Theoclymenus called him away from his men and took him by the hand.

"Telemachus, that bird did not fly on your right without a god behind it. I knew it for an omen the moment I looked at it. There is no family in Ithaca more kingly than yours. You will have the power here, always."

"Stranger, I only wish that word may be fulfilled. Then you would very soon know my friendship, and get so many gifts from me that anybody meeting you would call you a lucky man."

And he turned to Peiraeus, whom he trusted more than any of his crew, and asked him to take the stranger home and look after him and honour him until he came himself; and Peiraeus said he would, and would keep him as long as he stayed, and there would be no want of hospitality.

Then he went aboard and told the crew to embark and cast off the cables, and they went aboard and sat down at the oars.

And Telemachus bound his good sandals under his feet and picked up his heavy spear with the sharp bronze point off the deck of the ship. And they cast off the cables, and pushed her out, and sailed for the town, as the son of Odysseus had told them.

And his feet carried him on, fast, until he came to the yard where his pigs were, thousands of them, and where the good swineherd slept beside them, always loyal to his masters.<sup><a href="#book-15-note-3">3</a></sup>

---

## NOTES TO BOOK FIFTEEN

<a id="book-15-note-1"></a>
1. **Theoclymenus, and the long pedigree.** The poem introduces this man by giving five generations of his family before it tells you what he wants, which is a passage most readers find heavy going, and it is worth knowing why it is there. He is a seer, from the most famous seer-family in Greek legend — the line of Melampus, who understood the speech of birds, and of Amphiaraus, who went to the war at Thebes knowing it would kill him because his wife had been bribed with a necklace to send him. To name that ancestry was to establish, in the only way available, that this stranger's prophecies are worth listening to. He is also a murderer on the run, taken aboard without hesitation and without any questions asked about the killing — which tells you something about how blood-guilt worked. A man who had killed within his own tribe had to leave, immediately and permanently, and the family of the dead man would pursue him; but exile discharged the obligation, and elsewhere he was simply a stranger, and strangers come from Zeus.

<a id="book-15-note-2"></a>
2. **What Eumaeus was, and what he is.** He is the son of a king, stolen as a small child and sold; and it is worth being plain that his story is not offered as an outrage. It is offered as a piece of ordinary bad luck of the kind that happened constantly on that sea. What the poem does with it is quieter and stranger: it gives the finest manners in the book to a slave, and lets him tell a prince's biography in a hut, at night, to a beggar who is really a king. Everybody in that room is in disguise, one way or another. — Two details reward a second look. The woman who steals him has herself been stolen — taken by pirates from her own country, sold, and now trying to buy her way home with somebody else's child — and the poem gives her a name, a father and a city, which it did not have to do. And Eumaeus, who has been a slave since he was five, has himself bought a slave, Mesaulius, with his own savings, as he mentioned in passing at the end of the last book. He is not outside the system. Nobody in this poem is outside it.

<a id="book-15-note-3"></a>
3. **Two birds, one book.** The poem frames this book with omens and it is doing it deliberately. At the start, an eagle takes a tame goose out of the yard of a great house, and Helen reads it: the wild thing comes down from the mountain and carries off the creature that has been fattening at home. At the end, a hawk strips a dove in flight and the feathers fall between the young man and his ship, and the seer reads that one. Both mean the same thing and neither of them needs to be spelled out to the reader, which is why the poem does not spell it out. Notice, though, who is allowed to interpret. A woman at a gate and a fugitive murderer picked up at a beach — the two people in this book with the least standing of anybody in it — are the two who can see what is coming. The kings say nothing.

---

*Book Sixteen: In Which a Father and a Son Are Alone in a Room, and Only One of Them Knows It.*


<div class="page-break"></div>

<!-- Source: book/odyssey-book-16.md -->

# THE ODYSSEY
### Retold in English, with Explanations

---

## BOOK SIXTEEN
### In Which a Father and a Son Are Alone in a Room, and Only One of Them Knows It

---

At first light, in the hut, Odysseus and the good swineherd lit a fire and got their breakfast ready and sent the herdsmen out with the droves of pigs.

And the dogs, who bark at everybody, did not bark. They went fawning round somebody coming up the path.

Odysseus noticed it, and heard the sound of feet.

"Eumaeus — somebody is coming. A friend of yours, or somebody the dogs know, because they are not barking; they are making a fuss of him. And I can hear footsteps."

He had not finished saying it when his own son stood in the doorway.

The swineherd jumped up in amazement, and the bowls he had been mixing the bright wine in fell out of his hands. And he went to meet his master and kissed his head and both his beautiful eyes and both his hands, and the tears came pouring down.

The way a loving father greets a son who comes back in the tenth year out of a far country — an only son, a late child, for whom he has suffered a great deal — that is how the swineherd put his arms round godlike Telemachus and kissed him all over, as though he had got out from under his own death.

"You have come, Telemachus. Sweet light. I thought I should never see you again once you had gone off in the ship to Pylos. Come in, dear child, and let me have the pleasure of looking at you, newly here from somewhere else. You do not often come out to the farm and the herdsmen; you stay in the town — as though it were any pleasure to you to look at that destructive crowd of suitors."

"So be it, old friend. I have come out here for your sake — to see you with my own eyes, and to hear from you whether my mother is still at home, or whether some other man has married her by now, and the bed of Odysseus is lying empty, with nothing on it, and the cobwebs gathering."

"She is in your halls, with a steady heart, enduring; and the nights and the days waste away for her, wretchedly, while she cries."

He took the bronze spear from him, and Telemachus stepped in over the stone threshold. And as he came in, his father got up from his seat to make room for him.

And Telemachus stopped him. "Sit down, stranger. We shall find a seat somewhere else in our own farmyard; here is a man who will put one out."

So Odysseus sat down again, and the swineherd heaped green brushwood for the young man and threw a fleece on top; and Telemachus sat down there, and the swineherd set out platters of roast meat left over from the night before, and heaped bread into a basket, and mixed honey-sweet wine in an ivy bowl, and sat down opposite. And they put out their hands to the good things in front of them.

"Old friend, where does this stranger come from? How did the sailors bring him to Ithaca? Who did they say they were? Because I do not suppose he came here on foot."

And Eumaeus told him what he had been told: a Cretan, who had wandered through a great many cities of men, with a god driving him about; who had run away from a Thesprotian ship and come to the farm. "And now I put him in your hands. Do as you like. He says he is your suppliant."

"Eumaeus, that is a hard thing to say to me. How am I to take this stranger into my house? I am young, and I cannot yet trust my own hands to defend a man if somebody starts on him. My mother's heart is divided two ways: whether to stay here with me and keep the house, respecting her husband's bed and what the people say, or to go now with whichever of the Greeks courting her in the halls is the best man and offers most.

"But since this stranger has come to *your* house, I shall clothe him in a cloak and tunic, good clothes, and give him a two-edged sword and sandals for his feet, and send him on wherever his heart tells him to go. Or if you like, keep him here on the farm and look after him, and I shall send the clothes out here and all his food, so that he is not a drain on you and your men.

"But I will not have him go up there among the suitors. They are far too full of insolence and violence, and they will make a mockery of him, and that would be a bitter grief to me. It is hard for one man to get anything done against a crowd, however strong he is; they are a great deal stronger."

---

And the much-enduring Odysseus said:

"Friend, since it is right that I should answer — my heart is torn open, listening to you tell what these suitors get up to in your halls, against the will of a man like you.

"Tell me: do you put up with it willingly? Or do the people of your country hate you, following some voice from a god? Or do you blame your brothers, who are the men a fighter relies on when a serious quarrel comes?

"I wish I were as young as I am angry, and were the son of Odysseus, or Odysseus himself — then let some stranger cut my head off my neck if I did not walk into the halls of that man and make myself a plague to every one of them. And if they beat me down by weight of numbers, one against so many, I would rather be killed in my own house than have to watch these disgraceful things going on and on: guests knocked about, servant women dragged through the fine halls, wine drawn off and wasted, men eating up food idly and endlessly, for a thing that is never going to be brought off."

"Stranger, I shall tell you exactly. The people are not hostile to me and there is no quarrel with them. And there are no brothers to blame, either. Zeus made this a single line: Arceisius had one son, Laertes; Laertes had one son, Odysseus; and Odysseus left one son — me — in his halls, and had no joy of me.

"So the house is full of enemies. All the chief men of the islands — Dulichium, Same, wooded Zacynthus — and everyone who is anybody in rocky Ithaca, they are all courting my mother and wearing the house away. And she neither refuses the hateful marriage nor can bring herself to end it; and they eat my living away, and before long they will tear me to pieces too."

Then he turned to the swineherd. "Eumaeus, go quickly and tell my mother that I am back safe from Pylos. And come straight back here; tell nobody else. There are a great many Greeks planning trouble for me."

"Shall I take the same message to Laertes as I go? The old man used to look after his farm, whatever grief he had for Odysseus, and eat and drink with the servants when he felt like it. But they say that since you went off in the ship he has not eaten or drunk, and has not looked at the work of the farm, but sits grieving and crying, and the flesh is wasting off his bones."

"Sad as it is, we shall let him alone. Tell my mother, and have her send the housekeeper out to him quietly, and she can tell the old man."

And he sent the swineherd off; and Eumaeus tied his sandals on and went to the town.

---

And Athena did not fail to notice that the swineherd had gone. She came up to the hut in the likeness of a woman, tall and beautiful and skilled at fine handwork, and stood in the doorway where Odysseus could see her.

Telemachus did not see her at all; the gods do not appear plainly to everybody. But Odysseus saw her, and so did the dogs, and they did not bark; they whimpered and shrank away across the yard.

She signalled with her eyebrows. Odysseus understood and came out of the hall, past the great wall of the yard, and stood in front of her.

"Son of Laertes. Speak to your son now and hide it no longer, so that the two of you can plan the killing of the suitors and go into the town. And I shall not be far away; I am ready for the fight."

And she touched him with her golden wand. She put a freshly washed cloak and tunic about him first, and made him taller and younger; the brown came back into his skin, his cheeks filled out, and his beard turned dark again.

Then she went away, and Odysseus went back into the hut. And his own son stared at him and was frightened, and turned his eyes away, in case this was a god.

"Stranger — you look different than you did a moment ago. Your clothes are not the same, and your skin is not the same. You must be one of the gods who hold the wide sky. Be gracious to us. We will give you acceptable offerings and worked gold. Spare us."

"I am no god. Why do you compare me to the immortals?

"I am your father. The one you have been grieving for, and suffering for, and putting up with other men's violence for."

And he kissed his son, and let a tear fall to the ground, which until then he had held back, every one of them.

And Telemachus did not believe him.

"You are not Odysseus. You are not my father. Some god is deceiving me, to make me cry harder. No mortal man could arrange this by his own devising — not unless a god came himself and easily made him young or old, whichever he wanted. Just now you were an old man in filthy clothes; now you look like one of the gods."

"Telemachus, it is not right for you to be so amazed that your father is in the house, or to stand there wondering. No other Odysseus is ever going to come here. I am he. I have suffered a great deal and wandered a great deal, and I have come in the twentieth year to my own country.

"This is Athena's doing. She makes me whatever she likes, because she can; one moment a beggar, the next a young man with fine clothes on his body. It is an easy thing for the gods who hold the wide sky to glorify a mortal man or to bring him low."

And he sat down. And Telemachus threw his arms round his good father and wept.

And in both of them the longing to cry rose up, and they cried out loud, harder than birds — sea-eagles, or vultures with hooked claws, whose young the country people have taken out of the nest before they could fly. That is how pitifully the tears fell from under their eyelids.

And the light of the sun would have gone down on the two of them crying, if Telemachus had not suddenly said: "But what ship brought you here? What sailors? Who did they say they were? Because I do not suppose you came to Ithaca on foot."

---

There is the reunion, and I want to point at one thing in it and then leave it alone.

He does not prove anything.

Every other recognition in this poem has a token attached: there will be a scar in a few books' time, and a piece of furniture at the very end, and each of them is a hard fact produced under pressure to satisfy somebody who has decided not to be fooled. Here there is nothing of the kind. His father simply says *I am your father*, and the boy says he does not believe it, and the man says it again and adds that Athena did the rest — and that is the whole of the evidence, and it is accepted.

Which makes sense, when you think about it, because there is nothing available. Telemachus was an infant in arms when this man sailed. He has no memory of a face, no voice to compare, no scar he was ever shown. He cannot recognise his father; he can only be told, and decide. And what settles it is not proof at all: it is the crying, which goes on for so long that the poem says the sun would have set on it.

He is the only person in the book who has to take it on trust.

---

Odysseus told him the truth: that the Phaeacians had brought him and put him ashore asleep, and given him bronze and gold and woven cloth, which was now stored in a cave by the will of the gods; and that Athena had sent him here to plan how the suitors might be killed.

"Now tell me the number of them, so that I know how many there are and what sort of men. Then I shall turn it over in my own mind and decide whether the two of us can take them on alone, or whether we should look for help."

"Father, I have always heard of your great name — that you were a mighty spearman and a wise head in council. But this is a very large thing you have said. Two men cannot fight a crowd of strong ones.

"The suitors are not ten, and not twice ten. They are a great many more than that. Count them here, and now. From Dulichium there are fifty-two picked young men, with six servants; from Same, twenty-four; from Zacynthus, twenty; and from Ithaca itself, twelve, all of them the best. And with them are Medon the herald and the divine singer, and two attendants who are skilled at carving meat.

"If we go against all of that inside the hall, I am afraid your revenge would turn out bitter and terrible when you came to take it. Think whether you can find a helper — somebody who would stand up for us both with a ready heart."<sup><a href="#book-16-note-1">1</a></sup>

"Then I shall tell you, and you turn it over. Do you think Athena and father Zeus will be enough for us, or shall I think about another helper?"

"Those are excellent helpers you name, though they sit up high among the clouds and hold power over all men and all immortals."

---

Then Odysseus gave him the plan, and it is worth having in full, because everything from here to the end of the poem runs on it.

"In the morning, go home and join that overbearing crowd. The swineherd will bring me to the town later, looking like an old beggar in a bad way. And if they insult me in the house, let the heart in your breast put up with it while I am badly treated. Even if they drag me by the feet through the hall and out of the door, or throw things at me — watch it and endure it. Tell them to stop being foolish, certainly, and coax them with gentle words. They will not listen; their day is standing beside them.

"And I shall tell you something else; keep it in your mind. When Athena, who thinks of everything, puts it into my head, I shall nod to you. And the moment you see it, take all the weapons of war that are lying in the hall and carry them up and store them in the corner of the high chamber — every one of them.

"And when the suitors miss them and ask you, put them off with soft words. Say: *I have laid them away out of the smoke, because they are not what they were when Odysseus left them and went to Troy; they are spoiled, as far as the breath of the fire has reached them. And besides, the son of Cronos (Zeus) has put a bigger fear in my heart — that you may quarrel over your wine and wound each other and disgrace the feast and the courtship. Iron by itself draws a man on.*<sup><a href="#book-16-note-2">2</a></sup>

"But leave two swords behind for the two of us, and two spears, and two oxhide shields, where our hands can snatch them up.

"And nobody is to know that Odysseus is in the house. Not Laertes, not the swineherd, not any of the servants, and not Penelope herself. You and I alone will find out how the women stand; and let us test some of the men as well, and see who honours us and fears us in his heart, and who does not care and slights you, young as you are and worthy as you are."

"Father, I think you will find out what sort of spirit I have in due course; I am not soft in the head. But I do not think this particular plan will profit the two of us, and I ask you to consider it. You will be a very long time going round the farms testing every man, while at their ease those others go on eating your goods in the halls, without sparing anything.

"The women I do agree you should find out about — which of them dishonour you and which are innocent. But I would rather not go round the farms testing the men now. Let us see to that later, if you really know some sign from Zeus."

---

Meanwhile the ship that had brought Telemachus from Pylos came in to the town, and they hauled her up and carried the gifts to the house of Clytius, and sent a herald to the house of Odysseus to tell Penelope that her son was out in the country and had ordered the ship into the city, so that she should not be frightened and cry.

And the herald and the good swineherd met, both of them carrying the same message to the lady. And when they reached the house, the herald said it out loud in the middle of the servant women: "Your dear son, my queen, has come back from Pylos." And the swineherd went up close to Penelope and told her quietly everything her son had told him to say; and when he had said it all he went out through the courtyard and back to his pigs.

And the suitors were dismayed, and went out and sat down in front of the wall of the yard, outside the gates.

Eurymachus spoke first. "Friends, this is a large thing that Telemachus has brought off in the most insolent way — this journey. And we said it would never happen. Come, let us launch a black ship, the best there is, and get a crew of rowers together, to go quickly and tell the others to come home."

He had not finished when Amphinomus turned in his place and saw a ship inside the deep harbour, with men taking the sails down and oars in their hands. And he laughed pleasantly and said: "There is no need to send any message. They are here. Either some god told them, or they saw her going past themselves and could not catch her."

So the men from the ambush came up from the shore and went to the assembly, and would not let anybody else, young or old, sit down with them.

And Antinous said:

"So the gods have got the man out of trouble. Day after day our lookouts sat on the windy heights, one relieving another; and at sunset we never slept on shore but stayed at sea in the fast ship waiting for the bright Dawn, lying in wait for Telemachus so as to catch him and kill him. And meanwhile some god has brought him home.

"So let us think here about a miserable end for him. He must not get away. I do not believe our business will ever be brought off while he is alive. He is shrewd himself in judgement and planning, and the people are not showing us any particular favour any more.

"Come — before he calls the Greeks to assembly. Because I do not think he will be slack about it. He will be full of anger, and he will stand up in front of everybody and tell them how we plotted his death and failed to catch him; and they will not approve when they hear an ugly thing like that. Take care they do not do us harm, and drive us out of the country, and we go off to somebody else's.

"Let us get in first and take him out in the fields, well away from the town, or on the road. And let us keep his living and his goods, dividing them fairly among ourselves, and give the house to his mother to keep, and to whichever of us marries her.

"But if that does not please you, and you want him to live and keep everything his father left him — then let us stop gathering here and eating up his treasure, and let each man court her from his own house with wedding gifts. And she can marry the one who gives most and comes as her destined husband."

Nobody said anything at all.

Then Amphinomus stood up and spoke among them — the son of Nisus, and the leading man from Dulichium, and the one whose conversation pleased Penelope most, because he had a decent mind.

"Friends, I would not want to kill Telemachus. It is a dreadful thing to kill a man of royal blood. Let us first find out what the gods think about it. If the decrees of great Zeus approve, I shall kill him myself and tell everybody else to. But if the gods turn us away from it, then I say we stop."

They all thought that was well said, and got up and went back into the house of Odysseus and sat down on the polished chairs.

---

Hold on to Amphinomus. He is the only one of the hundred and eight who is ever given a good motive for anything, and he has just talked the others out of a murder; and Penelope likes him, and the poem says so plainly and tells you why. Nothing more will be made of him for two books. He is not going to be spared.

---

But Penelope had heard. The herald Medon had been standing outside the courtyard while they wove the plot inside, and he came and told her; and she came down the long stairs to the hall with her women, and stood by the doorpost with her bright veil in front of her face, and spoke to Antinous by name.

"Antinous. Insolent man. Contriver of wickedness. They say you are the best of all the men of your age in Ithaca for judgement and for speech. You were never any such thing.

"Madman — why do you spin out death and doom for Telemachus, and take no notice of suppliants, whose witness is Zeus? It is an unholy thing to plot evil against one another.

"Do you not know that your own father came here as a fugitive, in terror of the people? They were furious with him, because he had joined up with Taphian pirates and raided the Thesprotians, who were at peace with us. They wanted to destroy him, and tear the heart out of him, and eat up all that great living of his.

"And Odysseus held them off and stopped them, angry as they were.

"And now you eat up his house without paying for it, and court his wife, and try to kill his son, and grieve me terribly. I tell you to stop, and to make the others stop."

And Eurymachus answered her — smoothly.

"Daughter of Icarius, wise Penelope. Take heart. Do not let these things trouble your mind. That man does not exist, and never will, who will lay hands on Telemachus your son while I am alive and looking at the light of the sun.

"Because I tell you this, and it will be brought to pass: his black blood would run round my spear at once. Odysseus himself used to sit me on his knees, often, and put roast meat in my hands and hold the red wine to my lips. So Telemachus is far the dearest of all men to me, and I tell him to have no fear of death — not from the suitors. From the gods it cannot be avoided."

So he said, cheering her up; and he was arranging Telemachus's death in his own mind while he said it.

And she went up to her bright upper room and cried for Odysseus, her own husband, until Athena cast sweet sleep on her eyelids.

---

And in the evening the good swineherd came back to Odysseus and his son. They were getting supper ready, having sacrificed a yearling pig; and Athena had come first and struck Odysseus with her wand and made him an old man again and put the shabby clothes back on him — in case the swineherd looked him in the face and knew him, and went off and told Penelope and did not keep it in his heart.

Telemachus spoke first. "You are back, Eumaeus. What is the news in the town? Are the lordly suitors home from their ambush yet, or are they still out there watching for me?"

"I did not care to go about the city asking. My heart told me to give my message and come straight back. But a fast messenger from your crew met me, a herald, and he got to your mother first. And there is one thing I do know, because I saw it with my own eyes. I was above the town, where the hill of Hermes is, when I saw a fast ship coming into our harbour, with a great many men in her, and she was loaded with shields and double-edged spears. I thought it was them. I do not know."

And Telemachus smiled, and looked across at his father — and took care not to catch the swineherd's eye.

Then they finished the work and laid out the meal and ate; and when they had had enough of eating and drinking they thought about bed, and took the gift of sleep.

---

## NOTES TO BOOK SIXTEEN

<a id="book-16-note-1"></a>
1. **A hundred and eight men.** This is the only place the poem does the arithmetic, and it is worth writing down, because the vagueness of "the suitors" can make them feel like a crowd of extras. Fifty-two from Dulichium with six servants; twenty-four from Same; twenty from Zacynthus; twelve from Ithaca itself, and those the best men on the island. A herald, a singer, and two carvers. That is a hundred and eight armed young men of good family, plus staff, against two — and shortly against four. Telemachus gives the figures because he is trying to talk his father out of it, and his objection is entirely sound. Note also what the numbers say about Ithaca: the twelve local men are outnumbered eight to one by outsiders. This is not a village quarrel. It is most of the aristocracy of four islands, camped in one house, waiting for a kingdom to fall vacant.

<a id="book-16-note-2"></a>
2. **"Iron by itself draws a man on."** The excuse Telemachus is coached to give for clearing the weapons out of the hall has two halves, and the second half is a proverb: the mere presence of a weapon pulls a man towards using it. It is offered here as a piece of ordinary wisdom that no one would think to argue with — of course you do not leave spears standing about a room where men are drinking — and it is doing double work, because it is also a perfectly accurate description of what is about to happen in that room. The plan depends on the suitors accepting a commonplace about human nature and failing to notice that it is being used against them.

---

*Book Seventeen: In Which an Old Dog Waits on a Dunghill, and a Stool Is Thrown.*


<div class="page-break"></div>

<!-- Source: book/odyssey-book-17.md -->

# THE ODYSSEY
### Retold in English, with Explanations

---

## BOOK SEVENTEEN
### In Which an Old Dog Waits on a Dunghill, and a Stool Is Thrown

---

When Dawn came up, rosy-fingered, Telemachus tied his good sandals under his feet and picked up his heavy spear, ready for the town.

"Old friend, I am going to the city, so that my mother can see me. I do not think she will stop her miserable crying and her weeping until she looks at me with her own eyes. And here is what I want you to do. Take this unlucky stranger to the town so that he can beg his dinner there; whoever likes will give him a crust and a cup. I cannot possibly carry every man in the world; I have troubles enough of my own. And if the stranger is annoyed at that, it will be the worse for him. I like to say what I mean."

"My friend, I have no wish to be kept here either. It is better to beg one's dinner in a town than in the fields; whoever likes will give me something. I am not of an age to stay about a farm and do everything a master tells me. Go on. This man will guide me, as you have said, when I have warmed myself at the fire and the sun has got up. These clothes of mine are miserably thin, and the frost before dawn might finish me; and you say the town is a long way off."

So Telemachus went off out of the yard, walking fast, sowing trouble for the suitors.

And when he came to the fine house he set his spear against a tall pillar and stepped in over the stone threshold.

Eurycleia saw him long before anybody else, as she was spreading fleeces over the carved chairs, and she came straight to him crying, and the other women of the house came crowding round and kissed his head and his shoulders in welcome.

And Penelope came out of her room, looking like Artemis (goddess of the hunt) or golden Aphrodite (goddess of love), and threw her arms round her son crying, and kissed his head and both his beautiful eyes.

"You have come, Telemachus. Sweet light. I thought I should never see you again, after you went off to Pylos in a ship, secretly, against my will, to ask after your father. Come, tell me what sight you had of him."

"Mother, do not stir up crying in me, and do not set my heart going in my breast, when I have just got out from under a sheer destruction. Wash, and put clean clothes on, and go upstairs with your women, and promise a full offering to all the gods, in the hope that Zeus may grant us a day of requital. I am going to the assembly, to call in a stranger who came with me from Pylos. I sent him on ahead with my crew, and told Peiraeus to take him home and look after him and honour him until I came."

She did as he said.

And Telemachus went out through the hall with his spear in his hand, and two swift dogs went with him; and Athena poured a supernatural grace over him, so that all the people stared at him as he came. And the lordly suitors gathered round him with fine words on their lips and plans for trouble in their hearts; but he kept clear of the crowd of them and went and sat down with Mentor, and Antiphus, and Halitherses, who had been his father's friends from the beginning.

And Peiraeus came up bringing Theoclymenus through the town, and Telemachus went straight to the stranger.

"Peiraeus, keep the gifts at your house for the moment. If the suitors kill me quietly in the halls and divide up my father's goods among them, I would rather you had them and enjoyed them than any of those men. And if I manage to sow death and doom for them, then bring them to my house and be glad with me."

And he brought the stranger home; and there they bathed and oiled and dressed him and sat him down, and the housekeeper brought bread and a great many good things.

And Penelope sat opposite them by the doorpost of the hall, leaning back in her chair, spinning fine yarn.

"Telemachus, I shall go upstairs and lie down on that bed of mine which has become a bed of sorrows, always wet with my tears since the day Odysseus went off to Troy with the sons of Atreus. And you could not bring yourself, before those insolent men came into this house, to tell me plainly about your father's homecoming, if you have heard anything."

So he told her: how Nestor had received him kindly at Pylos, like a father receiving a son, but knew nothing; how he had been sent on to Sparta, and how Menelaus had told him what the old man of the sea had reported — that Odysseus was alive on an island, weeping, in the house of the nymph Calypso, who was holding him there against his will, and that he had no ship and no crew to carry him over the wide back of the sea.

And her heart was stirred in her breast as she listened.

And then Theoclymenus spoke.

"Honoured wife of Odysseus — this man has no clear knowledge of it. Listen to me instead. I shall prophesy to you exactly, and hide nothing.

"Let Zeus be my witness first of all, and this table of hospitality, and the hearth of Odysseus that I have come to: Odysseus is already here, in his own country. He is sitting still somewhere or moving about, and he is learning about these evil deeds, and he is planting the seed of destruction for every one of the suitors."

"Ah, stranger — I only wish that word may be fulfilled. Then you would very soon know my friendship, and get so many gifts from me that anybody who met you would call you a lucky man."

---

Meanwhile the suitors were amusing themselves in front of the hall with the discus and the throwing spear, on the levelled ground where they always did it, in their usual insolent style; and when it was dinner time and the flocks came in from the fields all round, Medon called them in to eat.

And Odysseus and the good swineherd were setting out from the farm for the town. Eumaeus gave him a staff, and slung a wretched wallet round him, full of holes, on a twisted cord.

And on the way, where the road runs by a spring — a fine built spring with cold water flowing out of the rock, and a grove of water-loving poplars round it in a circle, and an altar of the nymphs above it where every traveller made an offering — they met Melanthius, the son of Dolius, coming down with the pick of the goats for the suitors' dinner, and two herdsmen with him.

And when he saw them he abused them, shockingly.

"There you are: the vile leading the vile. The god always brings like to like. Where are you taking this pig, you miserable swineherd — this disgusting beggar, this spoiler of feasts? He will stand rubbing his shoulders against a great many doorposts, begging for scraps, and no swords and no cauldrons.

"If you gave him to me to look after my farm, and sweep out the stalls, and carry green stuff to the kids, he could drink whey and put some muscle on his thigh. But since he has learnt nothing but bad habits he will not go near an honest job; he would rather go cringing round the neighbourhood begging food for that bottomless belly of his.

"And I will tell you this, and it will happen. If he goes to the house of great Odysseus, a great many footstools thrown from men's hands will fly round his head and be broken on his ribs, as he gets pelted through the house."

And as he passed he kicked Odysseus on the hip, stupidly; and did not knock him off the path. He stood firm.

And Odysseus considered whether to go for him with the staff and take the life out of him, or lift him up bodily and dash his head on the ground. And he held it in and endured it.

But the swineherd looked the man in the face and cursed him, and lifted up his hands and prayed aloud.

"Nymphs of the spring, daughters of Zeus — if ever Odysseus burned you the thigh pieces of lambs and kids, wrapped in rich fat, then grant me this prayer. Let that man come back. Let some god guide him home. He would knock all this display out of you, all these airs you flaunt as you go swaggering about the town, while worthless herdsmen ruin the flocks."

"Listen to the cunning dog talk. One day I shall take him off in a black ship well away from Ithaca and sell him for a good price. And I only wish Apollo would strike Telemachus down in the halls today, or that the suitors would do for him — as surely as the day of homecoming is lost for Odysseus, far away."

And he left them going slowly along, and went on quickly and reached the house and went in and sat down among the suitors, opposite Eurymachus, who liked him best of all of them.

---

The two of them came up and stopped outside; and the sound of the hollow lyre came out to them, because Phemius was striking up a song. And Odysseus took the swineherd's hand.

"Eumaeus, this must be the fine house of Odysseus. Anybody could pick it out of a crowd of buildings. One part leads on to the next; the courtyard is finished off with a wall and a coping, and the double doors are strong. No man could force it. And I can tell there are a great many men at dinner in there, because the smell of roast is coming out, and the lyre is going, which the gods have made the companion of a feast."

"You have picked it out easily enough; you are not a fool in other things either. But let us think what we are going to do. Either you go in first and I stay here; or you stay and I go first. Do not wait about outside, in case somebody sees you and throws something at you or hits you."

"I understand. My mind takes it in. Go in first; I shall stay here. I know all about being hit and having things thrown at me. My heart is patient, because I have had a great deal of trouble on the sea and in war. Let this be added to it.

"But there is no hiding a ravening belly, that cursed thing, which gives men so much trouble. It is for the belly's sake that ships with good benches are fitted out and sent over the barren sea to bring harm to enemies."

---

And while they were talking, a dog that had been lying there raised his head and pricked up his ears.

Argos. Odysseus's own dog, whom he had bred himself and never had the use of, because he went off to holy Ilios first. In the old days the young men used to take him out after wild goats and deer and hares. Now he lay where he had been thrown, on the deep pile of mule dung and cattle dung that was heaped in front of the doors until the servants got round to carting it away to manure the great estate. There lay the dog Argos, full of vermin.

And when he saw Odysseus standing near he wagged his tail and dropped both his ears; and he had not the strength to get any closer to his master.

And Odysseus looked away and wiped a tear off, easily, so that Eumaeus should not see it, and asked him a question at once.

"Eumaeus, it is a strange thing that this dog is lying here on the dung heap. He is well made; though I cannot tell whether he had any speed to go with the looks, or whether he was one of those table dogs that gentlemen keep for show."

"That is the dog of a man who died a long way off. If he were still in body and in action what he was when Odysseus left him and went to Troy, you would be astonished if you saw his speed and his strength. Nothing he ever chased in the deep wood got away from him; he was a wonder at following a scent.

"But now he is in a bad way. His master has died somewhere abroad, and the women do not care and will not look after him. Servants stop doing their work properly the moment their masters are no longer over them. Zeus who sees everything takes away half a man's worth on the day that slavery comes on him."<sup><a href="#book-17-note-1">1</a></sup>

And with that he went into the house, straight in among the suitors.

And the fate of black death took hold of Argos, at once, when he had seen Odysseus in the twentieth year.

---

I shall not do anything to that, because it does not need me. I shall only point out two things and then let it alone.

The first is that the dog is the first creature in Ithaca to know him. Not his son, who had to be told; not the nurse, who will find the scar in a few books' time; not his wife, who will make him prove it. A half-dead animal on a manure heap, with no evidence at all, gets it right instantly and has plainly been getting it right, and waiting, for twenty years.

The second is what Odysseus does about it. He looks away and wipes his face where the swineherd cannot see, and then asks a casual question about the animal's breeding. He does not go to him. He cannot: the whole plan depends on it, and it would cost him everything, and he knows it. So the only creature in the country who recognises him gets nothing at all — no word, no hand, no acknowledgement — and dies about ninety seconds later.

---

Telemachus saw the swineherd first, and nodded to him and called him over; and Eumaeus looked round and picked up a stool and sat down opposite, and Telemachus cut off a portion of meat and gave him bread out of the basket.

And Odysseus came in behind him, like an old and pitiful beggar, leaning on a stick, with wretched clothes on his body, and sat down on the ash-wood threshold inside the doorway, leaning against the cypress doorpost.

And Telemachus took a whole loaf and as much meat as his two hands would hold, and told the swineherd to carry it over to him and tell him to go round the suitors and beg from each of them: "Shame is a bad companion for a man in need."

So the beggar took it, and prayed for the young man, and ate.

And when the singer had finished, the suitors made a noise through the hall; and Athena came and stood by Odysseus and told him to go and gather scraps from them, so that he might learn which of them were decent and which were lawless — and even so she was not going to save a single one of them from destruction.

So he went from left to right, holding his hand out, exactly like a man who had been begging all his life. And they pitied him and gave him something, and wondered at him, and asked each other who he was and where he came from.

And Melanthius the goatherd spoke up.

"Listen to me, suitors of the famous queen. I have seen this stranger before; the swineherd brought him here. I do not know for certain who he says he is."

And Antinous turned on Eumaeus.

"You notorious swineherd. What did you bring this fellow into the town for? Have we not enough vagabonds already, disgusting beggars who spoil a feast? Do you think it a small thing that they gather here and eat up your master's living, that you have called this one in as well?"

"Antinous, that is not well said, noble as you are. Who ever goes out and invites a stranger from abroad, unless he is one of the men who work for the public good — a prophet, or a healer of sicknesses, or a carpenter, or a divine singer, who gives delight with his song? Those are the men who are asked for all over the boundless earth. Nobody would invite a beggar to make trouble for himself.

"But you are always harder than any of the suitors on the servants of Odysseus, and hardest of all on me. And I do not care, so long as sensible Penelope is alive in these halls, and godlike Telemachus."

"Be quiet. Do not answer him at any length. Antinous is always harsh, and provoking, with ugly words; and he stirs up the others too."

And then he turned on Antinous himself.

"You take care of me exactly as a father takes care of his son, telling me to drive this stranger out of the hall with a hard word. God forbid. Take something and give it to him; I do not grudge it — I tell you to. And do not worry about my mother in this matter, or any of the servants in the house of Odysseus.

"But that is not the thought in your mind at all. You would very much rather eat a great deal yourself than give any of it away."

"Telemachus, you great orator, you unstoppable temper — what a thing to say. If all the suitors gave him as much as I am going to, this house would keep him off for three whole months."

And he pulled out the footstool from under the table where he had been resting his shining feet, and showed it to him.

But all the others gave, and filled the wallet with bread and meat.

---

And Odysseus was on his way back to the threshold to eat what the Greeks had given him, when he stopped beside Antinous and spoke to him.

"Give, friend. You do not seem to me the worst of the Greeks, but the best; you look like a king. So you ought to give a better piece of bread than the others, and I should sing your praises all over the boundless earth.

"Because I too once lived in a house among men, a rich man in a wealthy house, and I gave often to a wanderer, whoever he was and whatever he came needing. I had servants past counting and everything else that men live well on and are called rich for.

"And Zeus made nothing of it all. He put it in my heart to go off to Egypt with roving pirates, a long voyage, so that I should be destroyed."

And he told him the shape of it: the crews who would not be held, the plundering, the country roused, the men killed and the men led off alive into slavery.

"And they gave me to a friend of theirs to take to Cyprus. And from there I have come here, and I have had nothing but trouble."

And Antinous answered him.

"What god has brought this nuisance here to spoil our dinner? Stand out there in the middle, away from my table, or you will find yourself back in a bitter Egypt and a bitter Cyprus. What a bold and shameless beggar you are. You go up to every man in turn, and they give recklessly, because there is no holding back and no grudging when a man is being generous with somebody else's goods, and every one of them has plenty of it in front of him."

And Odysseus drew back and said:

"Well, well. So your looks are better than your sense. You would not give a suppliant so much as a grain of salt out of your own house, you who are sitting at another man's table and cannot bring yourself to take up a piece of bread and hand it over — with all that in front of you."

That made Antinous angrier still, and he glared at him and spoke.

"Now I do not think you are going to get out of this hall in one piece, since you have started on abuse."

And he took up the footstool and threw it, and hit him on the right shoulder, at the base of the back.

And Odysseus stood there like a rock. The blow from Antinous did not so much as shift him. He shook his head in silence, deep down planning trouble.

And he went back and sat down on the threshold and put his well-filled wallet down and spoke to the suitors.

"Hear me, suitors of the famous queen, while I say what my heart tells me. There is no grief in a man's mind and no pain when he is hit fighting for his own property — for his cattle, or his white sheep. Antinous hit me because of my miserable belly, that cursed thing which brings so much trouble on men.

"But if there are gods anywhere for beggars, and avenging spirits, then let the end of death come for Antinous before ever he is married."

"Sit and eat quietly, stranger, or get out. Otherwise the young men will drag you through the house by the hand or the foot for talking like that, and skin you alive."

And every one of the others was extremely angry, and one of the arrogant young men would say:

"Antinous, you did wrong to hit that unlucky wanderer. You are a doomed man, if there happens to be some god up in the sky. And the gods do put on the shape of strangers from far countries, and take every kind of form, and go about the cities watching to see which men are violent and which are law-abiding."

Antinous took no notice whatever.

And Telemachus nursed a great grief in his heart at his father being struck; but he did not let a single tear fall to the ground. He shook his head in silence, deep down planning trouble.<sup><a href="#book-17-note-2">2</a></sup>

---

Penelope heard about it upstairs, and said, among her women: "May Apollo the famous archer strike *you* like that, Antinous." And the housekeeper Eurynome said: "If our prayers were answered, not one of them would ever see the fair-throned Dawn again."

"Nurse, they are all hateful, because they plan wickedness. But Antinous is like black death itself. Some unlucky stranger is going through the house begging alms of the men, because want drives him; and all the others filled his wallet and gave him something. And Antinous threw a footstool and hit him on the right shoulder."

And she sent for the swineherd and told him to bring the stranger to her, so that she could greet him and ask whether he had heard anything of Odysseus.

"My queen, I only wish the suitors would be quiet. He tells such tales as would put a spell on your heart. I had him three nights and kept him three days in my hut — he came to me first, when he ran away from a ship — and he had not got to the end of the story of his troubles.

"It is like watching a singer who has been taught by the gods to sing songs of longing to men, and they cannot stop listening while he goes on. That is how he held me, sitting beside me in the hut. He says he is a friend of Odysseus's family and lives in Crete. And he says he has heard that Odysseus is close by, alive, in the rich country of the Thesprotians, and is bringing a great deal of treasure home."

"Go and call him here, so that he can tell it to my face."

And then Telemachus sneezed loudly, and the whole house rang with it; and Penelope laughed, and her words came out fast.

"Go and call the stranger to me. Did you not hear my son sneeze at everything I said? So may death be brought about for every one of the suitors; not one of them shall get away from death and the fates. And here is another thing; keep it in your mind. If I find that everything he says is true, I shall dress him in a cloak and a tunic, good clothes."<sup><a href="#book-17-note-3">3</a></sup>

So the swineherd went and gave the message.

"Eumaeus, I should be glad to tell the whole truth to wise Penelope, because I know all about that man; the two of us have had the same troubles. But I am afraid of that crowd of hard suitors, whose insolence and violence reach the iron sky. Just now, when I was going through the hall doing no harm to anybody, that man hit me and hurt me, and neither Telemachus nor anybody else did anything about it.

"So tell Penelope to wait in the hall until the sun goes down, eager as she is. And then let her ask me about her husband's homecoming, and give me a seat nearer the fire; because the clothes I have on are poor, as you know, since it was you I first appealed to."

And the swineherd went back with that, and Penelope was surprised he had not come. "You are not bringing him, Eumaeus. What does the vagrant mean by that? Is he unusually afraid of somebody? Or is he ashamed of himself in the house? A shy beggar is a bad beggar."

And when Eumaeus explained, she said: "The stranger is no fool. He is guessing at what may very well be true. I do not think there are any other men on earth quite so outrageous, or so given to reckless behaviour."

Then the swineherd went back to Telemachus and told him he was going out to the farm to look after the pigs, and to see to their living and his; and Telemachus told him to have his supper first and come back in the morning and bring good victims for sacrifice.

So he sat down again and ate and drank his fill, and then went back to his pigs, leaving the courtyard and the halls full of feasters.

And they took their pleasure in dancing and singing, because by now the evening had come on.

---

## NOTES TO BOOK SEVENTEEN

<a id="book-17-note-1"></a>
1. **Argos, and what Eumaeus says over him.** The dog's name simply means *swift*, or *bright* — an entirely ordinary name for a hunting dog, of the sort a man would give an animal without thinking about it, which is part of the point. — What deserves as much attention as the dog is the sentence the swineherd attaches to him, because it is one of the bleakest things anybody says in this poem: that Zeus takes away half a man's worth on the day slavery comes upon him. Eumaeus is himself a slave. He is explaining, without self-pity and as a piece of general knowledge, why the women of the house no longer bother to feed an old dog — servants stop doing their work well once nobody is over them — and in the middle of it he states, as a fact about the world, that people like him are worth half what they were. He is at that moment the most honourable person in the book, and he has just cleaned up after the suitors' goats. The poem sets his opinion of himself beside his conduct and says nothing.

<a id="book-17-note-2"></a>
2. **The stool, and the suitors' own unease.** Notice who objects. It is not Telemachus, who says nothing and lets no tear fall; and it is not Eumaeus, who has already been slapped down once. It is the other suitors — the anonymous ones, the crowd — who tell Antinous he did wrong, and their reason is worth having in full: *you are a doomed man, if there happens to be a god about; the gods put on the shape of strangers and go round the cities watching who is violent and who is not.* They are exactly right, in every particular, including the disguise. And having said it they go back to their dinner. Nobody gets up. It is a very precise picture of how a bad thing carries on happening in a room full of people who can all see it is wrong: the objection gets made, out loud, by somebody with no stake in it, and then the plates are passed.

<a id="book-17-note-3"></a>
3. **The sneeze.** A sneeze at the moment a wish is spoken was a good omen, and a well-attested one — the idea outlived antiquity by a very long way, and is the distant ancestor of blessing somebody who sneezes. What makes this one delightful is the timing and the fact that Penelope *laughs*. She has just finished saying she hopes every suitor in the house will die; her son sneezes somewhere down the hall; and she takes it, quite seriously and also with real amusement, as heaven signing the document. It is the only time she laughs in the poem.

---

*Book Eighteen: In Which Two Beggars Fight for a Sausage, and a Wife Comes Downstairs.*


<div class="page-break"></div>

<!-- Source: book/odyssey-book-18.md -->

# THE ODYSSEY
### Retold in English, with Explanations

---

## BOOK EIGHTEEN
### In Which Two Beggars Fight for a Sausage, and a Wife Comes Downstairs

---

Then a beggar came in, a public one, who used to go begging round the town of Ithaca, and who was famous for a greedy belly and eating and drinking without stopping. He had no strength and no muscle, though he was very big to look at.

His name was Arnaeus; his mother had given him that at birth. But all the young men called him Irus, because he ran errands for anybody who asked.<sup><a href="#book-18-note-1">1</a></sup>

He came in and tried to drive Odysseus out of his own house.

"Get away from the door, old man, before you get dragged out by the foot. Do you not see them all winking at me and telling me to haul you out? I would be ashamed to. Get up, or the two of us will be settling it with our hands."

And Odysseus looked at him from under his brows.

"You strange man. I am doing you no harm and saying nothing about you, and I do not grudge it if somebody gives you something, even a good deal. This threshold will take both of us, and you have no call to be jealous over other men's property. You look to me like a vagrant, the same as I am; it is the gods who hand out prosperity.

"Do not push me too far with your hands, or you will make me angry; and old as I am I shall spoil your chest and your lips with blood. And I should have a quieter day of it tomorrow, because I do not think you would come back a second time to the hall of Odysseus."

"Listen to the tramp rattling away, like an old woman at the oven.
