I shall work him over with both hands and knock every tooth out of his jaws onto the floor, the way you do with a pig caught in the corn. Put your belt on, and let all these gentlemen see us fight. How are you going to take on a younger man?"

Antinous heard them squabbling on the polished threshold, and laughed with real pleasure.

"Friends, there has never been anything like this. What sport the god has brought into this house. The stranger and Irus are challenging each other to a fight. Let us set them on."

They all jumped up laughing and gathered round the two beggars in their rags.

"Listen to me, suitors," said Antinous. "There are goats' paunches lying at the fire that we set aside for supper, stuffed with fat and blood. Whichever of the two wins and proves the better man can stand up and take whichever of them he likes. And he shall always eat with us afterwards, and we will let no other beggar come in and beg among us."

They all liked that. And Odysseus, with cunning in his mind, said:

"Friends, there is no possible way for an old man worn down with trouble to fight a younger one. But my belly tells me to — my belly, that does all the harm — so that I get myself beaten. But swear me all a great oath first: that no man of you, out of favour to Irus, will hit me with his heavy hand and put me down for him unfairly."

They swore it. And Telemachus said: "Stranger, if your proud heart tells you to defend yourself against this man, then have no fear of any other Greek here, because whoever strikes you will have more men to fight. I am the host; and the princes Antinous and Eurymachus agree, and they are both sensible men."

---

Then Odysseus pulled his rags up and belted them round his loins, and out came his thighs, big and handsome, and his broad shoulders showed, and his chest and his powerful arms; and Athena stood beside him and made the limbs of the shepherd of the people greater still.

The suitors were extremely surprised, and one would look at the man beside him and say: "Irus will very soon be un-Irused, and it will be trouble he asked for. What a thigh the old man shows from under those rags."

And Irus's spirit went badly to pieces. The servants had to belt him up and bring him out by force, terrified, with the flesh trembling on his bones.

And Antinous rounded on him. "You braggart. Better if you had never been born, if you are shaking like that at an old man worn out by the misery he carries about with him. I will tell you plainly, and it will be brought about: if he beats you, I shall put you on a black ship and send you to the mainland to king Echetus, who mutilates everybody — and he will cut off your nose and your ears with the pitiless bronze and tear away your privates and give them raw to the dogs to eat."<sup><a href="#book-18-note-2">2</a></sup>

That made him tremble a great deal more; and they led him into the middle, and both men put their hands up.

Then Odysseus considered whether to hit him so as to knock the life out of him where he stood, or to fell him gently and stretch him out. And gently seemed better, in case the Greeks looked too closely at him.

So when they had their hands up, Irus hit him on the right shoulder, and Odysseus hit him on the neck under the ear and crushed the bones inside, and the red blood came up through his mouth at once, and he went down in the dust bellowing, with his teeth chattering and his heels drumming on the ground.

And the lordly suitors threw up their hands and died laughing.

And Odysseus took him by the foot and dragged him out through the doorway into the courtyard and propped him against the wall and put his staff in his hand.

"Sit there now and keep the pigs and the dogs off. And do not go setting yourself up as lord over strangers and beggars, you miserable creature, or you may get something worse."

Then he slung the shabby bag over his shoulders, with all its holes, and went back and sat down on the threshold.

And they went in laughing and made him welcome. "May Zeus and the other gods give you whatever you want most, stranger, since you have stopped that insatiable creature begging round the country. We shall very soon be shipping him over to king Echetus."

And Odysseus was glad at the sound of it.

---

I should like you to hold two things about that scene at once, because the poem plainly does.

It is funny. A hall full of men roaring, a bragging beggar who cannot fight being belted into the ring by servants while his knees knock, and a supposed old man who turns out, when he lifts his rags, to have the thighs of a wrestler. The suitors' joke about being *un-Irused* is a genuine joke and it is meant to be laughed at, and the poem is enjoying itself.

And underneath it, look at what is actually happening. A man with nothing is being made to fight another man with nothing, by rich men, for the amusement of the rich men, with a bag of tripe as the prize; and when he loses, the sponsor of the entertainment promises to have him shipped to a foreign torturer who will cut pieces off him. Nobody objects. The oath Odysseus asks for — that none of them will join in and hold him down — was not a foolish precaution.

Irus is a bully and a fool and he picked the fight. He is also the only person in this book who tries to defend that doorway from an intruder, and he is thrashed for it by the intruder, in front of the men who are actually stealing the house.

---

Then Amphinomus took two loaves out of the basket and brought them to him, and pledged him in a golden cup.

"Good health, father stranger. May you have prosperity in time to come; you are held down by a great many troubles now."

And Odysseus answered him.

"Amphinomus, you strike me as a man of good sense; you are your father's son, and I have heard his good name — Nisus of Dulichium, a good man and a rich one. They say you are his, and you seem a reasonable man. So listen to me, and take in what I say.

"Of everything that breathes and moves upon the earth, the earth raises nothing feebler than a man.

"While the gods give him prosperity and his knees are quick, he thinks he will never suffer anything in time to come. And when the blessed gods measure him out sorrow, he carries that too, unwillingly, with an enduring heart. Because the mind of men on the earth is like the day the father of gods and men brings on them.

"I too was once on my way to being a prosperous man, and I did a great many reckless things, giving way to my own strength and power, and trusting in my father and my brothers. So let no man ever be lawless. Let him keep whatever the gods give him in silence.

"And these are the sort of reckless things I see the suitors devising — wasting the property and dishonouring the wife of a man who I do not think will be away from his friends and his own country much longer. He is very near.

"May some god take you home out of his path. May you not meet him when he comes back to his own dear country. Because I do not think the suitors and he will be parted without blood, once he is under his own roof."

And he poured a libation and drank the honey-sweet wine and put the cup back into the prince's hands.

And Amphinomus went off through the hall with his head down and his heart heavy, because his spirit foresaw trouble. And even so he did not escape his fate; Athena had bound him too, to be beaten down by the hands and the spear of Telemachus.

And he sat down again in the chair he had got up from.

---

That is the only warning Odysseus gives anybody in this poem, and it is a real one — not a threat dressed as advice, but a genuine attempt to get one man out of the building before the roof comes in. He does it because Amphinomus brought him bread and spoke to him kindly, which nobody else in that hall has done.

And it does not work. Not because the man is stupid — he understands it perfectly; the poem says his heart foresaw trouble — but because he goes and sits down again in the same chair. Which is, I am afraid, what most people do.

---

Then Athena put it into the mind of Penelope to show herself to the suitors, so as to set their hearts fluttering and make herself more honoured than before in the eyes of her husband and her son.

She gave a little laugh, for no reason, and said: "Eurynome, my heart wants something it never wanted before: I want to show myself to the suitors, hateful as they are to me. And I should like to say a word to my son that would do him good — not to spend all his time with those overbearing men, who speak kindly to him and are planning harm."

"All of that is well said, child. Go and speak to your son. But wash first, and put oil on your cheeks. Do not go down with your face all stained with crying; it does no good to grieve endlessly. And your son is now the age you always prayed to see him."

"Eurynome, do not urge me to wash and oil myself out of kindness. The gods who hold Olympus destroyed my beauty on the day my husband went away in the hollow ships. But tell Autonoe and Hippodameia to come and stand beside me in the hall. I will not go among men alone. I am ashamed to."

And while the old woman was gone to call them, Athena thought of something else, and poured a sweet sleep over the daughter of Icarius (Penelope); and she sank back and slept where she sat, and all her joints let go.

And the shining goddess gave her immortal gifts, so that the Greeks should marvel at her. She washed her beautiful face with the ambrosial beauty that Aphrodite (goddess of love) uses when she goes into the lovely dance of the Graces; and she made her taller and fuller to look at, and whiter than new-sawn ivory.

Then she went away; and the women came in, chattering, and the sound of them woke Penelope, and she rubbed her cheeks with her hands.

"That was a soft sleep that wrapped me round, miserable as I am. I wish pure Artemis (goddess of the hunt) would give me so soft a death, now, this minute, so that I need not go on wasting my life away grieving and longing for the excellence of my husband, who was the best of all the Greeks."

And she went down from her bright upper room, not alone; two women went with her. And when she came among the suitors she stood beside the doorpost of the great hall, holding her shining veil in front of her face, and a faithful woman stood on either side of her.

And their knees went weak where they stood, and their hearts were bewitched with desire, and every one of them prayed to lie in her bed.

---

But she spoke to her son.

"Telemachus, your mind is no longer steady. When you were a child you had better judgement. Now you are grown and have come to the measure of a man, and any stranger looking at your height and your looks would say you were the son of a wealthy house; and your mind and your judgement are no longer what they were.

"What a thing to have happened in these halls — that you let this stranger be knocked about so shamefully. How would it be if a stranger, sitting in our house, came to harm from being handled like that? It would be your shame and your disgrace among men."

"Mother, I do not blame you for being angry. But I do notice things and understand them, both good and bad, and I am not the child I was.

"All the same, I cannot manage everything sensibly. These men sit on either side of me knocking me off balance, planning harm, and I have nobody to help me. And the fight between the stranger and Irus did not turn out the way the suitors wanted; the stranger was the better man.

"I wish to heaven the suitors were sitting in our halls at this moment with their heads hanging, beaten — some of them in the courtyard and some inside — the way Irus is sitting out there by the courtyard gate now, with his head lolling like a drunk, unable to stand up straight or get home, because his legs have gone."

---

Then Eurymachus said: "Daughter of Icarius, sensible Penelope, if all the Greeks in Argos could see you, there would be more suitors than these feasting in your halls from tomorrow morning; because you are beyond all other women in beauty and in stature and in the balance of the mind inside you."

"Eurymachus, the immortals destroyed my excellence and my beauty and my figure on the day the Greeks embarked for Ilium (Troy), and my husband Odysseus went with them. If he were to come home and take care of my life, my name would be greater and better than it is. As it is I am in trouble; a god has let loose so much of it on me.

"When he was going he took me by the wrist of my right hand and said: *Wife, I do not think all the Greeks will come home from Troy unhurt. So I do not know whether a god will spare me or whether I shall be caught there. Take care of everything here. Look after my father and my mother in the house as you do now, or more, while I am away. And when you see our son with a beard on his face, then marry whom you like and leave your house.*

"That is what he said, and all of it is coming about. The night will come when a hateful marriage finds me, whose happiness Zeus has taken away.

"But here is what grieves me to the heart. This was never the way of suitors before. Men who want to court a good woman, the daughter of a rich house, and to compete with each other for her, bring in their own cattle and their own fat sheep and make a feast for the bride's friends, and give her splendid gifts. They do not eat up somebody else's living for nothing."

And Odysseus was glad, because she was drawing gifts out of them and charming their hearts with soft words, while her mind was set on something else entirely.

And Antinous said: "Daughter of Icarius, whatever gifts any of the Greeks wants to bring here, take them; it is not right to refuse a gift. But we shall not go back to our own lands, or anywhere else, until you marry the best man among us."

So they all sent their heralds to fetch presents. Antinous's man brought a great embroidered robe, very beautiful, with twelve golden brooches on it fitted with curved clasps. Eurymachus's brought a chain of gold strung with amber beads, that shone like the sun. Two men brought Eurydamas a pair of earrings, three drops to each of them, with a great grace shining out of them. Another brought Peisander a necklace. And every one of the Greeks gave something fine.

And the queen went up to her upper room, and her women carried the beautiful presents up behind her.

---

Now: watch what has just happened, because it is one of the cleverest things anybody does in this poem and it is done in about nine sentences.

She comes down looking better than she has looked in twenty years, at a moment she did not choose and by an intervention she does not know about. She reproaches her son in front of everybody for allowing a guest to be abused, which puts her firmly on the side of the household and the law. She then quotes her absent husband's own parting instructions, which have the effect of announcing that she is now, technically, free to marry — and she gets the sob in the right place.

And then she observes, sweetly, that the gentlemen have not been doing this properly. Real suitors bring cattle. Real suitors bring gifts.

Within a minute there are heralds running all over Ithaca and the property is flowing the right way up the road for the first time in three years.

Her husband is sitting ten feet away in rags watching it, and the poem says he was *glad* — glad because she was getting presents out of them while her mind was on something else. He does not admire her because she is loyal, or because she is sad, or because she is beautiful, though she is all three. He admires her because she is working the room.

That is the marriage this whole poem has been walking towards, and here is the first glimpse of the two of them in the same space, doing the same thing, on the same side, and only one of them knows it.

---

Then they turned to dancing and singing and enjoyed themselves and waited for the evening to come on; and the dark evening came on them while they were enjoying themselves.

And they set up three braziers in the hall to give light, and put dry firewood in them, long seasoned and newly split, and mixed torches in; and the maids of enduring Odysseus took turns to keep the flame going.

And Odysseus said to them:

"Maids of Odysseus, of the master who has been away so long — go into the house where the honoured queen is. Sit with her and turn the spindle and comfort her, or card the wool in your hands. I will provide the light for all these gentlemen. Even if they want to sit here till the golden Dawn, they will not tire me out. I am very used to enduring."

And the women laughed and looked at one another. And Melantho abused him — a girl with pretty cheeks, the daughter of Dolius, whom Penelope had brought up herself and treated like her own child and given toys to whenever she wanted them. And even so she had no grief in her heart for Penelope; she was Eurymachus's lover.

"You miserable stranger, you must be out of your wits, if you will not go off and sleep at a smithy or a lodging-house instead of standing here talking loudly among all these lords, and not the least bit frightened. Either the wine has your wits, or your mind is always like this and you talk nonsense. Are you so beside yourself because you beat that tramp Irus? Take care a better man than Irus does not stand up against you and knock your head about with his strong hands and throw you out of the house covered in blood."

And Odysseus looked at her from under his brows. "You bitch. I shall go straight over there and tell Telemachus what you have said, and he will cut you to pieces where you stand."

And that frightened the women off. They fled through the hall with their knees shaking, because they thought he meant it.<sup><a href="#book-18-note-3">3</a></sup>

---

And he took his stand beside the burning braziers and kept the light going, looking at all of them; and his mind was turning over other things, which were not going to be left unfinished.

But Athena would not let the arrogant suitors leave off their biting insults, so that the pain should sink deeper still into the heart of Odysseus.

And Eurymachus started it, raising a laugh at him.

"Listen to me, suitors of the glorious queen. It cannot be without a god's hand that this man has come to the house of Odysseus. At any rate the torchlight seems to be coming from the man himself — off the top of his head, where there is not one hair, no, nor even a few."

And then to Odysseus: "Stranger, would you be willing to work for hire, if I took you on at a farm on the boundary — your wages guaranteed — gathering stones for walls and planting tall trees? I would keep you in bread all the year round and give you clothes for your body and sandals for your feet. But since you have learned nothing but bad habits, you will not want to work; you would rather beg round the country and feed that bottomless belly of yours."

And Odysseus said:

"Eurymachus, I only wish there could be a contest between the two of us in the spring, when the days grow long — in a hayfield, and I with a curved scythe in my hands and you with another, and plenty of grass, and the two of us at work with nothing to eat until it was fully dark.

"Or oxen to drive, the best there are, big tawny beasts, both of them well fed on grass, the same age and the same strength, and their power not easy to wear out; and a field of four acres, with the soil giving way under the plough. Then you would see whether I could cut an unbroken furrow all the way.

"Or if Zeus were to raise a war somewhere this very day, and I had a shield and two spears and a bronze helmet fitted to my temples — then you would see me in among the front-line men, and you would not be standing there making jokes about my belly.

"But you are extremely insolent and your mind is hard, and you think you are a great man and a strong one because you keep company with a few worthless people. If Odysseus were to come back to his own country, those doors, wide as they are, would very soon be too narrow for you as you ran out through them."

Eurymachus went black with rage. "You wretch, I shall very soon do you an injury for talking so freely among all these men, and not the least bit frightened. Either the wine has your wits, or your mind is always like this and you talk nonsense. Are you so beside yourself because you beat that tramp Irus?"

And he snatched up a footstool. And Odysseus sat down quickly at the knees of Amphinomus of Dulichium, out of the way of Eurymachus; and the stool hit the wine-steward on the right hand, and the jug went down with a clang and the man went over backwards in the dust, groaning.

The suitors made an uproar in the shadowy hall, and one would look at the man beside him and say: "I wish this stranger had died somewhere else before he came here; then he would not have made all this trouble. Now we are brawling about beggars, and there will be no pleasure in a good dinner, because the worse things are winning."

And Telemachus said: "Sirs, you are mad. You are no longer hiding what the food and drink are doing to you; some god is driving you. Now that you have dined well, go home and go to bed whenever your heart tells you. I am not driving anybody out."

They bit their lips and stared at Telemachus, astonished that he had spoken so boldly.

And Amphinomus said: "Friends, when a fair word has been spoken, nobody should take offence and answer it roughly. Do not manhandle the stranger, or any of the servants in the house of godlike Odysseus. Come — let the steward pour a drop into the cups so that we can make our libations and go home to bed. And leave the stranger in the hall of Odysseus for Telemachus to look after; it is to his house that he has come."

That pleased them all. And when they had poured and drunk as much as they wanted, they went off to their own houses to sleep.

---

## NOTES TO BOOK EIGHTEEN

<a id="book-18-note-1"></a>
1. **Irus, who is not called Irus.** His name is Arnaeus. *Irus* is a nickname the young men of the town gave him, and it is a joke: it is made from Iris, the goddess who carries messages for the gods, because this man will carry a message for anybody who pays him in food. It is the sort of name that sticks to a person and slowly replaces him, and the poem tells you his real one exactly once, in the line before it stops using it. There is a second turn of the same joke a page later, when the suitors say he is about to be *un-Irused* — which in Greek is a single coined word, made by putting a negative in front of his nickname, and is the kind of thing a hall full of drunk young men would find extremely funny.

<a id="book-18-note-2"></a>
2. **King Echetus.** He is mentioned three times in this poem and nowhere else in Greek literature, always in the same breath as mutilation, always as a threat, and always to somebody helpless. Nobody knows whether he was a figure from some lost story or simply a bogey — the equivalent of naming a place people are sent and do not come back from. What matters is that Antinous produces him casually, as a piece of ordinary banter, to frighten a beggar into fighting; and that nothing in the scene suggests anybody present thought the threat outlandish. It is worth remembering when the reckoning comes, and readers begin to feel that it goes too far.

<a id="book-18-note-3"></a>
3. **Melantho, and what the poem tells you about her.** Four facts, in one sentence, delivered without comment: Penelope raised her from a child, treated her as her own daughter, gave her whatever toys she asked for — and she feels nothing for Penelope, and sleeps with Eurymachus. She is the sister of Melanthius the goatherd, who kicked Odysseus at the spring in Book Seventeen; the two of them are the household's answer to Eumaeus and the cowherd, and the poem is arranging its servants into two columns. — She is also one of the twelve women who will be hanged in Book Twenty-Two, and I will not pretend her behaviour here is anything but cruel. But I said in Book Two that I would keep the question open, and I shall: the poem gives her a motive that is entirely her own, and gives her a lover who is the second most powerful man in that hall, and never once asks what a young slave woman's alternatives were when he came looking for her.

---

*Book Nineteen: In Which a Husband and a Wife Talk All Night, and an Old Woman Washes His Feet.*


<div class="page-break"></div>

<!-- Source: book/odyssey-book-19.md -->

# THE ODYSSEY
### Retold in English, with Explanations

---

## BOOK NINETEEN
### In Which a Husband and a Wife Talk All Night, and an Old Woman Washes His Feet

---

Odysseus was left behind in the hall, turning over the killing of the suitors with Athena's help. And he spoke quickly to Telemachus.

"Telemachus, we must get the weapons of war stowed away, every one of them. And when the suitors miss them and ask you about it, put them off with soft words: *I have laid them away out of the smoke, because they are no longer what they were when Odysseus left them behind and went to Troy; they are quite spoiled, as far as the breath of the fire has got at them. And here is a better reason, which some god put into my mind: I was afraid you might quarrel when you were in drink and wound one another and shame the feast and the courtship. Iron by itself draws a man on.*"

Telemachus called out to Eurycleia. "Nurse, shut the women up in their rooms while I put my father's weapons away in the store — good weapons, standing about neglected in the house, going dull with the smoke, since my father went away. I was a child then. I want to lay them away where the breath of the fire will not reach them."

"Child, I only wish you would take charge of the house and look after all your property. But who is to go with you and carry a light, if you will not let the maids come out?"

"This stranger. I will not have a man idle who eats my bread, however far away he has come from."

So she shut the doors of the hall. And the two of them jumped up, Odysseus and his son, and carried in the helmets and the bossed shields and the sharp spears; and Athena went in front of them with a golden lamp and made a beautiful light.

And Telemachus said suddenly: "Father, this is a great marvel I am looking at. The walls of the hall and the fine panels and the crossbeams of pine and the pillars standing up — they are all shining in my eyes as though there were a fire in here. Some god must be inside, one of those who hold the wide sky."

"Be quiet. Hold your thoughts in and ask no questions. This is the way of the gods who hold Olympus. Go to bed now. I shall stay here, to try the maids a little more, and your mother; and in her grief she will ask me about everything."

So Telemachus went off through the hall by the light of the blazing torches, to the room where he always slept, and lay down and waited for morning. And Odysseus was left in the hall, turning over the killing of the suitors with Athena's help.

---

Then Penelope came down out of her room, looking like Artemis (goddess of the hunt) or like golden Aphrodite (goddess of love). They set her chair by the fire where she always sat, worked with ivory and silver, which the craftsman Icmalius had made long ago; and he had put a footstool on it, part of the same piece, and a great fleece was thrown over it.

And the women came out and cleared away the piles of bread and the tables and the cups the men had been drinking from; and they threw the fire out of the braziers onto the ground and heaped fresh logs on them, for light and for warmth.

And Melantho started on Odysseus for the second time.

"Stranger, are you going to be a nuisance here all night as well, wandering about the house and spying on the women? Get out of doors and be satisfied with your dinner, or you will be hit with a torch and go out that way."

And Odysseus looked at her from under his brows.

"Strange woman, why do you come at me with such anger in your heart? Is it because I am dirty and wearing bad clothes on my body and I beg round the country? Necessity is on me. That is what beggars and vagrants are like.

"I too once lived in a house of my own among men, and I was rich, and my house was rich; and I gave a great many times to a wanderer, whoever he was and whatever he came in need of. And I had servants past counting and everything else that men live well by and are called wealthy for.

"And Zeus brought it all to nothing; he chose to. So take care, woman, that you do not lose all the beauty you shine with among the maids at present — in case your mistress grows angry with you and turns hard, or Odysseus comes home; there is still some share of hope left. And if he really has died and is never coming back, still there is his son Telemachus, who by the grace of Apollo is a grown man now; and there is not a woman in these halls behaving badly who will escape his notice, because he is not a child any longer."

Penelope heard him and rounded on the girl.

"You bold and shameless creature. You are not hiding your monstrous behaviour from me in the least, and you shall wipe it off with your own head. You knew perfectly well — you heard it from me — that I meant to question this stranger in my halls about my husband, because I am in great distress."

Then she said to the housekeeper: "Eurynome, bring a chair over and put a fleece on it, so the stranger can sit and talk to me and listen; I want to ask him some things."

---

She began where anybody would begin. "Stranger, this I shall ask you myself, first of all. Who are you, and where do you come from? Where is your city, and who are your parents?"

And he turned it aside without seeming to.

"Lady, no mortal on the boundless earth could find fault with you. Your name goes up to the wide sky, like the name of a blameless king, a god-fearing man ruling over many strong people and upholding justice, so that the dark earth bears him wheat and barley, and the trees are heavy with fruit, and the flocks never fail to bear, and the sea gives fish, all because of his good leadership; and the people prosper under him.

"So ask me anything else you like here in your house, but do not ask about my family and my own country, in case you fill my heart still fuller of pain by making me remember. I am a man of many sorrows. And it is not fitting for me to sit crying and grieving in another person's house; endless mourning does no good. One of your women might be angry with me, or you might yourself, and say I was swimming in tears because my head was heavy with wine."

"Stranger, the immortals destroyed my excellence and my beauty and my figure on the day the Greeks embarked for Ilium (Troy), and my husband Odysseus went with them. If he were to come and take care of my life, my name would be greater and better. As it is I am in trouble; a god has let loose so much of it on me.

"All the nobles who rule the islands — Dulichium and Same and wooded Zacynthus — and those who live in clear-seen Ithaca itself, are courting me against my will and wearing away my house. And so I take no thought for strangers or suppliants or heralds, but I waste my heart away wanting Odysseus.

"They press on with the marriage, and I wind my schemes.

"First a god breathed it into me to set up a great loom in the hall and weave at a wide fine web; and I said to them: *Young men, my suitors — since Odysseus is dead, be patient about the marriage, however eager you are, until I finish this cloth; I do not want my spinning wasted. It is a shroud for the lord Laertes (father of Odysseus), against the day the pitiless end of death takes him. I will not have the Greek women in this country talking against me, that a man who won so much should lie without a covering.*

"So I said, and their proud hearts agreed. And after that I wove at the great web by day, and unravelled it by night, when I had torches set beside me. Three years I kept it from them and got away with it. But when the fourth came round with the seasons, then my women told them — shameless creatures — and they came and caught me at it, and shouted at me; and I finished it, against my will, because I had to.

"And now I cannot escape the marriage, and I cannot think of any other trick. My parents are pressing me to marry, and my son is angry as he watches his living eaten up, because he understands it now; he is a man, well able to look after a house that Zeus grants honour to.

"But tell me your family, all the same, and where you come from. Because you are not sprung from the oak in the old story, or from a rock."

---

And Odysseus told her a lie.

He told her he came from Crete, from the great city of Cnossus, where Minos was king; that his father was Deucalion, and his brother Idomeneus, who had gone off to Troy in the beaked ships; and that his own name was Aethon, and he was the younger of the two.

And he told her he had met Odysseus there — that the wind had driven Odysseus off course past Malea on his way to Troy and forced him into an awkward anchorage; that he had come up to the city looking for Idomeneus, calling him a dear and honoured friend, and had missed him by ten days or eleven; that he himself had taken Odysseus in and entertained him properly out of the household stores, and gathered barley and wine and cattle for sacrifice out of the public store for the men who were with him; and that they had stayed twelve days, penned in by a North Wind that some hard god had raised, and had put to sea on the thirteenth when it dropped.

He made all these lies of his sound like the truth as he told them.

And as she listened, the tears ran down and her face melted. The way the snow melts on the high mountains, that the East Wind thaws when the West Wind has piled it up, and as it melts the rivers run full — that is how her lovely cheeks melted as she cried for her husband, who was sitting there beside her.

And Odysseus pitied his wife in his heart as she grieved.

But his eyes stood in his head as though they were made of horn or iron, and he did not move them; and by guile he kept his tears back.

---

There is nothing in the poem I find harder than that pair of sentences, and I do not think the poem finds it easy either.

He pities her. The text says so plainly, and gives him the emotion before it gives him the concealment. And then it describes the concealment with a piece of physical detail so precise that you can feel him doing it: the eyes held still, not blinking, because a blink would spill it.

Everything he has been praised for in eighteen books is in that stillness. It is the same faculty that got him out of the cave and off the beach at Scheria and past the dogs at the farm, and it is not being used on an enemy. It is being used to watch his wife cry over him for as long as it takes.

I shall not tell you whether he is right. He has been told by a goddess to trust nobody, and there are a hundred and eight armed men in the town, and one loose word from a servant would finish him and his son together. The reasoning is sound. What the poem does is refuse to let the soundness of the reasoning make the thing comfortable, and it does that by giving him the pity first.

---

Then she decided to test him.

"Now, stranger, I think I shall try you, and find out whether you really did entertain my husband there in your halls with his companions, as you say. Tell me what sort of clothes he was wearing, and what kind of man he was himself, and tell me about the companions who went with him."

"Lady, it is hard to say, after so long. It is twenty years now since he went away from there and left my country. But I shall tell you as my heart pictures it.

"Odysseus was wearing a fleecy purple cloak, doubled over; and there was a brooch on it made of gold with a double clasp, and the front of it was worked in a curious way. A hound was holding a dappled fawn down between his forepaws and gripping it as it struggled; and everybody was amazed at it, at the way the two of them were gold and yet the hound was throttling the fawn and looking at it, and the fawn was writhing with its feet and trying to get away.

"And I noticed the tunic on his body, shining like the skin of a dried onion, it was so soft; and bright as the sun. A great many women looked at it and wondered.

"But I will tell you something else, and you must take it in. I do not know whether Odysseus wore those clothes at home, or whether one of his crew gave them to him when he went aboard the fast ship, or whether some host did; because Odysseus was dear to a great many men, and few Greeks were his equal.

"I gave him a bronze sword myself, and a fine purple cloak with a double fold, and a fringed tunic, and I sent him off with honour in his well-benched ship.

"And there was a herald attending him, a little older than he was, and I will tell you about him too. He was round in the shoulders and dark-skinned and curly-headed, and his name was Eurybates; and Odysseus honoured him above the rest of his companions, because the two of them thought alike."

And she cried still harder, because she knew the tokens Odysseus had given her, and they were unmistakable.<sup><a href="#book-19-note-1">1</a></sup>

And when she had had her fill of weeping she said: "Stranger, until now you have only been pitied in this house; from now on you shall be loved and honoured. I gave him those clothes myself, the ones you describe. I folded them and brought them out of the store-room and put the bright brooch on them to be an ornament for him.

"And I shall never welcome him home again, coming back to his own dear country. It was an evil fate that took Odysseus off in the hollow ship to see that Ilium (Troy) that should not be named."

---

I want to point at the brooch, because of what he does with it.

He is asked for proof and he produces it, and he produces the right thing: not the sword, which she never saw, but the cloak she folded with her own hands and the pin she fastened on it. And the thing worked on that pin is a hound holding down a fawn and watching it struggle.

He picked that out of twenty years of memory and described it to her, in detail, twice — the gold that seems to move, the fawn's feet working, the eyes of the dog on it — while she sat opposite him and wept and did not know who she was talking to.

The poem does not remark on it. It simply hands you a little golden object, in a room where one person is being slowly and deliberately held, and lets it lie there.

---

Then he told her the rest of what he had told the swineherd — that he had heard of Odysseus close by, in the rich country of the Thesprotians, alive, and gathering treasure to bring home; that his ship and his companions had been lost off Thrinacia because the crew ate the cattle of the Sun; that the Phaeacians had honoured him like a god and were ready to send him home; and that he had gone to Dodona to ask the great oak of Zeus how he should come back to his own country, openly or in secret.

"So he is safe, and he will be here very soon. He will not be far from his friends and his own country much longer. And I shall swear you an oath on it. Let Zeus be my witness first, and this table of hospitality, and the hearth of Odysseus that I have come to: all of it will happen exactly as I say. Within this very month Odysseus will come here — as the old moon goes out and the new one comes in."

"Ah, stranger. I wish that word might be fulfilled. Then you would know my friendship soon enough, and get so many gifts from me that any man who met you would call you a lucky one.

"But this is how it will be, I think, in my heart. Odysseus is not coming home, and you will not get your passage from here, since there are no such masters in this house as Odysseus was among men — if there ever was such a man — to welcome honoured strangers and send them on their way.

"But come, women, wash him, and make up a bed — a bedstead and blankets and bright rugs — so that he can lie warm until the golden Dawn. And in the morning bathe him and rub him with oil, so that he can sit in the hall beside Telemachus and think about his breakfast. And it will be the worse for any man of them who annoys him and grieves his heart; that man will get nothing done here after that, however furiously he rages.

"Because how are you to find out about me, stranger — whether I really am better than other women in judgement and careful sense — if you sit down to eat in my hall unwashed and badly dressed? Men do not live long. If a man is harsh himself, and his mind is harsh, everybody prays that he may suffer while he lives, and when he is dead they all mock him. But if a man is blameless, and his mind is blameless, strangers carry his name far and wide across the world, and a great many people call him a good man."

"Honoured wife of Odysseus, cloaks and bright rugs became hateful to me on the day I left the snowy mountains of Crete behind me and went off in my long-oared ship. I shall lie down as I have lain through many sleepless nights before this. I have spent a great many nights on a poor bed, waiting for the bright Dawn.

"And footbaths give me no pleasure either. No woman of those who are servants in your house is going to touch my foot — unless there is some old and faithful one who has suffered as much in her heart as I have. I should not begrudge such a woman touching my feet."

"Dear stranger, no man so sensible has ever come to my house out of all the strangers from far away; everything you say is so well judged. I have an old woman with an understanding heart, who nursed and reared that unlucky man and took him in her arms the day his mother bore him. She shall wash your feet, weak as she is.

"Come now, sensible Eurycleia, get up and wash a man of your master's own age. Odysseus's feet must be like this by now, and his hands like this. Men grow old quickly in bad fortune."

---

The old woman covered her face with her hands and let the hot tears come.

"Oh, my child. I can do nothing for you. Zeus must have hated you above all men, god-fearing as your heart was. No mortal ever burned so many fat thigh-pieces to him, or such chosen sacrifices, as you gave him — praying that you might come to a sleek old age and bring up your glorious son. And now he has taken your day of homecoming away from you alone.

"I suppose the women in some strange country mocked at him the way these bitches all mock at you here, when he came to some great lord's fine house; and it is to get away from their insults and their taunting that you will not let them wash you.

"But the daughter of Icarius, sensible Penelope, has told me to, and I am not unwilling. I shall wash your feet, for Penelope's sake and for your own, because the heart in me is stirred with sorrow.

"And listen to what I am going to say. A great many hard-tried strangers have come here, but I do not think I ever saw a man so like another as you are like Odysseus — in your build, and your voice, and your feet."

"Old woman, everybody who has seen the two of us with their own eyes says the same: that we are extraordinarily like one another. You have noticed it yourself, and said so."

So the old woman took the shining cauldron she used for washing feet and poured cold water into it and added hot.

And Odysseus sat down at the hearth and turned quickly towards the dark, because it came to him all at once that when she handled him she might notice the scar, and everything would come out.

---

She came up and began to wash her master. And she knew the scar at once.

He had been given it long ago by a boar, with its white tusk, on Parnassus, when he had gone there to visit Autolycus and the sons of Autolycus — his mother's father, who was the finest man alive at thieving and at swearing oaths, a skill the god himself had given him, Hermes (the god of travellers, of luck, and of theft), because Odysseus's grandfather used to burn him acceptable offerings of the thighs of lambs and kids, and Hermes went along with him willingly.

Autolycus had come once to the rich country of Ithaca and found his daughter's son newly born; and Eurycleia had set the baby on his knees as he finished his supper, and said: "Autolycus, find a name yourself now for your child's own child. He has been prayed for a long time."

And Autolycus said: "Son-in-law, daughter — give him the name I say. I have come here as a man who has been angry with a great many people, men and women both, over the fruitful earth. So let his name be **Odysseus**, the man of anger. And when he is grown and comes to his mother's family's great house on Parnassus, where my property is, I shall give him some of it and send him home happy."<sup><a href="#book-19-note-2">2</a></sup>

So he had gone there for the gifts, when he was a young man; and Autolycus and his sons had welcomed him and clasped his hands, and his grandmother Amphithea had put her arms round him and kissed his head and both his beautiful eyes; and they had killed a five-year-old bull and feasted all day.

And at first light they had gone out hunting, the dogs and the sons of Autolycus, and Odysseus with them, up the steep wooded mountain, into the windy hollows. The sun was just striking on the fields, coming up out of the deep-flowing Ocean, when the beaters came into a glade. The dogs went in front, tracking, and the sons of Autolycus behind them, and Odysseus close up behind the dogs with his long spear swinging.

There was a great boar lying in a thick lair, where the force of the wet winds never blew and the bright sun never struck through and the rain could not get in, it was so thick; and there was a great heap of fallen leaves in it. And the noise of the feet of men and dogs came round him as they closed in, and he came out of the lair against them with his back bristling and his eyes flashing, and stood at bay close in front of them.

Odysseus went in first, holding the long spear up in his heavy hand, wanting to strike. And the boar was too quick for him and came in sideways above the knee, and tore a long gash in the flesh with his tusk, and did not reach the bone. And Odysseus hit him in the right shoulder, and the point of the bright spear went clean through, and he went down in the dust with a scream and the life flew out of him.

And the sons of Autolycus busied themselves over the carcass and bound up the wound of faultless godlike Odysseus skilfully, and stopped the black blood with a charm; and they went back quickly to their father's house, and healed him, and gave him splendid presents, and sent him off gladly to Ithaca. And his father and his honoured mother were glad when he came, and asked about everything, and about the scar, and how he had come by it. And he told them the whole story properly.

---

That is where the name came from, and the poem has kept it back for nineteen books.

I told you in Book Nine that *Odysseus* is built on a verb meaning to be angry with, to hate, to deal out pain, and that it runs both ways at once — the man who is hated, and the man who causes trouble. Here at last is the naming itself, and it is done by a grandfather who is famous for thieving and for perjury, over his supper, with the baby on his knees. He does not name the child for a hope, or a god, or an ancestor. He names it after his own bad temper.

And the poem produces the whole story here, of all the places — inside the sentence where an old woman's hands are moving down a leg towards the mark that will tell her who he is. It is the longest digression in the poem and it arrives at the worst possible moment, and readers have complained about it for two thousand years. I think the placing is the point. Everything is suspended: the water, the hands, the room, the wife eight feet away. And into that gap the poem pours the one thing it has never told you, which is what this man's name means and who gave it to him.

Then the hands find the scar.

---

The old woman took the scar in the flat of her hands and knew it by the touch, and let the foot go. The leg dropped into the basin, and the bronze rang, and it tipped over, and the water went out on the floor.

And joy and grief took hold of her at the same moment, and both her eyes filled with tears, and her voice would not come out.

She put her hand on his chin and said: "You are Odysseus. Dear child. And I never knew you — not until I had handled the whole body of my master."

And she looked across at Penelope, wanting to tell her that her husband was in the room.

And Penelope could not meet her eye and did not notice, because Athena had turned her mind aside.

And Odysseus felt for the old woman's throat with his right hand and took hold of it, and pulled her closer to him with the other.

"Mother. Do you want to destroy me? You nursed me yourself at your own breast. And now, after suffering a great deal, I have come in the twentieth year to my own country. But since you have found me out, and a god has put it in your heart — be quiet. Let nobody else in this house hear of it.

"Because I will tell you plainly, and it will be brought about. If a god beats the lordly suitors down under me, I shall not spare you, nurse though you are and though you nursed me, when I kill the other serving women in my halls."

"My child, what a thing to let past the barrier of your teeth. You know how firm I am, and how unyielding. I shall hold as hard as solid stone, or iron.

"And I will tell you something else; take it in. If a god beats the lordly suitors down under you, then I shall tell you about the women in the halls — which of them dishonour you and which are innocent."

"Nurse, why would you tell me about them? There is no need. I shall take note of every one of them myself and find them out. Keep it to yourself, and leave the rest to the gods."

---

Sit with that for a moment, because it is the coldest thing he does in the poem.

An old woman who fed him at her own breast has just recognised him, from a scar, on her knees, with her hands in the water; and she is crying with joy; and his response is to take her by the throat.

He does it for the same reason he does everything, and the reason is good: she was on the point of calling across the room, and if she had, he and his son would both be dead by morning. And he does not merely silence her. He tells her that when the killing starts he will kill her too if she is among the women who have gone over, nurse or no nurse.

She is not offended, which is the strangest part. She says only that she will hold like stone, and then offers to give him the names — and he refuses even that, because he does not want the list from her. He wants to watch them himself.

---

Then she went off to fetch more water, since the first lot was all spilled; and when she had washed him and rubbed him with oil, Odysseus pulled his chair nearer the fire again to get warm, and hid the scar under his rags.

And Penelope said:

"Stranger, I shall ask you one small thing more myself, because it will soon be time for rest — for anybody on whom sweet sleep comes, however troubled he is. But a god has given me sorrow past all measuring. All day I take a kind of pleasure in mourning and grieving while I see to my own work and the women's in the house; and when the night comes and sleep takes everyone, I lie on my bed, and the sharp cares come crowding thick about my beating heart and torment me while I mourn.

"And my heart goes to and fro in doubt — whether to stay with my son and keep everything safe, my property and my servants and my great high-roofed house, respecting my husband's bed and what the people say; or to go now with whichever of the Greeks courting me in the halls is the best man and brings the most gifts.

"My son, while he was a child and thoughtless, would not let me marry and leave my husband's house. Now he is grown and has come to the full measure of manhood, and he prays me to go out of the hall again, because he is troubled about his property, which the Greeks are eating in front of him.

"But listen to this dream of mine, and interpret it for me.

"I have twenty geese about the house that come out of the water and eat wheat, and it warms me to watch them. And a great eagle with a crooked beak came down off the mountain and broke all their necks and killed them; and they lay strewn about the hall in a heap, and he went up into the bright sky.

"And I cried and wailed, in the dream, and the Greek women gathered round me while I grieved bitterly because the eagle had killed my geese.

"And he came back and perched on a jutting roof-beam, and checked my crying with a mortal man's voice, and said: *Take heart, daughter of far-famed Icarius. This is no dream but a waking vision, a good one, and it will be brought about. The geese are the suitors; and I who was the eagle a moment ago am your husband, back again, and I shall let loose a cruel death on all of them.*

"And the honey-sweet sleep let me go. And I looked round and saw the geese in the hall pecking at their wheat by the trough, exactly where they always are."<sup><a href="#book-19-note-3">3</a></sup>

"Lady, there is no way of turning that dream aside and reading it otherwise. Odysseus himself has told you how he means to bring it about. Destruction is plain for every one of the suitors; not a man of them will get away from death."

"Stranger, dreams are awkward things, and hard to read, and they do not all come true for people.

"There are two gates for shadowy dreams. One is made of horn and one of ivory. The dreams that come through the sawn ivory deceive us, and bring words that come to nothing. The ones that come out through the polished horn bring true things to pass, when a mortal sees them.

"But I do not think my strange dream came from there. If it had, it would have been very welcome to me and to my son.

"And I will tell you something else; take it in. This coming dawn is the evil-named one that will take me out of the house of Odysseus. Because now I mean to set them a contest: the axes, which he used to stand up in a row in his halls, like the props of a ship, twelve of them altogether; and he would stand a long way off and shoot an arrow through the whole line.

"Now I shall set this contest before the suitors. And whichever man most easily strings the bow in his hands and shoots an arrow through all twelve axes — with him I shall go, and leave this house of my marriage, so beautiful, and so full of everything a life needs, which I think I shall remember even in my dreams."

"Honoured wife of Odysseus. Do not put this contest off any longer in your halls. Odysseus of the many devices will be here before these men can handle that polished bow and string it and shoot an arrow through the iron."

"Stranger, if you were willing to sit beside me in the hall and give me pleasure, sleep would never be shed on my eyelids. But people cannot go without sleep forever. I shall go up to my room and lie down on my bed, which has become a bed of mourning for me, always wet with my tears since the day Odysseus went off to see that Ilium that should not be named. I shall lie down there; and you lie here in the house — either put something on the floor, or let them set a bedstead for you."

And she went up to her bright upper room, and her women went with her; and when she had gone up she cried for Odysseus, her own dear husband, until Athena cast a sweet sleep on her eyelids.

---

I shall not tell you what she knows, because I do not think anybody can, and I would rather leave you holding the question than hand you a bad answer.

Consider only the order of events. She has spent the evening with a stranger who described her husband's clothes, down to the pin she fastened herself. He has sworn her a formal oath, on the hearth, that Odysseus will be here inside the month. She has told him a dream in which an eagle kills the suitors and announces that he is her husband — and then said, immediately, that she does not think it was a true dream, which is a thing people say when they have been told something they want too much to believe.

And then, that same night, having waited twenty years and put the marriage off by every device she could invent, she announces that tomorrow she will bring out her husband's bow and marry whichever man can use it.

It may be despair. She says it is: this is the evil dawn, my son is grown, I cannot hold them off any longer. It may be that a woman who has been listening very carefully all evening has decided to put a bow into the room and see what happens. The poem does not say, and the argument has run for two thousand years without settling.<sup><a href="#book-19-note-4">4</a></sup>

What I will say is this. Whatever she does or does not suspect, she has just arranged the one contest in the world that her husband cannot lose and no other man can win, on the one night he happens to be sitting by her fire, and she has done it herself, without being asked, without being told to, and against her own interest.

---

## NOTES TO BOOK NINETEEN

<a id="book-19-note-1"></a>
1. **The tokens.** In a poem full of recognitions this is the first, and it establishes the pattern all the others follow: not a face, not a voice, but a *thing that only two people could know*. Penelope does not ask what her husband looked like; she asks what he was wearing, which is the harder question and the better one. Anybody who had seen Odysseus could describe his build. Only somebody who was there could describe the pin. — Note also what she does with the answer. She does not leap up. She weeps, and says that from now on he will be honoured in her house, and then goes on talking. Every recognition in this poem is followed immediately by a test of some kind, and by somebody keeping their head.

<a id="book-19-note-2"></a>
2. **The name, and the man who gave it.** See Book Nine, note 1, where the meaning was set out and the story promised. Here it is: Autolycus, the hero's grandfather on his mother's side, celebrated for two accomplishments — theft and perjury — both of them gifts from Hermes, who was pleased with his offerings. He arrives, finds a newborn on the premises, and is invited to name it; and he chooses a name that means, roughly, *the one who gives and gets grief*, on the grounds that he himself has been angry with a great many people in his time. It is the only naming scene in the poem and it explains a good deal, including where the cleverness came from and why nobody in this family expects the world to be simple.

<a id="book-19-note-3"></a>
3. **The gates of horn and ivory.** This is the passage's most famous line and it is a pun, which is why it works in Greek and merely sounds handsome in English. The Greek for *horn* is close to a verb meaning to fulfil or bring to pass, and the Greek for *ivory* is close to a verb meaning to deceive. So true dreams come through the gate whose name sounds like *fulfil*, and false ones through the gate whose name sounds like *deceive*. It is not an explanation; it is a piece of wordplay offered as one — and Penelope, who has just been told a dream that says exactly what she wants to hear, uses it to argue herself out of believing it. That is the real point of the passage, and it is heartbreakingly ordinary: it is what people do with good news they cannot afford to trust.

<a id="book-19-note-4"></a>
4. **Does she know?** The central argument of *Odyssey* criticism, and nobody has won it. The case for yes: she suddenly finds this beggar dearer than any guest she has had; she asks him for exactly the proof he can give; she tells him her most private dream; she comes down and announces the contest of the bow within an hour of being given a sworn oath that her husband will arrive this month; and the contest she chooses is one only her husband can win. The case for no: the poem says several times that Athena put things into her mind, which would be a strange way to describe a woman acting on her own conclusions; she says plainly and repeatedly that she does not believe he is coming; and when the truth finally arrives she does not behave in the least like someone who suspected it. — My own view, for what it is worth, is that the question may be badly posed. People are perfectly capable of knowing a thing and not knowing it at the same time, and of taking an action for reasons they could not state if you asked them. The poem gives us her behaviour and withholds her mind, and it does that on purpose, and it does it to nobody else in the book.

---

*Book Twenty: In Which Nobody Sleeps, and the Last Dinner Is Served.*


<div class="page-break"></div>

<!-- Source: book/odyssey-book-20.md -->

# THE ODYSSEY
### Retold in English, with Explanations

---

## BOOK TWENTY
### In Which Nobody Sleeps, and the Last Dinner Is Served

---

Odysseus lay down to sleep in the forecourt. He spread an undressed oxhide on the ground and heaped over it a great many fleeces from the sheep the Greeks had been killing, and Eurynome threw a cloak over him when he had lain down. And there he lay awake, turning over trouble for the suitors in his mind.

And the women came out of the hall, the ones who had been going with the suitors, laughing among themselves and making merry together. And the heart in his breast was stirred, and he debated hard, in his mind and in his heart, whether to rush out and deal death to every one of them, or to let them lie with the arrogant suitors this one last time. And the heart inside him growled.

As a bitch stands over her tender puppies and growls at a man she does not know, and is ready to fight him, so the heart growled inside him at their wickedness. And he struck himself on the breast and spoke to his own heart.

"Endure this, heart. You put up with something fouler than this on the day the Cyclops, who had no restraint in him, ate my strong companions. And you held out, until cunning got you out of that cave when you had thought you were dead."

So he spoke, rebuking the heart in his own breast; and his heart held firm and stayed obedient. But the man himself went on tossing from side to side.

As a man turns a paunch stuffed with fat and blood this way and that over a blazing fire, wanting it roasted quickly, so he rolled from side to side, working out how he was ever going to lay hands on the shameless suitors, one man against so many.<sup><a href="#book-20-note-1">1</a></sup>

And Athena came down to him from the sky, in the likeness of a woman, and stood over his head.

"Why are you awake, unluckiest of all men? This is your house. Your wife is in it, and your son — and a son any man would be glad of."

"Goddess, everything you say is right. But my heart keeps working at this: how am I to lay hands on the shameless suitors, alone as I am, when they are always here in a body? And there is a bigger thing than that which I keep turning over. If I do kill them, by the will of Zeus and yourself, where am I to escape to afterwards? I ask you to think about that."

"You obstinate man. Most people are content to trust a weaker friend than I am — a mortal, who does not know as much. I am a god, and I have guarded you the whole way through, in every one of your troubles. I shall put it plainly: if fifty companies of mortal men stood round the two of us, wanting to kill us in a fight, you would drive their cattle and their fat sheep away afterwards. So let sleep take you. It is a weariness to lie awake and keep watch all night. You are coming up out of your troubles now."

And she poured sleep over his eyelids and went back to Olympus.

---

But as sleep took hold of him, loosening the cares of his heart, his true wife woke, and sat up in her soft bed and cried; and when she had had her fill of crying she prayed first of all to Artemis (goddess of the hunt, whose arrows bring a quiet death to women).

"Artemis, honoured goddess, daughter of Zeus — I wish you would put an arrow in my breast this minute and take my life away. Or let a storm wind catch me up and carry me off down the misty ways and throw me out where the circling Ocean pours in, the way the storm winds carried off the daughters of Pandareus.

"The gods had killed their parents and left them orphans in the house; and Aphrodite (goddess of love) fed them on cheese and sweet honey and good wine, and Hera (queen of the gods) gave them beauty and sense beyond all other women, and holy Artemis gave them height, and Athena taught them how to do glorious work with their hands. And while Aphrodite was going up to high Olympus to ask Zeus to arrange happy marriages for them, the storm winds snatched the girls away and handed them over to the hateful Furies to look after.

"I wish those who live on Olympus would blot me out that way, or that Artemis of the lovely hair would strike me, so that I might go down under the hateful earth still looking at Odysseus, and never gladden the heart of a lesser man.

"An evil is bearable when a person cries all day, with a heavy heart, but sleep takes hold of them at night; because sleep makes you forget everything, good and bad, once it has closed your eyelids. But some god sends me bad dreams as well.

"This very night there was somebody lying beside me, like him, looking as he did when he went away with the army; and my heart was glad, because I thought it was not a dream but the truth at last."

She said that, and the golden Dawn came up.

And Odysseus, lying there, heard the sound of her crying; and in the drowsy state between sleeping and waking it seemed to him that she already knew him, and was standing beside his head. So he gathered up the cloak and the fleeces he had been lying on and put them on a chair in the hall, and carried the oxhide out of doors, and lifted his hands and prayed to Zeus.

"Father Zeus, if you gods brought me over the dry land and the water to my own country of your own will, after you had afflicted me so badly — then let one of the people waking in this house speak a word of omen for me, and let some other sign be shown to me outside."

And Zeus the counsellor heard him, and thundered at once out of shining Olympus, from high up above the clouds; and Odysseus was glad.

And a woman grinding grain spoke the word, close by, in the house, where the king's mills stood. Twelve women in all worked at them, making barley meal and wheat flour, which is the marrow of men. The others were asleep, having ground their wheat, but this one alone had not finished yet, because she was the weakest of them. She stopped her mill and spoke the words that were a sign for her master.

"Father Zeus, who rule over gods and men — you have thundered loudly out of the starry sky, and there is not a cloud anywhere. You must be showing somebody a sign.

"Bring about what I am going to say, wretched as I am. Let this be the very last day the suitors take their sweet dinner in the halls of Odysseus. They have loosened my knees with the miserable work of grinding their meal. Let them eat their last supper now."

And Odysseus was glad at the word of omen and at the thunder of Zeus, because he believed he was going to make the guilty pay.<sup><a href="#book-20-note-2">2</a></sup>

---

The other women were gathering in the fine house by now and kindling the unwearying fire on the hearth; and Telemachus got out of bed and dressed and slung his sharp sword over his shoulder and tied his good sandals under his shining feet, and took up his heavy spear with the sharp bronze point.

He stopped in the doorway and said to Eurycleia: "Dear nurse, did you honour the stranger in the house with a bed and food, or is he lying about uncared for? Because that is my mother's way, sensible as she is. She will honour a worse man blindly, and send a better one away without honour."

"You should not blame her now, child, when she is not to blame. He sat and drank his wine as long as he wanted, and said he was not hungry any more, because she asked him. And when he began to think about bed and sleep, she told the women to make one up for him. But he was like a man who is completely miserable and out of luck, and he refused to sleep in a bed under blankets. He lay in the forecourt on an undressed oxhide and some sheepskins, and we threw a cloak over him."

So Telemachus went out through the hall with his spear in his hand, and two swift dogs went with him, and he made his way to the assembly place. And Eurycleia set the women to work: sweeping the house and sprinkling the floors, putting the purple covers on the chairs, wiping down the tables with sponges, cleaning the mixing bowls and the two-handled cups. Twenty of them went off to the spring for water, and the rest worked in the house, deft about their business.

And the suitors' men came in and began splitting wood skilfully; and the women came back from the spring. And Eumaeus came after them, driving three fat hogs, the best of the whole herd. He left them to feed in the fine yard, and he spoke to Odysseus kindly.

"Stranger, are the Greeks looking at you any better now, or are they still treating you badly in the halls, as before?"

"Eumaeus, I only wish the gods would pay them back for the outrage they commit in another man's house, insolently, without a shred of shame in them."

And while they were talking, Melanthius the goatherd came up, driving in the best goats of all his flocks for the suitors' dinner, and two herdsmen came with him; and he tied the goats under the echoing colonnade and spoke to Odysseus again with his usual sneer.

"Stranger, are you still going to be a nuisance here in this house, begging off the gentlemen? Are you never going to clear out? I do not think the two of us are going to part without tasting each other's fists, because you beg past all decency. There are other dinners among the Greeks."

Odysseus did not answer him a word. He shook his head in silence, turning over trouble in the depths of him.

And a third man came in, Philoetius, a leader among men, bringing a barren heifer and some fat goats for the suitors; the ferrymen had brought them over, who take anybody across who comes their way. He tied the animals up carefully under the echoing colonnade, and came and stood beside the swineherd.

"Who is this stranger, swineherd, who has just come to our house? What family does he claim? Where are his people and his father's fields? Poor man. He has the build of a king about him; but the gods bring misery on men who have wandered a long way, once they have spun trouble for them, kings included."

And he took Odysseus by the hand and said:

"Good day, father stranger. May you have some happiness in the time to come; you are held down by a great many troubles at present.

"Father Zeus, no god is more deadly than you. You have no pity for men, though you made them yourself; you let them get acquainted with misery and hard pain.

"I broke out in a sweat when I saw you, and my eyes are full of tears, because I thought of Odysseus. I expect he is dressed in rags like these too, wandering about among people somewhere, if he is still alive and looking at the sunlight.

"And if he is dead already and in the house of Hades — then I grieve for faultless Odysseus, who set me over his cattle when I was only a boy in the country of the Cephallenians. They have increased past counting since then. No man's herd of broad-browed cattle could have grown better.

"And now other men order me to drive them in for themselves to eat. They take no notice of the son in the house and no notice of the anger of the gods, because they are in a hurry to divide up the property of a master who has been away too long.

"And here is the thing that keeps turning over in my heart. It is a very bad business, while the son is alive, to take the cattle and go off to another country, to strangers. And it is worse still to stay here in misery, minding cattle that belong to other men. I would have run long ago and gone to one of the other great kings, because this is past bearing. But I keep thinking about that unhappy man, and hoping he may come from somewhere and scatter the suitors through the halls."

"Cowherd," said Odysseus, "since you seem to be neither a bad man nor a fool, and I can see for myself that you have sense in your mind, I shall tell you something and swear a great oath on it. Let Zeus be my witness first, and this table of hospitality, and the hearth of Odysseus that I have come to: Odysseus will come home while you are still here, and you shall see with your own eyes, if you want to, the killing of the suitors who lord it in this house."

"Stranger, I wish the son of Cronos would bring that word about. Then you would find out what my strength is, and how these hands of mine obey me."

And Eumaeus prayed to all the gods in the same way, that clever Odysseus might come back to his own house.

---

Meanwhile the suitors were weaving death and destruction for Telemachus. But a bird came over on their left, an eagle flying high with a trembling dove in its claws; and Amphinomus said: "Friends, this plan of ours will not run smoothly — the killing of Telemachus. Let us think about dinner instead." That pleased them all, and they went into the house and laid their cloaks on the chairs and benches and set about killing sheep and goats and fat hogs and a heifer from the herd.

And Telemachus put Odysseus in the great hall itself, beside the stone threshold, on a shabby stool at a small table, and gave him a portion of the inner meat and poured wine for him in a golden cup.

"Sit there now among the gentlemen and drink your wine. I shall keep the taunts and the hands of all the suitors off you myself, because this is not a public house; it is the house of Odysseus, and he won it for me. And you, suitors, hold your tongues from insults and your hands from blows, so that no quarrel and no fighting starts."

They all bit their lips and were astonished at Telemachus, that he spoke so boldly. And Antinous said: "Hard as it is, let us take what Telemachus says, though he threatens us a good deal. Zeus did not allow it, or we should have stopped him talking in these halls before now, clear speaker though he is."

Telemachus took no notice of him at all.

And by now the heralds were bringing the holy sacrifice for the gods through the town, and the long-haired Greeks were gathering in the shady grove of Apollo, who shoots from far off.<sup><a href="#book-20-note-3">3</a></sup>

And in the house they roasted the outer meat and drew it off the spits and divided the portions and had a splendid dinner; and the men who were serving put down a portion in front of Odysseus equal to their own, because Telemachus had told them to.

But Athena would not let the arrogant suitors leave off their bitter insulting altogether, so that the pain might sink deeper still into the heart of Odysseus.

There was a man among them with a lawless mind, whose name was Ctesippus, and he lived on Same; and trusting in his enormous wealth he was courting the wife of the long-absent master of the house. And he spoke up now to the arrogant suitors.

"Listen to me, my lords. The stranger has had an equal portion for some time, as is only proper; it would not be decent or right to cheat the guests of Telemachus, whoever comes to this house. But come — I shall give him a guest-gift myself, so that he can pass it on as a present to the bath-woman, or to one of the other slaves in the house of Odysseus."

And with that he picked up an ox's foot out of the basket where it lay, and threw it with his heavy hand.

And Odysseus avoided it by turning his head aside a little, and smiled in his heart a very grim smile indeed; and the foot hit the well-built wall.

And Telemachus rounded on Ctesippus.

"It has turned out a great deal better for your life that you did not hit the stranger; he got out of the way of your missile himself. Otherwise I should have run you through the middle with my sharp spear, and your father would have been arranging a funeral here instead of a wedding.

"So let nobody in my house make a display of unseemly behaviour. I notice everything now and I understand it, the good and the bad alike; before this I was a child.

"But even so we put up with watching all this — sheep slaughtered and wine drunk and food eaten — because it is hard for one man to hold back a great many. Still: do me no more harm out of your hostility. And if you are set on killing me with the sword, then I would rather have that. It would be far better to die than to go on watching these disgraceful things forever — guests knocked about, and men dragging the serving women shamefully through this beautiful house."

They all went very quiet. And after a while Agelaus said:

"Friends, when a just word has been spoken nobody should take offence and answer it back angrily. Do not manhandle the stranger, or any of the servants in the house of godlike Odysseus.

"But I would say a gentle word to Telemachus himself and to his mother, in the hope that it pleases them both. As long as the hearts in your breasts still hoped that Odysseus would come home, nobody could blame you for waiting and keeping the suitors in the house; that was the better course, if Odysseus had come back. But now it is perfectly plain that he never will.

"So go and sit beside your mother and tell her this: to marry the best man, the one who offers the most, so that you can keep everything your father owned, eating and drinking, while she looks after somebody else's house."

"Agelaus, I swear by Zeus and by my father's sufferings, who has died somewhere far from Ithaca or is wandering still — I am not putting my mother's marriage off in any way. I tell her to marry whoever she likes, and I offer gifts past counting.

"But I am ashamed to drive her out of the hall against her will by saying so outright. God forbid that."

---

And then Athena stirred up unquenchable laughter in the suitors and knocked their wits sideways.

They were laughing now with jaws that seemed to belong to somebody else. The meat they were eating was fouled with blood, and their eyes were filling with tears, and their hearts had turned towards wailing.

And Theoclymenus, who saw as a prophet sees, spoke among them.

"You poor wretches, what is this trouble you are suffering? Your heads and your faces and your knees are wrapped in night. There is a burning sound of wailing going up, and your cheeks are wet with tears. The walls are sprinkled with blood, and the fine crossbeams too. The porch is full of ghosts and the courtyard is full of them, hurrying down into the dark under the earth. And the sun has died out of the sky, and an evil mist has run over everything."

And they all laughed at him very merrily, and Eurymachus said: "This stranger has just come from abroad and he has lost his mind. Quick, young men, take him out of doors and see him to the assembly place, since he finds it dark in here."

"Eurymachus, I am not asking you for an escort. I have eyes and ears and both my feet and a perfectly sound mind in my breast. I shall take myself out through that door, because I can see the evil coming for you, and not one of the suitors will get away from it — not one of you who insult men and plan wanton things in the house of godlike Odysseus."

And with that he went out of the hall and came to the house of Peiraeus, who was glad to see him.

---

I must stop for a moment over that passage, because it is the strangest in the poem and a reader who is not warned may take it for nonsense.
